paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. Fyodor Pavlovitch owned land, but he was not very nice or smart in his life. Still, he knew how to make money. He started out poor, but when he died, he had saved up a lot of money. He was strange, and many people in town remembered him because he died in a sad and dramatic way. I will tell about his death later.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was married two times. He had three sons: Dmitri (called Mitya) from his first wife, and Ivan and Alexey from his second wife. His first wife was Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov. She came from a rich family. People wondered why someone like her would marry a man like Fyodor Pavlovitch. Maybe she wanted to show she was independent, or maybe she thought Fyodor Pavlovitch was interesting. They ran away together before getting married, which made it even more exciting for her. But they didn’t really love each other.

Soon after running away, Adelaïda Ivanovna realized she did not like her husband at all. They fought a lot. Even though her family gave her money, Fyodor Pavlovitch took it all from her. He tried to take her house and land too, but her family stopped him. People said Adelaïda Ivanovna was stronger than Fyodor Pavlovitch, and sometimes she even hit him. One day, she left him and ran away with a poor student, leaving little Mitya behind. After she left, Fyodor Pavlovitch brought many women to his house and drank a lot. He went around telling everyone stories about how sad he was that his wife left.

Some people teased Fyodor Pavlovitch, saying he seemed happy to play the part of a sad husband. He liked to tell funny stories about his troubles. Then he found out where Adelaïda Ivanovna had gone—she was in Petersburg with the student. He wanted to go after her, but instead, he just drank more. Soon, her family got news that Adelaïda Ivanovna had died in Petersburg. She died either from sickness or hunger. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard, he was drunk. Some say he laughed and thanked God; others say he cried like a child. Maybe he did both. People are often more simple and honest than we think.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was not a good father. When his wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, died, he forgot all about their little boy, Mitya (whose full name is Dmitri Fyodorovitch). Fyodor Pavlovitch was busy with parties and drinking. The only person who cared for Mitya was Grigory, a loyal family servant. Grigory took care of Mitya, fed him, and changed his clothes. If not for Grigory, no one would have looked after the child.

Mitya’s mother’s family also forgot about him at first. His grandfather had died, and his grandmother was sick in Moscow. Her daughters were married and busy. So, for almost a year, Mitya lived in Grigory’s cottage. If his father had remembered him, he would have sent him away anyway, because Mitya would have been in the way. Then, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a cousin of Mitya’s mother, came back from Paris. Pyotr was a smart and important man who liked to talk about his time in big cities and about famous people he knew. He owned a big estate near the town and often argued with the local monastery about land. When Pyotr learned about Mitya, he decided to help. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him he wanted to take care of Mitya. Fyodor Pavlovitch acted surprised and pretended he didn’t even know he had a son at home.

Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to act in silly ways, even if it didn’t help him. Pyotr worked hard and became Mitya’s guardian, along with Fyodor Pavlovitch. Mitya had a small property from his mother. Pyotr took charge, but he didn’t have his own family and soon wanted to go back to Paris. He left Mitya with a lady cousin in Moscow. Later, when there was a big revolution in Paris, Pyotr forgot about Mitya, too. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya went to live with her married daughter. He changed homes again after that. These are the main things you need to know about Mitya for now.

Mitya (Dmitri Fyodorovitch) was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s sons who thought he had money of his own. He had a wild childhood and moved from place to place. He didn’t finish school, went to military school, got in trouble, fought a duel, lost his rank, and later earned it back. He spent a lot of money and got into debt. He did not get any money from his father until he became an adult. When he finally met his father as a grown-up, they talked about his property. Mitya didn’t like his father. He only stayed a short time, took some money, and made a deal for more payments. But he never got a clear answer about how much money there was. His father noticed that Mitya believed he had more money than he really did, and Fyodor Pavlovitch was glad, because it suited his plans. He thought Mitya just wanted quick cash and sent him small amounts over time. Four years later, Mitya came back, angry, wanting to settle everything. He found out he had nothing left. He had already gotten all his money in bits and pieces, and maybe even owed his father now. Mitya was shocked and thought his father had cheated him. This is where the big trouble in the story begins. Before telling that part, we need to learn about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s other two sons.

Soon after his first son, Mitya, turned four, Fyodor Pavlovitch married again. His new wife was Sofya Ivanovna, a very young girl from another province. Sofya had lost her parents as a child and lived with a rich old lady, who both helped and treated her badly. Sofya was gentle and quiet. Once, she was so unhappy living with the old lady that she tried to hang herself, but was saved in time.

Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Sofya to marry him, but was first refused. Then he suggested they run away together, and Sofya agreed because she was only sixteen and very unhappy. The old lady was angry and gave them nothing. Fyodor did not care about money this time; he was attracted by Sofya's beauty and innocence.

After marrying Sofya, Fyodor treated her badly. He often brought other women into the house and did not respect her. Grigory, the servant, felt sorry for Sofya and once chased the other women away. All the trouble made Sofya very nervous and sick, and sometimes she lost her mind. Still, she had two sons, Ivan and Alexey. When Sofya died, Alexey was almost four years old. After her death, Fyodor forgot about his sons, just as he did with Mitya. Grigory took care of Ivan and Alexey. The old lady who raised Sofya found the boys living in poor conditions and blamed Sofya for being ungrateful.

Three months after Sofya died, the old lady arrived in town. She went to Fyodor's house and slapped him twice, then pulled his hair. Without saying much, she went to see the boys, saw they were dirty, and hit Grigory too. She wrapped the boys in a rug and took them away in her carriage. Grigory did not complain and even bowed to the old lady as she left.
Fyodor Pavlovitch thought it was fine that the old lady took the boys. He even told everyone about the slaps he got.

The old lady soon died, but in her will she left Ivan and Alexey one thousand roubles each for their education, with rules to make the money last until they were twenty-one. Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the main heir, was honest and took care of the boys. He especially liked Alexey, who lived with his family for a long time. Yefim made sure the boys' money doubled over the years and paid for their schooling himself. Ivan was a quiet and serious boy who knew his father was not a good man. Ivan was very smart and left Yefim’s house at thirteen to study in Moscow. He worked hard, teaching and writing short newspaper stories to earn money. Later, Ivan wrote a famous article that many people read. Even people in the nearby monastery talked about it, and they were surprised to learn he was Fyodor Pavlovitch’s son. Soon after, Ivan came to visit his father.

People wondered why Ivan, who was smart and proud, chose to visit the father who had ignored him. Even Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a relative, was surprised to meet Ivan and thought he was impressive.
Miüsov said, “Ivan is proud and doesn’t need money. Why is he here? He doesn’t drink or party, but his father seems to need him. They get along very well!”
Ivan truly did have a good influence on his father, who behaved better when Ivan was around.
Later, people learned that Ivan partly came to help his older brother Dmitri, whom he met for the first time on this visit. They had written letters before about something important to Dmitri.
Ivan was like a peacemaker between his father and Dmitri, who were fighting and almost went to court.

The family was together for the first time, and some members met each other for the first time. The youngest brother, Alexey, had already been living in town for a year. It is hard to describe Alexey, but you should know that he was already wearing a monk’s robe and living in the monastery, where he wanted to stay.

Alyosha was twenty years old. His brother Ivan was twenty-four, and his oldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. Alyosha was not a fanatic or a mystic. He just loved people and wanted to escape from the bad things in the world. That’s why he wanted to be a monk. He found a kind and wise monk named Zossima, who became very important to him. Alyosha was a little strange, even as a child. He lost his mother when he was four, but he remembered her all his life. His favorite memory was of his mother praying for him in front of a holy picture, crying and hugging him tight. Alyosha was quiet and didn’t talk much, but he liked people and trusted them. He never judged or criticized anyone, even when he saw bad things at his father’s house. If something bothered him, he just left the room quietly. His father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, didn’t trust him at first, but soon he loved Alyosha very much, even if he was drunk and silly about it.

Everyone liked Alyosha, even when he was little. When he lived with Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the whole family loved him like their own son. At school, Alyosha was quiet and liked to read in corners, but he was still a favorite among the children. He was never mean or proud, and he never fought back if someone was rude to him. If someone teased him, he would soon act as if nothing happened. The other boys sometimes made fun of him because he was shy about rude talk, especially about women. They would try to tease him, but he just stayed quiet, and finally they left him alone. Alyosha was always one of the best students, but never the very first.

When Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha still had two years left at school. The widow went to Italy with her family, so Alyosha went to live with some distant relatives he didn’t know. Alyosha never worried about who paid for him to live there. Unlike his brother Ivan, who worked hard to pay his own way, Alyosha didn’t care about money. If he ever got money, he would give it away or forget about it.

Alyosha didn’t finish school. A year before finishing, he told the ladies he wanted to visit his father. They didn’t want him to go, but gave him money and new clothes. He gave some money back, saying he would travel cheaply. When he arrived at his father’s house, he didn’t say why he left school. Soon, people noticed he was looking for his mother’s grave. His father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, didn’t remember where it was, but the servant Grigory showed Alyosha the grave and told him he had paid for the tombstone himself. Alyosha just listened and left quietly.

Fyodor Pavlovitch had not lived in town for years. After his wife died, he moved away for a while and made more money. When he came back, he acted even more wild and careless. He opened many taverns, drank a lot, and only Grigory kept him out of trouble. When Alyosha came home, even his father started acting a little better.
Not long after seeing his mother’s grave, Alyosha said he wanted to become a monk. He told his father this was his strong wish, and that the elder Zossima at the monastery had impressed him.
Fyodor Pavlovitch listened and said, “So you want to be a monk, my gentle boy?”

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was half drunk, joked about monks and money, but told Alyosha he would support him. He said, “I’ll never desert you, and I’ll pay for you if they ask. You don’t spend much money, anyway.” Then he started rambling about hell and hooks, wondering if devils would drag him down when he died. He asked Alyosha to pray for him, because he had sinned a lot.
Alyosha said kindly, “But there are no hooks there.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch answered, “Maybe there are only shadows of hooks. When you live with the monks, you’ll know more. Go, find out the truth, and then tell me. It’s better for you to be there than here with me. You’re like an angel. I hope nothing bad ever touches you. I’ll wait for you. You’re the only one who hasn’t judged me.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch started crying. He was a bad man, but he could also be very emotional.

Some people might think Alyosha was weak or sickly, but he was actually a healthy, strong young man with red cheeks and bright eyes. He was handsome and calm. Even though Alyosha believed in miracles, he was not a silly dreamer. He was a realist—someone who wanted to see the truth and believe in it with all his heart. For Alyosha, faith was more important than miracles. If he believed in something, he really believed it.

Some might say Alyosha was not smart because he didn’t finish school, but that’s not true. He just wanted to find truth and do good things right away, even if he had to give up everything for it. Alyosha wanted to live for God and for what he believed was right. If he hadn’t believed in God, he would have lived very differently. He wanted to do the right thing, not just give a little, but give everything, as he thought Jesus wanted.

Alyosha thought, “I can’t just give a little; I want to give everything to God.” Maybe he remembered going to church with his mother when he was small. In the monastery, he met someone special—an elder named Zossima. In Russian monasteries, an elder is like a wise guide who helps people with their souls. This tradition was old but had been forgotten for some time. Zossima was the third elder at their monastery, and now he was very old and sick. Many people came from far away to see Zossima because he was so wise and kind.

An elder is someone you choose to listen to and obey, hoping to learn to be a better person. People who follow an elder tell him everything and try to do what he says, so they can grow stronger inside. This tradition is not just about rules, but about learning and changing your heart.

There are many stories about elders. One old story says a young man who did not obey his elder could not rest in peace until he was forgiven. In more recent times, even important church leaders said only the elder could release someone from his promise. That’s why elders were both respected and sometimes not liked. Some people thought this was too much power, but many people, rich and poor, came to elders for help and advice. Elders could help people become better, but sometimes people worried it might make some too proud.

Elder Zossima was 65 years old. He used to be a soldier. Alyosha lived with him and cared for him, but Alyosha could come and go as he wished. Alyosha liked helping Zossima and admired how wise and kind he was. Many people came to Zossima for advice, and he often seemed to know what was troubling them even before they spoke.

Alyosha saw that people came to Zossima worried or sad, but left happy. Zossima was not strict; he was cheerful and loved to help everyone, even those who made mistakes. Most of the monks loved Zossima and thought he was a saint. Some people believed miracles would happen because of him. Alyosha believed Zossima was truly holy and that he could help sick people get better.

Alyosha did not doubt the stories of miracles or the love people had for Zossima. He was glad when crowds of poor people and sick children came to see Zossima and ask for his blessing. People would cry, kiss his feet, and bring sick children for help. Zossima would pray for them and bless them. Even when he was very sick, people waited days just to see him. Alyosha understood that these people needed to believe in someone good and holy.
The people thought, “There is so much wrong in the world, but somewhere there is someone holy who knows the truth. If he is here, then truth is not gone, and maybe one day the world will be good.”

Alyosha felt the same way. He believed Zossima was a true saint who would bring honor to the monastery even after he died. Alyosha’s heart was full of hope and happiness because he believed in Zossima.
Alyosha dreamed that one day, because of people like Zossima, everyone would be good and love each other, and there would be no more rich or poor—just people living together like God’s children.

When Alyosha’s two brothers, Ivan and Dmitri, came to town, it made a big impression on him. He became friends with Dmitri faster than with Ivan. Ivan was smart and serious, and Alyosha wasn’t sure what Ivan thought about him. Dmitri was not as educated as Ivan, but he spoke about Ivan with respect. Alyosha learned from Dmitri that there was a big problem between Dmitri and their father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and that Ivan was involved too. Alyosha thought the two brothers were very different.

Around this time, the whole family decided to meet in Elder Zossima’s cell. Their father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, suggested it, maybe as a joke, hoping they would get along better in front of the elder. Dmitri, who had never met Zossima, agreed, even though he thought his father was trying to scare him. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was visiting nearby, also wanted to come, partly because he was curious about the elder and partly because he had business with the monastery. Even though Zossima was sick, he agreed to see them, and the day was set.
Zossima just smiled and said to Alyosha, “Who made me a judge over them?”

Alyosha was worried about the meeting. He knew Dmitri would take it seriously, but the others might not. He thought Ivan and Miüsov were only coming out of curiosity, and his father might try to make fun of the elder. Alyosha cared a lot about Zossima and didn’t want anyone to hurt his feelings. He thought about warning Zossima, but decided not to. Instead, he sent a message to Dmitri asking him to keep his promise to behave. Dmitri wasn’t sure what promise Alyosha meant, but replied that he would try his best to stay calm.
Dmitri wrote, “I would rather bite my tongue than be rude to the sainted man you love so much.” But Alyosha still felt uneasy about the meeting.

It was a warm, sunny day at the end of August. After church, some visitors came to see the elder. The first to arrive was Miüsov in a fancy carriage with his young cousin, Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. Kalganov was about twenty and planning to go to university, though he had not decided where yet. He was tall, strong, and looked thoughtful. Sometimes he seemed lost in his own world. He was usually quiet but could be talkative when alone with someone. He was always nicely dressed and was friends with Alyosha.

Next, Fyodor Pavlovitch came in an old carriage with his son Ivan. Dmitri was supposed to come too, but he was late. The visitors left their carriages at the hotel and walked to the monastery. Miüsov and the others had never been here before, and Miüsov was curious. As people left the church, a few important guests were among them, like some ladies and an old general. Beggars came up to the visitors, but only Kalganov gave a coin to an old woman and told her to share it. He felt embarrassed, even though no one said anything.
The visitors thought someone would welcome them, since one had given a big donation and another was a rich landowner. But no official came to meet them.
Miüsov looked at the tombstones and almost made a joke about them, but stopped himself. He was starting to get annoyed.
“Who can we even ask for help here? We need to find out where to go,” Miüsov said.
Just then, an older man named Maximov came up. He was bald and wore a summer coat. He was friendly and said he was a landowner from Tula. He wanted to help them.
Maximov told them, “Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, over there, past the trees.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “We know it's past the trees, but we forgot the way. We haven’t been here in a long time.”
Maximov offered to show them the way, saying, “Come with me! I’m going there too.”
So they left through the gate and walked toward the trees. Maximov hurried along, looking at everyone with big, curious eyes.
Miüsov said, “We are here to see the elder for our own business, so thank you, but you don’t have to come with us.”
Maximov said he had already been there, calling the elder a “chevalier parfait,” snapping his fingers.
Miüsov asked, “Who’s a chevalier?”
Maximov replied, “The elder, Zossima, he’s wonderful!”
Suddenly, a pale monk wearing a cap came up and stopped them.
The monk bowed and said, “The Father Superior invites all of you to have dinner with him after your visit, at one o’clock. Maximov, you too.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was excited about the invitation. “We promise to behave here,” he said. He asked Miüsov if he would come too.
Miüsov agreed, saying he wanted to see the customs. He joked that Fyodor Pavlovitch’s company was the only problem.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said Dmitri was not there yet.
Miüsov said it would be better if Dmitri did not come at all. He thanked the monk for the dinner invitation.
The monk said, “Now, I am supposed to take you to the elder.”
Maximov said he would go straight to the Father Superior instead.
The monk replied, “The Father Superior is busy right now. But you can go if you want.” Maximov hurried back to the monastery.
Miüsov called Maximov rude as he left. Fyodor Pavlovitch said Maximov looked like someone named von Sohn.
Miüsov asked how he could know that, and Fyodor Pavlovitch said he could always tell from people’s faces.
Miüsov warned Fyodor Pavlovitch again to behave or he would leave. He told the monk he was worried about Fyodor Pavlovitch. The monk just smiled quietly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “Here’s the hermitage! We’ve arrived, but the gates are shut,” and he made the sign of the cross.
Fyodor Pavlovitch talked about the saints painted on the gates and how women were not allowed inside. He asked the monk if the elder saw ladies.
The monk explained women could come to special rooms outside the hermitage, and the elder would visit them if he felt well enough. Madame Hohlakov and her sick daughter were waiting there now.
Fyodor Pavlovitch joked about rules for women at other holy places. Miüsov threatened to leave again if he kept talking like that.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “Look how nice it is here!” and stepped inside.
There were no roses, but many beautiful flowers everywhere, even around the church and the elder’s house.
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked if it was like this when the last elder, Varsonofy, was here. He joked that Varsonofy used to hit people with a stick. The monk said that wasn’t true.
The monk told them to wait while he announced them.
Miüsov warned Fyodor Pavlovitch one last time to behave.
Fyodor Pavlovitch teased Miüsov, asking if he was worried about his sins, since people said the elder could tell why people were visiting just by looking at them.
Miüsov was annoyed but didn’t answer, as they were called inside.
Miüsov thought to himself that he was getting angry and might start an argument inside.

Almost at the same time, everyone entered the small room where Father Zossima (the elder, a wise and holy monk) had just come in. Two other monks were already there: Father Librarian and Father Païssy (a smart, gentle monk who was often sick). In the corner stood a young man about twenty-two. He was a student learning about religion and lived at the monastery. He looked respectful and serious, but since he was not as important as the others, he did not bow to the guests.

Father Zossima came in with a young helper (a novice) and Alyosha (his gentle student). The two monks bowed deeply and kissed Father Zossima’s hand. Father Zossima blessed them and bowed back, asking for their blessing too. They all did this very seriously. Miüsov (a proud visitor) thought it was all just for show. He had wanted to be polite and get the elder's blessing, but when he saw the monks bowing and kissing hands, he changed his mind. Miüsov just made a regular bow and sat down. Fyodor Pavlovitch (Alyosha’s father) copied Miüsov in a silly way. Ivan (Alyosha’s brother) bowed politely but did not kiss any hands. Kalganov (a young friend) was so nervous he forgot to bow at all. Father Zossima saw this and simply asked everyone to sit. Alyosha blushed, feeling embarrassed. He was worried things would go badly.

Father Zossima sat on an old, leather sofa. The visitors sat in a row on old chairs. The monks sat by the door and window. The student, novice, and Alyosha stayed standing. The room was small and plain, with only simple furniture, two flower pots, and many holy pictures. One lamp burned in front of a very old icon (a special picture of the Virgin Mary). There were also a Catholic cross, some fancy art, and some cheap pictures of saints. On the other walls were portraits of important Russian bishops.

Miüsov looked at the room and then at Father Zossima. Miüsov liked to think he could judge people well. He thought Zossima looked strange: small, bent, with thin wrinkled skin and sharp, shining eyes. His beard was tiny and his lips were thin. His nose was sharp, almost like a bird’s beak.

Suddenly, the little wall clock struck twelve, and Fyodor Pavlovitch spoke up, noticing his son Dmitri was missing. He tried to make jokes in front of everyone, calling Father Zossima a “sacred elder” and talking about how he was always on time. Miüsov snapped at him, saying he was not a king. Fyodor Pavlovitch just joked more, telling a silly story about once making a joke to an important policeman and ruining his business, and then about another time when his words got him in trouble. Miüsov was annoyed and said Fyodor Pavlovitch was acting foolish again.

Father Zossima watched them both quietly. Fyodor Pavlovitch kept talking, saying he knew he was being silly, and that sometimes he couldn’t help himself. He even compared himself to a little devil and told another story he claimed was about Diderot, a famous philosopher, but Miüsov said he was lying. Fyodor Pavlovitch admitted he made up part of the story, saying he just wanted to be funny and liked to play the fool.

Miüsov was so angry he stood up, forgetting himself. He felt embarrassed, as this was supposed to be a special, respectful visit. Usually, important people would come to see the elder, kneeling and feeling lucky to be there. But now Fyodor Pavlovitch was making a joke out of everything. Alyosha was almost crying, embarrassed by his father. Ivan just sat quietly, not helping at all.

Miüsov apologized to Father Zossima for the foolishness and tried to leave, but Father Zossima kindly stopped him and asked him to stay, saying he was welcome as a guest. Fyodor Pavlovitch then asked the elder if he was annoying him. Father Zossima told him not to worry, to make himself at home, and not to be ashamed of himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch joked that it was dangerous to let him be himself, but then stood up and loudly said how much the elder’s words had touched him. He fell to his knees and asked, “What must I do to gain eternal life?” It was hard to tell if he was being serious or just playing around again.

Father Zossima smiled gently and told him, “You already know what to do. Don’t drink too much, don’t say bad things, don’t chase after wrong pleasures, don’t love money, and close some of your taverns. Most of all, don’t lie.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch joked, “You mean about Diderot?” Father Zossima answered, “No, not just that. Don’t lie to yourself. If you lie to yourself, you won’t know what is true anymore. Then you stop respecting yourself and others, and you stop loving. Then you fill your life with bad things. Also, people who lie to themselves often take offense easily and enjoy feeling insulted, even if nothing happened. But please, sit down, and don’t pretend so much.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch quickly kissed the elder’s hand, saying he liked what the elder had said. He admitted he had lied his whole life, and then asked a question: Was it true that a saint once picked up his own head after being killed and walked around with it? The elder said no, that story was not true.

Fyodor Pavlovitch said that Miüsov had told him the story years ago, and that it shook his faith. Miüsov denied it, but Fyodor Pavlovitch kept teasing that it was Miüsov’s fault. Miüsov got upset and said Fyodor Pavlovitch ruined everything he touched.

Then Father Zossima stood up and told everyone he had to leave for a few minutes because others were waiting to see him. He smiled and told Fyodor Pavlovitch not to lie. Alyosha and the novice hurried to follow Father Zossima out. Alyosha was relieved the elder was not upset. As Father Zossima walked away to meet more people, Fyodor Pavlovitch tried to stop him, saying he had only been acting foolish on purpose to test the elder. He promised to be quiet now and let Miüsov speak.

Near the wooden porch below, about twenty peasant women were waiting. They had heard that Father Zossima (the elder) was coming out soon, so they gathered together. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, waited too, but in a special place for important women.

Madame Hohlakov was rich, pretty, and always dressed nicely. She was about thirty-three and had been a widow for five years. Her daughter was fourteen and could not walk, so she sat in a long chair with wheels. The girl was thin from being sick but had a happy face and big, dark eyes. They planned to travel for her health but were delayed. They were in town for business, not only for church, but had visited Father Zossima once three days ago. Even though he rarely saw visitors, they came again, hoping for the “happiness of seeing the great healer.”
Madame Hohlakov sat beside her daughter’s chair. Nearby stood an old monk visiting from a faraway monastery. He wanted Father Zossima’s blessing too.

When Father Zossima came out, he went first to the peasants waiting at the steps. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and blessed the women. One woman, who seemed crazy, was brought to him. When she saw him, she screamed and twisted as if in great pain. Father Zossima put his stole on her forehead and said a short prayer, and she became calm right away.
Many women began to cry with joy. Some tried to kiss his clothes, and others sang out happily.
Father Zossima blessed them all and spoke to some. He already knew the woman who had been screaming; she lived nearby and had come before.
He pointed to another woman, thin and with a face dark from the sun. She knelt and stared at him with wild eyes.
“From far away, Father, from far away!” the woman said, swaying and resting her cheek on her hand.
“Are you from the town?” Father Zossima asked.

“Yes, Father. We are town people, but really peasants. I came to see you. I have buried my little son. I have been to three monasteries, but they told me, ‘Go to Father Zossima.’ So I came. I was here yesterday at the service, and today I have come to you.”
“Why are you crying?” asked Father Zossima.

“It’s for my little son, Father. He was almost three years old. He was our last child. We had four, but now all are gone. I buried the first three, but this last one I cannot forget. I keep thinking of him and looking at his little clothes. I wail and cry. My husband, Nikita, is a driver. We are not poor. But now nothing matters. Nikita drinks when I am gone, but I don’t care. I left home three months ago. I don’t care about anything now.”

Father Zossima said, “Long ago, a saint saw a mother like you crying for her only child. The saint said, ‘Do you know how brave these little ones are before God? No one is bolder than children in Heaven. They say, “Lord, you gave us life, but took it back so soon. Make us angels!” And God does. So, mother, be glad and don’t cry—your son is with the angels and prays for you.’ Your little one is happy with God, so rejoice.”
The woman listened and sighed sadly.

“My Nikita tried to say the same,” she said. “He tells me our son sings with the angels. But he cries too. I wish I could just see my boy once more, hear him call me, or hear his little feet. But he is gone, Father. I will never see him again.” She pulled out her boy’s little sash and cried hard.

Father Zossima said, “Like Rachel in the Bible, you cry for your children and cannot be comforted. Mothers feel this pain. Don’t try to stop your tears, but remember, your boy is an angel and sees you and is happy when you remember him. One day, your sorrow will turn to gentle joy. I will pray for your son’s soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”

“A sweet name! I will remember him, and your sadness, and pray for your husband too. It is wrong to leave your husband. Your son sees from heaven that you are gone and is sad. He wants to see his parents together. Go back to your husband today.”

“I will go, Father, as you say. My Nikita is waiting for me,” the woman said. But Father Zossima turned to another old woman, dressed like a townsperson. She said her son Vasenka worked far away in Irkutsk, Siberia. He had not written for a year, and she didn’t know where to ask about him.
The woman said a rich lady told her, “Pray for your son as if he were dead, and he will write to you.” She wanted to know if this was right.

“Don’t do that,” said Father Zossima. “It is wrong to pray for the dead when your son is alive. Pray to the Mother of God for his health. I tell you, your son is alive and will soon return or send a letter.”
“Thank you, Father! God bless you for praying for us,” said the woman.
Then Father Zossima saw a young, sick-looking woman staring at him. She seemed afraid to speak.
“What is it, my child?” he asked.
“Forgive my soul, Father,” she whispered, kneeling at his feet. “I have sinned and am afraid.”
Father Zossima sat down on the step. The woman moved closer, still on her knees.
“I have been a widow for three years,” she whispered. “My husband beat me and was sick. I wished he would not get well. Then a thought came to me—”
“Wait,” said Father Zossima, listening close. The woman whispered her secret, then finished.
“Three years ago?” he asked.
“Yes. At first, I didn’t think about it, but now it worries me all the time.”
“Did you come far?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you confessed it?”
“Yes, twice.”
“Have you taken Communion?”
“Yes. But I am afraid to die.”

“Don’t be afraid,” said Father Zossima. “If you truly repent, God will forgive anything. There is no sin too big for God’s love. Keep being sorry and loving. Forgive your husband in your heart. If I, a sinner, can be kind to you, think how much more God loves you. Love is a great treasure. It can save everything.”
He blessed her, gave her a small ikon, and she bowed down, silent.
Father Zossima smiled at a healthy woman holding a baby.
“From Vyshegorye, dear Father,” she said.
“You brought your baby five miles to see me. What do you want?” he asked.
“I came just to see you. People said you were sick, but you look well! You’ll live many more years. God bless you! Many people pray for you.”
“Thank you, daughter,” said Father Zossima.
“I have a small favor. Here are sixty copecks. Give them to someone poorer than me.”
“Thank you, dear. Is this your little girl?”
“Yes, Father. Her name is Lizaveta.”
“May God bless you and your little Lizaveta! You have made me happy. Farewell, dear children.”
He blessed everyone and bowed low to them.

A kind lady stood nearby, watching the elder (the wise old monk) talk with the peasants and bless them. She felt so moved that she cried a little and wiped her tears. When the elder came to her, she greeted him happily.

“Oh, what a wonderful scene!” she said, her voice shaky because she was so touched. “Now I understand why people love you. I love people too, especially our Russian people—they are so great and simple!”
The elder asked, “How is your daughter? You wanted to talk to me again?”

The lady replied, “Yes, I prayed for this! We have come to thank you. You healed my daughter, Lise, just by praying for her and putting your hands on her last Thursday. We wanted to kiss your hands and tell you how grateful we are.”
The elder said, “Healed? But she is still in her chair.”

The lady quickly said, “But her night fevers stopped since Thursday! Her legs are stronger, she slept all night, and her cheeks are rosy. She even stood up by herself for a whole minute this morning! The doctor was amazed. Lise, thank him!”
Lise tried to look serious and thanked the elder by putting her hands together, but then she started laughing.
“It’s at him,” Lise said, pointing to Alyosha (Alexey Fyodorovitch), feeling a bit annoyed with herself for laughing.
Alyosha, who stood behind the elder, blushed and looked down.
The lady said, “Lise has a message for you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How are you?” She held out her gloved hand to Alyosha.
The elder turned to Alyosha, who went closer to Lise and awkwardly gave her his hand. Lise looked important.
“Katerina Ivanovna sent you this note,” Lise said, handing Alyosha a letter. “She wants you to visit her as soon as you can.”

Alyosha was surprised. “She wants to see me? Why?” he asked. The lady explained, “It’s about Dmitri Fyodorovitch and everything that happened. Katerina Ivanovna has made up her mind, but she needs to talk to you. Please go; it’s the right thing to do.”
“I’ve only seen her once,” Alyosha said, still confused.
“She is such a wonderful person. Think of all the pain she’s going through!” said the lady.
Alyosha read the note, which only asked him to come urgently. He agreed, “Very well, I will come.”
Lise cheered up. “Oh, I knew you would go! I always thought you were great, Alyosha. I’m glad to tell you so!”
“Lise!” said her mother, a bit stern but smiling.
The lady said, “You never come to see us, Alexey Fyodorovitch, though Lise says she’s happiest with you.”

Alyosha blushed again and smiled shyly. Meanwhile, the elder began talking to a monk who had been waiting nearby. This monk was from far away, from Obdorsk, and belonged to a poor monastery with only ten monks. The elder blessed him and welcomed him.
The monk suddenly asked, “How can you do such things?” He pointed at Lise, speaking of her being healed.
The elder said, “It’s too soon to say she’s healed. If she is better, it is only by God’s will. Please visit me, Father. I am sick, and I know I won’t live much longer.”
“Oh no! You will live a long time,” cried the lady. “You look so well and happy!”
The elder replied, “I feel better today, but I understand my illness. If I seem happy, that pleases me, because people are meant to be happy. All the good and holy people were happy.”
The lady sighed, “You speak so beautifully! But I suffer so much. Let me tell you what I couldn’t say before—I am suffering!”
She pressed her hands together in front of him.
The elder asked, “What are you suffering from?”
She answered, “From not having enough faith.”
“You mean faith in God?” asked the elder.
“No, not that. But I worry about life after death. No one can explain it, and it frightens me. You are wise, so I wanted to ask you. What will you think of me?”
She clasped her hands again.
The elder gently said, “Don’t worry about what I think. I believe you really are suffering.”

The lady said, “Sometimes I wonder if faith is real, or just comes from being scared of nature. What if, after I die, there is nothing? How can I get my faith back? I only believed when I was a child. How can I prove it’s true? No one else seems to care, but I do. It’s so hard!”
The elder said, “There’s no way to prove it, but you can become sure of it.”
“How?” she asked.
“By loving others and helping them. The more you love people, the more you will believe in God and your soul. If you forget yourself by loving others, you will have no doubt.”
“I dream of helping people,” said the lady. “Sometimes I want to leave everything and become a nurse. I think I could help anyone, no matter how sick.”
The elder said, “It’s good that you have such kind dreams. Maybe one day you will do good in real life.”

The lady asked, “But could I keep doing it for long? What if the sick person is unkind, or complains? I think I would stop loving people if they were not grateful. I want people to thank me and love me back.”
She looked at the elder, feeling upset with herself.

The elder said, “A doctor once told me he loved humanity, but the more he loved all people, the less he could stand being with anyone for two days. People annoyed him, but he still dreamed of helping everyone.”
The lady asked, “What can I do? Should I give up?”

The elder answered, “No. It’s good that you feel worried about this. Do your best, and it will count for something. If you only want approval for being honest, you will only dream about loving people and never really do it. Then you will stop thinking about the next life.”
“You have shown me the truth!” the lady cried. “I see now I just wanted your praise.”

The elder smiled. “If you are truly honest, that is good. If you can’t find happiness, remember you are on the right path. Don’t lie to yourself. Watch yourself carefully and try to avoid being mean or scared. Even when you feel weak, don’t be afraid. Love in real life is hard. People want to do good quickly and be praised, but true love takes work and patience. Sometimes, when you feel far from your goal, you are really about to reach it. God is guiding you. I must go now. Goodbye.”
The lady began to cry.
“Lise, Lise! Bless her—bless her!” she cried.
The elder teased, “She doesn’t deserve love. Why did you laugh at Alexey?”

Lise had been watching Alyosha and making fun of him because he was shy and wouldn't look at her. She tried to catch his eye, and when he finally looked, she smiled at him. Alyosha became even more embarrassed and tried to hide behind the elder. But he couldn’t help glancing at Lise again, and she laughed so much that the elder said, “Why do you make fun of him, naughty girl?”

Lise suddenly blushed and became serious. She spoke quickly, “Why has he forgotten everything? He used to carry me around when I was little. We played together. He taught me to read. When he left, he said he would never forget me, that we would be friends forever! And now he is afraid of me. Why? He could visit us, but he doesn’t. I shouldn’t have to invite him.”
Then she hid her face and started to laugh and cry at the same time. The elder smiled, blessed her, and Lise kissed his hand and pressed it to her eyes, still crying.
“Don’t be angry with me. I’m silly and good for nothing... Maybe Alyosha is right not to visit a silly girl like me.”
The elder said, “I will certainly send him.”

The elder (Father Zossima) had been away from his room for about twenty-five minutes. It was past half-past twelve, but Dmitri (one of the Karamazov brothers), who was the reason for the meeting, still hadn’t come. The other guests seemed to forget about him and were busy talking. Ivan (another Karamazov brother) and the two monks, Father Iosif and Father Païssy, led the conversation. Miüsov wanted to join in but was mostly ignored, which made him annoyed. Fyodor Pavlovitch (father of the Karamazov brothers) watched Miüsov with a sly smile and started to tease him in a whisper, saying Miüsov stayed just to show off his cleverness. Miüsov said he was about to leave, but Fyodor Pavlovitch joked he would be last to go. Then Father Zossima came back to the room. The room got quiet for a moment, but the elder smiled and looked at everyone as if asking them to keep talking. Alyosha (the youngest Karamazov brother) noticed Father Zossima looked very tired, but the elder wanted everyone to stay for some reason.

Father Iosif told Father Zossima they were talking about Ivan’s interesting article. Ivan had written about the Church and the State (government) and how they should work together. Ivan explained that he thought the Church should include the whole State, not just a small part of it. Some people disagreed, saying the Church should stay separate from the State. Father Païssy agreed with Ivan and said the Church should become the most important thing, as promised by God. Miüsov thought this idea was just a far-away dream and joked it was like something out of a story. He said he was worried the Church might start punishing people like the government does, but Ivan said if the world was all Church, the Church wouldn’t cut off or hurt people. Instead, if someone did something wrong, they would be separated from the Church, which would feel much worse than just going to jail. Ivan said the Church would try to help people become better, not just punish them.

Father Zossima joined the conversation and said that regular punishments like prison or exile don’t really help people change. Only when someone feels sorry in their heart and knows they did wrong against the Church and God, can they truly become better. The Church does not try to hurt people, but treats them with kindness, hoping they will change. Even if someone does something very bad, the Church still cares for them and does not give up on them. Father Zossima said that if the whole society was like the Church, maybe there would be less crime. The Church would help people change for the better. He said it might not happen soon, but someday, it could be true, because that is what God wants.

Father Païssy agreed, saying, “So be it, so be it!” Miüsov thought this was a strange idea, and said it was like making the Church more powerful than the State. Father Païssy said Miüsov was wrong; the idea wasn’t to make the Church into the State, but for the State to become more like the Church, full of goodness. Alyosha watched all of this and felt very moved by the conversation. He saw that Rakitin (another guest) was also listening quietly, but seemed excited.

Then Miüsov told a story. He said that in Paris, he once met a government worker who said that Christian socialists were more dangerous than other kinds because they believed in God and wanted to change things. Miüsov wondered if the people here were like those Christian socialists. But before anyone could answer, the door opened and Dmitri (the brother they had been waiting for) finally came in, surprising everyone.

Dmitri Fyodorovitch was twenty-eight years old. He looked older and was strong, but his face was thin and a bit sickly. His dark eyes looked serious but sometimes seemed sad or thoughtful, even when he was laughing. People said he had a quick temper and was not always steady. Lately, everyone in town had heard about the fights he had with his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Dmitri wore nice clothes, gloves, and a top-hat. He had a short mustache and short brown hair. He walked like a soldier. When he entered the room, he went straight to Father Zossima, the elder, and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima blessed him, and Dmitri kissed his hand.
Dmitri said, “Please forgive me for being late. Smerdyakov, my father’s servant, told me the wrong time.”
Father Zossima said, “It’s all right, you are only a little late.”

Dmitri thanked him and bowed again. Then he turned to his father and made a deep, respectful bow. Fyodor Pavlovitch quickly bowed back, trying to look serious. Dmitri then bowed to everyone else and sat down quietly to listen.
After Dmitri entered, the conversation started again. Miüsov didn’t want to continue the argument with Father Païssy and suggested Ivan Fyodorovitch should speak.
Ivan said that some people confused socialism and Christianity, and even the police sometimes made the same mistake.

Miüsov then told a story about Ivan. He said that Ivan once told a group that there was nothing in the world to make people love each other, except the belief in life after death. Ivan said that if people stopped believing in immortality, there would be no love or goodness—everything would be allowed, even bad things. Ivan also said that people who don’t believe in God would think selfishness and even crime were normal.
Dmitri asked, “So, if someone doesn’t believe in God, crime becomes sensible for them?”
Father Païssy answered, “Yes.”
Dmitri said, “I’ll remember that,” and stopped speaking. Everyone looked at him, surprised.
Father Zossima asked Ivan, “Is that really what you believe?”
Ivan replied, “Yes. Without belief in immortality, there’s no virtue.”
Father Zossima said, “You are lucky to believe that, or maybe very unhappy.”
Ivan asked, “Why unhappy?”
The elder said, “Because you probably don’t really believe in immortality or in what you wrote.”
Ivan blushed and said, “Maybe you are right, but I wasn’t just joking.”
Father Zossima said that Ivan’s heart was full of questions he couldn’t answer, and that caused him pain. He hoped Ivan would find his answer one day.
Ivan got up, received the elder’s blessing, and kissed his hand. Everyone was quiet and felt the moment was serious. Alyosha looked worried. Then Miüsov shrugged, and Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up.

Fyodor Pavlovitch loudly compared his sons Dmitri and Ivan to characters from a story, saying one was good and one was bad, and he himself was like a nobleman from that story. He asked the elder to judge them.
Father Zossima, looking tired, told Fyodor Pavlovitch not to make jokes or insult his family.
Dmitri stood up, angry. He said, “Sorry, Father Zossima. I am not educated, but you have been fooled. My father only wants to make a scene. But I think I know why—”

Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted that everyone blamed him. He said Dmitri was in debt to him, and that Dmitri had spent money badly. He accused Dmitri of falling in love with a good young woman, then of chasing after another woman, whom he called an “enchantress.” He said Dmitri wanted money from him for this woman, and that Dmitri had borrowed money from others. He threatened to tell more secrets.
Dmitri yelled, “Be quiet! Don’t you dare insult a good girl in front of me!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch pretended to cry and asked if Dmitri cared about his father’s blessing or would rather be cursed.
Dmitri called him a hypocrite.
Fyodor Pavlovitch told everyone that Dmitri had beaten up a poor captain in a tavern, just because the captain worked for Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Dmitri, shaking with anger, admitted he had hit the captain and was sorry. But he said the captain had tried to trick him, and that his father had tried to get him in trouble because of jealousy over the woman. Dmitri said he had come to make peace, but now his father had insulted him and the young lady, so he had to tell the truth.
Dmitri could not finish. Everyone was upset. The monks waited for Father Zossima to speak. The elder watched them, weak but calm. Miüsov felt ashamed.

Miüsov said the whole scene was a scandal and blamed Fyodor Pavlovitch. He said he didn’t know about the details and was only now learning that a father was jealous of his son over a woman, and tried to put him in prison.
Fyodor Pavlovitch screamed that if Dmitri were not his son, he would challenge him to a duel.
Dmitri looked at his father with disgust.
Dmitri said quietly, “I thought I was coming home with my fiancée to look after you, but I found only a bad, foolish man.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted again, saying the woman called a “creature” was better than anyone in Miüsov’s family, and that Dmitri had left his fiancée for her.
Father Iosif said, “Shameful!”
Kalganov, a young man, also cried, “Shameful and disgraceful!”
Dmitri, shaking with anger, asked if such a man as his father should be allowed to live and poison the world.
Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted to the monks, saying that even though the woman had made mistakes, Christ forgave people who loved much.
Father Iosif said, “It was not for that kind of love.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch went on mocking the monks, saying they thought eating simple food made them good.
Everyone agreed this was too much.
Suddenly, Father Zossima stood up. Alyosha helped him. Father Zossima went to Dmitri and bowed down so low his forehead touched the floor. Everyone was shocked.
Father Zossima said, “Good-bye! Forgive me, all of you!” and bowed to his guests.
Dmitri was amazed, then cried out, covered his face, and rushed out. The other guests hurried out too, forgetting to say good-bye. Only the monks stayed to get the elder’s blessing.
Fyodor Pavlovitch, now calmer, wondered aloud what Father Zossima’s bow meant.
Miüsov answered angrily that he didn’t know, but he wanted to leave and never see Fyodor Pavlovitch again.
The monk who had invited them to dinner met them outside.
Miüsov asked the monk to tell the Father Superior he was sorry he couldn’t come to dinner.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said loudly that Miüsov only left because of him, and that he would go home instead of eating at the monastery.
Miüsov said he was not Fyodor’s relative and never had been.
Fyodor Pavlovitch teased Miüsov about being related, said Ivan could stay if he wanted, and that Miüsov should go apologize for the trouble.
Miüsov doubted Fyodor Pavlovitch would really go home.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he was ashamed and would not stay for dinner after such a scene.
Miüsov still did not trust him, watching as Fyodor Pavlovitch walked away.
Miüsov asked Ivan if he would go to the dinner.
Ivan said yes, since he was invited.
Miüsov grumbled that they had to explain to the Father Superior that the trouble was not their fault.
Ivan agreed, saying at least their father wouldn’t be there.
Miüsov hoped so.
They all walked toward the dinner. The monk said the Father Superior had been waiting a long time and they were late. Miüsov was angry with Ivan.
Miüsov thought Ivan was acting like nothing happened and blamed it on the Karamazov nature.

Alyosha helped Father Zossima to his bedroom and sat him gently on the bed. The room was very small and simple. There was just a narrow bed, a thin mattress, and some holy pictures in the corner. Father Zossima looked very tired and breathed hard. He stared at Alyosha, thinking deeply.
“Go now, my dear boy,” Father Zossima said softly. “Porfiry will stay with me. You are needed at the Father Superior’s dinner. Hurry and help there.”

Alyosha wanted to stay, but Father Zossima said, “You are needed more with the others. If things get difficult, say a prayer. Remember, my son, this is not your place forever. When God takes me, you must leave the monastery and go out into the world.”

Alyosha was surprised. Father Zossima continued, “This is not your home for now. I bless you to work in the world. Your journey will be long. You will even get married one day and face many hardships before you return. But I trust you. Christ is with you. Don’t leave Him, and He won’t leave you. You will have deep sadness, but you will find happiness in it. Remember my words: in sorrow, find joy. Work hard, always. My time is short, so remember what I say.”
Alyosha’s face showed strong feelings. He wanted to cry.

Father Zossima smiled gently and said, “Why are you sad? When someone dies, people in the world cry, but here we rejoice and pray for them. Leave me now, I must pray. Stay close to your brothers—both of them.”
Father Zossima blessed Alyosha. Alyosha wanted to ask why the elder had bowed to Dmitri, but he was too shy. He believed it was something important and mysterious.

As Alyosha hurried to the monastery to help at dinner, he remembered Father Zossima’s words about his death. Alyosha felt scared and sad. He wondered how he could live without Father Zossima. He walked quickly through the trees, feeling heavy in his heart. Suddenly he saw Rakitin waiting on the path.
“Are you waiting for me?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes,” Rakitin grinned. “You’re going to the Father Superior’s big dinner. I won’t be there, but you go and help. Tell me—what does that strange bowing by Father Zossima mean?”
“What do you mean?” Alyosha asked.
“When Father Zossima bowed to your brother Dmitri, and even touched his forehead to the ground!”
“You’re talking about Father Zossima?” Alyosha checked.
“Yes,” said Rakitin.
“What did that mean?” Rakitin pressed.
“I don’t know, Misha,” Alyosha replied.
“I thought so. Everyone will talk about it. I think Father Zossima sensed something bad coming—a crime in your family,” said Rakitin.
“What crime?” Alyosha asked.

“It will be between your brothers and your rich old father. Father Zossima bowed to warn everyone. If something happens, people will say, ‘The holy man predicted it!’ That’s how these things go. He bows to a murderer and scolds a good man.”
“What crime? What murderer? What do you mean?” Alyosha stopped, shocked.
Rakitin asked, “Haven’t you thought about it? Be honest.”
“I have,” Alyosha admitted quietly.
“Really?” Rakitin was surprised.
“I didn’t really think it, but when you spoke, I felt I had,” Alyosha said.
“You see? You thought of a crime when you saw your father and Mitya today. So I’m right?”
“Wait,” Alyosha said nervously. “Why does this interest you?”

“I suddenly understood your brother Dmitri. He is honest but hot-tempered. If someone pushes him too far, he might hurt your father. But your father is also wild. If they don’t control themselves, it could end badly.”
“No, Misha, you are wrong. It won’t go that far.”

“But you’re shaking. Mitya is honest but also loves pleasure too much. All Karamazovs do. Even you, Alyosha, might be like that. All of you are intense and wild. Right now, your father, Dmitri, and Ivan are all fighting inside. You might get pulled in too.”
“You’re wrong about that woman. Dmitri despises her,” Alyosha said, shivering.
“Grushenka? No, he doesn’t. He left his fiancée for her! Sometimes a man can’t help loving a woman, even if he says he hates her. That’s how strong feelings can be.”
“I understand,” Alyosha said softly.
“Really? So you do think about these things!” Rakitin teased. “You look pure but you have Karamazov blood too. Grushenka keeps asking me to bring you to her. She’s very interested in you.”
“Thank her, but I’m not coming,” Alyosha said with a strained smile. “Finish what you were saying.”

“It’s simple. All of you Karamazovs are wild and greedy. Ivan writes about religion but doesn’t believe it. He wants Mitya’s fiancée, Katerina Ivanovna, for himself, and Mitya will let him have her so he can be with Grushenka. Your father is now crazy about Grushenka too. She plays with them both, waiting to see who will give her more. Mitya is ready to leave Katerina Ivanovna, a rich and beautiful girl, to marry Grushenka, who used to be with a rough old merchant. Ivan might end up with Katerina Ivanovna and her money. Your family is a mess, Alyosha! Ivan is waiting to see what will happen, and even Mitya said Ivan deserved Katerina more than he did. Even Katerina is unsure whom she likes better.”
“How do you know all this?” Alyosha asked, frowning.
“Why do you sound worried? You know I’m telling the truth.”
“You don’t like Ivan. He wouldn’t care about money,” Alyosha said.
“But Katerina is beautiful and rich. Sixty thousand rubles is a lot.”
“Ivan doesn’t care for money or comfort. Maybe he is looking for something else, maybe even suffering,” said Alyosha.
“What a strange idea,” Rakitin replied.
“Ivan’s mind is troubled,” Alyosha explained. “He wants answers to big questions.”

“You sound just like your elder,” Rakitin said, annoyed. “Ivan’s ideas are silly. He said if there is no soul, then anything is allowed. But people can still be good without believing in the soul. They can love freedom, equality, and kindness.”
Rakitin stopped, remembering something.
“That’s enough. Why are you smiling? Do you think I’m foolish?”
“No, Misha. I understand why you’re upset. Maybe you care about Katerina Ivanovna, and that’s why you don’t like Ivan. Are you jealous?”
“And jealous of her money too? Will you say that?” Rakitin asked.
“I won’t talk about money. I don’t want to insult you.”
“Fine, but why should I like Ivan? He insults me. Why can’t I insult him?”
“Ivan never says anything about you,” said Alyosha.
“But I heard he was talking about me at Katerina Ivanovna’s house. He joked that I would one day run a magazine and become rich by pretending to be a socialist but really caring only about money.”
“That really might happen, Misha,” Alyosha said with a friendly smile.
“You’re teasing me, Alyosha.”
“No, I’m joking. But how did you hear all this? You weren’t there, were you?”
“No, but Dmitri was, and I overheard him telling the story while I was in Grushenka’s bedroom.”
“Oh, right. I forgot—she’s a relation of yours.”
“A relation! Grushenka isn’t related to me!” Rakitin shouted, turning red. “Don’t insult me like that!”
Alyosha blushed. “Sorry, I didn’t know. But why do you call her bad names? I heard you visit her often and you’re not her lover. Why do you hate her so much? Does she really deserve it?”

“I have my reasons for seeing her. But as for being related—no. Your brother or father might be closer to her than I am. Look, here we are. You should go to the kitchen. What’s going on? Are we late? There’s your father and Ivan coming out, shouting. Miüsov is leaving in his carriage, and Maximov is running. There must have been trouble! Maybe they even had a fight!”
Rakitin was right to be surprised. There had been a big, shocking scene. It happened quickly and was worse than anyone expected.

Miüsov walked with Ivan to the Father Superior’s house. He felt bad for losing his temper earlier. Miüsov decided to be polite, friendly, and helpful. He wanted to show the monks he was not like Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he thought was rude and silly.
Miüsov made up his mind to give up his arguments with the monastery about fishing and wood-cutting. He didn’t really care about those things anymore.

These good feelings got even stronger when Miüsov saw the Father Superior’s dining room. The room was simple but very clean, with pretty flowers and a nice table full of food and drinks. Rakitin, who liked to find out everything, peeked into the kitchen and later told Alyosha about all the tasty dishes. Rakitin was smart, but Alyosha worried he was not a very good person inside, even if Rakitin thought he was.

Rakitin was not invited to the dinner. Only Father Iosif, Father Païssy, and another monk were there. Miüsov, Kalganov, Ivan, and Maximov arrived. The Father Superior, a tall old man with gray hair, greeted them. Miüsov tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior gently pulled it away. Ivan and Kalganov kissed his hand as peasants do.
Miüsov spoke politely to the Father Superior, saying sorry that Fyodor Pavlovitch had not come. He explained Fyodor Pavlovitch was upset after arguing with his son and asked for forgiveness.
The Father Superior listened kindly and replied that he was sorry Fyodor Pavlovitch was not there. He invited everyone to sit.
The Father Superior stood by the holy picture and said a prayer. Everyone bowed their heads.

Just then, Fyodor Pavlovitch came back, even though he had planned to leave. He remembered how people thought he was a fool, so he wanted to embarrass everyone. He told the coachman to wait and hurried back to the monastery, not really knowing what he would do.
Fyodor Pavlovitch walked into the dining room right after the prayer. He laughed loudly and said, “They thought I had gone, and here I am again!”
For a moment, everyone was quiet and stared at him. Miüsov became angry.
“No! This I cannot endure!” Miüsov said, grabbing his hat.
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked if he could come in. The Father Superior said yes and asked everyone to be friendly.
Miüsov was too upset and said, “No, no, it is impossible!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would go wherever Miüsov went. He started calling Maximov “von Sohn,” talking nonsense.
Maximov was confused and said he was not von Sohn. Fyodor Pavlovitch told a silly story about a man named von Sohn.
The monks wondered what was happening. Miüsov wanted to leave.

Fyodor Pavlovitch stepped further in and began a long, loud speech. He said he cared about his son, Alexey (Alyosha), and wanted to take him home. He complained about the way the monks confessed their sins and said he would write to the church leaders about it.
Fyodor Pavlovitch was talking nonsense, repeating old rumors about the monastery that were not true. But he could not stop himself.
Miüsov shouted, “How disgraceful!” Father Iosif and Father Païssy were upset, and Miüsov and Kalganov left the room.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would not visit again and that the monastery had caused him pain in his life, even though this was not true. He pretended to be very sad and angry.
The Father Superior bowed his head and spoke calmly, saying they would not hate anyone who was rude to them.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would take Alyosha away from the monastery. He told Ivan to come too and tried to invite Maximov, calling him von Sohn again. Then he left, shouting and waving his arms.
Rakitin pointed out Fyodor Pavlovitch to Alyosha.
Fyodor Pavlovitch yelled to Alyosha to come home for good and to take all his things.

Alyosha watched quietly. Fyodor Pavlovitch got into the carriage. Ivan went to join him without saying goodbye to Alyosha. Suddenly, Maximov ran up, trying to get into the carriage too, laughing and shouting, “Take me, too!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy and joked about Maximov being von Sohn. He invited Maximov to jump in.
But Ivan pushed Maximov away and climbed into the carriage.
Ivan told the coachman to drive on.
The carriage left. Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Ivan why he was angry since it was Ivan’s idea to come to the monastery.
Ivan told him to be quiet.
Fyodor Pavlovitch wished for some brandy, but Ivan did not answer.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would take Alyosha away from the monastery, even if Ivan did not like it.
Ivan turned away and stared at the road. They did not speak again all the way home.

The Karamazovs’ house was not in the middle of town, but not too far away either. It was a big, old, gray house with a red roof. Inside, there were lots of small cupboards, closets, and stairs. Rats lived there too, but Fyodor Pavlovitch (the father) did not mind them. He said they made him feel less lonely at night. Every evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch sent his servants to sleep in the lodge, a building in the yard, and locked himself inside the house. He liked food cooked in the lodge, so the servants carried the dishes across the yard, even in winter. The house was made for a big family, but now only Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan lived there. In the lodge, there were three servants: old Grigory, his wife Marfa, and a young man named Smerdyakov. Grigory was stubborn and always did what he thought was right, even if his reasons were strange. He was honest and could not be bribed. Marfa (his wife) always listened to Grigory, but after the serfs were freed, she wanted to leave and open a shop in Moscow. Grigory refused, saying it was their duty to stay with Fyodor Pavlovitch, no matter what.
“Do you know what duty means?” Grigory asked Marfa.
“I know what it is, but I don’t know why our duty is to stay here,” Marfa replied.
“Well, just accept it. That’s how it will be. Don’t talk back,” Grigory said.

So they stayed, and Fyodor Pavlovitch paid them their wages. Grigory knew Fyodor Pavlovitch listened to him and often needed his help. Sometimes, Grigory even stopped people from hurting Fyodor Pavlovitch and then gave him a good talk after. Fyodor Pavlovitch was not only scared of being beaten; sometimes, he just needed someone loyal nearby. At night, if Fyodor Pavlovitch felt scared or lonely, he sometimes went to wake Grigory just to talk for a bit. If Grigory was calm, Fyodor Pavlovitch felt better. Sometimes, Alyosha, another son, stayed with Fyodor Pavlovitch. Alyosha was always kind to his father, even though Fyodor Pavlovitch was not a good man. This surprised Fyodor Pavlovitch, and he realized he learned something new from Alyosha.

Grigory had never liked Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna (Dmitri’s mother), but he had always protected Sofya Ivanovna, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second wife, who was poor and often called “crazy.” Grigory cared about Sofya and would not let anyone say bad things about her. Grigory was quiet and serious, but he did love Marfa, and she knew it.

Marfa was clever, maybe even more careful than Grigory about money, but she always listened to him and respected him. They did not talk much, only about what was needed each day. Grigory liked to think by himself, and Marfa was used to his silence. He only hit Marfa once, long ago, after she danced in a special way that reminded him of her time as a servant in a rich family. After that, Marfa stopped dancing, and Grigory never hit her again.

Grigory and Marfa never had children who lived. One baby was born, but it died soon after. Grigory liked children and took care of Dmitri (Fyodor Pavlovitch’s oldest son) when his mother left. Later, he looked after Ivan and Alyosha, too. When his own baby was born, Grigory was very sad to see it had six fingers. He was so upset he stayed away from everyone until the baby’s christening.
The priest asked, “Why shouldn’t the baby be christened?”
Grigory said quietly, “Because it’s a dragon.”
The priest was surprised. “A dragon? What do you mean?”
Grigory did not want to explain more. He just said, “It’s a mistake of nature.”

The others laughed and christened the baby anyway. Grigory prayed hard but still felt the same way. He hardly looked at the baby while it lived, but when it died two weeks later, he was very sad. He put the baby in its little coffin himself and cried at the grave. After that, Grigory became more religious, reading holy books alone and often wearing his big glasses. He liked the Book of Job and a book by Father Isaac the Syrian, even if he did not understand it all. He also listened to new religious ideas from people called Flagellants, but he did not join them. Reading about religion made him even more serious.

Grigory was always a little mystical. When his baby died, something strange happened the night after the burial. Marfa woke up because she heard a baby crying. She was scared and woke Grigory. He thought it sounded like a woman moaning. He got up, took a lantern and the key, and went into the garden. He heard the noise from the bath-house. Inside, he found Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (called Stinking Lizaveta), a poor girl who could not talk and wandered the streets. She had just given birth to a baby and was dying. Her story is told in another chapter.

Grigory noticed something strange about Lizaveta. Lizaveta was a very small woman, not even five feet tall. She had a big, red face and her eyes stared without really seeing. She almost never wore shoes, even in winter, just a simple, rough dress. Her hair was dark and curly and always messy with dirt and leaves because she slept outside, even on the ground. Her father was named Ilya. He was sick, poor, and drank too much. He would beat Lizaveta when she came home, so she stayed away. Many people in town felt sorry for her because she was slow and thought she was special to God. People tried to give her warm clothes and boots, but she always left them behind and went back to being barefoot. Once, a governor visited, saw Lizaveta, and said it was wrong for her to be dressed like that, but nothing changed. When her father died, people liked her even more since she was an orphan. Even the town boys never teased her. Lizaveta would walk into any house, and people would give her food or money. If she got money, she gave it to the church. If she got a roll, she handed it to someone else, even rich ladies, and never kept anything for herself except black bread and water. She never stole, even if she saw lots of money. She almost never went to church, and slept outside or sometimes at her old home. People were surprised she stayed healthy, but she was very strong for her size. Some said she acted this way out of pride, but that didn’t make sense, as she could hardly speak, only making little noises.

One warm, bright night in September, five or six men left a club very late. They walked along a path behind houses. There, they saw Lizaveta sleeping under some bushes. The men laughed and made mean jokes about her. One wondered if anyone could think of Lizaveta as a woman. The others said no, but Fyodor Pavlovitch disagreed loudly, trying to make the others laugh at his silly behavior. He was acting wild because his first wife had just died. The others laughed at him, but nobody thought he was serious. Eventually, they all left. Later, Fyodor Pavlovitch said he had gone with them, but no one knew for sure. Months later, people found out Lizaveta was going to have a baby. Everyone was upset and wanted to know who had hurt her. Soon, people started saying it was Fyodor Pavlovitch, though no one could prove it. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t care what the townspeople said.

Grigory tried hard to defend Fyodor Pavlovitch. He argued with people and said Lizaveta was not his fault. Grigory blamed Karp, a criminal who had been hiding in town, and people believed this for a while. Still, people were even kinder to Lizaveta. A kind widow named Kondratyev took Lizaveta into her house, planning to keep her safe until her baby was born. But on the last day, Lizaveta escaped and went into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. No one knew how she climbed the tall fence, but she did, even though she was about to have her baby.

Grigory ran to get Marfa and an old midwife. They saved the baby, but Lizaveta died in the morning. Grigory took the baby home, put it on Marfa’s lap, and said, “This child is an orphan and belongs to everyone, but most of all to us. Our own lost child sent him to us. Take care of him and be sad no more.”

Marfa raised the baby. He was named Pavel, and people also called him Fyodorovitch because they thought Fyodor Pavlovitch was his father. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t mind and found it funny, though he said the boy was not his. The townspeople liked that Fyodor Pavlovitch accepted the baby. Later, Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him the last name Smerdyakov, after his mother’s nickname.
Smerdyakov grew up to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second servant. He lived with Grigory and Marfa and worked as the cook. There is more to tell about Smerdyakov, but that will come later in the story.

Alyosha stood for a moment, not sure what to do after his father shouted at him from the carriage. But he didn’t just stand still—Alyosha always tried to act. He went to the kitchen to see what his father had done upstairs, then set off on his way, hoping for answers as he walked. His father’s loud orders to come home “with his mattress and pillow” didn’t scare him at all. Alyosha knew his father liked to shout just to make a scene, like a shopkeeper in town who once smashed his own dishes when drunk but was sorry later. Alyosha believed his father would let him return to the monastery soon, maybe even that night. He also felt sure that his father wouldn’t hurt him, and, in fact, Alyosha thought nobody in the world would ever want to hurt him. He trusted this completely and walked on without fear.

But Alyosha was also worried about something else. He was nervous about seeing Katerina Ivanovna (a proud and beautiful woman), who had sent him a note asking to meet. Alyosha didn’t know exactly why he was afraid, but he always felt uneasy around her, even though she was trying to help his brother Dmitri out of kindness. The closer he got to her house, the more nervous he felt.

Alyosha thought Ivan (his brother’s friend) wouldn’t be there, since Ivan was probably with their father, and Dmitri wouldn’t be there either. So Alyosha would have to meet Katerina Ivanovna alone. He wanted to see Dmitri first and talk to him about the letter, but Dmitri lived far away and was probably out. After thinking a bit more, Alyosha crossed himself and bravely went toward Katerina Ivanovna’s house.

He knew the house well. Taking the main road would be slow, and his father might still be waiting for him, so Alyosha decided to take a shortcut through backyards and over fences. People he met along the way greeted him, and soon he was almost there.

Alyosha passed a small old house with a garden next to his father’s place. He remembered that a sick old woman lived there with her daughter, who used to work for rich families but now was poor. The daughter still wore fancy dresses, even though they got food from Alyosha’s father’s kitchen. Alyosha remembered a story about her dress with a long train, then suddenly saw something surprising in the garden.
Dmitri (also called Mitya) was in the garden, waving to Alyosha and signaling him to come over quietly. Alyosha hurried to him.
“Good thing you saw me! Climb over!” Dmitri whispered excitedly. “I was just thinking of you!”
Alyosha was happy to see his brother but didn’t know how to get over the fence. Dmitri helped him, and Alyosha jumped over easily.
“Great! Come with me,” Dmitri whispered.
“Where?” Alyosha whispered, looking around the empty garden.
“No one’s here. Why are you whispering?” Alyosha asked.

Dmitri laughed loudly, “Why am I whispering? I’m hiding here, but it’s funny how I started whispering anyway! Let’s go over there—just be quiet for now. I want to hug you, Alyosha. I was just wishing you were here.”
Dmitri led Alyosha to a hidden old summer-house at the back of the garden. Inside, Alyosha saw a half-empty bottle of brandy and noticed that Dmitri seemed very excited.
“Yes, it’s brandy,” Dmitri said, smiling. “But I’m not drunk, just having a little. Sit down. I could hug you so tight! In the whole world, I love only you!”

“Well, only you, and one woman I’m in love with, but that’s different. Sometimes you can love someone and hate them too. Sit here, and I’ll talk. I need to tell you everything because only you will understand. Tomorrow, everything changes for me—life will end and begin again. Have you ever felt like you’re falling into a deep hole? That’s how I feel, but I’m not scared. Where were you going?”
“I was going to see Father, but I wanted to visit Katerina Ivanovna first,” Alyosha answered.
“Both of them? That’s just what I wanted! I was waiting for you because I want you to go to Father and Katerina Ivanovna for me. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted you, my angel, to do it.”
“Did she ask you to come? Did she send a letter?” Dmitri asked.
“Yes, here’s her note,” Alyosha said, handing it over.

Dmitri was happy Alyosha had come the back way. “Listen, I need to tell someone everything. You’re my angel on earth. If someone is about to make a big change and asks a friend for help, wouldn’t the friend help?”
“I’ll do it,” said Alyosha, “but tell me what you want.”
“Don’t hurry. Things are different now. Sometimes I wish people could understand how I feel. But you do. Let me think…”
Alyosha decided to wait and listen. Dmitri sat, thinking hard, his head in his hand.

“Alyosha, you’re the only one who won’t laugh at me. I want to confess something. There’s so much suffering in the world. I’m not just someone who drinks and does bad things. I think about people who are lost, because I’m one of them.”

“We Karamazovs are like insects who follow their desires. Even you, Alyosha, have those feelings. Beauty is a strange thing—it can be wonderful and terrible at the same time. People are full of puzzles and don’t always know what to do with their feelings. God and the devil fight inside people’s hearts. But enough about that. Now, let me tell you what’s really happening.”
