Dmitri began, “Back then, I lived wildly. Father said I spent lots of money on girls, but that’s not true. I liked to spend money on fun—music, parties, and even giving gifts to ladies. Sometimes I liked adventures and doing bad things, even though I knew they were wrong. Once, at a winter picnic, I held a girl’s hand and made her kiss me. She thought I would marry her, but I ignored her for months. She married someone else and left town, still upset with me. I never told anyone about these things. I didn’t brag. But enough about that. I didn’t bring you here to talk about silly stories. I want to tell you something more important. Don’t be surprised that I want to tell you.”
Alyosha said quietly, “You think I’m upset about what you did, but really, I’m just like you.”
“You? That’s hard to believe!” Dmitri replied.
Alyosha explained, “We’re the same. You’re higher up on the ladder, but I’m on the bottom step. Anyone can climb up, but it’s the same ladder.”
“Then maybe people shouldn’t step on at all,” said Dmitri.
Alyosha nodded. “If they can help it, they shouldn’t.”
“But can you?” Dmitri asked.
“I don’t think so,” Alyosha answered.

Dmitri smiled and said, “Alyosha, you’re kind. Grushenka once said she would like to eat you up! But let’s move on. Father lied about me, but something similar happened once. You’re the first I’ve told, except Ivan—he knows everything, but he never speaks of it.”

Dmitri continued, “I was a lieutenant in the army, but people still watched me closely. I spent a lot of money and was popular in town, even though my colonel didn’t like me because I didn’t show him enough respect. The colonel had two wives, both gone, and a daughter named Agafya Ivanovna from his first wife. Agafya was kind and cheerful, a good dressmaker, and I was friends with her, but just as friends. The colonel also had a younger daughter, Katerina Ivanovna, from his second wife. She had just finished school and was coming home. She was smart, proud, and everyone was excited for her return.”

“When Katerina Ivanovna came, the whole town celebrated. I didn’t try to meet her at first, but later I did. She didn’t like me, and I wanted to get back at her. She was different from other girls—she was strong and smart, and I wasn’t.”
“I kept acting foolishly, drinking, and causing trouble. The colonel punished me. Around that time, Father sent me a lot of money, but I didn’t really understand why. We can talk about that later.”

“Then a friend told me the colonel was in trouble—people thought he stole government money. Soon, everyone turned away from him. I found Agafya and told her, ‘There’s 4,500 roubles missing from your father’s accounts.’”
“‘What do you mean? Everything was fine before,’ she said.”
“‘It’s not fine now,’ I answered.”
“She was scared.”
“‘Don’t frighten me! Who told you?’ she asked.”

“‘Don’t worry,’ I said. ‘I won’t tell anyone. But if your father can’t pay, he’ll be punished unless you send your young lady to me. I just got money. I’ll give her 4,000 roubles and keep the secret.’”
“‘You scoundrel!’ she shouted.”
“Agafya was angry, but she told Katerina Ivanovna everything. That’s what I wanted. Agafya and her aunt loved Katerina and always helped her.”

“Soon, a new major came. The colonel got sick and couldn’t give back the money. I knew he used to lend the money to a merchant named Trifonov, who would bring it back after making profits. But this time, Trifonov didn’t return the money. The colonel tried to kill himself, but Agafya stopped him just in time. That evening, when I was about to go out, Katerina Ivanovna suddenly came to my room.”
“No one saw her come. The old ladies I lived with kept quiet. Katerina Ivanovna came in bravely, but I could see she was worried.”
“‘My sister said you would give me 4,500 roubles if I came myself. I have come. Give me the money!’ she said.”
“She was trembling and scared. ‘Alyosha, are you listening?’”
Alyosha said, “I know you will tell the truth.”

Dmitri nodded, “I will. When I saw her, I felt two things at once—how beautiful and brave she was, and how badly I could hurt her. For a moment, I wanted to be cruel, but I also thought about marrying her the next day, to make things right. But then I pictured her refusing even to see me. That made me angry. I wanted to insult her.”
“‘Four thousand? I was joking. Maybe two hundred, but you came for nothing,’ I almost said.”
“If I had said that, she would have run away, and I would have felt terrible forever. I have never hated anyone else like I did for those few seconds, but it was close to love, too.”

“Instead, I went to the table, took out a five-thousand rouble note, and handed it to her politely. She bowed low, then ran away. After she left, I almost hurt myself with my sword, but I didn’t. I just kissed it. That’s what happened with Katerina Ivanovna. Now you and Ivan know. No one else.”
Dmitri stood up, wiped his forehead, then sat down again, facing Alyosha.
Alyosha said, “Now I understand the first part.”
Dmitri answered, “You understand the first half. That part was like a play, but now the second half is like a sad story, and it’s happening here.”
Alyosha said, “I don’t understand the second half yet.”
Dmitri replied, “Do you think I do?”
Alyosha asked, “Dmitri, tell me, are you still engaged to Katerina Ivanovna?”

Dmitri explained, “We didn’t get engaged right away. For six weeks after our first problem, Katerina Ivanovna didn’t send me any letters or messages, except she sent back the money I gave her, but only the change, and not even a note. After that, I spent the rest of my money on parties and got in trouble with my boss.

The lieutenant-colonel paid back the money he owed and then became very sick. He died soon after. Katerina Ivanovna and her family left for Moscow. The day she left, she sent me a small note that said, ‘I will write to you. Wait. K.’”

“In Moscow, everything changed for Katerina Ivanovna. A rich old lady who was her relative lost her other heirs, so she made Katya her favorite and gave her lots of money—eighty thousand roubles—to use for marriage.”

“Then, I got a letter from Katya. She said she wanted to marry me, even if I didn’t love her. She wrote kind things, saying she wanted to help me. I wrote back, but I was embarrassed because I mentioned her money. I also wrote to Ivan about all this. Ivan fell in love with her, too, and she respects him a lot. Sometimes I think she might really love him, not me, especially after everything that happened.”

“Yes, we are officially engaged. When I went to Moscow, there was a big ceremony. The general’s wife blessed us and liked me, but not Ivan. Katya and I talked a lot, and I promised her I would change my ways.”
“Today, I brought you here, Alyosha, so you could go to Katerina Ivanovna for me and tell her that I will never visit her again. Tell her, ‘He sends you his compliments.’”
Alyosha said, “But is that possible?”
Dmitri answered, “That’s why I’m sending you. I can’t tell her myself.”
Alyosha asked, “Where are you going?”

Dmitri said, “I’m going to Grushenka. When I started seeing Grushenka, I stopped being a good, honest man. I first went to see her because I was angry and wanted to scare her, but then I stayed. I spent three thousand roubles with her at Mokroe, buying food and drinks for everyone. Grushenka is tricky, and she laughed at the idea of marrying me. She made jokes, but nothing serious happened.”

Dmitri suddenly jumped up, looking very upset. He grabbed Alyosha and said, “I want you to know, Alyosha, that I’m not a thief, but I did a terrible thing. Katerina Ivanovna gave me three thousand roubles to send to someone in Moscow. But I spent that money with Grushenka. I lied about sending it and never showed her the receipt. When you go to Katya today, she’ll ask about the money. What will you say?”
Alyosha said, “Mitya, you are very unhappy, but things are not as bad as you think.”
Dmitri said, “I’m not going to hurt myself, Alyosha. I just don’t care anymore. I’m going to Grushenka.”
“If Grushenka wants to marry me, I will. If not, I’ll just stay near her, even if I have to be a servant for her guests.”
Alyosha said, “Katerina Ivanovna will understand. She will see your pain and forgive you.”
Dmitri said, “She won’t forgive everything. The best thing would be to pay back the three thousand roubles.”
Alyosha said, “I have two thousand. Ivan can give you another thousand. Take it and pay her back.”

Dmitri said, “You can’t do that, Alyosha. You’re too young and can’t get the money right now. You must go to Katya today and tell her my message, with or without the money. Tomorrow will be too late. I’ll also send you to our father.”
“Go to father first. Ask him for three thousand roubles.”
Alyosha said, “But, Mitya, he won’t give it to you.”

Dmitri replied, “I know he won’t. But I want to give him a chance to do the right thing. He made a lot of money from my mother’s savings. If he gives me just three thousand, I’ll leave him alone forever.”

“But father won’t give me the money, especially now that he thinks Grushenka might really marry me. He’s crazy about her too. I even know he has three thousand roubles ready in an envelope, waiting for Grushenka. Only his servant, Smerdyakov, knows about it. Father is sending Ivan away for a few days so that Grushenka can come while he’s gone.”
“I’m staying in a room nearby, watching in secret to see if Grushenka goes to father’s house.”
“Grushenka won’t come today, I think. Smerdyakov will tell me if she does. Father is drinking now. Go to him and ask for the three thousand.”
Alyosha said, “I will go. Will you wait here for me?”
Dmitri answered, “Yes. I’ll wait as long as it takes. But remember, you must go to Katerina Ivanovna today and tell her, ‘He sends his compliments.’”
Alyosha said, “And what if Grushenka comes today or soon?”
Dmitri replied, “If she comes, I’ll try to stop her.”
“If something bad happens, it could be murder. I couldn’t stand it.”
“Who will be murdered?” Alyosha asked.
“The old man, our father. I wouldn’t hurt Grushenka.”
“Brother, what are you saying?” Alyosha cried.
Dmitri said, “I don’t know. Maybe I won’t do anything, but maybe I will. Sometimes I hate our father so much I can’t stand it.”
Alyosha said, “I’ll go, Mitya. I believe God will help, and nothing terrible will happen.”
Dmitri replied, “I’ll wait for a miracle. If it doesn’t happen...”
Alyosha went thoughtfully to his father’s house.

Alyosha came home and found his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, still sitting at the table in the biggest room, which was old and fancy. There were big mirrors and old portraits on the walls. In one corner, there were special pictures called ikons, with a lamp that was lit at night. Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to stay up very late, sometimes until three or four in the morning. He would walk around or sit and think. He often sent the servants away, but Smerdyakov, the servant, usually stayed and slept on a bench in the hall.

When Alyosha walked in, dinner was finished, but there was still coffee and sweet fruit. Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to eat sweets and drink brandy after dinner. Ivan was there too, drinking coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood nearby. Everyone seemed happy, and Fyodor Pavlovitch was laughing loudly. Alyosha could tell his father was in a good mood and not too drunk.

“Here he is!” shouted Fyodor Pavlovitch when he saw Alyosha. “Come sit down! Have some coffee. I won't give you brandy because you’re fasting, but would you like some special liqueur? Smerdyakov, get it from the cupboard!”
Alyosha said no to the liqueur.
“That's fine, we’ll drink it,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch happily. “But have you had dinner?”
Alyosha said yes, even though he only had some bread and a drink called kvas at the monastery. He asked for hot coffee.

“Good! Alyosha wants coffee. Smerdyakov’s coffee is the best. He also makes great fish soup. You must try it one day. But didn’t I ask you to bring your mattress and pillow to stay here? Did you bring them?”
Alyosha smiled and said he didn’t bring them.

“You were scared this morning, weren’t you?” laughed Fyodor Pavlovitch. “I can’t be angry with you. Ivan, I love how Alyosha looks me in the eye and laughs. Alyosha, let me give you a father’s blessing.”
Alyosha stood up, but Fyodor Pavlovitch changed his mind.
“No, I’ll just make the sign of the cross on you. Sit down. Now, we have something funny for you—just your kind of thing! Balaam’s ass has started talking to us!” he said, laughing.
Fyodor Pavlovitch called Smerdyakov, the quiet servant, “Balaam’s ass.” Smerdyakov was about twenty-four, very quiet, and didn’t like to talk to people. He thought he was better than everyone.

Smerdyakov had been raised by Grigory and Marfa, but he wasn’t thankful or friendly. As a boy, he did strange things, like hanging cats and pretending to do church funerals for them in secret. Grigory caught him once and gave him a beating. Smerdyakov then hid for a week and never forgave Grigory for calling him names. Grigory taught him to read and write, and later, the Bible. But Smerdyakov asked tricky questions, like where did the light come from before the sun was made? Grigory got angry and slapped him. After that, Smerdyakov had his first epileptic fit, a sickness with sudden attacks. Fyodor Pavlovitch felt sorry for him, called a doctor, and stopped Grigory from hurting him. He started letting Smerdyakov come upstairs, and even gave him books to read.
Smerdyakov read a little but didn’t like the books. He said one wasn’t true and another was boring. So the bookcase was locked again.
After a while, Marfa and Grigory noticed Smerdyakov was picky with his food. He would look at every bite, hold it up to the light, and take a long time before eating.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about this, he decided Smerdyakov should become his cook. He sent him to Moscow to learn. Smerdyakov came back looking older, very neat, and always wearing clean clothes. He was still quiet and didn’t want to talk to anyone. He was a great cook, and Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him well. Smerdyakov spent most of his money on fancy clothes and nice-smelling things. His sickness got worse, so when he was ill, Marfa had to cook, which Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't like.
One day, Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Smerdyakov, “Are your fits worse because you want a wife? Should I find one for you?” Smerdyakov got angry and said nothing.

Fyodor Pavlovitch trusted Smerdyakov. Once, when Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk, he lost some money outside. The next day, he saw the money on the table. Smerdyakov had found it and brought it in. Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him a reward and liked him, even though Smerdyakov was always silent.

Sometimes Smerdyakov would just stop and stare, lost in thought. He didn’t talk about what he was thinking. Some people are like this—they just think quietly to themselves for a long time. Smerdyakov was one of them, and kept his thoughts and feelings hidden deep inside.

Grigory went shopping in the morning and heard a story from the shopkeeper Lukyanov. The story was about a Russian soldier who was captured far away in Asia. The captors told the soldier to stop being a Christian and become a Muslim, or he would die painfully. The soldier refused, so they tortured him and took off his skin, but he still praised Christ until he died. Grigory told this story at the dinner table. Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to laugh and talk after dinner, especially with Grigory. Today he was in a good mood. He joked that the soldier should be made a saint, and his skin put in a church, so people would come and give money.
Grigory did not like Fyodor Pavlovitch making fun of the story. Smerdyakov, who was waiting by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often helped at the table since Ivan came to town.
Fyodor Pavlovitch saw Smerdyakov smile and asked, “What are you grinning at?”
Smerdyakov said loudly, “I think if the soldier had pretended to stop being a Christian to save his life, it wouldn’t have been a sin. He could have done good things later to make up for it.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “No, that’s wrong. If you do that, you go to hell.”
Just then, Alyosha came into the room. Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy to see him.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “We’re talking about your subject, Alyosha!” and made Alyosha sit down.
Smerdyakov said, “It’s not a sin, and there shouldn’t be any punishment if it’s fair.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch laughed and asked, “What do you mean by ‘fair’?” He nudged Alyosha.
Grigory was angry and called Smerdyakov a rascal.
Smerdyakov answered calmly, “Wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch. If I was captured and told to stop being a Christian, I could decide for myself. There would be no sin.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “You’ve said that before. Prove it.”
Grigory muttered, “Soup-maker.”
Smerdyakov said, “If I say I’m not a Christian and curse God, then I am cut off from the church right away. Even thinking about it counts. Isn’t that true, Grigory Vassilyevitch?”
Smerdyakov looked pleased as he asked Grigory, but he was really answering Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Fyodor Pavlovitch whispered to Ivan, “He’s saying all this for you. He wants you to praise him. Praise him!”
Ivan listened seriously.
Fyodor Pavlovitch told Smerdyakov to wait and asked Ivan to listen again.
Ivan bent down and listened.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “I love you like I love Alyosha. Want some brandy?”
Ivan thought, “You’re a bit drunk,” but looked at his father.
Ivan watched Smerdyakov with interest.
Grigory suddenly shouted, “You’re already cursed! How dare you argue?”
Fyodor Pavlovitch told Grigory not to scold Smerdyakov.
Smerdyakov said, “Wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch. If I’m cut off from the church, I’m like someone who was never baptized. Isn’t that true?”
Fyodor Pavlovitch told him to hurry up and finish.

Smerdyakov went on, “If I’m not a Christian anymore, then I didn’t lie to my enemies. God already took away my Christianity because of my thoughts. If I’m not a Christian, it’s not my fault. No one blames a person who was never Christian. God wouldn’t punish someone just for being born differently. God can’t tell a lie.”
Grigory was shocked and stared at Smerdyakov, not understanding everything. Fyodor Pavlovitch laughed loudly.

Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “Alyosha, what do you think? Smerdyakov, you talk like a clever person, but it’s nonsense. Even if you fool your enemies, you still gave up your faith in your heart and are cursed for it. In hell, they won’t be nice to you. What do you say?”
Smerdyakov answered, “Yes, I gave up my faith in my heart, but that’s not a special sin. Many people do that.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, “How is that normal?”
Grigory hissed, “You lie!”

Smerdyakov calmly said, “Grigory Vassilyevitch, the Bible says if you have faith, you can tell a mountain to move and it will. But you can’t do that, and neither can anyone else. Maybe one or two people in the world can, but they are hiding somewhere. Does that mean everyone else will be punished? I think God will forgive people if they are sorry.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy and said, “So you think there are two people who can move mountains? Ivan, write that down!”
Ivan smiled and agreed, “That’s how people believe.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “See? Ivan agrees. That’s Russian faith, isn’t it, Alyosha?”
Alyosha said seriously, “No, Smerdyakov does not have real Russian faith.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch said, “I’m not talking about Smerdyakov’s faith, just the idea about the two people in the desert. Isn’t that Russian?”
Alyosha smiled and said, “Yes, that’s very Russian.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch told Smerdyakov, “You talk nonsense. We all have little faith because we’re too busy. But you denied your faith when you could have shown it. So it is a sin.”

Smerdyakov replied, “It might be a sin, but not a big one. If I truly believed, I’d face torture and not give up my faith. But if I tried to move a mountain and it didn’t work, I might start to doubt. At a scary moment, anyone could be afraid. If I doubt, I hope God will forgive me anyway.”
The argument was over. Suddenly, Fyodor Pavlovitch (the father) stopped smiling and started to look angry. He drank more brandy than he should have.

“Go away, all of you!” he yelled at the servants. “Smerdyakov, leave now. I’ll send you your gold coin later. Don’t cry, Grigory. Go see Marfa, she’ll help you. Why can’t we have peace after dinner?” He sounded annoyed as the servants left.
Fyodor Pavlovitch turned to Ivan (his middle son). “Smerdyakov always hangs around you now. Why does he like you so much?”
Ivan answered, “I haven’t done anything. Smerdyakov just thinks highly of me. But he’s really just a servant and a mean man.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch talked some more about Smerdyakov and about Russian peasants in general. He said he didn’t really like them and thought they needed to be punished sometimes. He bragged about liking clever people and made fun of Russia.

Then Fyodor Pavlovitch told a strange story about people punishing girls and how he liked to joke about it. He also said he was sorry for being rude to Alyosha’s (his youngest son’s) elder that morning. He wondered if God existed, and asked Ivan and Alyosha what they believed.
Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly asked, “Ivan, is there a God or not? Tell me the truth.”
Ivan said, “No, there is no God.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Alyosha, “Is there a God?”
Alyosha answered, “There is.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch then asked Ivan, “Is there life after death?”
Ivan said, “No, there isn’t.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Alyosha, “Is there immortality?”
Alyosha said, “Yes. In God is immortality.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch sighed and said maybe Ivan was right, and wondered why people believed for so long. He asked Ivan again if there was a God. Ivan said, “No, there is not.”
“Who is laughing at mankind, Ivan?” Fyodor Pavlovitch asked.
“Maybe the devil,” Ivan replied, smiling.
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, “Is there a devil?”
Ivan said, “No, there’s no devil either.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch complained about people inventing God, but Ivan said without God there would be no civilization or brandy.
Fyodor Pavlovitch worried he had hurt Alyosha’s feelings. Alyosha said, “I’m not angry. Your heart is better than your head.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch asked Ivan if he loved Alyosha. Ivan said yes.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, now very drunk, said he was rude to the elder that morning because he was excited. He also said the elder was smart and even told stories about him. Then he got confused and admitted he was mixing up stories.
Ivan said, “I’m going away. You’ve had too much brandy.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch begged Ivan to go to Tchermashnya, but accused him of wanting to stay and watch him instead.
Fyodor Pavlovitch became angry and tried to start an argument. He said Ivan looked at him with mistrust, but Alyosha’s eyes were kind. He told Alyosha not to love Ivan.
Alyosha said, “Don’t be mean to my brother. Stop picking on him.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch complained his head hurt and told Ivan to take away the brandy. Then he suddenly started to smile slyly.

Fyodor Pavlovitch tried to cheer up and promised to visit Ivan in Tchermashnya, saying he would show him a poor girl there. He talked about how he liked all women and didn’t think any woman was ugly. He told a long story about Alyosha’s mother, how she used to laugh in a special way, and about a time she got upset with him and he took her to the monastery. He said he never insulted her, except maybe once, when he tried to stop her praying. He remembered how upset she got.

As Fyodor Pavlovitch spoke about his mother, Alyosha started to look upset. Suddenly, Alyosha jumped up, hid his face, and began to cry just like his mother had done. Fyodor Pavlovitch was shocked at how much Alyosha looked like his mother in that moment.
Fyodor Pavlovitch shouted, “Ivan, get water! He’s just like his mother!” He told Ivan that Alyosha was upset about his mother.
Ivan angrily reminded Fyodor Pavlovitch that Alyosha’s mother was his mother too. For a second, Fyodor Pavlovitch seemed to forget that Ivan and Alyosha had the same mother.
Fyodor Pavlovitch was confused, then started to laugh drunkenly.
Suddenly, there was a loud noise and shouting from the hall. The door flew open and Dmitri (the oldest son) rushed in. Fyodor Pavlovitch was terrified.
“He’ll kill me! Don’t let him get me!” Fyodor Pavlovitch screamed, grabbing onto Ivan.

Grigory and Smerdyakov hurried into the room after Dmitri. They had tried to stop him from coming in, just like Fyodor Pavlovitch (their master) had told them before. When Dmitri paused to look around, Grigory quickly ran and closed the doors to the inner rooms. He stood in front of them, arms wide, ready to block Dmitri. Dmitri yelled and rushed at Grigory.

Dmitri tried to move Grigory, but Grigory pushed him back. Dmitri, very angry, hit Grigory hard. Grigory fell to the floor, and Dmitri jumped over him and broke open the door. Smerdyakov, pale and scared, stayed by Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“She's here!” Dmitri shouted. “I saw her come to the house but I couldn't catch her. Where is she?”

Fyodor Pavlovitch stopped being scared when he heard Dmitri shout about Grushenka. He yelled, “Hold him! Hold him!” and ran after Dmitri. Grigory got up, still dizzy. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. Something crashed in the next room; Dmitri had knocked over a big glass vase.

Ivan and Alyosha grabbed their father and pulled him back. Ivan said, “Why are you chasing him? He might hurt you!” Fyodor Pavlovitch insisted that Grushenka must be in the house. He was shaking and upset.
Ivan said, “You saw she hasn't come.” Fyodor Pavlovitch argued she could have come in another way, but Ivan reminded him that the other entrance was locked and he had the key.
Dmitri came back. He had found the other door locked, and the windows were all closed, so Grushenka could not have come in.

Fyodor Pavlovitch screamed, “Hold him! He’s been stealing money!” He rushed at Dmitri, but Dmitri grabbed his father by the hair and threw him down, then kicked him in the face. Ivan and Alyosha pulled Dmitri away.

Ivan shouted, “You’ve killed him!” Dmitri, breathing hard, said, “If I haven’t, I’ll come again and do it!” Alyosha told Dmitri to go away. Dmitri asked Alyosha if Grushenka had been there, but Alyosha said no one had seen her. Dmitri insisted he saw her and left, telling Alyosha to give a message to Katerina Ivanovna.

Ivan and Grigory helped Fyodor Pavlovitch into a chair. His face was bloody, but he listened carefully to Dmitri. Fyodor Pavlovitch still thought Grushenka was in the house. Dmitri looked at him angrily and said, “I don’t regret hurting you! I curse you and disown you!” Then he ran out.

Fyodor Pavlovitch whispered for Smerdyakov, still thinking Grushenka was there. Ivan shouted that she was not there and told Smerdyakov to get water. Smerdyakov brought water, and they put Fyodor Pavlovitch to bed. He soon fell asleep. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing-room. Smerdyakov cleaned up the broken vase, while Grigory stood looking sad.
Alyosha told Grigory he should rest because of his hurt head, but Grigory said, “He’s insulted me.” Ivan said, “He insulted his father too.” Grigory repeated, “He’s insulted me.”

Ivan whispered to Alyosha that if he hadn’t stopped Dmitri, Dmitri might have killed Fyodor Pavlovitch. Alyosha said, “God forbid!” Ivan said that sometimes bad people hurt each other and deserve it, but Alyosha shuddered and promised not to let anyone be killed. Ivan left to walk in the yard.

Alyosha sat by his father’s bed for about an hour. Fyodor Pavlovitch woke up and asked where Ivan was. Alyosha said Ivan was outside. Fyodor Pavlovitch looked at himself in the mirror and saw his swollen nose and bruised forehead.

Fyodor Pavlovitch told Alyosha he was afraid of Ivan, but not of Alyosha. He asked if Grushenka had been there, and Alyosha said no. Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy to hear that Grushenka would not marry Dmitri. He was so glad that he squeezed Alyosha’s hand and had tears in his eyes.

Fyodor Pavlovitch told Alyosha to take an image of the Mother of God home and said Alyosha could return to the monastery. Then he asked Alyosha if he would see Grushenka and find out who she wanted to choose. Alyosha said he would ask if he saw her, but Fyodor Pavlovitch said Grushenka was tricky and not to trust her.

Fyodor Pavlovitch asked where Dmitri had sent Alyosha. Alyosha said, “To Katerina Ivanovna.” Fyodor Pavlovitch wondered if it was for money, but Alyosha said no. Fyodor Pavlovitch told Alyosha to visit him in the morning and not to tell Ivan.
Alyosha promised, and Fyodor Pavlovitch said goodbye, thanking Alyosha for helping him. Alyosha asked how his father felt, and Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would be well tomorrow.

Outside, Alyosha found Ivan sitting and writing. Alyosha told Ivan their father was awake and letting him go back to the monastery. Ivan said he would like to see Alyosha tomorrow. Alyosha said he might be at the Hohlakovs’ or Katerina Ivanovna’s.
Ivan guessed that Dmitri had asked Alyosha to give Katerina Ivanovna a message, and Alyosha was embarrassed. Ivan asked if Dmitri wanted Alyosha to say goodbye to her.
Alyosha asked Ivan how things would end between their father and Dmitri. Ivan said no one could know, but they must not let Dmitri into the house.

Alyosha asked if anyone had the right to decide who should live. Ivan said people often wish things in their hearts, but that doesn't mean they act on them. Ivan asked if Alyosha thought he was like Dmitri and could hurt their father. Alyosha said he didn't think that, and Ivan thanked him. They shook hands warmly, closer than ever before.

Alyosha left his father’s house feeling tired and sadder than before. His mind felt confused. He was worried about how things would end between his father and his brother Dmitri, and the woman named Grushenka. He had seen them together and knew things were only getting worse. Alyosha also realized even more people were involved than he first thought. Ivan, his other brother, had started to talk to him more, but now Alyosha felt a little scared by this. Alyosha was headed to Katerina Ivanovna’s house, not feeling shy like before, but hoping she could help. He had to tell her what happened and about the three thousand roubles Dmitri lost. Dmitri asked Alyosha to explain the whole scene with their father, too.

It was getting dark when Alyosha arrived at Katerina Ivanovna’s large house. She lived with two aunts. One aunt was Agafya Ivanovna’s aunt, who had cared for Katerina Ivanovna before. The other aunt was from Moscow. Both aunts always did what Katerina Ivanovna wanted. Katerina Ivanovna only listened to her benefactress, an old general’s widow, who was still in Moscow.
When Alyosha rang the bell, the maid seemed to know he was coming. He heard people moving quickly and skirts rustling—some women had just left the room.

Alyosha was surprised that his visit made such a fuss, but he was led into a big, fancy room. There were many sofas, flowers, pictures, and even an aquarium. Two cups of chocolate and some cakes were left on the table. He could tell he had interrupted visitors. Suddenly, Katerina Ivanovna came in, smiling and happy to see him. A servant brought in candles.
“Thank God! You’ve come at last! Sit down,” Katerina Ivanovna said.

Alyosha remembered meeting Katerina Ivanovna before. She was proud and strong, and her eyes were bright and serious. He had told Dmitri, “You’ll be happy with her, but maybe not always peaceful.” Now, seeing her again, Alyosha realized he might have been wrong. She looked friendly and sincere, but also very excited.
Katerina Ivanovna said, “I was so eager to see you, because I can learn the truth from you and no one else.”
Alyosha answered awkwardly, “I came because Dmitri sent me.”
Katerina Ivanovna nodded. She said she wanted Alyosha to tell her honestly what he thought of Dmitri after today. She wanted to know the exact message Dmitri sent.
Alyosha said, “He told me to give you his compliments and to say he would never come again.”
“Did he really say ‘compliments’?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“He made me repeat that word,” Alyosha said.
Katerina Ivanovna blushed.
She asked Alyosha if Dmitri had insisted on using that word because he was upset and acting brave. Alyosha agreed.

Katerina Ivanovna asked about the money, the three thousand roubles. Alyosha told her Dmitri felt ashamed and hopeless about it. Katerina Ivanovna explained she knew about the money and had tried to help Dmitri secretly. She just wanted him to trust her and not feel ashamed in front of her.
Katerina Ivanovna began to cry.
Alyosha said he had to tell her what happened between Dmitri and their father.
Alyosha explained how Dmitri had tried to get the money, fought with their father, and then sent his “compliments” and goodbye before going to Grushenka.
Katerina Ivanovna laughed a little and said Dmitri would never marry Grushenka, because it was just passion, not real love.
Alyosha said maybe Dmitri would marry Grushenka.
Katerina Ivanovna said Grushenka was an angel and told Alyosha to meet her. She called for Grushenka to come in.
Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna) answered with a sweet voice.

Grushenka came in, smiling. Alyosha stared at her, expecting to see a terrible woman, but she looked kind and pretty, with a soft voice and gentle movements. She seemed happy and friendly, with a childlike look in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna sat her down and kissed her.
Katerina Ivanovna said it was their first meeting, but she knew Grushenka would bring peace and joy.
Grushenka said, “You did not disdain me, sweet young lady,” still smiling.
Katerina Ivanovna joked and kissed Grushenka’s hand, calling her an angel.
Grushenka said maybe she didn’t deserve such kindness.

Katerina Ivanovna said Grushenka was noble and generous, but just unlucky in love. She explained Grushenka had once loved another man who left her, and now he might be coming back. The old merchant who cared for Grushenka was like her father and had saved her from sadness.
Grushenka said Katerina Ivanovna was in a hurry about everything.
Grushenka admitted she could be selfish and had played with Dmitri’s feelings for fun.
Katerina Ivanovna reminded Grushenka she promised to tell Dmitri she loved someone else and wouldn’t be with him.
Grushenka said she didn’t really promise that.
Grushenka explained she could change her mind anytime and might go back to Dmitri.
Katerina Ivanovna was surprised and hurt.
Grushenka said maybe she’d feel sorry for Dmitri and help him.
Grushenka asked if Katerina Ivanovna could still like her, knowing she was silly and changeable. She took Katerina Ivanovna’s hand and said she should kiss it just as Katerina had kissed hers.
Grushenka said maybe she would do whatever Katerina wanted, but only if she wanted to, with no promises.
She held Katerina’s hand near her lips, but seemed to be thinking.
Suddenly, Grushenka said, “After all, I think I won’t kiss your hand,” and laughed.
Katerina Ivanovna asked, “Why not?”
Grushenka said, “So you’ll remember you kissed my hand, but I didn’t kiss yours.”
Grushenka looked at her with sharp eyes.
Katerina Ivanovna jumped up, angry, and called Grushenka “insolent.”
Grushenka said she would tell Dmitri how Katerina kissed her hand, but she didn’t kiss Katerina’s.
Katerina Ivanovna shouted at Grushenka to go away.
Grushenka said it wasn’t nice to say such things.
Katerina Ivanovna screamed, calling Grushenka a bad name.
Grushenka replied that Katerina had once visited men for money, showing she knew Katerina’s secret.
Katerina Ivanovna screamed again and tried to attack Grushenka, but Alyosha held her back.
Alyosha told Katerina Ivanovna not to fight or speak anymore.
The two aunts and a maid ran in to help Katerina Ivanovna.
Grushenka said she would leave and asked Alyosha to walk her home.
Alyosha begged her to go quickly.
Grushenka laughed and told Alyosha she had done this on purpose and would tell him a story on the way home.
Alyosha was upset and Grushenka left, laughing.
Katerina Ivanovna started crying and shaking. Everyone tried to calm her down.
One aunt said she had tried to warn Katerina Ivanovna about inviting Grushenka.
Katerina Ivanovna cried that Grushenka was a tigress and wished Alyosha hadn’t stopped her from attacking Grushenka.
She said Grushenka deserved to be punished in public.
Alyosha quietly left the room.
Katerina Ivanovna shouted that Dmitri was a scoundrel for telling Grushenka about her past.
Alyosha wanted to say something but didn’t know what.
Katerina Ivanovna told Alyosha to go and begged him to come back tomorrow and not judge her.
Alyosha walked outside, feeling like he might cry.
The maid ran after him and gave him a letter from Madame Hohlakov that had been left for him.
Alyosha took the letter without thinking and put it in his pocket.

Alyosha walked quickly from the town to the monastery. It was almost night, and the road was empty. When he reached the cross-roads, he saw someone waiting under a willow tree. Suddenly, the person ran at him, shouting, “Your money or your life!”
“So it's you, Mitya!” Alyosha cried, surprised and a little scared.
Dmitri (Mitya) laughed loudly. “Ha! You didn’t expect me! I was waiting here because I knew you’d pass by. Come on, tell me the truth. Crush me if you want. But what’s wrong?”
“Nothing, brother—just that you frightened me. Oh, Dmitri! I keep thinking about Father’s blood. You almost killed him. You cursed him. And now you’re making jokes.”

“Well, look at this dark, windy night,” said Dmitri. “I was waiting here and suddenly thought, why go on living in misery? I almost wanted to end it all. But then I heard you coming, my dear brother, the one I love most. I wanted to hug you, but instead decided to play a silly joke. Forgive me for scaring you. Now tell me, what happened? What did she say? Was she angry?”
“No, not angry, Mitya. I found them both there.”
“Both? Who?”
“Grushenka at Katerina Ivanovna’s.”
Dmitri was shocked. “Impossible! Grushenka with her?”

Alyosha told Dmitri everything that happened at Katerina Ivanovna’s house. Dmitri listened closely, his face growing darker and angrier as he heard the story. But then, suddenly, Dmitri’s face changed and he burst out laughing uncontrollably. “So she wouldn’t kiss her hand! She ran away! The other one called her a tigress! That’s just like her. She should be punished, but I must get better first. She’s amazing in her own way. So she ran home? I’ll go to her! Alyosha, don’t blame me.”
“But Katerina Ivanovna!” Alyosha said sadly.

“I see her too, and I understand her now. She’s so proud and brave. You say her aunt tried to stop her? But Katya wouldn’t listen. She thought she could charm Grushenka, but she was really chasing her own dream. Alyosha, how did you get away from those women? Did you run? Ha ha!”
“Brother, you hurt Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about what happened that day. She brought it up and insulted her. Wasn’t that terrible?”
Dmitri frowned and hit his forehead. He realized what he had done and remembered Katerina Ivanovna’s words: “Your brother is a scoundrel!”
“Yes, I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day.’ I was drunk at Mokroe, but I was crying and praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. But now, it’s all ruined. That’s how women are.”

Dmitri looked down. “Yes, I am a scoundrel. Tell her I accept that name. Good-bye. You go your way, I go mine. I don’t want to see you again unless I have to. Good-bye, Alexey.” Dmitri squeezed Alyosha’s hand and walked away quickly toward the town.
Alyosha watched him go, surprised at how suddenly Dmitri left.

But then Dmitri turned back. “Alexey, one more thing just for you!” He tapped his chest. “Something terrible is going to happen to me. I’ve never done anything as bad as what’s on my heart now. I could stop it, but I won’t. I told you everything, but not this. I’ll carry out my plan, and you’ll see later. Don’t pray for me—I don’t deserve it. Good-bye!” Dmitri hurried away for good.
Alyosha walked toward the monastery, confused and worried about what Dmitri meant.
He went around the monastery and through the pine woods to the hermitage. He was let inside, even though it was late. His heart shook as he went into Father Zossima’s room.

In the cell, he found Porfiry (a young monk) and Father Païssy, who came often to check on Father Zossima. Alyosha found out that Father Zossima was getting worse and couldn’t hold his usual evening talk with the other monks. Usually, the monks would come in, confess their sins and troubles out loud, and Father Zossima would listen, bless them, and give advice. Some monks didn’t like this and thought it was wrong, but others believed it was good for their souls. Alyosha knew that sometimes monks pretended to confess just to have something to say.

Father Païssy whispered, “He is weaker and sleepy. He woke up for five minutes, sent his blessing to the brothers, and asked for their prayers. He remembered you, Alexey, and said, ‘His place is there, not here, for a while.’ He cares about you. But remember, if you go back to the world, it must be to do your elder’s work, not for fun.”

Father Païssy left. Alyosha felt sure Father Zossima was dying. He decided to stay at the monastery and not leave, even though he had promised to visit his father and friends. Alyosha went into Father Zossima’s bedroom, knelt, and bowed to the ground, seeing the elder sleeping peacefully.

Alyosha went back to the other room. He took off his boots and lay down on the hard sofa he used as a bed. He took off his cassock and prayed for a long time. While praying, he remembered the little pink note Lise (the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov) had given him. He finished his prayer, then opened the letter.

Lise wrote, “Alexey Fyodorovitch, I am writing to you without anyone knowing, not even Mama. I love you. I have loved you since I was a child. My heart chooses you, and I want us to be together someday. But you must leave the monastery first. When you come tomorrow, I don’t know how I’ll act. Please, don’t look at me right away, or I might laugh.”
“I hope you don’t think badly of me for telling you this secret. I might cry today. Good-bye until we meet.—Lise. P.S. You must come!”

Alyosha read the note in surprise, then smiled softly. He felt peaceful and happy. He put the letter away, crossed himself, and lay down. He prayed that God would help everyone and bring them joy. Then Alyosha fell asleep, feeling calm and safe.

Alyosha woke up very early, before the sun came up. Father Zossima felt weak but wanted to get out of bed and sit in his chair. His mind was clear, and his face looked tired but happy and kind. He told Alyosha, “Maybe I won’t live through today.” He wanted to confess and take the sacrament right away, as he always did with Father Païssy. After communion, the monks did the last prayers for him. Many monks came into the small room, so some had to leave to make space. Alyosha stayed close by as Father Zossima sat in his chair and tried to talk to everyone, even though his voice was weak.

Father Zossima joked, “I’ve talked so much while teaching you all these years, that now it’s harder for me to be quiet than to speak, even though I’m weak, dear Fathers and brothers.” He looked at everyone with love.
Alyosha remembered some of what Father Zossima said. He spoke about many things, wanting to share everything in his heart before he died. He wanted everyone to feel his joy and love.

Father Zossima said, “Love one another, Fathers. Love all God’s people. We are not better than people outside these walls. In fact, coming here means we know we are worse and need help. Every monk should remember he is responsible for all people and all their sins. This is true for everyone, not just monks. When we know this, our hearts can love everyone in the world. Pray for others, even those who hate you or do wrong. Don’t be proud. Don’t hate anyone, not even people who don’t believe in God. Pray for them all. Take care of your heart, confess your own sins, and always trust God. Don’t love money or be greedy. Have faith.”
Father Zossima’s words were sometimes hard to follow because he was very tired and excited, but everyone listened closely and remembered what he said.

When Alyosha left the room for a moment, he saw that all the monks waiting outside were excited and nervous. Some looked worried, others were very serious. Many expected something special to happen after Father Zossima died, even though it seemed a little silly to some. Father Païssy looked the most serious.

A monk came to tell Alyosha that Rakitin was there with a letter from Madame Hohlakov. The letter said that a woman named Prohorovna had come the day before to ask Father Zossima if she could pray for her son Vassenka, who had gone far away and not sent news for over a year. Father Zossima told her not to pray for him as if he was dead, because that was wrong, but then he forgave her and said her son was alive and would soon come or send a letter. Madame Hohlakov wrote that this came true: as soon as Prohorovna got home, there was a letter from her son saying he was coming back to her soon.

Madame Hohlakov wanted Alyosha to tell everyone about this miracle. But everyone already knew. Rakitin also wanted Father Païssy to know he had something very important to talk about. Alyosha gave the letter to Father Païssy to confirm the story.
Even Father Païssy, who was usually very serious, couldn’t hide his feelings. He smiled a little and his eyes shone.
Father Païssy said, “We shall see greater things!”
The other monks repeated, “We shall see greater things yet!”
But Father Païssy told everyone not to talk about it too much yet, because maybe it was just a coincidence, even though he didn’t really believe that himself.

Soon the whole monastery and many visitors heard about the miracle. One monk from Obdorsk, who had come the day before, was very surprised. He had asked Father Zossima the day before how he could do such miracles.

This monk from Obdorsk didn’t know what to think. The night before, he had visited Father Ferapont, an old monk who lived alone and was known for fasting and not talking much. Father Ferapont didn’t like Father Zossima or the “elders,” and some monks agreed with him. Some thought he was a great saint, others thought he was a little crazy, but people liked his strange ways.

Father Ferapont lived in a small, old wooden hut near the bees. He took care of many holy icons and burning lamps. He ate very little and spoke to almost no one, even to the monk who brought him bread. Some visitors believed he could talk to angels and only spoke to them instead of people.

The monk from Obdorsk went to see Father Ferapont, feeling nervous. It was late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting outside his little hut, under a big elm tree. The monk bowed to ask for a blessing.
Father Ferapont said, “Do you want me to bow to you? Get up!”
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit with me. Where are you from?” Father Ferapont asked.
The monk answered that he came from the Obdorsk monastery, St. Sylvester.
Father Ferapont said he had been there before and asked if Sylvester was well.
Father Ferapont asked about how they fasted at the other monastery. The monk explained their rules, but said Father Ferapont fasted even more, eating only bread and water.
Father Ferapont asked, “And mushrooms?”
He said, “I could live in the forest on mushrooms and berries, but they can’t give up bread. That is why they are in trouble with the devil.”
Father Ferapont asked if the monk had seen devils among the others, and then told stories of seeing devils on some of the other monks, like one hiding under a cassock or in a pocket.
The monk asked, “You can see spirits?”
Father Ferapont said yes, and told a story about catching a devil’s tail in the door and making the sign of the cross until it died.
The monk then asked if it was true that Father Ferapont spoke with the Holy Spirit.
Father Ferapont said, “He does come down sometimes.”
The monk asked, “How does He come?”
“As a bird,” said Father Ferapont.
He explained, “Sometimes as a dove, sometimes as a swallow, goldfinch, or blue-tit.”
The monk asked how he could tell, and Father Ferapont said, “He speaks in human language.”
The monk asked what He said, and Father Ferapont replied, “Today He told me a fool would visit and ask silly questions. You want to know too much.”

After a pause, Father Ferapont pointed to the tree and said, “At night, those branches become Christ holding out His arms for me. It’s terrifying. He might take me away—just like Elijah in the Bible.”

The monk went back to his room, feeling confused but also thinking Father Ferapont must be very holy because he fasted so much. He was more impressed by Father Ferapont than by Father Zossima, and thought maybe strict fasting made people see miracles. He was curious and kept asking questions to everyone about the new “miracle” from Father Zossima, but Alyosha didn’t notice him much at the time.
Alyosha was called back to Father Zossima, who was now in bed again, very tired. Only Father Païssy, Father Iosif, and Porfiry were there. Father Zossima looked at Alyosha and asked:
“Is your family expecting you?”
He reminded Alyosha, “Didn’t you promise to see them today?”
Alyosha said, “I did promise—to my father, my brothers, and others.”
Father Zossima told him, “You should go. Don’t worry. I won’t die before you come back to hear my last words. I will give you my last gift. Go keep your promise.”

Alyosha left right away, even though it was hard to go. He was happy to hear he would be able to say goodbye. He hurried to finish his business in town and return. Father Païssy also said some kind words to him as they left together.

Father Païssy told Alyosha, “Remember, the world’s science tries to explain away everything holy, but it doesn’t see the whole truth. Faith has lasted for centuries, and even people who say they don’t believe still follow Christ’s teachings in their hearts. Remember this as you go into the world. It will help you when you face hard times.”

Father Païssy blessed Alyosha. As Alyosha left, he felt happy to have made a new and caring friend in Father Païssy. He thought maybe Father Zossima wanted Father Païssy to help him after he was gone. Alyosha knew Father Païssy wanted to protect his heart and help him stay strong.

First, Alyosha went to visit his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch. On his way, he remembered that his father had told him to come without Ivan (his brother) seeing him. Alyosha wondered why, but decided his father was just excited yesterday and didn’t really mean it. He was happy when Marfa Ignatyevna (the servant) told him that Ivan had gone out two hours ago.

Alyosha went inside. His father was sitting alone at the table, wearing slippers and an old coat. He was looking at some papers but not really paying attention. The house was empty except for him, because Smerdyakov (another servant) had gone out shopping, and Grigory (the main servant) was sick in bed. Fyodor Pavlovitch looked tired. He had big purple bruises on his forehead, which was wrapped with a red handkerchief, and his nose was swollen and bruised too. He looked angry and glared at Alyosha when he came in.
“The coffee is cold,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said grumpily. “I won’t offer you any. I only ordered fish soup today. Why did you come?”
“I wanted to see how you are,” Alyosha said.

“I told you to come yesterday, but it doesn’t matter. You always come poking in anyway,” his father replied, sounding unfriendly. Then he got up and looked at himself in the mirror, fixing his handkerchief.
“Red is better. White looks like I’m in a hospital,” he said. “How is your elder?” (He meant the wise monk who taught Alyosha.)
“He is very sick, he might die today,” said Alyosha. But his father wasn’t listening.
“Ivan’s gone out,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly. “He’s trying to steal Mitya’s (Dmitri’s) fiancée. That’s why he’s here,” he said with a mean look.
“Did he tell you that?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, he told me three weeks ago! Do you think Ivan wants to kill me too? He must have some reason for coming here.”
“Why do you say such things?” asked Alyosha, feeling upset.

“He doesn’t ask for money, but he’s not getting any from me. I want to live as long as possible, so I need my money. When I get old, girls won’t want to come to me, so I need to save up. I plan to keep sinning until the end. People pretend not to sin, but everyone does. Your paradise, Alyosha, isn’t for me. I think when you die, you just sleep forever. You can pray for me if you want, or not! That’s how I see things. Ivan talks fancy, but he doesn’t know much. He just sits and smiles.”

“Why won’t he talk to me? If he does, he acts proud. Ivan is a scoundrel! And I’ll marry Grushenka if I want to. If you have money, you can get anything. Ivan is scared I’ll marry Grushenka, so he’s trying to get Mitya to marry her instead. Then Ivan can go after Mitya’s rich fiancée. Ivan is a scoundrel!”
“You’re so angry! Maybe you should rest,” said Alyosha.
“You say that and I’m not mad at you. If Ivan said it, I’d be angry. Only with you am I nice sometimes. Otherwise, I’m bad-tempered.”
“You’re not bad, just mixed-up,” Alyosha said, smiling.

“Listen. I wanted to get Mitya put in jail for what he did yesterday. These days, people don’t care about fathers, but it’s still against the law to beat up your old father. I could send Mitya to prison.”
“Are you going to do that?” Alyosha asked.
“Ivan talked me out of it. But there’s another reason.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch leaned closer and whispered to Alyosha.

“If I send Mitya to jail, Grushenka will hear and go visit him. But if she hears he beat me up, maybe she’ll give him up and come to me instead. She always does the opposite of what you expect. Want some brandy? Or coffee with brandy in it? It’s tasty.”
“No, thank you. I’ll just take a roll,” said Alyosha, putting a bread roll in his pocket. “You shouldn’t drink brandy either,” he added.
“You’re right, it makes me more nervous. Just one glass.” Fyodor Pavlovitch took out the brandy, poured a glass, drank it, and locked it back up.
“That’s enough. One glass won’t hurt me.”
“You seem happier now,” Alyosha said.

“I love you, Alyosha, even without brandy. But with scoundrels, I’m a scoundrel. Ivan isn’t going to Tchermashnya—he just wants to see how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They’re all scoundrels! I don’t really know Ivan. He’s not like us. I won’t leave him anything when I die. And I’ll crush Mitya like a beetle! I was thinking of giving Mitya some money to leave for good, but now I changed my mind. I’ll keep my money. Don’t say anything to him, or he’ll get his hopes up. By the way, is his fiancée, Katerina Ivanovna, going to marry him? You saw her yesterday, right?”
“She won’t leave him,” said Alyosha.
“See how these ladies love a scoundrel like Mitya? If I were young again, I’d be a hero too. But Mitya won’t have Grushenka. I’ll crush him!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was angry again. “You can go. There’s nothing for you to do here.”
Alyosha went to say goodbye and kissed his father on the shoulder.
“Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, surprised. “We’ll see each other again, won’t we?”
“Of course. I just felt like it,” said Alyosha.
“Well, come again soon. I’ll make fish soup for you next time! Come tomorrow, you hear?”
As soon as Alyosha left, Fyodor Pavlovitch poured himself another half glass of brandy.
“No more!” he muttered, locking the cupboard. Then he went to bed, lay down, and quickly fell asleep.

Alyosha left his father's house and walked towards Madame Hohlakov's home. He was glad his father didn't ask about Grushenka (a woman Alyosha met yesterday). Alyosha thought his father and Dmitri (his brother) were both still angry and planning something. Alyosha hoped he could find Dmitri today.

As Alyosha walked, he saw a group of schoolboys near a small bridge. The boys were about nine to twelve years old. Some had school bags, some wore coats, and some had boots. They were talking loudly and holding stones. Alyosha liked children, so he stopped to watch. He noticed another boy across the ditch, standing alone by a fence. This boy looked about ten, was pale and small, and watched the group carefully. Alyosha guessed they had argued at school.

Alyosha spoke to a curly-haired boy in the group. He said, “When I was your age, I carried my school bag on the left, not the right.” Another boy said, “He is left-handed.” A third added, “He even throws stones with his left hand.”

Just then, the boy by the fence threw a stone at the group. It almost hit the left-handed boy. The boys shouted for Smurov (the left-handed boy) to throw back. He did, but missed. The boy across the ditch threw another stone, hitting Alyosha on the shoulder.

The boys laughed and shouted, “He aimed at you, Karamazov!” Then all six threw stones at the lonely boy. One stone hit his head, but the boy jumped up and threw stones back. Soon, both sides were throwing stones fast.

Alyosha yelled, “Stop! Six against one isn't fair. You could hurt him.” He ran forward to protect the lone boy. Some boys stopped throwing. One boy in a red shirt said, “He stabbed Krassotkin with a penknife in class. It bled, but Krassotkin didn't tell. He deserves a beating.” Alyosha asked, “But why? Do you tease him?” The boys yelled that the lonely boy was now throwing at Alyosha. They threw stones again. The boy across the ditch was hit in the chest, screamed, cried, and ran away up the street. The boys teased him, calling him “Wisp of tow.”

The oldest boy said, “You don't know how mean he is, Karamazov.” Alyosha asked, “Is he a tell-tale?” The boys just looked at each other. One boy told Alyosha to catch up with the boy, who was now waiting up the street and looking back. The boys laughed and told Alyosha to ask him about “wisp of tow.” Alyosha guessed this was how they teased him and said he would not ask that. He wanted to find out why they hated the boy.

Alyosha crossed the bridge and walked toward the lonely boy, even though the other boys warned him he might get hurt. The boy waited for Alyosha. He was small, wore an old coat that was too short, had bare arms, a patch on his pants, and a hole in his boot. His pockets were full of stones. Alyosha stopped two steps away. The boy saw Alyosha didn't want to fight, so he relaxed a little and said, “I am alone, and there are six of them. I’ll beat them all, alone!”

Alyosha said, “One of the stones must have hurt you.” The boy shouted, “But I hit Smurov on the head!” Alyosha asked, “Did you throw a stone at me on purpose?” The boy looked angry and said, “I don't know you. Do you know me?” Alyosha said, “I don't know you and I don't tease you. Goodbye.”

The boy shouted, “Monk in silk trousers!” He thought Alyosha would fight him, but Alyosha just walked away. Suddenly, the boy threw a big stone at Alyosha’s back. Alyosha turned and said, “So you throw stones from behind? Is it true you attack on the sly?” The boy threw another stone, hitting Alyosha’s elbow. Alyosha asked, “Aren’t you ashamed? Why did you do that? What have I done to you?” The boy just waited, thinking Alyosha would fight him.

Suddenly, the boy rushed at Alyosha, grabbed his hand, and bit his finger hard. Alyosha cried out and pulled his finger free, which was bleeding. He used his handkerchief to stop the bleeding. The boy watched him the whole time.

Alyosha said, “You see how badly you bit me. Isn't that enough? Now, tell me, what have I done to you?” The boy looked surprised. Alyosha said, “I don’t know you. This is the first time I’ve seen you. But you must be angry at me for some reason. Why did you hurt me?” Instead of answering, the boy started crying loudly and ran away. Alyosha watched him run and decided he would try to find out the reason later, when he had more time.

Alyosha walked quickly to Madame Hohlakov’s house. It was a big, pretty stone house with two floors. Madame Hohlakov didn’t live there all the time, but she owned it because it came from her family. She spent more time in Moscow or at another estate. As soon as Alyosha came in, Madame Hohlakov hurried out to meet him.
“Did you get my letter about the new miracle?” she asked fast, looking excited and worried.
“Yes,” Alyosha said.
“Did you show it to everyone? He made the son better for his mother!”
“He is dying today,” Alyosha said quietly.
“I know, I know! I wish I could talk to you about all this. But, listen, Katerina Ivanovna is here now!”
“That’s good,” Alyosha said. “She told me to visit her today.”

“I know what happened yesterday, and how badly that person acted. It was terrible! Your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch—what do you think of him? But it’s not him in there with Katerina Ivanovna, it’s your other brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch. They’re talking seriously. I can only guess what’s happening! It’s like a sad story. I’m so glad you’re here! But wait, I need to ask you: why was Lise so upset? When she heard you were here, she started crying.”
Lise (Madame Hohlakov’s daughter) called out from behind a door, “Maman, it’s you who are upset, not me!” She sounded like she wanted to laugh.
“No wonder, Lise! You make me so worried. Lise has been sick all night with a fever. Dr. Herzenstube says we have to wait. When you came, she screamed and wanted to be in this room.”
“Mamma, I didn’t know he came. I didn’t want to be in here because of him.”
“That’s not true, Lise. Yulia told you Alyosha was coming. She was watching.”
“Mamma, that’s silly. But if you want to be clever, tell Alyosha he was silly to come after what happened yesterday. People are laughing at him.”
“Lise, you go too far! I’m glad Alyosha is here. I need him. Oh, I’m so unhappy!”
“What’s wrong, mamma?”
“Everything! Lise’s moods, her sickness, that doctor, even the miracle! It’s too much. Tell me, will Father Zossima live till tomorrow?”
Alyosha said, “Could you please give me a clean rag? I hurt my finger and it hurts a lot.”
Alyosha showed his finger, wrapped in a bloody handkerchief. Madame Hohlakov screamed and shut her eyes.
“Oh no, what a terrible wound!”
When Lise saw Alyosha’s finger, she opened the door fast.
“Come here! Why didn’t you say anything? He might have bled a lot, mamma! How did it happen? He needs water, quick! Mamma, get some water right now!”
“Should we call Dr. Herzenstube?” Madame Hohlakov asked.
“Mamma, you’ll drive me crazy! Dr. Herzenstube never knows what to do! Just get water, please! Go tell Yulia to hurry!”
“It’s not bad,” Alyosha said, trying not to worry them.
Yulia ran in with water. Alyosha put his finger in it.
“Mamma, bring some lint and that bottle for wounds. It’s in your bedroom cupboard,” Lise said.
“I’ll get it. You’re very brave, Alyosha. How did it happen?” Madame Hohlakov hurried away.
Lise asked Alyosha quickly, “How did you get hurt? Then I have something else to ask you.”
Alyosha quickly told Lise about meeting the schoolboys and how one bit his finger.
“Why do you spend time with schoolboys?” Lise asked, sounding upset. “You’re a boy yourself! But you must find out more about that boy. Now tell me, does your finger hurt too much to talk?”
“No, it’s fine now.”
“That’s because it’s in the water. The water will get warm soon. Yulia, bring ice and more water. Now, will you give me the letter I sent you yesterday? Hurry, mamma will come back soon.”
“I don’t have the letter,” Alyosha said.
“Yes, you do. It’s in your pocket. I’m sorry for my joke. Give it back.”
“I left it at home.”
“Please bring it to me later.”
“I can’t today. I’m going back to the monastery and may not visit for a few days. Father Zossima—”
“Four days? Did you laugh at my letter?”
“No, I didn’t laugh.”
“Why not?”
“Because I believed you.”
“You’re teasing me!”

“No, I really did. When Father Zossima dies, I’ll leave the monastery and finish my studies. When you’re old enough, we’ll get married. I think you’d be a good wife. Father Zossima wants me to marry.”
“But I’m in a wheelchair,” Lise said, blushing.
“I’ll push you myself, but I think you’ll get better.”
“You’re silly, Alyosha! Mamma, why are you so slow?”
“Don’t shout, Lise. I couldn’t find the lint. Did you move it?”
“How could I know he’d come with a hurt finger? But maybe I would have done it on purpose! Mamma, you’re funny.”
“Never mind about being funny. I’m just tired out by everything.”
“That’s enough about Dr. Herzenstube,” Lise said, laughing. “Alyosha fought with a boy and got bitten. He wants to get married! Isn’t that funny, mamma?”
Lise kept laughing and looked slyly at Alyosha.
“Why talk about marriage, Lise? And what if the boy was sick?”
“Mamma, boys don’t have rabies!”
“Why not? If a mad dog bites a boy, he could bite others. You bandaged his finger so well, Lise! Do you still hurt, Alyosha?”
“Not much now.”
“Are you afraid of water?” Lise asked.
“That’s enough, Lise. I was too quick to say the boy was sick. Katerina Ivanovna just heard Alyosha is here. She wants to see him.”
“Mamma, go see them yourself. Alyosha’s finger hurts.”
“No, I can go,” Alyosha said.
“You’re leaving?”
“I’ll see them and then come back. But I want to see Katerina Ivanovna soon and then return to the monastery.”
“Go straight back to your monastery, Alyosha. I want to sleep. I didn’t sleep last night.”
“Lise, I wish you would sleep!” Madame Hohlakov said.
“I can stay a few more minutes,” Alyosha said softly.
“Please take him away, mamma,” Lise said. “He’s a monster.”
“Lise, you’re silly today. Let’s go, Alyosha. Maybe she will sleep after seeing you. How lucky!”
“Mamma, you’re so sweet! I must kiss you,” Lise said.

“And I kiss you, Lise. Listen, Alyosha,” Madame Hohlakov whispered. “I won’t say much, but you’ll see. It’s strange—Katerina Ivanovna loves your brother Ivan, but tries to love Dmitri. It’s like a play! I’ll go in with you, and stay if they let me.”

In the living room, Katerina Ivanovna looked upset but determined. Ivan Fyodorovitch was getting ready to leave as Alyosha (his brother) and Madame Hohlakov came in. Alyosha was worried because he had heard people say Ivan loved Katerina Ivanovna and might want to take her away from Dmitri (their other brother). Alyosha cared about both his brothers and didn’t want them to fight. Dmitri said having Ivan as a rival helped him, but Alyosha didn’t understand how. Alyosha always thought Katerina Ivanovna loved Dmitri, not Ivan, but now he wasn’t sure.

Madame Hohlakov had just said Katerina Ivanovna loved Ivan, not Dmitri, and was only pretending to love Dmitri because she felt she should. Alyosha began to think maybe this was true. He wondered, “What if she doesn’t love Ivan or Dmitri at all?” He was confused and didn’t know what to think.
Alyosha felt bad thinking so much about who loved whom. He wondered why he cared so much, but he couldn’t help it. He felt this was very important for his brothers.

Ivan had called Dmitri a “reptile” the day before. Alyosha worried their family might fight even more. He loved both brothers and wanted to help, but he didn’t know what was best for them. He wanted to do something, but he was confused and unsure.
When Alyosha came in, Katerina Ivanovna quickly asked Ivan to stay and made Alyosha sit beside her. Madame Hohlakov sat near Ivan.
Katerina Ivanovna spoke to them all. She said Alyosha had seen her act badly the day before. She wasn’t sure if she still loved Dmitri. She felt sorry for him, which didn’t feel like love.
Alyosha realized Katerina Ivanovna was being honest and probably didn’t love Dmitri anymore.
Katerina Ivanovna said she had made a big decision last night, and Ivan agreed with her.
She wanted Alyosha to tell her if he thought she was right. She said hearing his opinion would help her be calm.
Alyosha said he wanted her to be happy but didn’t know much about love.

Katerina Ivanovna said the most important thing was honor and duty. She had decided that even if Dmitri married someone else, she would never leave him. She would always be there for him as a friend and sister, ready to help him when he was unhappy. She wanted him to know she loved him and kept her promise, even if he betrayed her.
She was breathing hard and looked upset. Ivan then spoke.
Ivan said her feelings were true. He said other women would be wrong to act this way, but for her, it was right because she was so honest.
Madame Hohlakov said this was just because of what happened yesterday.

Ivan answered that for Katerina Ivanovna, this decision would last her whole life. She would always think about her promise and her suffering, but in the end, she would feel proud for keeping her word.
Ivan’s words sounded a little mean, and he seemed to be making fun of her.
Madame Hohlakov disagreed again.
Katerina Ivanovna cried and begged Alyosha to say what he thought.
She said she was upset and tired, but felt strong with her two friends there.
Ivan suddenly said he had to go to Moscow soon, maybe the next day.
Katerina Ivanovna’s face changed. She looked surprised, then quickly became happy and cheerful.

She said she was sad to lose Ivan, but also glad because he could visit her aunt and Agafya in Moscow and explain everything to them so she didn’t have to write a hard letter. She rushed off to write the letter.
Madame Hohlakov reminded her that she still wanted Alyosha’s opinion.
Katerina Ivanovna stopped and said she hadn’t forgotten. She insisted Alyosha must decide.
Alyosha was upset and didn’t understand why Katerina Ivanovna acted glad Ivan was leaving.
Alyosha said she was acting, pretending to be glad about Ivan leaving, but really she was hiding her true feelings.
Alyosha continued, saying she said she was sad to lose Ivan but at the same time said it was good he was leaving. He thought she was pretending.

Alyosha said he wasn’t sure how to say it, but he thought maybe Katerina Ivanovna never loved Dmitri or Ivan. He thought Dmitri never really loved her, either. He said someone needed to tell the truth.

Alyosha suggested bringing Dmitri so Katerina Ivanovna could join his hand with Ivan’s and stop the confusion. He said she was torturing Ivan because she really loved him, but was pretending to love Dmitri out of duty.
Katerina Ivanovna got very angry and called Alyosha a “religious idiot.”
Ivan laughed and stood up to leave.

Ivan said Alyosha was wrong. He said Katerina Ivanovna never cared for him (Ivan), even though she knew he loved her. She only kept Ivan close to get back at Dmitri for hurting her. Ivan said Katerina Ivanovna actually loved Dmitri even more when he insulted her. He said she needed to feel like a hero for staying loyal to someone who treated her badly. Ivan said goodbye and left, saying he would never come back and did not want to take her hand.
Alyosha tried to call Ivan back, feeling it was his fault Ivan was leaving, but Ivan did not return.
Katerina Ivanovna went into the next room.
Madame Hohlakov told Alyosha he had acted like an angel and said she would try to stop Ivan from leaving.
Katerina Ivanovna returned with money in her hand.

She calmly asked Alyosha for a favor. She explained that Dmitri had hurt a poor man named Snegiryov by dragging him by the beard in front of people, including his son. She wanted Alyosha to take two hundred roubles to Snegiryov’s family to help them, but not as a payment for what happened—just as a kind act. She asked Alyosha to do this for her and then left the room quickly.
Alyosha wanted to say something to Katerina Ivanovna, but Madame Hohlakov pulled him away.
Madame Hohlakov said Katerina Ivanovna was proud but kind. She explained that everyone hoped Katerina Ivanovna would marry Ivan because he loved her, not Dmitri, who didn’t care for her.
Alyosha pointed out that Katerina Ivanovna had been crying and was hurt.
Madame Hohlakov said never to trust a woman’s tears and that she usually sided with the men.
Alyosha felt guilty, blaming himself for what had happened.
Madame Hohlakov kept telling him he had acted like an angel.
Alyosha said he had thought Katerina Ivanovna loved Ivan, so he spoke up—but now he worried about what would happen.
Just then, the maid ran in and said Katerina Ivanovna was ill and crying.
Lise, Madame Hohlakov’s daughter, was worried too.
Madame Hohlakov told Lise not to scream and said that Katerina Ivanovna’s crying was a good sign. She told Alyosha to hurry and deliver the money and then come back.
Madame Hohlakov hurried away. Alyosha wanted to see Lise before leaving.
Lise told him not to come in, but to talk through the door. She wanted to know why people called him an angel.
Alyosha said it was because he had done something silly and said goodbye.
He told Lise he was very sad but would be back soon. Then he ran out of the room.

Alyosha felt very sad. He thought he had made things worse by getting involved in a love problem he didn't understand. He remembered that Father Zossima had sent him to help people get along, but now he worried he had only caused more trouble. He promised himself to be more careful in the future.

Katerina Ivanovna asked Alyosha to do something, so he went to Lake Street. His brother Dmitri lived nearby. Alyosha wanted to see Dmitri before going to the captain, even though he guessed Dmitri was avoiding him. He also kept thinking about Father Zossima, who was very sick.

Alyosha kept wondering about the little boy Katerina Ivanovna had mentioned. He thought it must be the same boy who bit his finger before. Thinking about this helped him forget his worries for a while. He decided not to feel bad anymore and just do what he had to do. He ate some bread from his pocket and felt better.

Dmitri wasn't home. The people who owned the house seemed nervous and told Alyosha that Dmitri hadn't slept there for three nights. Alyosha guessed they were protecting Dmitri and thought that was kind of them.

Alyosha found the captain’s house. It looked old and crooked, with a muddy yard and a cow. Inside, he asked some old women where to find the captain. They pointed him to a door. Alyosha was about to go in, but heard it was very quiet inside and decided to knock first. After a moment, someone shouted, "Who's there?"

Alyosha went inside. The room was crowded and messy, with beds, a stove, and rags hanging up. There were three windows, but they let in little light. On the table was some leftover food and a nearly empty bottle of vodka. Several people were in the room: a thin, sick-looking woman; a young girl with reddish hair; another girl who was hunched over with crutches nearby; and a small, weak man with reddish hair and a short beard. The man jumped up and wiped his mouth when he saw Alyosha.
The girl by the window said loudly that Alyosha must be a monk begging for money. The man answered her quickly, then turned back to Alyosha and asked why he had come.
Alyosha saw that the man acted nervous and angry at the same time. He wore old, mismatched clothes that looked too small for him.
Alyosha introduced himself as Alexey Karamazov.
The man said he was Captain Snegiryov and wanted to know why Alyosha was there.
Alyosha said he just wanted to talk.
Captain Snegiryov quickly brought Alyosha a chair and sat very close to him.
The captain said his full name and explained he used to be in the army but had lost his position. Now he often said "sir" because he had become poor.
Alyosha said he came about "that business."
The captain wanted to know what business.
Alyosha explained it was about the fight between his brother Dmitri and the captain.
Suddenly, a boy’s voice came from behind a curtain. Alyosha saw it was the same boy who had bitten him. The boy was sick in bed but looked at Alyosha without fear.
The captain was surprised and asked if it was Alyosha’s finger the boy had bitten.
Alyosha explained what happened: there were other boys throwing stones at the captain's son, and when Alyosha tried to help, the boy bit him.
The captain wanted to punish his son, but Alyosha said he didn’t want that.
The captain became very upset. He asked if Alyosha wanted him to hurt himself to make up for what happened. He acted strange and angry.

Alyosha spoke gently and said he understood now. He thought the boy was angry because he loved his father and saw Alyosha as the brother of the man who hurt him. Alyosha said his brother Dmitri was sorry and wanted to apologize.
The captain asked if Dmitri would kneel and say sorry in public, and Alyosha said yes.
The captain became emotional and introduced his family: his two daughters and his son. He said they were all he had, and he loved them very much.
The girl by the window, Varvara, told her father to stop acting foolish.
The captain told Alyosha to stand up and meet his wife, Arina Petrovna, who was sick and could barely move. He kissed his wife's hand.
The wife greeted Alyosha, calling him the wrong name, and told him to sit down. She talked about how she used to be healthy but now was very sick.
The hunchback girl, Nina, started crying.
Varvara called her father a fool.
The mother began talking about the past and how people talk about her. She said only her son Ilusha loves her and asked her family to forgive her.
She started crying, and the captain tried to comfort her, wiping her tears.
Alyosha said he understood.
Ilusha, the sick boy, told his father to stop.
Varvara got angry at her father’s behavior.
The captain told Alyosha they should go outside to talk. He introduced Nina, saying she was like an angel.
He also said Varvara was like an angel, even though she called him names. Then he quickly took Alyosha outside to finish their talk.
The captain said, “The air outside is nice, but not in my apartment. Let’s walk slowly. I’m glad you care about what happens to me.”
Alyosha replied, “I have something important to say, but I don’t know how to start.”

The captain guessed, “You must have business with me. You wouldn’t visit for no reason. Or maybe you’re here because of the boy, but that’s unlikely. Let me tell you what happened before. A week ago, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch pulled my beard in anger and dragged me out of the tavern to the market-place. The schoolboys were coming out then, with Ilusha among them. When Ilusha saw me, he ran up, hugged me, and begged Dmitri, ‘Let go, it’s my father! Forgive him!’ He even kissed Dmitri’s hand. I’ll never forget Ilusha’s little face at that moment.”
Alyosha promised, “My brother will truly say sorry, even if he has to kneel in the market-place. I’ll make him!”

The captain replied, “So, it’s your idea, not his? Let me tell you, your brother did stop and let me go, saying, ‘You are an officer and I am an officer. If you want, find someone to be your second and challenge me to a duel. I will give satisfaction, though you are a scoundrel.’ That’s what he said. But if I fight him and die, who will take care of my family? If I’m only hurt, I’m still another mouth to feed. Ilusha is just nine. Should I make him beg in the streets? It’s foolish to talk about duels.”
Alyosha repeated, “He will ask your forgiveness! He will bow to you in the market-place!”

The captain went on, “I thought about going to court, but Agrafena Alexandrovna told me not to. She said if I try, she’ll tell everyone I was beaten for being dishonest and have me fired. Fyodor Pavlovitch also wants to use papers I signed to sue me. If I lose my jobs, how will I earn money? That’s why I kept quiet and you saw how we live. By the way, did Ilusha hurt your finger much?”
Alyosha answered, “Yes, it hurt a lot. He was very angry and was upset at me because I’m a Karamazov. But he was also throwing stones at other boys. That’s very dangerous.”
The captain said, “He was hit by a stone himself today, right on the chest. He came home crying and now he’s sick.”
