Alyosha added, “He attacks first because he’s upset about what happened to you. I heard he even stabbed a boy, Krassotkin, with a pen-knife.”
The captain said, “That’s dangerous. Krassotkin is someone important here. We might hear more about it.”
Alyosha said, “Maybe you shouldn’t send Ilusha to school until he calms down.”

The captain agreed, “Yes, he is so angry. Let me tell you more. Since the beard incident, the boys tease him about the ‘wisp of tow’—my beard. Schoolboys can be cruel. But Ilusha stands up for me. He isn’t ashamed of me, even when the rich children make fun of us. When he kissed your brother’s hand and cried ‘Forgive father,’ it hurt him deeply. After that, he got a fever and was sick all night. The next day, I got drunk to forget my troubles. Mamma cried too. We spent our last money. The boys kept teasing Ilusha, calling him ‘wisp of tow’ and saying, ‘Your father was dragged out of the tavern and you begged forgiveness.’”

The captain continued, “A few days later, Ilusha came home pale. At home, mamma and the girls got involved. Varvara said we never do anything sensible. I took Ilusha for a walk, like we do every evening to the big stone by the field. Ilusha’s hand was cold and thin. He said, ‘Father, don’t forgive what he did to you!’ At school they said Dmitri paid me ten roubles. I told him that wasn’t true and I wouldn’t take money. He trembled and kissed my hand, begging me to challenge Dmitri. I explained I couldn’t. He then promised when he grew up, he would challenge Dmitri himself. He said, ‘I could kill you, but I forgive you, so there!’ He thought about this for two days and couldn’t sleep.”

“But then he started coming home beaten. I learned he was standing up to his whole class. I got worried and took him for another walk. He asked, ‘Are rich people stronger than anyone?’ I said yes. He said he would get rich, become an officer, and then no one would dare hurt us. He wanted us to move to a better town. We dreamed about buying a horse and cart and moving away together. He was so happy dreaming about the horse.”

“But yesterday everything changed. He was very sad after school, even on our walk. I tried to cheer him up, talking about our plans, but he was silent and his fingers shook. At the big stone, I sat down and talked about flying kites. Suddenly, Ilusha hugged me tight and cried hard, saying, ‘Father, he insulted you!’ We both cried. I thanked God no one saw us. You must thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. But I won’t hurt my boy just to please you.”
The captain sounded grumpy again, but Alyosha could tell he trusted him. Alyosha wanted to help.
Alyosha said, “I wish I could be friends with your boy! Could you help with that?”
The captain answered, “Of course, sir.”

Alyosha said, “Now, I have a message. My brother Dmitri also hurt his fiancée, Katerina Ivanovna. She asked me to bring you this money—not from Dmitri or me, but just from her, to help you after you were both insulted. She wants you to take these two hundred roubles as a gift from a sister to a brother. Please take them.” Alyosha held out the money.
They stood near the big stone, no one else around. The captain was shocked to see so much money.
He took the notes and stared quietly, surprised.
“Is this really for me? Two hundred roubles! I haven’t seen so much in years! And she says she’s like a sister? Is that true?”
“I promise it’s true,” said Alyosha.
The captain blushed.
“If I take it, will you think I’m bad?” the captain asked. “You’re telling me to take it, but will you secretly look down on me?”
“No! No one will know but you, me, her, and her friend,” Alyosha promised.
The captain got excited. “You don’t know what this means to me now.”

“With this money, I can help mamma and Nina, my hunchback daughter. Doctor Herzenstube said Nina needs medicine and baths, but we can’t afford it or even get water easily. Nina is always in pain but doesn’t complain. She eats the leftovers and thinks she’s a burden, but really, she is our angel and keeps us together. Even Varvara, who works hard and gave us her savings for school, can’t go back to Petersburg now. Now I can buy medicine, get help, and feed everyone. It feels like a dream!”
Alyosha was happy he could help.

The captain said quickly, “Now maybe Ilusha and I can really leave, buy a horse and cart, and move to another province for work. I have an old friend who might give me a job. Maybe I can pay off my debts and we can all go.”
“You’ll have enough!” Alyosha said. “Katerina Ivanovna will send more if you need it, and I can help, too. Moving away would be best, especially for Ilusha. Write to us, and we’ll always be friends.”
Alyosha wanted to hug him, but stopped. The captain looked strange, his lips moving with no sound.
“What is it?” asked Alyosha.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, do you want to see a trick?” the captain asked, sounding strange.
“What trick?” asked Alyosha.
“A pretty trick,” whispered the captain, making a funny face.
“What’s wrong? What trick?” Alyosha was worried.
Suddenly, the captain crumpled the money in his hand, threw it on the sand, and shouted, “Do you see?”
He stomped on the money, breathing hard.
“So much for your money! So much for your money!” he yelled over and over.
He stood up tall, looking very proud.

“Tell those who sent you that the ‘wisp of tow’ does not sell his honor,” he said, raising his arm. Then he ran a few steps, turned back, and blew a kiss to Alyosha. He ran again, then turned with tears in his eyes and said,
“What would I tell my boy if I took money for our shame?”

Then he ran away. Alyosha watched, very sad. He knew the captain didn’t plan to throw away the money until the last moment. Alyosha didn’t follow him because he understood why. When the captain was gone, Alyosha picked up the crumpled notes. They were dirty but still good. He put them in his pocket and went to tell Katerina Ivanovna what happened.

Madame Hohlakov met Alyosha at the door. She was worried and upset. Katerina Ivanovna had fainted after her crying, and now she was very sick with a fever. The doctor, Herzenstube, had been called, and the aunts were already there. Everyone was waiting in Katerina Ivanovna’s room, hoping she would not get worse.

Madame Hohlakov looked very serious. She kept saying how serious the situation was. Alyosha wanted to tell her what had happened to him, but she stopped him. She asked Alyosha to go sit with Lise and wait.

Madame Hohlakov whispered to Alyosha that Lise had been sorry for laughing at him before. Lise had almost cried because she felt bad. Madame Hohlakov explained that Lise cared a lot about Alyosha’s opinion and thought of him as her best childhood friend. She told Alyosha to go and cheer Lise up, because he always made her happy.
“Come in, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Lise said.
Alyosha came in. Lise looked embarrassed and blushed. She quickly started talking about something else.

Lise said her mother had told her about the two hundred roubles Alyosha was supposed to give to a poor officer, and about how the officer had been insulted. Lise asked if Alyosha had given him the money.
Alyosha said he had not given the money to the officer, and that it was a long story.

Alyosha began telling Lise what happened. As he spoke, he forgot his embarrassment, and Lise listened closely. Alyosha told her about Ilusha and the officer, and how the man had trampled on the money instead of taking it. Lise was touched and surprised.
Lise cried out, “So you didn’t give him the money! You let him run away! You should have gone after him!”
Alyosha said, “No, Lise; it’s better I didn’t go after him.” He walked around the room, thinking.
Lise asked, “How is it better? Now they have no food!”
Alyosha explained that the officer would still get the money the next day. He said he had made a mistake, but maybe that was for the best.
Lise wanted to know what mistake Alyosha meant.

Alyosha said the officer was a very sensitive man, and he was embarrassed for being so happy about the money. Alyosha explained that when he offered to help the man even more, the man felt ashamed and angry. Alyosha believed the officer would think about the money all night and would probably come back to accept it the next day.
Lise was surprised and asked why this was better.

Alyosha said that if the officer had taken the money right away, he would have felt bad later and might have returned it angrily. Now, because the officer had already shown his pride by refusing the money, it would be easier for him to accept it tomorrow.
Alyosha was happy and said, “And then he will take it!” Lise clapped her hands.
Lise said, “Now I understand! Alyosha, how do you know all this? I could never have thought of it.”
Alyosha said it was important to make the officer feel equal, or even better than them, even though he was taking money.
Lise joked that Alyosha was good, but sometimes formal. She asked, “Are we being mean by thinking so much about what the officer will do, as if we know everything about him?”
Alyosha said it was not mean, because everyone is the same inside. He said Father Zossima once told him to care for people like children or like the sick in hospitals.
Lise said, “Let’s care for people like the sick!”
Alyosha agreed and said he would try, though sometimes he was impatient.
Lise said she was happy.
Alyosha was glad to hear it.
Lise told Alyosha to check if her mother was listening at the door.
Alyosha checked and said no one was listening.
Lise blushed and took Alyosha’s hand. She said she wasn’t joking when she wrote to him yesterday; she was serious.
Suddenly, Lise kissed Alyosha’s hand three times.
Alyosha said happily, “I knew you were serious.”
Lise laughed and blushed, still holding his hand.
Alyosha, also blushing, said he wanted to make her happy but didn’t know how.
Lise teased Alyosha, saying, “You’re cold and rude! You act like you’re sure I’ll be your wife.”
Alyosha laughed and asked, “Was it wrong for me to be sure?”
Lise said it was “delightfully right.”
Alyosha kissed Lise on the lips.
Lise was surprised. Alyosha was embarrassed.
Alyosha said, “Forgive me. Maybe I was stupid. You said I was cold, so I kissed you.”
Lise laughed and covered her face, but then became serious.
She said, “We must wait to kiss more. We’re not ready. Tell me, why do you choose me? I am sick and not smart. I don’t deserve you.”

Alyosha said she did deserve him. He would be leaving the monastery soon and needed to marry. He thought Lise was the best person for him, because she knew him since childhood and was more innocent and happy than he was.
Lise asked, “Like a martyr? How?”
Alyosha said Lise’s questions showed she could suffer and think deeply.
Lise, very happy, asked what kind of suit Alyosha would wear when he left the monastery.
Alyosha said he would wear whatever Lise liked.
Lise described a blue velvet coat, white vest, and gray hat. She asked if Alyosha believed she didn’t care for him before.
Alyosha said he knew she cared.
Lise joked that he was hard to deal with.
Alyosha explained he pretended not to know she cared, to make things easier for her.
Lise said that made it worse and better at the same time. She told Alyosha about how she tested him with her letter, and was happy he didn’t bring it to give back.
Alyosha said he had the letter with him after all.
He showed the letter to Lise from a distance.
But he said he wouldn’t give it back; she could only look at it.
Lise teased, “You told a lie!”
Alyosha laughed and said, “If you like, I told a lie so I wouldn’t have to give the letter back. It’s precious to me.”
Lise was happy and again asked if her mother was listening.
Alyosha asked why she wanted to check; he didn’t want to suspect her mother.
Lise said that mothers had a right to spy on daughters.
Alyosha disagreed.
Lise said she would spy on Alyosha after they were married, and read all his letters.
Alyosha said, “If so, but it’s not right.”
Lise admitted that spying was wrong, but she would do it anyway.
Alyosha laughed and said she wouldn’t find anything.
Lise asked if Alyosha would give in to her when they disagreed.
Alyosha said he would, except in the most important things.
Lise promised to give in to him in everything, and even promised never to spy on him since he thought it was wrong. Then she asked why he seemed sad lately.
Alyosha said he had a secret sorrow, and she must love him to notice.
Lise wanted to know what the secret was.
Alyosha said he would tell her later.
Lise guessed that Alyosha’s brothers and father were worrying him.
Alyosha agreed.
Lise said she didn’t like Alyosha’s brother Ivan.
Alyosha said his brothers and father were destroying themselves and others, and wondered if even God could help them. He said he was a Karamazov too, even though he was supposed to be a monk.
Alyosha said, “Perhaps I don’t even believe in God.”
Lise was gentle and quiet, but Alyosha didn’t answer. He seemed troubled by his own thoughts.
Alyosha said his dear friend, the best man in the world, was dying. He felt very close to him and would be left alone. He told Lise that in the future, they would be together.
Lise said, “Yes, together forever! You can kiss me now.”
Alyosha kissed her.
Lise told him to go back to his friend and said she would pray for them. She asked if they would be happy.
Alyosha said he believed they would be.
Alyosha decided not to visit Madame Hohlakov but found her waiting by the door. He saw she had been waiting for him on purpose.
Madame Hohlakov told Alyosha that everything was nonsense and childish, and that he must not take it seriously.
Alyosha asked her not to tell Lise that, because it would upset her.
Madame Hohlakov wanted to know if Alyosha had just agreed to make Lise feel better.
Alyosha said he was serious.
Madame Hohlakov said she would never let him visit again and would take Lise away.
Alyosha asked why, since it was all far away and they would have to wait more than a year.
Madame Hohlakov said she was very unhappy and that this was a great blow. She made a joke about a play and asked about the letter Lise had written. She demanded to see it.
Alyosha changed the subject and asked about Katerina Ivanovna.
Madame Hohlakov said Katerina Ivanovna was still sick and unconscious, and that the aunts and doctor were upset. She again begged to see the letter.
Alyosha said he would not show the letter, even if Lise gave permission. He promised to come back tomorrow, and left.
Alyosha ran out into the street.

Alyosha knew he had to hurry. While saying goodbye to Lise (his friend), he thought of a way to find his brother Dmitri. Dmitri was hiding from him. It was almost three o’clock. Alyosha really wanted to go back to the monastery to see his wise and dying teacher, but finding Dmitri was more important. Alyosha felt something bad was about to happen. He didn’t know exactly what, but he wanted to warn Dmitri. He thought, “If anything happens, at least I tried to help. I won’t regret it later.”

Alyosha planned to surprise Dmitri by climbing over the fence, just like he did the day before. He would hide in the summer-house in the garden. If Dmitri didn’t come, Alyosha would wait there quietly, not letting anyone know he was around. Dmitri might come to the summer-house if he was waiting for Grushenka (the woman Dmitri loved). Alyosha decided to do this, even if it meant not returning to the monastery today.

Everything went smoothly. Alyosha climbed over the fence at the same place as before and sneaked into the summer-house. He didn’t want the housekeeper or Foma (the servant) to see him, because they might tell Dmitri or not let him in.

The summer-house was empty. Alyosha sat down to wait. The place looked older and sadder than before. He noticed a ring on the table from spilled brandy. While waiting, silly thoughts came into his head. He wondered why he sat in the same spot as yesterday. Waiting made him feel gloomy. After about fifteen minutes, Alyosha heard a guitar playing nearby. Some people were sitting on a garden seat not far away. Alyosha remembered seeing that seat yesterday. He wondered who was there.
A man started to sing and play the guitar.
Then a woman spoke and asked, “Why haven’t you visited us for so long, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you look down on us?”
The man answered politely but acted very important. Alyosha guessed it was Smerdyakov (the servant), and the woman was Marya Kondratyevna (the daughter of the house, visiting from Moscow).
Marya Kondratyevna said she loved poems and asked Smerdyakov to sing more. Smerdyakov sang again.
Marya Kondratyevna liked his singing better last time and said so. Smerdyakov said poetry was silly. Marya Kondratyevna disagreed.
Smerdyakov said nobody talks in poems, and if everyone did, we wouldn’t say much. He called poetry useless. Marya Kondratyevna told him he was very smart.
Smerdyakov talked about his hard childhood and how people teased him because he didn’t have a father. He said he hated Russia, and hearing people use certain words made him angry.
Marya Kondratyevna said he’d act differently if he were a young soldier, but Smerdyakov said he didn’t want to be a soldier and would get rid of all soldiers if he could.
Marya Kondratyevna asked who would protect them if there were no soldiers. Smerdyakov talked about Napoleon attacking Russia in 1812 and said maybe it would have been better if Russia had lost.
Marya Kondratyevna said she liked Russian boys better than foreign ones. Smerdyakov said it depended on what you liked.

Marya Kondratyevna said he acted like a fancy foreigner. Smerdyakov said people were bad everywhere, but in Russia, people were dirtier and needed to be punished. He said Fyodor Pavlovitch (their father) was right about that, even if he was crazy.

Marya Kondratyevna reminded him that he respected Ivan Fyodorovitch (another brother). Smerdyakov complained that Ivan called him a smelly servant. He said Dmitri was even worse, wasting money and acting badly. Smerdyakov said he was just a cook, but could do great things if given the chance.
Marya Kondratyevna thought duels sounded exciting. Smerdyakov explained that it was scary when someone pointed a gun at you.

Suddenly, Alyosha sneezed. The singing and talking stopped. Alyosha got up and walked over to them. He saw Smerdyakov looking fancy, and Marya Kondratyevna wearing a long blue dress. She was young but had a very round, freckled face.
Alyosha asked, “Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” Smerdyakov stood up slowly; Marya Kondratyevna did too. Smerdyakov said he didn’t know where Dmitri was or care.
Alyosha explained he just wanted to know if Smerdyakov had seen Dmitri. Smerdyakov said he knew nothing.

Alyosha said Dmitri thought Smerdyakov always told him news about the house, like when Grushenka came. Smerdyakov just looked at him. Then Smerdyakov asked how Alyosha got in, since the gate was locked. Alyosha said he climbed the fence and apologized to Marya Kondratyevna for sneaking in.

Marya Kondratyevna said it was fine; Dmitri often came that way too. Alyosha said he really needed to find Dmitri for something very important. Marya Kondratyevna said Dmitri never told them where he went.

Smerdyakov complained that Dmitri always bothered him with questions and even threatened him twice. Alyosha was surprised. Smerdyakov said Dmitri had a bad temper and might hurt him if he let Grushenka in. Smerdyakov was scared of him.
Marya Kondratyevna added that Dmitri once threatened to “pound him in a mortar.” Alyosha thought maybe that was just angry talk and wished he could warn Dmitri.

Smerdyakov then said, “Ivan Fyodorovitch (your brother) sent me this morning to Dmitri's place with a message: he wanted Dmitri to go eat with him at the restaurant in the market.” Smerdyakov didn’t find Dmitri at home. The landlady said Dmitri had left. Smerdyakov guessed Dmitri might be at the restaurant with Ivan now. He begged Alyosha not to mention he told him, because Dmitri might hurt him.

Alyosha repeated, “Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Smerdyakov said yes, at the Metropolis tavern. Alyosha was excited and thanked Smerdyakov, saying he would go there right away. Smerdyakov reminded him not to tell anyone he had helped. Alyosha promised he would keep it a secret and would just act as if he came by chance. Marya Kondratyevna offered to open the gate, but Alyosha said he would climb the fence again.

Alyosha hurried to the tavern, feeling nervous. He couldn’t go inside wearing his monk’s robe, but planned to ask for his brothers at the door. Just as he reached the tavern, a window opened, and Ivan called down to him, asking Alyosha to come up. Alyosha said he wasn’t sure about his clothes, but Ivan said he was alone in a private room and would come meet him. A minute later, Alyosha was sitting with Ivan, who was eating dinner alone.

Ivan was sitting in a part of the tavern behind a screen, so people couldn’t see him, but he wasn’t in a private room. There were waiters running around, and only one other person, an old retired soldier, was drinking tea in the corner. The tavern was noisy with shouts, music, and the sound of billiard balls. Alyosha knew Ivan didn’t like taverns and almost never came to them, so he guessed Ivan was only here to meet Dmitri. But Dmitri hadn’t arrived.
Ivan smiled when he saw Alyosha. “Shall I order you some soup or fish? You can’t just drink tea,” he said. Ivan had just finished dinner and was having tea.
“I’d like some soup, please, and tea after. I’m hungry,” Alyosha replied happily.
“And cherry jam? You loved cherry jam when you were little.”
“You remember that? I still like it. Please order some.”
Ivan called the waiter and asked for soup, cherry jam, and tea.

Ivan said, “I remember a lot about you, Alyosha. When you were eleven and I was fifteen, we weren’t really close. When I went to Moscow, I didn’t think of you much. Later, when you came to Moscow, we only met once. And now I’ve been here for three months, but we haven’t talked much. Tomorrow I’m leaving, and I was just thinking how I might see you to say goodbye. Then you walked in.”
“So you really wanted to see me?” Alyosha asked.

“Yes, very much. I wanted us to really get to know each other before I leave. I’ve noticed you looking at me these past three months, always expecting something. At first, it annoyed me, but now I respect you. You stand firm, Alyosha. And I think you care about me. Do you?”
“Yes, I love you, Ivan. Dmitri says you’re like a tomb, but I say you’re a riddle. I still don’t understand you, but today I understood something new.”
“What’s that?” Ivan asked with a laugh.
“You won’t be mad? I realized you’re just as young as other people your age, just a nice, young boy. Did I insult you?”

“Not at all!” Ivan said warmly. “It’s funny, but I’ve been thinking about how young and green I am too. Even if I lose faith in everything, I still want to live. I love life, even if I don’t understand it. I love spring leaves, the blue sky, and sometimes people, even if I don’t know why. I want to travel in Europe, even though I know it’s just a graveyard of the past. But I want to go. I love life with my whole heart. Do you understand what I mean, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed.
“I understand, Ivan. I think it’s good to love life,” Alyosha said. “Everyone should love life more than anything.”
“More than the meaning of life?” Ivan asked.
“Yes, love it even if you don’t understand it. Then you’ll find its meaning. You already love life, Ivan. That’s half the work done.”
“And what’s the other half?” Ivan asked.
“You have to help people who seem lost, maybe they aren’t lost after all. Let’s have tea. I’m glad we talked, Ivan.”
“You’re feeling inspired,” Ivan smiled. “Are you really leaving the monastery?”
“Yes, my elder told me to go out into the world.”
“Then we’ll see each other again outside. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” Alyosha answered, telling Ivan about his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan listened closely and asked questions.
“Smerdyakov asked me not to tell Dmitri what he told me,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and thought for a while.
“Are you worried about Smerdyakov?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, he bothers me. I wanted to see Dmitri, but now I don’t need to,” Ivan said.
“Are you really leaving soon, brother?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes.”
“What will happen with Dmitri and father?” Alyosha asked worriedly.

“Why do you keep asking? What does it matter to me? Am I my brother’s keeper?” Ivan said sharply, but then he smiled. “That’s what Cain said about his brother. But I can’t stay here to look after them. I’ve finished my business and I’m going. You saw me finish it just now.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna’s?”

“Yes, I’ve set myself free. Dmitri thought I was trying to steal Katerina Ivanovna from him, but I wasn’t. He even said I should have her. But now it’s all over. I feel so light-hearted, I almost wanted to order champagne to celebrate being free. It’s been going on for six months, and suddenly it’s over.”
“You mean your love for her?” Alyosha asked.
“If you want to call it that. I liked her, and she liked me, but suddenly it’s all gone. I laughed about it after talking to her.”
“You seem very happy about it,” Alyosha said.

“Yes! I didn’t really love her after all. She still attracts me, but it’s easy to leave her. Maybe she’ll take years to realize she doesn’t care for Dmitri, only for me. But I’m leaving for good. By the way, how is she now?”
Alyosha told him Katerina Ivanovna had been very upset and was now unconscious.
“I don’t think Madame Hohlakov is lying,” Alyosha said.
“I suppose I won’t go to her again. There’s no need.”
“Shall I order champagne to celebrate my freedom?” Ivan joked. “I’m so glad!”
“No, let’s not drink,” Alyosha said. “I feel a bit sad.”
“You’ve been sad for a while,” Ivan noticed.
“Are you leaving tomorrow morning?”
“Maybe. I only ate here today to avoid eating with father. I can’t stand him. But why do you worry about me leaving? We still have time to talk.”
“If you’re going tomorrow, how is that lots of time?”
“It doesn’t matter,” Ivan laughed. “We have enough time to talk about what matters. Why do you think we met here? To talk about Katerina Ivanovna? Or Russia? Or something else?”
“No.”
“Then you know. We want to talk about the big questions, like God and what we believe. That’s what you’ve been hoping to ask me, isn’t it?”
“Maybe,” Alyosha smiled. “Are you making fun of me, Ivan?”

“No, I’m not laughing. I want to be friends. Russian boys always talk about big questions in places like this, like whether God exists or not, or about changing the world. Even if they never meet again, that’s what they talk about.”
“Yes, Russians care about questions like God and immortality most of all,” Alyosha agreed.
“Sometimes it’s silly, but I like one Russian boy named Alyosha very much.”
“That was nice!” Alyosha laughed.
“So, where should I begin? Shall we talk about God?”
“Start where you want. Yesterday you said at dinner that there was no God,” Alyosha said seriously.
“I only said that to tease you,” Ivan replied. “But really, maybe I do accept God. Isn’t that a surprise?”
“If you’re not joking,” Alyosha said.

“No, I’m serious. Some people say that if there was no God, people would have to invent Him. It’s amazing that people even thought up the idea of God. I don’t try to figure out if God made people or people made God. I’ll tell you straight: I accept God. But if God made the world, He made it according to our minds, which only understand simple things. Some smart people think there are things we can’t understand, like maybe two lines that never meet could meet somewhere in infinity. Since I can’t understand that, I can’t expect to understand God either. So I just accept God and His wisdom, and I believe that everything will make sense in the end. But even if all suffering is fixed in the end, and everything is forgiven, I still don’t accept this world. I believe in God, but I can’t accept the world He created. That’s how I feel, Alyosha. That’s my belief. You wanted to know what I believe in, so now you know.”
“Why did you start our talk in such a silly way?” Alyosha asked.
“Because Russians always talk about these things in a silly way. Also, the simpler you are, the closer you are to the truth. I wanted to show my real feelings.”
“Will you explain why you don’t accept the world?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, I’ll explain,” Ivan said gently. “I don’t want to turn you away from your faith, Alyosha. Maybe I hope you can help me.” Ivan smiled in a way Alyosha had never seen before.

Ivan began, “I want to tell you something, Alyosha. I don’t understand how people can really love their neighbors. It’s easy to love people far away, but not the ones close by. I read about Saint John the Merciful, who took a sick, dirty beggar into his bed and tried to help him. I think he only did it because he felt he had to, not because he truly loved the beggar. When you know someone up close, it’s hard to really love them.”
Alyosha said, “Father Zossima talked about that. He said it’s hard for some people to love others when they see their faces. But there is a lot of love in the world, Ivan. I know that for sure.”

Ivan replied, “I don’t know about that, and most people feel like I do. Maybe people just can’t love like Christ did. He was God, and we’re not. Even if I’m in pain, no one else truly knows how much I hurt. Sometimes people don’t care because I might smell bad or look strange. People think beggars should ask for help in newspapers instead of in person. It’s easier to love people in stories or from far away, but not close up. But let’s talk about children instead. It’s easier to love children, even when they are messy. Grown-ups have done wrong things, but children haven’t. They are innocent. Do you like children, Alyosha? I know you do. Sometimes even cruel people like children. I knew a criminal who had hurt families, but while in prison, he loved watching children play. He even made friends with a little boy. I don’t know why I’m telling you all this, Alyosha. My head hurts and I feel sad.”

Ivan continued, “I met a man from Bulgaria who told me how some soldiers did terrible things to people there. They burned villages and hurt children in horrible ways. They even made games out of hurting babies, right in front of their mothers. Sometimes people say animals are cruel, but people can be much worse. Tigers only bite, but people can be cruel on purpose and in ways animals cannot imagine.”

Ivan went on, “I collect stories like these. Some are from other countries, but I also have stories from here. In Russia, people often beat others with rods. Once, a boy named Richard was given to cruel people when he was six. They treated him worse than a dog, made him work in the cold, and barely fed him. When he grew up, he committed a crime and was sentenced to die. Many kind people came to visit him in prison, taught him about God, and cried for him. They called him their brother, but still took him to be executed. In Russia, we have our own kind of cruelty. Once, a father and mother beat their daughter with a birch rod. The father was happy that the rod hurt more. They kept beating her while she screamed for help, and when the case went to court, people said it was normal. The father was not punished. People even cheered for him.”

Ivan said, “I have even more stories about Russian children. Some parents, who seemed like good people, secretly hated their little girl. They hurt her, hit her for no reason, and even locked her outside at night in the cold. Her own mother did terrible things to her. The poor child would cry and pray to God in the dark, not understanding why she was hurt so much. Why is this allowed to happen, Alyosha? People say it’s because we need to know good and evil, but I don’t think it’s worth it. No lesson is worth the suffering of a little child. I’m sorry if I’m making you sad, Alyosha. I’ll stop if you want.”

Ivan added, “Let me tell you one more story. A long time ago, a rich general owned a lot of land and many servants. One day, a little boy hurt the general’s favorite dog by accident. The general got very angry. The next day, he called everyone to watch. He made the boy stand in front of his mother and set his dogs on the child. The dogs killed the boy in front of everyone. What should happen to the general, Alyosha?”
Alyosha said quietly, “He should be shot.”
Ivan shouted, “See! Even you, Alyosha, have anger inside you.”

Ivan became quiet and said, “I only talked about children to make my point. There is so much suffering in the world. I don’t understand why things are this way. People lost paradise because they wanted freedom, but I still want justice. Not just someday, but now. I want to see the world made right. But what about the children? Why do they have to suffer for others’ mistakes? It’s not fair. If their pain is needed for everyone’s happiness, I don’t want that happiness. I can’t accept it. Even if there is a heaven where all is made good, it’s not worth the tears of one suffering child. I don’t care about punishing the bad people or sending them to hell. I just don’t want children to suffer at all. If that’s the price for harmony, I return my ticket. It’s not God I reject, but the way things are.”
Alyosha whispered, “That’s rebellion.”
Ivan replied, “Maybe, but I want to live. Let me ask you, Alyosha. If you could make everyone happy forever, but you had to hurt one little child to do it, would you agree?”
Alyosha said softly, “No, I wouldn’t.”
Ivan asked, “Do you think people could be happy knowing their happiness was built on a child’s suffering?”
Alyosha answered, “No, I can’t believe that. But there is someone who can forgive everything—Jesus. He gave his innocent life for all. The world is built on him.”
Ivan said, “Ah! You bring in Jesus. I was waiting for that. I even made up a story about Him. It’s not a poem, but I remember it. Want to hear it?”
Alyosha said, “Yes, I’m listening.”
Ivan said, “It’s called ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ It’s a strange story, but I want to tell it to you.”

Ivan began to tell Alyosha a story. He said, “This is a story from long ago, in the 1500s, back when people liked to put heavenly beings, like angels and Jesus, into plays and poems. In those days, people believed that holy people could visit earth, and there were even stories about the Virgin Mary going down to hell to help sinners. My story is like those old tales. In it, Jesus comes back to earth, but not to stay forever—just for a short visit. It’s been fifteen hundred years since people last saw Him, but they still believe He will return.”

Ivan continued, “Jesus comes to Seville, Spain, during the time of the Inquisition. This was a scary time when the Church punished people for their beliefs. The day before, almost a hundred people had been burned for being heretics, and everyone important was there to watch.”

Jesus arrives quietly, but people know right away who He is. They gather around Him. He smiles kindly, and people feel His love. He blesses them, and even just touching Him or His clothes can heal. A blind old man asks Jesus to help him see, and suddenly the man can see. The crowd cries and throws flowers at Jesus’ feet. Then, they bring a small white coffin with a dead girl inside. Her mother begs Jesus to bring her back. Jesus says softly, “Maiden, arise!” and the girl sits up, alive, holding her flowers.

Just then, the Grand Inquisitor (the head of the Inquisition, an old, tall man) walks by. He sees Jesus and the miracle. His face turns dark. He orders his guards to arrest Jesus. The people are so afraid of the Grand Inquisitor that they move aside without a word. The guards take Jesus to a dark prison cell. That night, the Grand Inquisitor comes alone to see Jesus.

The Grand Inquisitor says, “Is it really You? Don’t speak. I know what You would say, but You can’t add anything to what You said long ago. Why have You come to get in our way? Tomorrow, I will burn You at the stake as the worst heretic. The same people who kissed Your feet today will help me burn You tomorrow, just because I say so.”
Alyosha, surprised, asks Ivan, “Does Jesus say anything back?”

Ivan explains, “No, Jesus is silent. The Grand Inquisitor tells Him that the Church has taken over His work. The people believe they are free, but really, they have given up their freedom to the Church. The Grand Inquisitor says, ‘We have made people happy by taking away their freedom and giving them rules to follow.’”

Ivan tells how the Grand Inquisitor reminds Jesus of the three temptations in the wilderness, when the devil asked Jesus to turn stones into bread, jump from the temple, and rule the world. The Grand Inquisitor thinks Jesus made things too hard by giving people freedom instead of taking care of them and making them obey.

The Grand Inquisitor explains, “If You had given people bread, they would have followed You like sheep. But You wanted them to choose You freely. Now, most people are too weak for this freedom. They just want someone to tell them what to do.”

The Grand Inquisitor says the Church now gives people what they really want—miracles, mystery, and authority. He says, “We have fixed Your work. We rule people and make them happy, even if we have to trick them. We took power, even though it means siding with the tempter instead of You. People are happier this way. Only we, the leaders, must carry this heavy secret and be unhappy.”

He continues, “People will thank us for taking their freedom, because they are too weak and want to be cared for like children. We will let them sin, but forgive them, so they will love us even more. They will tell us all their secrets, and we will decide everything for them. We will promise them heaven, but really, only we will know the truth.”

Ivan finishes the story: “When the Grand Inquisitor stops talking, he waits for Jesus to answer. Jesus says nothing, but gently goes up to the old man and kisses him on his lips. The Grand Inquisitor shudders, then opens the door and lets Jesus go, telling Him never to come back. Jesus leaves quietly.”
Alyosha asks, “And the old man?” Ivan replies, “The kiss stays in his heart, but he sticks to his idea.”
Alyosha is upset and asks how Ivan can live or love anything with such sad thoughts in his heart. Ivan says he will try to find the strength to keep going, but maybe only until he is thirty.
Alyosha asks if Ivan believes “everything is lawful,” meaning, if there are no rules, can anyone do anything? Ivan says, “Yes, if there is no God, everything is allowed.”
Alyosha gets up and, instead of saying anything, kisses Ivan on the lips, just like Jesus did in the story.
Ivan laughs and says, “You stole that from my story! Thank you.”

As they leave, Ivan tells Alyosha, “If I can love life, it will be because I remember you. But please, don’t talk to me about these things anymore. If I ever feel lost at thirty, I promise I’ll come find you, wherever you are.”
Ivan and Alyosha go their separate ways. Alyosha hurries to the monastery, thinking about everything that happened and feeling both sad and hopeful.

Ivan left Alyosha and walked back to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s (his father’s) house. As he walked, Ivan felt very sad and upset, but he didn’t really know why. He had felt sad before, and it wasn’t strange now—he was leaving everything behind and planning to start a new life. Still, Ivan couldn’t explain exactly what he wanted or hoped for.

Ivan tried to stop thinking about his feelings, but that didn’t help. He felt like something was bothering him, like when you see something out of place and it annoys you until you fix it. He got closer to the house, feeling more and more annoyed.
At last, Ivan reached the gate and suddenly realized what was making him upset.

Smerdyakov (the servant) was sitting on a bench near the gate. As soon as Ivan saw Smerdyakov, he knew this was the person who was bothering him. Ivan remembered how he had felt gloomy when Alyosha talked about Smerdyakov earlier. Ivan wondered why someone like Smerdyakov could bother him so much.

Ivan had started to really dislike Smerdyakov lately. At first, when Ivan moved to the town, he was interested in Smerdyakov and talked with him a lot. They discussed ideas and even talked about strange things, but Smerdyakov never explained himself clearly. He always seemed to be hiding something or asking sneaky questions. After a while, Smerdyakov started acting like he and Ivan had a secret understanding, which made Ivan even more uncomfortable. Only recently did Ivan realize this was why he disliked Smerdyakov so much.

Ivan tried to walk past Smerdyakov without saying anything, but Smerdyakov stood up, showing he wanted to talk. Ivan stopped, which made him feel even more annoyed. Smerdyakov gave Ivan a look as if they had something important to say to each other.
Ivan wanted to tell Smerdyakov to go away, but instead, he heard himself ask softly, “Is my father still asleep, or has he woken up?”
This surprised Ivan, and he even sat down on the bench with Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov faced him, looking serious.
“Your father is still asleep,” Smerdyakov said slowly, acting like Ivan was the one who started the conversation. “I’m surprised at you, sir,” he added, looking down and playing with his shoe.
Ivan asked, “Why are you surprised at me?” even though he didn’t want to be curious.
Smerdyakov smiled and said, “Why don’t you go to Tchermashnya?” (a nearby town).
Ivan was surprised. “Why should I go to Tchermashnya?”
Smerdyakov said, “Your father has asked you to.”
Ivan lost his patience and shouted, “Say what you want!”
Smerdyakov calmly replied, “Nothing really, just talking.”
After a pause, Smerdyakov said, “I’m in a terrible position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don’t know how to help myself.” Ivan sat down again.

Smerdyakov continued, “Your father and your brother Dmitri are both crazy. Your father keeps asking about Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka). If she doesn’t come, he blames me. Dmitri comes at night with his gun and threatens me if I don’t let him know if Grushenka comes. They both get angrier every day. I’m so scared sometimes I feel like I’ll die.”
Ivan asked, “Why did you start spying for Dmitri?”
Smerdyakov said, “I didn’t want to, but Dmitri made me. He keeps threatening me. I’m sure I’ll have a long fit tomorrow.”
Ivan asked, “What do you mean by a long fit?”
Smerdyakov explained, “A fit that lasts hours, maybe days. Once it happened for three days. I fell from the garret then. The doctor helped me, but I might have died.”
Ivan asked, “How do you know you’ll have a fit tomorrow?”
Smerdyakov replied, “You can’t tell, but I feel it coming.”
Ivan said, “You fell from the garret then.”
Smerdyakov said he still climbs to the garret and could fall again, or fall down the cellar steps.
Ivan said, “You’re talking nonsense. Are you pretending you’ll be sick tomorrow?”
Smerdyakov answered, “If I pretended to have a fit, it would be to save my life. If Grushenka comes while I’m sick, your father can’t blame me for not telling him.”
Ivan got angry. “Dmitri won’t hurt you. He’s just angry. He won’t kill you.”
Smerdyakov said, “He’d kill me first. And I’m afraid people will think I helped him if something bad happens to your father.”
Ivan asked, “Why would they think that?”
Smerdyakov said, “Because I told him the secret signals.”
Ivan asked, “What signals? Tell me clearly.”

Smerdyakov explained: Fyodor Pavlovitch locks himself in at night and gave Smerdyakov secret knocks to use if Grushenka comes, or if something happens. No one else is supposed to know these signals, but now Dmitri knows too.
Ivan asked, “Did you tell Dmitri? How could you?”
Smerdyakov said he was scared and told Dmitri so Dmitri would trust him.
Ivan said, “If you think Dmitri will use the signals, don’t let him in.”
Smerdyakov said, “If I have a fit, I can’t stop him.”
Ivan said, “How do you know you’ll have a fit?”
Smerdyakov said, “I feel it coming. I’m too scared.”
Ivan said, “If you’re sick, let Grigory (the other servant) watch.”

Smerdyakov said, “I can’t tell Grigory without permission. Besides, Grigory is sick, and Marfa Ignatyevna (Grigory’s wife) is going to give him her special medicine tomorrow, which makes them both sleep for a long time. So if I’m sick and they are asleep, no one will stop Dmitri.”
Ivan was shocked. “It sounds like you’re planning all this!”
Smerdyakov answered, “Why would I plan it? It depends on Dmitri.”
Ivan asked, “Why would Dmitri come to see father if Grushenka doesn’t come?”
Smerdyakov said, “Dmitri might come because he’s angry or suspicious. He also knows Fyodor Pavlovitch has an envelope with three thousand roubles for Grushenka. Dmitri thinks the money is his, too.”
Ivan shouted, “Dmitri wouldn’t steal or kill father for money!”

Smerdyakov answered, “He needs money badly. He told me himself that his father owes him three thousand. Also, if Grushenka marries Fyodor Pavlovitch, she’ll get everything, and you and your brothers will get nothing. But if your father dies now, Dmitri could get some money, since there’s no will.”
Ivan shuddered and looked upset.
Ivan then asked, “Why do you want me to go to Tchermashnya? If I go, look at what could happen here.”
Smerdyakov answered softly, “Exactly.”
Ivan pressed, “What do you mean?”
Smerdyakov said, “I feel sorry for you. If I were you, I’d leave rather than stay in such a mess.”
Ivan called Smerdyakov an idiot and a scoundrel, then nearly attacked him, but stopped himself and walked toward the gate.
Ivan turned and said angrily, “I’m leaving for Moscow tomorrow morning.”
Smerdyakov calmly replied, “That’s best. You can always be sent for if something happens.”
Ivan stopped again. Smerdyakov now looked nervous and expectant, as if waiting for Ivan to say something.
Ivan shouted, “Couldn’t I be sent for from Tchermashnya, too, if something happened?”
Smerdyakov muttered, “Yes, from Tchermashnya, too,” looking worried.
Ivan asked, “Is it because Tchermashnya is closer? Or to save me money?”
Smerdyakov answered, “Exactly so...” but Ivan laughed suddenly and walked through the gate, still laughing, though he didn’t really feel happy at all. He was nervous and upset.

Ivan came into the drawing-room and saw his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch. Ivan was upset and did not want to talk. He waved his hands and shouted, “I am going upstairs to my room, not in to you. Good-by!” He hurried past his father without looking at him. Fyodor Pavlovitch was surprised and wanted to say something, but just stood there, watching Ivan walk away.
Fyodor Pavlovitch turned to Smerdyakov (the servant) and asked, “What's the matter with him?” Smerdyakov answered, “Angry about something. Who can tell?”

“Let him be angry then,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch. He told Smerdyakov to bring in the tea and asked if there was any news. Fyodor Pavlovitch then went on asking questions about his visitor, which Smerdyakov did not like. Soon it was late, and the house was locked up. Fyodor Pavlovitch walked around the rooms, waiting for a secret knock at the door. He kept looking out into the dark, but saw nothing.

Ivan stayed up late that night, until two o’clock. He was restless and could not think clearly. He had strange feelings, like wanting to go and hit Smerdyakov, but he did not know why. Sometimes he felt scared for no reason. He even felt angry at his brother Alyosha and at himself. He hardly thought about Katerina Ivanovna, though he remembered telling her he would go to Moscow. But deep down, he thought, “That’s not true. I might not go.”

Later, Ivan remembered how, that night, he quietly opened his door and went out to listen to his father downstairs. He stood on the stairs, listening for a long time, holding his breath. He called this a shameful thing to do and felt bad about it later. He didn’t hate his father just then; he was just curious about what he was doing, waiting for someone to knock. Ivan did this twice that night.

At about two o’clock, when the house was quiet, Ivan finally went to bed and slept well. He woke up early the next morning, feeling full of energy. He got up, packed his things, and was ready to leave. When Marfa Ignatyevna (the housekeeper) came in to ask about tea, Ivan was in a hurry but looked cheerful. He told his father that he was leaving for Moscow in an hour and asked for horses. Fyodor Pavlovitch was not surprised and did not seem sad to see Ivan go. Instead, he remembered something important he wanted Ivan to do.
“Do me a favor, my boy,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch. “Go to Tchermashnya on the way. It’s just a bit out of your way, but I have business there.”
Ivan said, “I can’t. The train leaves for Moscow at seven o’clock tonight. I’ll barely make it.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch begged him to go, saying he needed someone to talk to a merchant named Gorstkin about selling some timber. He explained that Gorstkin might pay more than another buyer and that it was important to make a deal soon.
Ivan said, “Let the priest do it.”

But Fyodor Pavlovitch insisted the priest wasn’t good at business. He told Ivan to watch Gorstkin’s beard—if he got cross and his beard shook, he was telling the truth. If he stroked his beard and grinned, he was lying. Fyodor Pavlovitch wrote a note for Ivan to give to Gorstkin.
Ivan said he wouldn’t be any good at this job.
Fyodor Pavlovitch still tried to persuade him, saying that Ivan was clever and just needed to see if Gorstkin was serious.
Ivan finally said in a bitter way, “You want me to go to that place yourself, then?” Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t notice Ivan was upset and took this as a yes.
“Then you’ll go? I’ll write the note now,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Ivan replied, “I’ll decide on the way.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch told Ivan to write to him if the deal was real, and promised he could go to Venice after.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was happy, wrote the note, and had lunch brought in. He didn’t talk about Dmitri. When Ivan left, his father tried to kiss him, but Ivan only shook hands. Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed this and stopped himself.
“Good luck to you! Come visit again. Christ be with you!” called Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Ivan got into the carriage.
“Good-by, Ivan! Don’t be too hard on me!” his father called out.

Smerdyakov, Marfa, and Grigory came out to say goodbye. Ivan gave them each some money. Smerdyakov helped with the rug. Ivan suddenly said, “I am going to Tchermashnya,” and laughed in a strange way. Smerdyakov answered, “It’s always worth talking to a clever man,” looking at Ivan in a special way.

As the carriage rolled away, Ivan looked at the fields and trees and felt happy for a moment. He tried to talk to the driver, but realized he wasn’t really listening. The air was fresh, and he thought about Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna, but these thoughts floated away. They reached the station, changed horses, and hurried to Volovya. Ivan wondered what Smerdyakov really meant. At the station, the drivers argued about taking him to Tchermashnya.
Ivan decided, “I won’t go to Tchermashnya. Can I still catch the train?”
“Yes, if we hurry,” said a driver.
Ivan asked if someone could tell his father he hadn’t gone to Tchermashnya.
Mitri, one of the drivers, said he could do it.
Ivan gave Mitri some money and laughed. Mitri laughed too and promised to do it.

At seven o’clock, Ivan got on the train to Moscow. He told himself, “Away with the past. I want a new life and no news from the old one.” But instead of being happy, Ivan felt very sad and upset all night. As the train got near Moscow, he thought, “I am a scoundrel.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch was glad Ivan had left and drank brandy. Suddenly, something bad happened. Smerdyakov fell down the cellar steps and had a fit. Marfa heard his scream and called for help. They found Smerdyakov shaking and foaming at the mouth, but he was not badly hurt. They carried him out with help from neighbors. Fyodor Pavlovitch was worried. Doctor Herzenstube came and said the fit was strong and could be dangerous. Smerdyakov was moved to a room near Grigory and Marfa’s.

More troubles came for Fyodor Pavlovitch that day. Marfa cooked dinner, but the soup and chicken tasted bad. She said the chicken was old and she wasn’t a cook. Grigory also became sick with back pain. That evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch was very nervous because he expected Grushenka (the woman he loved) to visit. Smerdyakov had told him she would come. Fyodor Pavlovitch waited and listened carefully, hoping she would knock on the window. He was excited and sure she would come this time.

When Alyosha walked into Father Zossima’s small room, he was surprised. He thought he would find Father Zossima very sick or maybe even unconscious. Instead, Father Zossima was sitting up in his chair, looking happy and smiling, though he was weak. There were four visitors with him: Father Iosif, Father Païssy, Father Mihaïl (the warden), and Father Anfim (a very old monk). Porfiry, a young helper, was also there. All these monks were his friends. They had come early and waited for him to wake up, because Father Païssy believed Father Zossima’s promise that he would get up and talk to them one last time, just as he said he would.
The room was very small, so everyone had to squeeze in on chairs. It was getting dark, but lamps and candles made the room bright.
When Alyosha stood shyly in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled and held out his hand.
“Welcome, my dear Alyosha, I knew you would come,” he said.
Alyosha walked up, bowed down to the floor, and began to cry. He felt so many emotions inside.

Father Zossima gently put his hand on Alyosha’s head and said, “Don’t cry for me yet. See, I am still sitting up and talking. Maybe I will live for many more years, as the kind woman from Vishegorye wished. God bless her and her little girl, Lizaveta.” Then he asked Porfiry if he had given the sixty copecks the woman gave to someone poorer, like he asked.
Porfiry said he had given the money to a poor widow whose house had burned down, just as Father Zossima told him.
“Get up, Alyosha,” Father Zossima said. “Have you seen your brother?” Alyosha thought it was odd he only asked about one brother.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” Alyosha replied.
“I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to.”
“I only saw him yesterday. I couldn’t find him today,” said Alyosha.
“Try again tomorrow. Hurry, maybe you can still stop something bad from happening. I bowed down because of the great suffering he will have.”
Father Zossima stopped and looked worried. His words sounded strange. Alyosha asked, “Father, what suffering do you mean?”

“Don’t ask, Alyosha. Yesterday, I saw something in his eyes that scared me. It was like seeing his whole sad future there. I sent you to him because I hoped your kind face would help him. But everything is in God’s hands. Remember, when a seed dies, it grows into much fruit. Alyosha, I have often blessed you in my heart. I think you will go out into the world and live like a monk in your soul. You will have enemies, but even they will love you. You will have trouble, but you’ll find happiness in it and help others be happy, too. That’s who you are.”

Then Father Zossima told his friends why Alyosha was so dear to him. He explained that, when he was a child, he had an older brother who died at seventeen. That brother had been a sign from God for him. He felt Alyosha reminded him of his brother, not just in face but in spirit. Sometimes, he almost thought Alyosha was his brother come back to inspire him. He told Porfiry, the young helper, that he loved him too, even if he seemed to love Alyosha more. Father Zossima said his brother was the most important person in his life, and now, at the end, memories of his brother filled his heart.

(Merged) This last talk with Father Zossima was remembered and written down later by Alyosha Karamazov. Maybe Alyosha added things from other talks, but this is what he remembered. Father Zossima spoke most of the time, but sometimes others joined in, or Father Païssy read from the Bible. That evening, Father Zossima seemed stronger than before, as if love gave him new energy, though he would soon die. Now, the story continues as Alyosha wrote it.

Father Zossima began telling about his life. He was born in a northern town called V. His father was a gentleman, but not important. He died when Zossima was only two, so Zossima did not remember him. His mother kept their small house and enough money to care for her two sons: Markel, the elder brother, and Zossima. Markel was eight years older, quiet, and kind. Six months before Markel died at seventeen, he became friends with a smart man who had been sent away from Moscow. Markel visited him often, but then the man left town.
When Lent started, Markel refused to fast and even said, “There is no God,” which made everyone upset. Zossima was only nine, but shocked to hear such things.

During Lent, Markel became very sick with a disease called consumption. The doctor said he would not live through the spring. Their mother begged Markel to go to church and take the sacrament, but this made him angry. Still, he soon realized he was truly sick, and became thoughtful. He said once at dinner that he probably wouldn’t live another year.

Three days later, it was Holy Week. Markel started going to church, saying, “I’m doing this to please you, Mother.” She cried with both joy and sadness. But soon he was too ill and had to stay in bed, so the priest came to their house.

It was a beautiful Easter time. Markel coughed at night but in the morning sat up in a chair, smiling gently. He seemed changed—sweet and loving. The old nurse would light the lamp before the holy picture, and now Markel wanted her to light it, not stop her.
“Light it, dear,” he said. “You are praying when you light it. I am praying when I watch you. We both pray to the same God.”
These words seemed strange to the family, but they made their mother cry and smile. Markel said, “Mother, don’t cry. Life is joyful.”
“How can you be joyful when you are so sick at night?” she asked.
“Don’t cry, Mother,” he answered. “Life is paradise, but we don’t see it. If we did, we’d have heaven on earth.”
Everyone was surprised by his new, kind words. When friends visited, Markel thanked them for loving him and wondered why he didn’t understand love before.
When the servants came in, Markel said, “Dear people, why do you do so much for me? If I lived, I would serve you, for everyone should serve each other.”
Their mother thought it was just his illness talking.
Markel said, “There must be masters and servants, but I want to serve my servants, too. And I believe that everyone has sinned against everyone, and I most of all.”
“How could you have sinned more than robbers or murderers?” his mother asked, smiling through tears.
“Mother, believe me. We are all responsible for everyone else and everything. I don’t know how to explain it, but I feel it.”

Every day, Markel grew sweeter and more loving. When the doctor came, Markel joked, “Do I have another day left?” The doctor said, “You have many days,” but Markel replied, “Why count? One day is enough for happiness. Why do we fight? Let’s love each other.”
The doctor told their mother privately that Markel wouldn’t live long and that the sickness was hurting his mind.

Markel’s window looked out to a lovely garden. He loved to watch the birds and asked even their forgiveness, saying, “Birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” He cried tears of joy, thinking everything was beautiful and he hadn’t noticed before.
“You take too much blame on yourself,” his mother said.
“It’s for joy, not sadness, that I cry,” Markel answered. “If I have sinned against all, they forgive me, too. That is heaven. Am I not in heaven now?”
Zossima remembered going into Markel’s room one evening. Markel put his hands lovingly on Zossima’s shoulders and looked at him quietly.
“Go play now, enjoy life for me too,” Markel said.

Zossima ran out to play, and he remembered those words all his life. Markel died three weeks after Easter, always happy and loving until the end. His death was talked about in the town. Zossima cried at his funeral, and though he was young, the memory stayed in his heart forever.

After Markel died, Zossima’s mother decided to send him to school in Petersburg, hoping for a good future for him, though it was hard for her. She took him there, and he never saw her again. She died three years later, always sad over her two sons.

Zossima kept precious memories from his childhood, especially of reading the Bible at home. He loved a picture book called “A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament” and learned to read with it. He remembered going to church with his mother one Easter week, seeing the smoke from the incense and hearing the story of Job for the first time, which touched his heart.

Zossima said he always remembered that story of Job, how Job lost everything but still said, “Blessed be the name of the Lord.” Even though people sometimes questioned God for letting Job suffer, Zossima saw that the story showed mystery and hope. He said, as people get older, even deep sorrow can become gentle, happy memories. He felt his life was ending, but each day felt closer to a new, wonderful life with God.

Zossima said that priests sometimes complain about being poor and not able to teach the Bible. But he thought they could still find a little time to read the Bible to children, even just once a week. If they did this with love and kindness, people would understand. He gave examples of Bible stories that touched people’s hearts, like Joseph’s brothers selling him, and Joseph forgiving them later. He believed these stories would help people and make them grateful, and even help the priests in their daily lives.

Zossima loved the Bible and said even a small story can grow in someone’s heart. He encouraged priests to read simple stories, like Esther, Jonah, and the parables of Jesus, so people, especially children, would learn and remember them. He believed the people would be thankful and help the priests more.
Zossima said that to help people, priests should show a good example and share God’s Word, because people’s hearts are hungry for it.

When Zossima was young, he traveled across Russia with Father Anfim to collect money for their monastery. One night, they stayed by a river with fishermen. A young man joined them, and he loved the forest and birds. They talked about how everything in nature is made by God and shows His greatness.
Zossima told the boy that all animals are gentle and innocent, and that Christ loves them too, because the Word of God is for all.
The boy asked, “Is Christ with them too?”

Zossima said, “Yes, Christ is with all creation.” He told a story about a saint who fed a wild bear, and the bear walked away peacefully. The boy was happy to hear that Christ loved the bear too. That night, the boy slept peacefully, and Zossima prayed for him.

When I was young, I spent almost eight years at a military school in Petersburg. There, I learned many new things, but also became rude and wild. I acted proud and careless, especially because I had money and liked to have fun.
I never opened my Bible during those years, even though I always carried it with me. I didn't know then how important it would be for me later.

After four years of this life, our regiment moved to the town of K. The people there liked parties and were very friendly. I met a kind and smart young woman from a respected family. I liked her and thought she liked me too. But I wasn’t really in love; I just admired her goodness. I didn’t want to give up my fun life, so I waited instead of telling her my true feelings.

When I returned after two months away, I found that she had married a rich landowner. He was older, well-educated, and important in society. I was shocked and angry, especially when I learned everyone else knew about their engagement except me. I felt embarrassed and wanted revenge.

I insulted her husband in front of many people and challenged him to a duel. Back then, officers often fought duels even though it was against the rules. My friend from the regiment agreed to help me.

The night before the duel, I became very angry and hit my servant, Afanasy, very hard. Later, when I woke up early in the morning, I felt awful. I realized I was not upset about the duel, but because I had been so cruel to Afanasy. I remembered my brother Markel saying that we are all responsible for each other.
I hurried to Afanasy’s room and asked him to forgive me. He was surprised, and I knelt at his feet. He cried, and I left feeling happier and lighter.

At the duel, my opponent shot first, but he only grazed my cheek. I threw my pistol away and asked his forgiveness for insulting him. The others were surprised, but I explained that it was better to tell the truth and repent, even during a duel. My opponent wanted to shake hands, but I said maybe later, when I had changed more.

Afterward, my fellow officers were confused. Some said I had disgraced the regiment, others said I was brave. I told them I had already decided to leave and become a monk. They laughed, but were kind to me and even tried to change my mind.

The people in the town also laughed, but they liked me. At a gathering, the young woman for whom I had fought the duel thanked me sincerely, and her husband did too. A serious man named Mihail, whom I barely knew, also came to talk to me.
Mihail was respected, rich, and known for helping others. Soon, he started visiting me every evening. He never talked much about himself, but always asked about my thoughts and feelings.
We often talked about how people should care for each other and how heaven is inside everyone. Mihail believed that one day, people would understand this and stop being so selfish and alone.
One night, Mihail suddenly told me, “I murdered someone.” I was shocked, but he explained everything over several days.

Fourteen years before, Mihail had fallen in love with a woman, but she loved someone else. In anger, he broke into her house and killed her. He tried to make it look like a servant had done it. The servant was blamed and died in prison, but no one suspected Mihail.

Mihail felt sad about losing the woman he loved, but not about the murder at first. He tried to do good things and help people, hoping this would make up for his crime. He got married and had children, but he felt guilty. He wondered how he could teach his children goodness when he had done something so wrong.
His guilt grew stronger, and he thought about confessing. Watching me ask for forgiveness after my duel gave him the courage to decide to tell the truth.
Mihail worried about his wife and children. He asked me what he should do. I told him to confess and trust that his children would understand one day.
For more than two weeks, Mihail kept coming to see me. Some days he was ready to confess, other days he was afraid. He worried that people would not believe him, or that his family would suffer.
I showed him some verses from the Bible to encourage him. Finally, Mihail decided to confess.

On his birthday, Mihail gathered many people and confessed to the crime. He showed them the things he had taken from the murdered woman as proof. Most people thought he was insane and did not believe him.
Soon after, Mihail became very ill. His wife and the townspeople blamed me, thinking my talks with him had made him sick. I was not allowed to visit him at first.

When I finally saw Mihail, he was weak but peaceful. He told me he was glad he had confessed, and now he felt God’s mercy near him. He also told me that one night he almost came back to kill me, because he was so angry and afraid, but he did not do it.

Mihail died a week later. Many people came to his funeral, but afterward, the townspeople blamed me and avoided me. Some began to believe Mihail’s story and asked me about it, but I said nothing. Soon, I left the town and entered a monastery. To this day, I remember Mihail in my prayers, because he suffered greatly.
This part is about a Russian monk and why he is important.

What is a monk? Some people today laugh at monks or think badly of them. They say some monks are lazy or act badly. But there are also many good monks who are gentle and pray quietly. These monks keep the love of God safe in their hearts. Maybe, one day, these gentle monks will help save Russia. They keep the true image of Christ safe, waiting for the right time to help the world.

I believe monks are important. Some people in the world have forgotten about God and only care about science and their own wishes. They think freedom means doing whatever you want. But this only leads to sadness and selfishness.

People are told to want more and more things, thinking this is freedom. The rich end up lonely and sad. The poor feel jealous and angry because they can’t get what they want. People say the world is becoming kinder, but this isn’t true.

Don’t believe that wanting more makes people happy or free. People start to care only about money, fancy things, and showing off. If they can’t get what they want, they may even hurt themselves or others. The poor often become sad and drink too much. Is this real freedom? I knew a man who said he fought for freedom, but he almost gave up everything just for a piece of tobacco!

People who only care about themselves can’t really help others for long. Instead of love and togetherness, there is more fighting and loneliness. When people are trapped by their wants, they forget about others and feel alone. There are more things in the world now, but less joy.

Life in a monastery is different. Monks follow rules, pray, and give up extra wants. People laugh at this, but it brings real freedom and joy. Who can do more for others—the person who is trapped by things, or the one who is free inside? Monks are sometimes told they don’t help people, but true monks do care. In the past, great leaders came from among the monks. This can happen again. The Russian monk has always cared for the people. Monks must remember to care for and teach the peasants, for the peasants have God in their hearts.

Peasants have their own problems. Bad habits like drinking hurt them and their families. Even children work too hard in factories, get sick, and see bad things. Children need sunshine, play, and love. Monks should hurry to help and teach people to stop hurting children.
Even though peasants do wrong, they know it is wrong and feel sorry. They still believe in God and goodness.

The rich and clever try to make rules without God. Some say there is no right or wrong. In some places, people are angry and fight the rich. But angry fighting is not the answer. God will save Russia through the people’s faith and kindness.
I have always noticed how most Russian people have dignity and are not jealous, even if they are poor. They respect others but know they are people, too.

Poor people are often kinder than the rich. I dream that one day, the rich will feel sorry for having too much, and the poor will forgive them. Real equality comes from seeing everyone as valuable, not just sharing money. The image of Christ will shine from our people.
Once, I met my old servant, Afanasy, in a town. He was so happy to see me! He took me to his house.
Afanasy was married with two children. They lived simply but were kind. They made tea for me and brought their children for me to bless.
I told Afanasy I would pray for his family. He was surprised to see me, his old master, as a monk. He cried.
I told him not to be sad, but to be happy for me.
Afanasy didn’t say much, but he was very gentle and caring.
He asked what happened to my money.
I told him I gave it to the monastery. We all share what we have.
When I was leaving, Afanasy gave me money for the monastery and also some for myself. He wanted to help me on my journey.
I left happy, thinking about how good it was that God let us meet again.
I never saw Afanasy again. We used to be master and servant, but now we were just people, joined by kindness. I hope one day all people can feel this way toward each other.
When I was young, I sometimes got mad at servants. But my brother once said, “Do I deserve to have another person serve me?” That made me think.
There will always be servants, but we should treat them kindly, like family. Why can’t I also serve my servant? One day, people will want to help others, not boss them around.
I believe that one day, people’s greatest happiness will be in doing kind things, not in showing off or being greedy. People may laugh at this idea, but I believe it will happen with Christ’s help.
If people try to make a good world without Christ, it won’t work. They may dream of unity, but without love, it leads to fighting. Only Christ’s love can save us from destroying each other.
Once, when I said we should treat servants kindly, people laughed at me. But I think I was right.
Young people, don’t forget to pray. Prayer helps you grow inside. Pray for everyone, even those you don’t know. Many people die alone, but your prayer can help them feel loved.

Don’t be afraid of people’s sins. Love everyone, even when they do wrong. Love everything—animals, plants, and people. If you love everything, you will see the mystery of God in the world. Love children, for they are pure and help us be kinder. Father Anfim taught me to love children. He always shared sweets with them.
When you see people do wrong, don’t use force. Use humble love. It is the strongest thing in the world.
Watch yourself every day. Even if you are mean to a child without noticing, the child will remember. Love is a teacher, but it takes work to learn to love always.
My brother once asked birds to forgive him. That may sound silly, but everything in the world is connected. If you are kinder, animals and children will be happier.
Pray for joy. Be happy like children. Don’t say, “Evil is too strong, and we are weak.” Instead, take responsibility for the world’s problems. If you do, you will see that you can help.

The pride of Satan is hard to understand, so don’t try to use that as an excuse. God asks us to do what we can understand. Even if much is hidden from us, we have a special sense of belonging to another, better world.
God planted seeds from different worlds here, and everything grows because it feels connected to those worlds. If we lose that feeling, we lose our happiness and love for life.

Remember, you cannot judge others unless you see that you could do the same wrong. If you feel sorry for someone’s crime, take it on yourself and forgive them. Even if they don’t change, don’t lose hope. Someday, someone will understand and be better. That is what the saints believed.

Keep working to help others. If you forget to do good, get up and do it right away. If others won’t listen to you, serve them quietly. Even if you are alone, pray and love the earth. If only two good people are together, that is enough to keep love alive.
If you do wrong and feel sad, be glad that others are good.

If you see evil and feel angry, do not wish for revenge. Instead, take the suffering on yourself. Remember, if you had been a light to others, maybe they wouldn’t have done wrong. If your goodness doesn’t help them now, it might help someone in the future. The joy you feel is your reward.

What is hell? I think it is the pain of not being able to love. When we are alive, we can love and do good. If we waste that chance, after death we see others loving, but we cannot join them. That is the real suffering.

Some think hell is burning fire, but I think the worst pain is inside, not outside. Even if people in heaven forgive those in hell, it will only make them sadder because they cannot love back. But maybe, by accepting this, they can still feel a little love.
Some people are proud and angry even in hell. They refuse to accept love and keep hurting themselves with their own hate. They wish for everything to end, but it never will.
Father Zossima’s death was a surprise. He seemed cheerful, but then he felt pain in his chest. He smiled, knelt on the floor, and quietly died, praying and kissing the ground.
The news spread quickly. The monks and people in the town heard about it, and crowds came to the monastery. Something surprising happened afterward, and people remember that day even now.

Father Zossima’s body was prepared for burial by Father Païssy. Monk bodies are not washed; instead, Father Païssy wiped the body with warm water, making the sign of the cross on the forehead, chest, hands, feet, and knees. He dressed Father Zossima in his monk’s clothes and put a special hood on his head. An icon of Jesus was placed in his hands, and his face was covered with black cloth. Early in the morning, they placed him in his coffin and set it in the big room where he used to meet people. Since Father Zossima was a priest and a strict monk, monks read the Gospel over him. Father Iosif began reading after the service. Father Païssy wanted to keep reading, but he and the head of the monastery were busy because there was a strange excitement among the monks and visitors. People came from the town, and the crowd grew more restless. Father Païssy and the Superintendent tried to calm everyone.

When morning came, people started bringing sick children to Father Zossima's coffin. They believed the elder’s body could heal them. It was clear that many people in town thought Father Zossima was a saint, not just the poor, but also richer people.

Father Païssy thought this excitement and hope for miracles was not proper. He tried to tell the monks to be calm and not expect something amazing right away, since monks should not act like people in the world.

But most people did not listen to him. Secretly, Father Païssy also hoped for a miracle, but he was bothered by how impatient everyone was. He especially disliked seeing Rakitin and the monk from Obdorsk in the crowd. He felt suspicious of them, though he knew he shouldn’t judge.
The monk from Obdorsk was the most restless. He hurried everywhere, asking questions and whispering to people, looking impatient and even angry.

Rakitin was there because Madame Hohlakov, who was very curious but not allowed in, sent him to watch and write her letters about everything that happened. She thought Rakitin was very religious, but he just acted in whatever way would help him.

It was a sunny day, and many visitors walked around the graves near the church. Father Païssy remembered he hadn’t seen Alyosha since the night. He soon spotted Alyosha sitting by himself, hiding behind a tombstone in the garden. Alyosha was crying hard, his face in his hands, shaking with sobs. Father Païssy stood by him for a while.
“Enough, dear son, enough,” said Father Païssy gently. “Why do you cry? This is the greatest day for him. Think where he is now!”
Alyosha looked at him, his face puffy from crying, but turned away and hid his face again.
“Maybe it is good to cry,” said Father Païssy softly. “Jesus sent you those tears.”
Father Païssy thought Alyosha’s tears would help to heal his heart. He walked away quickly because he felt he might start crying too.

Time passed. Monks kept reading prayers and the Gospel by Father Zossima’s coffin. Before three o’clock, something happened that no one expected. It was small, but caused a big stir in the town and the monastery. It was something that would change Alyosha’s heart and mind forever.

When Father Zossima’s body was put in the coffin before dawn, someone suggested opening the windows, but most people ignored it. They thought the body of such a holy man would not show any sign of decay, and they expected something special to happen.
