But soon after midday, people started to notice something and kept quiet at first. By three o’clock, it was obvious: a smell was coming from the coffin. News spread quickly among the monks and visitors, and then to the town. Unbelievers were happy, but some believers were also pleased, remembering how Father Zossima himself had said people sometimes like to see the good fall.

The smell of decay from the coffin grew stronger. This had never happened before in their monastery to someone so respected. In the past, holy monks had died and their bodies had decayed too, but no one made a fuss. Some monks in the past had even had bodies that did not decay and were thought to be saints. Now, many people were upset or shocked.

One monk, Job, who died at 105, was famous for being very holy, and his tomb was respected. Another, Father Varsonofy, was also remembered as a saint. There were stories that these two did not decay and that their bodies even smelled sweet.

Even with these stories, it was hard to explain why people were acting so foolishly at Father Zossima’s coffin. Some monks disliked the idea of elders, and others were jealous of Father Zossima’s fame. Some were happy about the quick decay, since it seemed to prove he wasn’t a saint. Others who loved him felt ashamed or upset.

As the smell grew, monks would walk into the cell, stay a short time, and hurry out to tell others. Some looked sad, but some were clearly happy. Even though most monks had loved Father Zossima, now the ones who disliked him seemed to be in charge.

Educated visitors from town soon came to see for themselves. Peasants mostly stayed outside. After three o’clock, more and more people arrived because of the news. Father Païssy kept reading the Gospel out loud, but soon he heard people whispering, “This is God’s judgment, not man’s.” The first to say this out loud was a respected man from town, but the monks had been whispering it already. The mood was changing, and people stopped hiding their true feelings.
Some monks said, pretending to be sad, “Why did this happen? He was so thin, there was little to decay.”
Others quickly added, “It must be a sign from heaven.” They said if decay was normal, it would take longer, but this was too fast, so it must be a message from God.

Gentle Father Iosif tried to say that not all saints’ bodies stay untouched, and that the Orthodox Church does not teach this as a rule. On Mount Athos, he said, the real sign was the color of the bones after many years, not the body right after death.
But most monks ignored him and even made fun of his words. They wanted to stick to old beliefs and not listen to new ideas.
Some sneered that monks on Mount Athos had forgotten true faith because they lived among the Turks and had no bells.

Father Iosif walked away, very sad, because he saw that people were becoming disobedient and things were getting out of control. Monks who loved the elder felt afraid and looked at each other in worry. Those who disliked elders became bold. Some said, “Father Varsonofy’s body did not decay, but he was holy, not just an elder.”

People started criticizing Father Zossima. Some said his teachings were too joyful, or that he did not believe in real fire in hell. Others said he liked sweet foods and tea, which was not proper for a strict monk. Some said he was proud because people knelt before him. Even older monks who had been silent now spoke against him, and their words influenced younger monks. The monk from Obdorsk listened and agreed, saying Father Ferapont was right. Just then, Father Ferapont arrived.

Father Ferapont rarely left his small hut, and he was not made to follow all the rules because people thought he was a very strict and holy man. Some monks even thought he was holier than all of them.
Father Ferapont especially disliked Father Zossima. News of the “sign” reached him, probably brought by the monk from Obdorsk.
Father Païssy, still reading by the coffin, knew what was happening outside, even if he couldn’t hear all the words. He waited calmly to see what would happen next.

Suddenly, there was a loud noise in the hallway. Father Ferapont stormed in, followed by a crowd of monks and townspeople. Most stayed outside, waiting to see what he would do. Father Ferapont raised his arms, and the monk from Obdorsk peeked in behind him.
Father Ferapont shouted, “Casting out I cast out!” and made the sign of the cross at all four corners of the room. Everyone knew he always did this to drive away evil spirits.
“Satan, go away!” he yelled again and again, making the sign of the cross.
He wore a rough robe tied with rope, his chest hairy, feet bare, and the chains he wore under his clothes clanked as he moved.
Father Païssy stopped reading and stepped toward him, waiting.
“Why have you come, Father? Why do you disturb the peace?” Father Païssy asked sternly.
“I came to drive out your visitors—the evil spirits,” shouted Father Ferapont. “I want to sweep them out with a broom.”
Father Païssy answered, “Maybe you are serving evil yourself. Who can say they are holy? Can you, Father?”

“I am not holy,” declared Father Ferapont loudly. “I do not let people bow to me. Your dead man did not even believe in devils. He gave medicine instead of fighting them. Now he stinks, which is a sign from God.”

(Father Ferapont was talking about a time when a monk saw evil spirits. Father Zossima told him to pray and fast, but also to take medicine. Some people thought this was wrong, and Father Ferapont was most upset.)
“Go away, Father!” commanded Father Païssy. “God will judge. Maybe this is a sign none of us understands. Do not trouble the others.”
“He did not fast properly, and that is why this happened. He liked sweets and tea, and now he is punished,” Father Ferapont shouted, getting more and more excited.
“You speak lightly, Father,” said Father Païssy, raising his voice. “I respect your fasting, but you talk like a silly child. Go away, I command you!”
“I will go,” said Father Ferapont, sounding sad but still angry. “You learned men look down on me. God has kept me safe from your cleverness.”

Father Païssy waited. Father Ferapont leaned his head on his hand, looked at the coffin, and sang softly, “Tomorrow they will sing a grand song over him, but over me just a simple one.” He shouted, “You are proud here!” and quickly left.

The crowd outside moved. Some followed him, but most stayed. Suddenly, Father Ferapont turned to the setting sun, raised his arms, and fell to the ground crying out, “My God has conquered! Christ has conquered the sun!” He sobbed like a child, his arms spread on the ground. Everyone rushed to him, and many started crying too.

People shouted, “He is the real saint! He should be elder!” Others said he would never be an elder because he would refuse it. The excitement grew, but just then the bell rang for service. People crossed themselves and hurried to church. Father Ferapont got up, crossed himself, and went back to his hut, still muttering. Father Païssy let Father Iosif read for him and went outside. The shouting did not disturb him, but he suddenly felt very sad. He realized it was because he saw Alyosha in the crowd and cared for him deeply.
Just then, Alyosha hurried past, not going to church. Their eyes met. Father Païssy saw that something big was changing in Alyosha.
“Have you lost your faith, too?” Father Païssy called sadly. “Are you joining those who doubt?”
Alyosha looked at him but quickly looked away, standing sideways and silent.
“Where are you going? The bell is calling us,” Father Païssy asked, but Alyosha did not answer.
“Are you leaving the hermitage without asking for a blessing?” Father Païssy said.
Alyosha gave a strange smile, looked at Father Païssy with a sad, strange look, waved his hand, and quickly walked away toward the gates.
“You will come back,” whispered Father Païssy, watching him go with sadness.

Father Païssy (a kind priest) was sure that Alyosha would come back. Father Païssy understood that Alyosha was having a hard time. Alyosha believed in God very much, but he still felt sad and upset. Later, Alyosha would remember this day as one of the hardest in his life. Alyosha was sad because his dear teacher, Father Zossima, had died and his body did not perform miracles. Instead, his body began to decay, and this made Alyosha very upset. Some people might laugh at Alyosha for being so sad, but his sadness showed how much he loved and cared.

Alyosha did not care about miracles for their own sake. He loved his teacher, Father Zossima, more than anyone else, and he wanted everyone to see how good and holy Father Zossima was. Alyosha had spent so much time loving and admiring his teacher that he forgot everything else, even his brothers Dmitri and Ivan, and his promise to help Ilusha’s father. He wanted justice for Father Zossima, and he wanted people to respect him. Everyone in the monastery hoped for miracles from Father Zossima, even wise people like Father Païssy, so Alyosha did too. But most of all, he wanted what was right.

Now, instead of being honored, Father Zossima was made fun of by others. Alyosha could not understand why such a good man was treated so badly. Why would God let this happen? Why didn’t God give a sign and help Father Zossima? Alyosha’s heart hurt because his beloved teacher seemed shamed in front of everyone. He wondered why God would let something so unfair happen.

Alyosha’s love for Father Zossima was so strong that he could not help feeling upset. He even remembered words from a talk with his brother Ivan, which now bothered him. Alyosha still loved God, but he was confused and hurt. Ivan’s words made him wonder about God’s world, and Alyosha felt even sadder.
It was getting dark when Rakitin (another young man from the monastery) saw Alyosha lying face down on the ground under a tree. Rakitin called out to him.

Alyosha sat up and leaned against the tree. He looked sad and tired. Rakitin teased him, asking if he was upset just because Father Zossima’s body had started to smell. Rakitin was surprised that Alyosha had believed in miracles.
Alyosha answered that he believed, he wanted to believe, and he would keep believing. Rakitin joked that Alyosha was angry at God for not giving Father Zossima a special honor.
Alyosha replied that he was not angry at God, but he just could not accept the world the way it was.

Rakitin changed the subject and asked if Alyosha had eaten anything. Alyosha could not remember. Rakitin offered him some sausage and vodka, thinking Alyosha would not want it. But Alyosha said yes to both.
Rakitin was surprised. He told Alyosha that Ivan had left for Moscow. Alyosha remembered his brother Dmitri for a moment, but he was too sad to care.
Rakitin talked about Madame Hohlakov, who was upset about Father Zossima too. Then Rakitin got an idea and asked if Alyosha wanted to go visit Grushenka (a woman in town). Alyosha agreed calmly.

Rakitin was shocked, but he took Alyosha by the arm and led him on the path. Rakitin was quiet, thinking about his own reasons for bringing Alyosha to Grushenka. Rakitin wanted to see Alyosha, who was always good, do something wrong, and he also hoped to get something for himself.
Rakitin thought, “Now is the perfect time,” and hurried Alyosha along.

Grushenka lived in a small wooden house near the big cathedral in town. The house belonged to the widow Morozov, who lived quietly with her two old nieces. Grushenka had rented the lodge for four years, thanks to her friend, the merchant Samsonov, who wanted the widow to watch over her. But soon, the widow stopped paying attention to Grushenka. People in town didn’t know much about Grushenka’s past. They whispered that when she was seventeen, an officer had betrayed her, then left and married someone else. Grushenka, whose real name was Agrafena Alexandrovna, was from a good family but had become poor until Samsonov helped her.

After four years, Grushenka changed from a sad, shy girl into a strong, proud woman. She was very clever with money and had saved up a small fortune, even working with old Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov to make money from bad debts. Many men tried to win her love, but except for Samsonov, she kept them all away.

Samsonov was very rich and strict. As he grew older and sicker, he trusted Grushenka more and more, though he never gave her much money. When he died, he left all his money to his sons, but he had given Grushenka some advice to help her in business.

Fyodor Pavlovitch first met Grushenka because of business, but soon he fell in love with her. Samsonov found this funny, but when Dmitri, Fyodor’s son, also fell in love with her, Samsonov became serious and told Grushenka to choose carefully between father and son.

Many people in town knew that both Fyodor and Dmitri Karamazov wanted to win Grushenka’s heart, but no one really understood how she felt. Grushenka lived simply with two servants, an old cook and the cook’s granddaughter. Her rooms were not fancy, but she managed with what she had.

One evening, Rakitin and Alyosha came to visit Grushenka. It was dark, and she was lying on a sofa, looking worried and waiting for someone. When she heard them, she was scared at first, thinking it was Dmitri, but the maid told her it was just visitors.

Grushenka was surprised and happy to see Alyosha, though she was a little upset at Rakitin for scaring her. She told them she had tricked Dmitri by saying she’d be at Samsonov’s house for the evening, but really she had come back to her lodge to wait for some news.
Grushenka was nervous, thinking Dmitri might be outside watching. She wanted the shutters closed so he wouldn’t see any light.

Rakitin asked why she was afraid of Dmitri. Grushenka explained she was expecting important news and didn’t want Dmitri to bother her. She had told him she’d be away until midnight, but she had run home quickly after leaving Samsonov’s house.
Grushenka said she was dressed up because she wanted to be ready to leave quickly if her special message arrived. Rakitin teased her about being dressed for a ball, but she said he didn’t understand.
Grushenka was truly happy to see Alyosha and invited him to sit with her. She said she never thought he would visit her, but she was glad he came, especially now.
Grushenka was in a good mood and teased Rakitin for being offended. She asked Alyosha why he seemed sad. Rakitin joked that Alyosha’s elder (Father Zossima) had died.

Grushenka, wanting to cheer Alyosha up, jumped into his lap and put her arm around him, asking if she could stay there. Alyosha didn’t say anything, but he felt different than he expected—he wasn’t afraid of her.
Rakitin reminded Grushenka she promised him champagne if he brought Alyosha. Grushenka agreed and told her maid Fenya to bring the bottle.
Rakitin asked about the message Grushenka was waiting for. She said her “officer” (the man who betrayed her before) was coming and might send a messenger any minute.
Rakitin wondered if Dmitri knew about the officer. Grushenka said he didn’t, or he would be furious. She tried to forget Dmitri and wanted to think only of Alyosha.
Grushenka told Alyosha she thought he was angry with her because of what happened with Katerina Ivanovna. She admitted she had acted badly but was glad things happened that way.

Grushenka told Alyosha she loved him with all her soul, but in a different way from the officer. She said she sometimes thought of him as her conscience and felt ashamed of herself when she thought about him.
Fenya brought in the champagne. Rakitin drank some, but Alyosha only tasted it and didn’t want any more. Grushenka also decided not to drink if Alyosha wouldn’t.
Rakitin teased Alyosha about grieving for his elder, and Grushenka was shocked to hear Father Zossima had died. She quickly got off Alyosha’s knee, feeling it wasn’t proper.
Alyosha spoke up and said Grushenka had a good heart and had been kind to him. He said he came looking for someone wicked but found a true sister instead. He told Rakitin not to judge.
Grushenka agreed and said she had wanted to tempt Alyosha, but now things were different. She told Rakitin to be quiet.

Grushenka told Alyosha a story about a wicked woman who gave away one onion to a beggar. When she died, her guardian angel tried to save her by pulling her from the lake of fire with the onion, but she was selfish and the onion broke, so she fell back in. Grushenka said she was like that woman, and the only good thing she’d done was give away one onion. She admitted she paid Rakitin to bring Alyosha to her.

Grushenka then told Alyosha she had wanted to ruin him because she thought he looked down on her. She explained how much pain she had felt because of the officer who betrayed her, and how angry and sad she had been for years. Now that the officer had written to her, she was struggling with her feelings, not knowing if she should forgive him or not.
Grushenka cried on the sofa. Alyosha tried to comfort Rakitin and said they should be merciful.
Alyosha said Grushenka was more loving than anyone thought and that even though she had suffered for years, she could still forgive.

Grushenka asked Alyosha if she should forgive the man who hurt her. Alyosha said she already had forgiven him. Grushenka agreed, but was unsure if her heart truly forgave. She said maybe she loved her tears and anger more than the man.
Grushenka said she might tear off her fancy clothes and send back all the money she had gotten. She was upset and shouted, saying maybe she would never see the officer or anyone again.
Rakitin said it was time to leave. Grushenka was sad that Alyosha would go and said he was the only one who had really pitied her.
Grushenka fell to her knees and thanked Alyosha, saying she had waited her whole life for someone like him to forgive her.
Just then, there was a noise, and Fenya ran in with a letter. It was from the officer, calling Grushenka to come to him in a carriage.
Grushenka said, “He whistles! Crawl back, little dog!” But then she decided to go and said goodbye to Alyosha and Rakitin, telling them to leave.
As Alyosha and Rakitin left, Grushenka called from her window for Alyosha to tell Dmitri she only loved him for one hour in her life and not to remember evil against her.
Rakitin was annoyed that things hadn’t turned out how he planned. He said the officer was just a poor man who wanted Grushenka’s money. Alyosha didn’t answer.
Rakitin became angry and left Alyosha alone. Alyosha walked back to the monastery, thinking deeply about everything that had happened.

It was very late when Alyosha (a gentle, kind young man) came back to the hermitage. The door-keeper let him in through a special door. It was nine o’clock, time for rest. Alyosha quietly entered the elder’s cell, where the coffin of Father Zossima (his beloved teacher) stood. Inside, Father Païssy was reading the Bible by the coffin. Porfiry, a young helper, was fast asleep in the next room. Father Païssy heard Alyosha come in, but didn’t look up. Alyosha went to a corner and knelt to pray.

Alyosha had many feelings all mixed together, but his heart felt sweet. He looked at the coffin, but the sad grief he’d felt earlier was gone. Now he felt joy, and he wasn’t surprised. The window was open, so the air was cool. Alyosha thought the smell from the coffin must have gotten stronger, but it didn’t bother him anymore. He prayed quietly, though sometimes his mind wandered. Still, he felt comfort and peace inside. Sometimes he prayed with love and thanks.
Soon, Alyosha stopped really praying as he got sleepy. He listened to Father Païssy’s reading but slowly started to doze off.
Father Païssy read, “And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there; and both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.”

Alyosha thought about the wedding and about people being happy. He remembered someone saying sad things, but thought that sometimes sad words help people. He also thought about his brother Mitya and Rakitin.
Father Païssy went on, “And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine.”

Alyosha loved this story. He remembered how Jesus did his first miracle at the wedding to make people happy. Alyosha remembered kind words from his elder and from Mitya, about how joy and forgiveness are important.

Alyosha thought about how the people at the wedding were poor, but Jesus and his mother were there. Jesus brought joy to everyone, even to simple, poor people. His mother knew He had come to help all people, not just to make sacrifices. Jesus did what his mother asked, even though it wasn’t a big miracle.

Suddenly, everything in the room seemed to change in Alyosha’s mind. It felt like he was at the wedding in Cana. He saw the guests and the happy couple. Then he thought he saw Father Zossima, who had died, getting up from the table and coming towards him.
Alyosha saw Father Zossima, looking joyful and alive, just like before he died. He, too, was at the wedding feast.
Alyosha heard Father Zossima’s kind voice, “Yes, my dear, I am called, too. Why are you hiding? Come join us.”
It was really Father Zossima’s voice.
The elder took Alyosha’s hand and helped him up.

“We are happy here,” said Father Zossima. “We are drinking new wine of joy. See all the guests? I am here because I gave an onion to a beggar. Many people here gave just a little, even just an onion. And you, kind boy, today you helped a hungry woman. Begin your good work, dear boy. Do you see the Sun, do you see Him?”
Alyosha whispered, “I am afraid. I dare not look.”

Father Zossima said, “Do not fear Him. He is great and wonderful, but also very loving. He became like us because He loves us. He changes water into wine so the guests will be glad. He is always calling new guests. Look, they are bringing new wine.”
Alyosha’s heart was full of happiness. He reached out, cried out—and woke up.

He was back in the cell, with the coffin and the open window. He was standing now, though he had fallen asleep kneeling. He walked straight to the coffin, brushing past Father Païssy, who noticed something strange was happening. Alyosha looked at the coffin and listened for Father Zossima’s voice, but no more words came. Suddenly, he turned and left the cell.

Alyosha did not stop on the steps. He hurried outside, wanting to be free and in the open air. The night sky was full of stars. The cathedral’s white towers and golden domes shone against the dark sky. The flowers around the house were asleep. The silent earth seemed joined with the silent stars above.

Alyosha looked up, then suddenly threw himself on the ground. He hugged the earth and kissed it, crying and promising to love it forever. In his heart he heard, “Water the earth with the tears of your joy and love those tears.”
Why was he crying?

Alyosha was so happy that he cried even for the shining stars. He felt close to the whole world and wanted to forgive everyone and ask forgiveness, not just for himself, but for all people. He felt that something strong and unbreakable had entered his soul. He felt he had changed forever. He had fallen to the ground a weak boy, but he stood up a strong and brave person. He would always remember this moment.
“Someone visited my soul in that hour,” Alyosha would say later, believing it with all his heart.
Three days later, Alyosha left the monastery, just as Father Zossima had told him to do.

Dmitri was very upset and restless after Grushenka left, but he didn’t know where she had gone or what had happened to her. For the past two days, he was running everywhere, feeling confused and worried. Alyosha couldn’t find him, and Ivan didn’t see him at the tavern. Dmitri’s landlady was hiding his whereabouts, just as he had told her.

Dmitri spent those two days rushing around, trying to fix his problems and save himself. He even left town for a few hours, even though it scared him to be away from Grushenka. Later, people would explain everything that happened, but for now, let’s just talk about the most important things that happened right before the terrible event that changed everything.

Grushenka had really loved Dmitri for a short time, but she also made him suffer sometimes. Dmitri never knew what Grushenka wanted. He couldn’t make her do anything, no matter how hard he tried. He guessed she was having a hard time making up her mind, and sometimes he thought she might even hate him. But Dmitri didn’t know what was really bothering Grushenka. For him, the main problem was still between him and his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Dmitri believed that Fyodor Pavlovitch wanted to marry Grushenka, and didn’t just want to buy her love for three thousand roubles. Dmitri thought Grushenka couldn’t decide which one of them was better for her.

Dmitri didn’t think much about the “officer,” the man from Grushenka’s past who had hurt her before. He knew about a letter the officer sent, but he didn’t believe the officer would really come back after so many years. Grushenka had shown Dmitri part of the letter, but hid the part that said the officer might return. Dmitri saw that she didn’t care much about the officer anymore, so he stopped worrying about it.

Dmitri felt sure that soon he would have to face his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and that this would decide everything. He hoped Grushenka would suddenly tell him, “Take me, I’m yours forever!” Then he would take her far away, marry her, and start a new life where no one would know them.
Dmitri dreamed of starting a good, new life with Grushenka. He hated the mess his life had become and thought that moving far away would help him become a better person.

But all this depended on what Grushenka decided. She might also pick Fyodor Pavlovitch and tell Dmitri to go away. Dmitri didn’t know what he would do if that happened. He hadn’t planned anything bad; he was just waiting and hoping for the best. But there was still a big problem.

If Grushenka chose him, how could he take her away without money? Fyodor Pavlovitch had stopped giving him money. Grushenka had some, but Dmitri was too proud to use hers. He wanted to pay for everything himself. He felt bad because he had already taken money from Katerina Ivanovna unfairly before and didn’t want to do something wrong again.
Dmitri kept worrying about where he could get the money he needed. Without it, he couldn’t do anything, and he was ashamed.

Dmitri might have known where to get the money, but to do it honestly, he had to first pay back the three thousand roubles he took from Katerina Ivanovna. He decided he would do anything to give her back the money. He would rather be called a thief or even go to jail than start a new life with Grushenka using stolen money.
Even though it seemed almost impossible to find so much money, Dmitri kept hoping something would happen to help him. He thought of wild ideas to get the money and soon decided to try one of them.

Dmitri decided to visit Samsonov, a rich merchant who had helped Grushenka before. Dmitri wanted to offer Samsonov a business plan so he could get the money he needed. He hoped Samsonov would want Grushenka to have a good life and would help him.

Dmitri didn’t think it was wrong to ask Samsonov for help. He believed Grushenka’s past was over, and if she married him, everything would be new. He also thought Samsonov was now just like a father to Grushenka and would want the best for her.
Dmitri was simple-hearted and really believed Samsonov would want to help Grushenka and make up for the past.
The next morning, after hardly sleeping, Dmitri went to Samsonov’s big, old house. Samsonov lived upstairs alone, while his family and workers lived downstairs.
The upper floor had fancy rooms, but Samsonov only stayed in his small bedroom, helped by an old servant and a boy. He could barely walk and didn’t talk much.

When Dmitri arrived, Samsonov first refused to see him. Dmitri sent a note saying his business was very important for Grushenka. After some thought, Samsonov agreed to meet him and called for his strong, tall son to be there as a witness.
Samsonov, helped by his son and servant, slowly came into the big drawing-room to meet Dmitri. The room was large and gloomy.
Dmitri, dressed nicely, hurried to meet Samsonov. He noticed how ill and swollen the old man looked. Samsonov sat down, very serious, making Dmitri feel nervous.
Samsonov asked Dmitri, “What do you want from me?”
Dmitri started talking quickly and nervously, full of hope but also scared. Samsonov just listened, not showing any emotion.
Dmitri believed his “guardian angel” had saved him and that Samsonov’s advice would work. He rushed off to try his new plan, feeling sure things would go well now.

But sadly, Samsonov was really just making fun of Dmitri. Later, Samsonov laughed about tricking him and told his son never to let Dmitri in again. Samsonov was angry and enjoyed seeing Dmitri so desperate.
After Dmitri left, Samsonov was still angry for a long time and even felt worse by evening.

Mitya (Dmitri Karamazov) needed to travel fast, but he didn’t have enough money for horses. He only had forty kopecks left. At home, he found his old silver watch that didn’t work anymore. He took it to a Jewish watchmaker in the market and sold it for six roubles.

“I didn’t expect that!” Mitya shouted happily. He quickly ran home with the money. Then he borrowed three more roubles from the people he lived with. They liked Mitya and gave him the money, even though it was all they had. Excited, Mitya told them that something big would happen today and explained everything about his plan and hopes. Now, with nine roubles, Mitya hired horses to go to Volovya station. This is why people later remembered that “at midday, the day before the big event, Mitya had no money, sold his watch, and borrowed three roubles in front of witnesses.”
This fact will be important later.

Mitya felt hopeful but also worried as he went to Volovya station. He was afraid Grushenka (a woman he loved) might visit his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, while he was gone. That’s why he left without telling her and told his landlady not to say where he went.
“I must get back tonight,” Mitya kept saying in the cart. He also thought he might need to bring Lyagavy (a peasant trader) back to sign a paper. But things didn’t go as he hoped.

First, he was late because his shortcut was much longer than he thought. Second, when he reached Ilyinskoe, the priest wasn’t home; he was in another village. Mitya went there with the tired horses, and by then it was almost dark.

The priest, a kind little man, told Mitya that Lyagavy was now at Suhoy Possyolok, staying in the forester’s cottage. Mitya begged the priest to take him there, and the priest agreed, but said they should walk because it wasn’t far. Mitya walked so fast the priest almost had to run to keep up.

Mitya talked nervously about his plans and asked for advice, but the priest mostly said, “I don’t know,” or “How can I tell?” When Mitya talked about fighting with his father over money, the priest got scared because he depended on Fyodor Pavlovitch. The priest also explained that Lyagavy’s real name was Gorstkin, and he didn’t like being called Lyagavy. Mitya should call him Gorstkin or else he wouldn’t listen.

Mitya was surprised, but said Samsonov had called him Lyagavy. The priest dropped the subject, but maybe he should have told Mitya that something seemed odd about the way Samsonov sent him. Mitya hurried on and was annoyed when he saw they had walked much farther than the priest said, but he stayed calm.

They went into the hut. The forester lived in one half, and Gorstkin (Lyagavy) was in the other. The room was too hot. There was a samovar, some bread, and bottles on the table. Lyagavy was asleep on the bench, snoring loudly. Mitya didn’t know what to do.

“I must wake him. My business is important. I need to get back today,” Mitya said nervously. But the priest and forester said nothing. Mitya tried to wake Lyagavy himself, shaking and pulling him, but Lyagavy didn’t wake up.
“He’s drunk,” Mitya thought. He tried everything, but the man only grunted and cursed.
Finally, the priest said, “You’d better wait a little. He’s not in a fit state.”
“He’s been drinking all day,” added the forester.
Mitya cried, “If only you knew how important this is to me!”
The priest said again, “Better wait till morning.”
“Till morning? That’s impossible!” said Mitya.
He almost tried to wake Lyagavy again but realized it was useless. The priest and forester were quiet.
Mitya was in despair. He was sweating and upset. The priest pointed out that even if Lyagavy woke up, he’d still be too drunk to talk. Mitya agreed to wait until morning.
Mitya said he would stay up with a light and start talking as soon as Lyagavy woke up. He said he’d pay the forester for the light and the room. Mitya also wondered where the priest would sleep.
The priest said he would go home on the forester’s horse. He wished Mitya good luck.
The priest left, happy to go, but wondered if he should tell Fyodor Pavlovitch about this strange event.

The forester went to his room, and Mitya sat waiting for Lyagavy to wake up. Mitya felt very sad and worried. The room was too hot, and he thought about Grushenka and what she might be doing. He jumped up, feeling upset.
“It’s a tragedy!” Mitya said, grinding his teeth. He looked at Lyagavy, who was a lean, curly-haired peasant with a long face. Mitya felt angry at him for no real reason.
Mitya felt it was humiliating that he had worked so hard and sacrificed so much, but now his future depended on this drunk man who just snored.
“Oh, the irony of fate!” Mitya cried, trying again to wake Lyagavy, but it didn’t work. He gave up and sat down.
“Stupid! How dishonorable!” Mitya said. His head started to hurt. He thought about leaving, but realized he couldn’t—he had no way to get out now.
His headache got worse, and he fell asleep sitting on the bench. He slept for hours. He woke up because his head hurt badly, and it took him a while to understand what was happening.

He realized the room was full of dangerous charcoal fumes from the stove, and he could have died. Lyagavy was still snoring. The candle was almost out. Mitya ran into the forester’s room and woke him up. The forester didn’t seem worried, but he did come to check.
“But he’s dead! What am I to do?” Mitya shouted.
They opened the doors, a window, and the chimney. Mitya got water, wet his own head, and put a wet rag on Lyagavy’s head. The forester wasn’t worried and said, “It’ll be all right now.”
The forester went back to sleep, leaving Mitya a lantern. Mitya tried to help Lyagavy for half an hour and decided not to sleep at all. But he was so tired that he lay down and fell asleep deeply.

He woke up very late, around nine o’clock. The sun was shining. The curly-haired peasant was awake, wearing his coat, and already drinking. Lyagavy was drunk again. Mitya saw that he was hopelessly drunk and stared at him. The peasant watched him silently.
Mitya said, “Excuse me, I’m Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of the old Karamazov whose copse you are buying.”
“That’s a lie!” said the peasant calmly.
“A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“I don’t know any Fyodor Pavlovitches,” said the peasant.
“You’re bargaining for the copse. Please wake up! Father Pavel brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and he sent me,” Mitya said quickly.
“You’re lying!” Lyagavy said again. Mitya felt cold with fear.
“Please! This isn’t a joke! You must understand me!” Mitya begged.
“You’re a painter!” said Lyagavy.
“No, I’m Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov. I have an important offer about the copse!” Mitya tried again.
The peasant stroked his beard.
“No, you did the job and turned out a scamp. You’re a scoundrel!” said the peasant.
“You’re mistaken!” Mitya cried, very upset. The peasant watched him with cunning eyes.
“Show me the law that allows roguery. You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand?” the peasant said.
Mitya stepped back, suddenly realizing the whole thing was foolish. He wondered how he could have wasted so much time on this drunk man.
“He’s dead drunk and will keep drinking for a week. What if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What have I done?” Mitya thought.

The peasant grinned at him. Mitya felt weak, like a child. He put on his coat and left the hut. He put fifty kopecks on the table for his stay. Outside, he saw only forest and didn’t know which way to go. He walked along a path, feeling lost and weak. Somehow, he made it out of the forest and saw empty fields.
“What despair! What death all around!” he said as he walked.

He met an old merchant in a hired cart. Mitya asked the way and found out the merchant was going to Volovya too. Mitya got in, and after three hours, they arrived. Mitya ordered horses to go to town and suddenly realized he was very hungry. While the horses were being harnessed, he ate an omelette, bread, sausage, and drank vodka. He felt a little better and made a new plan to get the money he needed before evening. “To think a man’s life can be ruined for only three thousand!” he said. He would have felt happier if he didn’t keep worrying about Grushenka.
At last, Mitya reached town and ran to see Grushenka.

This was the visit Mitya (Dmitri) made to Grushenka, the one she was so worried about. Grushenka was waiting for a message and was glad Mitya hadn’t come to see her that day or the day before. She hoped he wouldn’t come before she left. But suddenly, Mitya burst in. To get away from him, Grushenka said she had to go to Samsonov’s house to settle some business. Mitya walked with her, but at the gate she said goodbye and made him promise to come back at midnight to take her home. Mitya liked this idea. He thought, “If she’s at Samsonov’s, she can’t be going to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house.” He hoped she was telling the truth.

Mitya was a very jealous man. When Grushenka wasn’t with him, he imagined she was seeing someone else. But as soon as he saw her happy, smiling face, he stopped being jealous and felt ashamed for doubting her.
After leaving Grushenka at the gate, Mitya rushed home. He had a lot to do that day, but he felt lighter after their meeting.
Mitya wanted to find Smerdyakov right away to ask if Grushenka had visited Fyodor Pavlovitch the night before.
But before Mitya even reached his home, his jealousy returned.
He needed money urgently. He had almost no money left, and he remembered he could borrow some. He had a pair of nice pistols that he hadn’t pawned yet because he liked them a lot.

At the Metropolis tavern, Mitya knew a young official who liked collecting weapons. Mitya offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official wanted to buy them, but Mitya said no. The official gave him ten roubles as a loan, and they parted as friends.

Mitya hurried to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, planning to find Smerdyakov. He learned from Marya Kondratyevna (a woman who lived nearby) that Smerdyakov was sick and had fallen in the cellar. The doctor had visited, and even Fyodor Pavlovitch was worried. Mitya also found out that his brother Ivan had left for Moscow that morning.

Mitya was very upset about Smerdyakov being sick because now no one could watch the house for him. He asked the women if they saw anything strange the night before, but they said everything was normal. Mitya decided he needed to watch both Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house and Samsonov’s gate. But first, he had a new plan and needed to act quickly.
Mitya hurried home, cleaned up, and went to Madame Hohlakov’s house. He hoped to borrow three thousand roubles from her. He felt sure she would help him.

Mitya didn’t know Madame Hohlakov well, and she didn’t like him because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna. Madame Hohlakov wanted Katerina to marry Ivan instead. But Mitya thought if Madame Hohlakov wanted him away from Katerina, she might lend him money to make it happen.

Mitya’s plan was to offer Madame Hohlakov his rights to some land as security for the loan. He was excited about his idea, but he was nervous because this was his last hope. If she didn’t give him the money, he felt he would have nothing left to do but steal it.
At first, things seemed to go well. Madame Hohlakov welcomed him quickly and said she was expecting him.
Mitya said he came on important business and needed her help.
Madame Hohlakov told Mitya she could give him much more than three thousand roubles—she would save him.
Mitya was so happy, he thanked her with all his heart.
Madame Hohlakov said she had a great idea for him: he should go to the gold-mines and become rich. She promised he would make millions and become famous.
Mitya tried to remind her about the three thousand roubles, hoping she meant to give him the money right away.
But Madame Hohlakov just wanted him to promise he would go to the gold-mines.
She jumped up and ran to her desk, looking for something.
Madame Hohlakov handed Mitya a small silver icon on a cord from Kiev and put it around his neck. She said it would help him start a new life.
Madame Hohlakov sat down again and said he could now leave.
Mitya tried to thank her, but said he really needed the money soon. He started to confess that he loved someone else besides Katerina Ivanovna and needed the money because of that.
Madame Hohlakov told Mitya to forget about women and focus on going to the gold-mines. She said he would find the right woman later, after he came back rich.
Mitya finally asked her again, “Can I have the three thousand roubles today? If not, when?”
“What money?” Madame Hohlakov asked.
“The three thousand you promised,” said Mitya.
“Three thousand roubles? Oh, no, I don’t have three thousand,” Madame Hohlakov said calmly. Mitya was shocked.
Mitya reminded her that she had said it was as good as in his hands.
Madame Hohlakov said he misunderstood. She was talking about the gold-mines, not real money.
She said she had no money and wouldn’t give him any even if she did, because she wanted him to go to the gold-mines instead.
Mitya got very angry and hit the table with his fist.

He left the house upset and walked out into the street, crying like a child. He felt hopeless because he couldn’t pay his debt to Katerina Ivanovna. This shame weighed on him so much that it felt like a secret pain in his chest.
Suddenly he bumped into an old woman in the street. She yelled at him for not looking where he was going.
Mitya realized she was Samsonov’s servant, whom he’d seen before.
Mitya quickly asked, “Is Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka) there now?”
The old woman said Grushenka had been there but had already left.
“When did she go?” Mitya cried.
The old woman said Grushenka only stayed a minute, told a funny story, and then ran off.
Mitya yelled at her, not believing her, but then ran away.
He rushed to Grushenka’s house, but she had already left for Mokroe about fifteen minutes before.
Fenya, the servant girl, was in the kitchen with her grandmother. When Mitya ran in, Fenya screamed.
Mitya shouted, “Where is she?”
He fell at Fenya’s feet, begging her to tell him where Grushenka was.
Fenya said she didn’t know, even though she was scared Mitya might hurt her. She reminded him he had just seen Grushenka go out.
Mitya said, “She came back!”
Fenya swore Grushenka hadn’t come back.
Mitya shouted that Fenya was lying and ran out. He was in such a hurry that he grabbed a small brass pestle from the table and stuffed it in his pocket as he left.
Fenya cried out in fear, thinking, “Oh no! He’s going to hurt someone!”

Dmitri (called Mitya) was running fast. He thought, “Grushenka must be at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house! She went there after Samsonov’s, I’m sure.” Mitya didn’t go to Marya Kondratyevna’s house because he thought she and Smerdyakov were helping in the plan. He believed everyone was against him.

Mitya made a new plan. Instead of going straight to the house, he ran around the back way, through quiet streets and over a small bridge. He came to a lonely alley behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, where a tall fence stood. He remembered that Lizaveta once climbed over here, so he tried too. He pulled himself up and sat on top of the fence. From there, he saw the bath-house and the windows of the house glowing with light.

“Fyodor Pavlovitch’s bedroom is lit up. Grushenka must be there!” Mitya thought. He jumped down into the garden. Even though he knew Grigory and Smerdyakov were sick, he hid and listened. Everything was silent.

Mitya waited, hoping no one heard him. He slowly crept through the garden, careful not to step on branches. He moved quietly to the window. He hid behind some tall bushes under it, hardly daring to breathe.
Mitya waited a bit, but his heart pounded so fast he couldn’t wait much longer. He stood in the dark, just outside the light from the window.

He walked closer and peeked inside. He could see all of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s bedroom. There was a red screen in the middle. Mitya guessed Grushenka might be hiding behind it. Fyodor Pavlovitch was wearing a new, fancy dressing-gown and a red bandage on his head.
Fyodor Pavlovitch stood by the window, thinking. Then he poured himself a drink, sighed, and looked at his bruises in the mirror.
“He’s alone,” thought Mitya.
Suddenly, Fyodor Pavlovitch turned and looked out the window. Mitya quickly hid in the shadows.
Mitya wondered if Grushenka was behind the screen. But Fyodor Pavlovitch looked disappointed and sat at the table, resting his head on his hand. Mitya kept watching.
“He’s alone!” Mitya thought again. “If Grushenka was here, he would look different.”
Mitya felt upset. He wanted to know for sure if Grushenka was there. He decided to knock on the window, using a secret signal that meant, “Grushenka is here!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up and ran to the window. Mitya hid quickly.
“Grushenka, is that you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch whispered out the window, looking everywhere.
Mitya was now sure Fyodor Pavlovitch was alone.
Fyodor Pavlovitch leaned out farther, calling, “Where are you? Come here, I have a present for you!”
Mitya guessed the present was the three thousand rubles.
Fyodor Pavlovitch said he would open the door, almost climbing out the window to see better.
He was about to run outside to look for Grushenka.
Mitya watched him, feeling a huge wave of anger. He remembered how much he hated his father. Suddenly, Mitya pulled a brass pestle (a heavy tool) from his pocket.
At that moment, Grigory, who had been sick, woke up. He had taken medicine and gone to bed, while his wife Marfa Ignatyevna slept beside him. Smerdyakov was also asleep in the next room.

Grigory got up because he was worried about the house. Even though his back hurt, he remembered he had not locked the garden gate. He went outside and saw the gate was open. He also noticed Fyodor Pavlovitch’s window was open.
Suddenly, Grigory saw a shadowy person running in the garden.
“Good Lord!” Grigory shouted and chased after the person. The figure ran towards the bath-house, then to the fence. Grigory caught up just as the person was climbing over. He grabbed the man’s leg.
Grigory realized it was Mitya, the “parricide” (someone who kills their father).
Grigory shouted “Parricide!” loudly, but then fell to the ground, as if struck.

Mitya jumped back into the garden. He had the brass pestle in his hand and threw it into the grass. He bent over Grigory, whose head was bleeding. Mitya used his clean handkerchief to try to stop the blood, but it quickly turned red.

Mitya suddenly thought, “What am I doing?” He didn’t know if Grigory was dead or just hurt. “If I’ve killed him, I’ve killed him,” he said. Then Mitya climbed the fence, ran away holding the bloody handkerchief, and went back to the widow Morozov’s house.

After Mitya left earlier, Fenya had asked the porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, not to let Mitya in again. Nazar told his nephew Prohor to watch the gate, but forgot to warn him about Mitya. When Mitya arrived, Prohor let him in because he knew him.
“Where is Grushenka, Prohor?” Mitya asked.
Prohor answered, “She left for Mokroe two hours ago with Timofey.”
“Why?” Mitya cried.
“I don’t know. She went to see some officer. Horses were sent to get her.”
Mitya ran off to find Fenya, wild with worry.

Fenya was in the kitchen with her grandmother, getting ready for bed. They trusted Nazar Ivanovitch, so they hadn't locked the door. Suddenly, Mitya burst in, grabbed Fenya by the throat, and shouted at her.
“Tell me right now! Where is she? Who is she with at Mokroe?” Mitya yelled.
Both Fenya and her grandmother screamed in fear.
Fenya, terrified, said quickly, “I’ll tell you! Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I’ll tell you everything! She’s gone to Mokroe to see her officer.”
“What officer?” Mitya shouted.
“The officer she knew before, the one who left her five years ago,” Fenya answered, talking as fast as she could.

Mitya let go of Fenya. He stood there, very pale, realizing everything right away. Fenya sat frozen, scared, with her hands up like she was protecting herself. Her eyes were wide and staring at Mitya. There was blood on Mitya’s hands and on his face, which made Fenya even more frightened. The old cook looked at him in shock.
Mitya sat down on a chair, stunned and silent. He remembered Grushenka had told him about the officer and the letter she got a month ago. He wondered why he had forgotten about the officer until now.

Suddenly, Mitya started talking kindly to Fenya, acting like he hadn’t just scared her. He asked her questions, and Fenya answered quickly, wanting to help. She explained what happened that day: how Rakitin and Alyosha visited, how she watched for Grushenka, how Grushenka left, and how she called out to Alyosha to say, “Remember forever how I loved him for an hour.”
When Mitya heard this message, he smiled, his face less pale. Fenya noticed the blood on his hands and said, “Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’re all over blood!”
Mitya looked at his hands but didn’t care. He soon became quiet again. After about twenty minutes, he stood up, looking dreamy and smiled.

Fenya, kindly, pointed to his hands and asked what happened. Mitya said, “That’s blood, Fenya. That’s human blood. Why was it shed? But, Fenya… there’s a fence here, a high, scary fence. But tomorrow morning, Mitya will jump over it… You don’t understand, but you’ll know tomorrow. I won’t get in her way. I know how to move aside. She loved me for an hour—remember Mityenka Karamazov for that.” Then he left the kitchen. Fenya was even more scared by his sudden leaving.
Ten minutes later, Mitya went to see Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young man he had pawned his pistols with. Pyotr Ilyitch was just leaving to play billiards when Mitya arrived.
Seeing blood on Mitya’s face, Pyotr Ilyitch was shocked. “What happened?” he asked.
“I’ve come for my pistols and brought the money. Please hurry, I’m in a rush,” Mitya said.
Pyotr Ilyitch noticed Mitya was holding a big bundle of money, rainbow-colored notes, and his fingers were bloody. Everyone who saw him wondered at this sight.
Later, Pyotr Ilyitch said Mitya had thousands of roubles and seemed very strange, not sad but almost happy and rushed.
Pyotr Ilyitch asked, “What happened to you? Why are you covered in blood?”
He took Mitya to look in the mirror.
When Mitya saw his bloody face, he got angry and switched the money to his other hand. He tried to use his handkerchief, but it was soaked with blood, so he threw it on the floor.
“Do you have something to wipe my face?” he asked.
“You’d better wash,” Pyotr Ilyitch said, pouring water for him.
Mitya wondered aloud where to put his money. Pyotr Ilyitch told him to put it in his pocket or on the table.
Suddenly, Mitya said, “Let’s settle the pistols first. Here’s your money. I need them and can’t wait.”
Pyotr Ilyitch asked, “How did you get so much money?” He sent his boy, Misha, to change the notes.
Mitya told Misha to go to Plotnikov’s shop and order lots of food, sweets, and especially champagne, just like he did before.
Pyotr Ilyitch said, “You should go tell them yourself, or he’ll get it wrong.”
Mitya laughed, promised Misha a reward, and repeated the big order for food and drinks.
Pyotr Ilyitch told Mitya to come wash up and helped him take off his coat, which also had blood on it.
Mitya explained the blood must have come from his handkerchief and said he must have sat on it at Fenya’s.
They washed up. Pyotr Ilyitch made sure Mitya got clean, especially his hands and face.
Pyotr Ilyitch asked if Mitya had been fighting or even killed someone. Mitya laughed and said he had fought an old man, but they made up.
Pyotr Ilyitch scolded Mitya for always getting into fights and wanting so much champagne.
Mitya found his money and said he had three thousand roubles.
Pyotr Ilyitch asked if Madame Hohlakov had really given him the money, and Mitya teased him to go ask her in the morning.
Pyotr Ilyitch wondered why Mitya was spending all the money instead of going to Siberia, as he wanted before. Mitya said he was going to Mokroe.
“But it’s night!” Pyotr Ilyitch said.
“Once the lad had all, now he has nothing,” Mitya said sadly.
Mitya said, “I’m drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But that’s enough!”
Mitya began loading his pistols. Pyotr Ilyitch watched, worried.
Mitya looked at the bullet, wondering aloud if a person would look at the bullet before using it. He said it was just a silly thought, finished loading, then asked for a piece of paper.
Mitya wrote two lines, folded the paper, and put it in his pocket. He locked up the pistols and smiled at Pyotr Ilyitch.
“Now, let’s go,” Mitya said.
Pyotr Ilyitch asked if Mitya was thinking of hurting himself. Mitya said he wanted to live. He asked, “Do you know how to step aside for someone you love and someone you hate, and let them go on?”
“That’s enough, let’s go,” Mitya said.
“There’s a woman at Mokroe. That’s all you need to know,” Mitya answered.
Misha came back with change. Mitya gave money to Pyotr Ilyitch and Misha for helping.
Mitya invited Pyotr Ilyitch to Mokroe with him to drink and celebrate life. Pyotr Ilyitch said he was going to the “Metropolis” anyway.
Mitya wanted to drink at Plotnikov’s shop instead. He showed Pyotr Ilyitch the note he wrote: “I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish!”
Plotnikov’s shop was big and busy. Mitya and Pyotr Ilyitch arrived, and the workers were finishing packing a box of food and drinks for Mitya.
A cart with three horses and Andrey the driver was waiting. Andrey promised they would almost catch up to the others at Mokroe.
Mitya gave more orders for food, but he was forgetful and needed Pyotr Ilyitch’s help.
Pyotr Ilyitch argued about the price, and in the end, they agreed to send three hundred roubles’ worth instead of more.
Mitya pulled Pyotr Ilyitch into a back room to drink champagne. They sat at a little table.
Mitya said he loved life, but he had to “punish” himself for something wrong, like getting rid of a harmful insect. He said, “Let’s drink to life, and to one queen of queens!”
Pyotr Ilyitch agreed, and they drank. Mitya was excited but also sad, as if worried about something.
Mitya offered Misha, the boy, a drink to “golden-haired Phœbus, the sun of tomorrow.” Misha drank and left.
Mitya talked about women and said sadly, “My heart is sad, Pyotr Ilyitch.” He compared himself to Yorick from Hamlet.
Mitya asked Pyotr Ilyitch if he had ever stolen anything. Pyotr Ilyitch said he once took twenty copecks from his mother as a child and later gave it back.
Mitya said he did the exact same thing—stole twenty copecks from his mother at age nine and then gave it back.
Mitya stood up. Andrey called from the door that it was time to go.
Mitya asked for vodka for the driver, made sure his pistols were packed, and said goodbye to Pyotr Ilyitch, asking him not to think badly of him.
“You’re coming back tomorrow?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked.
“Of course,” said Mitya.
As Mitya was about to leave, Fenya ran up, begging, “Don’t hurt my mistress or the officer. He came first, he’ll marry her. Don’t take a life!”
Pyotr Ilyitch, realizing what Mitya might do, shouted, “Give me your pistols if you want to be honorable.”
“I’ll throw them away on the road,” Mitya said. He told Fenya he was sorry for hurting her and asked her to forgive him.
Andrey drove the horses quickly, and the bells rang as they left.
“Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyitch! My last tear is for you!” Mitya called.
Pyotr Ilyitch watched Mitya go, thinking he acted like a lunatic. He thought about staying to watch the packing, but left instead to play billiards at the tavern.
As he walked, Pyotr Ilyitch thought about Mitya, the officer, and the pistols. He figured nothing serious would happen—they would just drink and argue as usual.
At the tavern, Pyotr Ilyitch played billiards and told others Mitya had gotten three thousand roubles and gone to Mokroe with Grushenka. Everyone was surprised and talked about it seriously.
Someone wondered if Mitya had robbed his father.
People remembered Mitya had spoken about killing his father and needing three thousand roubles.
Pyotr Ilyitch listened but stopped talking about the blood on Mitya.
After a few games, Pyotr Ilyitch lost interest and left the tavern. He wanted to check if anything had happened at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house but wondered if it was his job to get involved.
He walked home, then remembered Fenya and wished he had asked her more questions. He turned back to Grushenka’s house, knocked on the gate, but no one answered.
He knocked loudly, filling the quiet street with noise.
“If they won't come, I’ll keep knocking!” he said, annoyed but determined to find out what was happening.

Dmitri Fyodorovitch (called Mitya) was riding fast in a cart pulled by three horses. He was heading to a place called Mokroe, about twenty versts away. The night was cool, the sky full of stars. The wind and the ride woke Mitya up a bit. He was filled with feelings about Grushenka, the woman he loved. He wanted to see her, maybe for the last time.

Mitya felt confused and upset, but mostly he just wanted to see Grushenka, his “queen.” He was not even jealous of her old boyfriend, who was with her now. This surprised him. He just wanted to see her, even if it hurt.

He thought, “She loved this man before me. I have no right to be angry. I should step aside and let her go.” Even though he made up his mind, Mitya still felt pain and worry inside. He remembered the note he wrote, saying he would punish himself, and the loaded pistol he carried.

Sometimes, he wanted to stop everything and end his troubles right there, but the feeling passed quickly. As they got closer to Mokroe, he stopped thinking about sad things and just wanted to see Grushenka, even if it was only for a second.
He thought, “She is with him now. I want to see her with him, and that’s all.” He felt a new, gentle kind of love for her and even wanted to step out of her life so she could be happy.
They had been riding almost an hour. Mitya and Andrey, the driver, were both quiet. Suddenly, Mitya got worried.
“Andrey! What if they’re asleep?”
Andrey said, “Maybe they’ve gone to bed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.” Mitya got upset, thinking he might not see Grushenka at all.
“Drive faster, Andrey! Hurry up!” Mitya shouted.
Andrey said, “Maybe they’re not in bed. Timofey said there were a lot of people there, playing cards.”
“Who are they?” Mitya asked.
Andrey explained, “Some are from our town, and some are strangers. They’re playing cards.”
“If they’re playing cards, maybe they’re still awake,” Andrey said.
“Faster, Andrey! Quicker!” Mitya said, getting more nervous.
Andrey then asked, “Fenya begged you not to hurt her mistress or anyone else. I’m the one driving you there... Forgive me, sir, but I worry about it.”
Mitya grabbed Andrey’s shoulders. “Are you a driver?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Then you know you can’t just run people over. If you hurt someone, you should punish yourself and go away.”
Andrey agreed, “That’s right, you shouldn’t hurt anyone, not even a horse. Everyone is made by God.”
Mitya asked, “Will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell, what do you think?”
Andrey answered, “I don’t know. When Jesus died on the cross, he went to hell and let out all the sinners. But the devil will still get the mighty and rich people who do wrong.”
Andrey said, “You’re like a child, sir. God will forgive you because you have a kind heart.”
“And you, do you forgive me, Andrey?”
“You’ve never hurt me, sir.”
“Forgive me for everyone, just you alone here, Andrey.”
“Oh, sir, your talk is strange. I feel afraid driving you.”
But Mitya was praying quietly, not listening.

Mitya prayed, “Lord, forgive me. Even if you send me to hell, I will still love you. But please, let me love Grushenka just a little longer. I will tell her, ‘You are right to leave me. Goodbye, and don’t worry about me.’”
“Mokroe!” Andrey pointed ahead.
In the darkness, they saw the village of Mokroe. Most people were asleep, but some lights were still on.
“Drive on, Andrey! I’m coming!” Mitya said, excited.
“They’re not asleep,” Andrey said, pointing to the inn with bright windows.
“They’re awake! Hurry, Andrey! Let everyone know I’m here!” Mitya shouted.
Andrey made the tired horses run faster and stopped in front of the inn.
Mitya jumped out. The innkeeper, Trifon Borissovitch, came out to see who had arrived.
“Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?” Mitya called.
The innkeeper ran down and greeted Mitya happily.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch! Is it really you?”

Trifon Borissovitch was a strong peasant who owned the inn. He could be strict, but acted very polite when it helped him. He was a widower with four daughters, and everyone in the village owed him money. He liked to make money from guests who drank too much.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, you’re back again!”
“Where is she?” Mitya asked.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna?” (That’s Grushenka.) “She’s here, too.”
“With whom?”
“Some strangers. One is a Pole, an official, and another is his friend.”
“Are they having a party? Do they have money?”
“Not much of a party,” said Trifon.
“There are two men from town, too. One is young, a relative of Mr. Miüsov. The other is Maximov, who has been to the monastery.”
“How is Grushenka?” Mitya asked.
“She just arrived. She’s sitting with them.”
“Is she happy?”
“No, she looks sad. She’s combing the young man’s hair.”
“The Pole?”
“No, the young one, Miüsov’s relative.”
“Kalganov.”
“Yes, Kalganov.”
“Are they playing cards?”
“They were, but now they’re drinking tea.”
“Are the gypsies here?” Mitya asked.
“No, the police sent the gypsies away. But we have Jewish musicians in the village. I can send for them.”
“Send for them! And get the girls too—Marya, Stepanida, and Arina. I’ll pay two hundred roubles!”
“For that money, I can get everyone. My daughters will sing for free. You gave the peasants champagne last time—”
“I spent over a thousand roubles here last time. Remember?” said Mitya.
“You did. I remember.”
“I’ve come to do it again,” said Mitya, showing his money.
“Bring wine, food, and the box Andrey has. Bring the girls, especially Marya.”
Mitya took out the box of pistols.
“Andrey, here’s fifteen roubles for the ride, and fifty for vodka. Remember Karamazov!”
“I’m afraid, sir. Give me five extra, but I won’t take more.”
“What are you afraid of?” Mitya asked. He gave Andrey five roubles and turned to Trifon. “Take me up quietly so I can look in without them seeing me. Are they in the blue room?”
Trifon showed Mitya to a dark corner where he could watch. Mitya looked inside. He saw Grushenka. His heart pounded.

Grushenka sat in a low chair, holding Kalganov’s hand. Kalganov seemed upset and talked loudly to Maximov, who was laughing. Two strangers were also there. One was short and angry-looking, the other was very tall. Mitya felt cold and nervous. He could not wait anymore. He put down the pistol box and walked into the blue room.
“Aie!” Grushenka screamed when she saw Mitya first.
Mitya (Dmitri Fyodorovitch) walked quickly to the table where everyone was sitting.
“Gentlemen!” he shouted, his voice shaky. “I'm all right! Please don’t worry. I just want to stay with you until morning. Only tonight, in this room.”
He looked at the fat little man smoking a pipe on the sofa.
The man took out his pipe and said, “Sir, we are here in private. There are other rooms.”
Kalganov, another guest, answered, “Is that you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Come, sit with us! How are you?”
Mitya happily shook Kalganov's hand. “I’m so glad to see you!”
“Ow! You squeezed my hand so hard!” Kalganov laughed.
Grushenka (Agrafena) smiled at Mitya, still a bit nervous, but glad he was acting friendly.
Maximov, another guest, said hello, and Mitya ran to greet him, too.

“I’m glad to see you, Maximov! Gentlemen, I came here to spend my last night in this room, with all of you. I want us to have music and fun like before. Let me buy wine for everyone!” Mitya took out a bundle of money.
Mitya was so excited he could hardly speak. The Polish man with the pipe stared at the money, then at Grushenka, looking puzzled.
“If my lady allows—” the Pole began.
Grushenka interrupted, “What does ‘suverin’ mean? You talk so funny! Sit down, Mitya, and don’t scare us. If you’re not going to, I’m glad you’re here.”
“Me? Scare you? Not at all!” Mitya said, waving his hands.
Suddenly, Mitya sat down hard on a chair and started crying, hugging the chair tightly.
“Oh, what are you doing?” Grushenka said. “You always cry when you see me! Why are you crying?”
Mitya quickly stopped, turned, and started laughing nervously.
“Cheer up!” Grushenka said. “I want you to stay, Mitya. If you leave, I’ll leave too!”
The Pole kissed Grushenka’s hand and said, “Whatever you wish. Please join us, Mitya.”
Mitya jumped up, ready to speak, but instead just said:
“Let’s drink, everyone!” Everyone laughed.
“I’m happy you brought champagne, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Don’t spend all your money, though. Where did you get it?”
Mitya quickly shoved his money back in his pocket, just as the innkeeper brought champagne. Kalganov poured the drinks.
Mitya shouted for more bottles and drank his glass quickly. Suddenly he looked much happier and smiled at everyone, especially Grushenka.
Mitya watched the two Polish men. One was short, with a pipe and a silly wig. The other was tall and looked tough. Mitya thought the tall one was the bodyguard of the short one.
Mitya didn’t really understand what Grushenka meant with some of her words, but he was just glad she was nice to him and let him sit by her.
Mitya looked around, wondering why everyone was so quiet.
Kalganov said, “We were all laughing at Maximov.”
Mitya looked at Maximov.
“He’s talking nonsense?” Mitya laughed happily.
“He says all our cavalry officers used to marry Polish women. That’s silly, isn’t it?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, very happy.
Kalganov wasn’t very interested in the Poles. He was more interested in Maximov, who often acted silly but was sometimes interesting.
Kalganov explained he had been traveling with Maximov since Mitya’s brother pushed Maximov off a carriage. Maximov kept saying silly things, so Kalganov was taking him back.
The Pole with the pipe said Maximov didn’t know Polish ladies.
The Pole could speak Russian, but liked to twist the words.
“But I married a Polish lady!” Maximov giggled.
“Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov asked.
“Was he really?” Mitya asked, excited.
Maximov explained that Polish ladies danced the mazurka with soldiers, sometimes jumping into their arms.
The tall Pole called Maximov a “lajdak,” which means scoundrel.
Grushenka got annoyed, “Why is he calling names?”
The Pole with the pipe said Maximov only knew servant girls, not real ladies.
The tall Pole agreed rudely.
“Let him talk, it’s more fun,” Grushenka said.
The little Pole said he wasn’t stopping anyone and went quiet.
Kalganov argued, “He’s never been in Poland! Were you married there?”
“No, in Smolensk. A soldier brought my future wife from Poland. He wanted to marry her, but she turned out to be lame,” Maximov said.
“So you married a lame woman?” Kalganov cried.
“They tricked me. I thought she just hopped for fun.”
“She was just happy to marry you!” Kalganov laughed.
“But after we were married, she told me she hurt her leg jumping a puddle as a child,” Maximov said, laughing.
Kalganov and Grushenka laughed hard. Mitya felt happier than ever.
Kalganov told Mitya that Maximov had two wives, and the second one ran away.
“Really?” Mitya asked, surprised.
“Yes, she took my money and left. A bishop once said, ‘One wife was lame, the other too quick-footed!’” Maximov smiled.
Kalganov explained Maximov often made up stories, even saying the writer Gogol wrote about him. Maximov claimed he was a character in Dead Souls.
Kalganov seemed truly excited about Maximov’s stories, and Mitya laughed along.
“Well, maybe he was beaten!” Mitya laughed.
“Not exactly, but—” Maximov started.
“Either you were beaten or you weren’t,” Mitya said.
The Pole with the pipe, looking bored, asked the tall Pole for the time. They didn’t have a watch.
Grushenka snapped at them, “Let people talk! Why should you stop them?”
The Pole said he wasn’t stopping anyone.
“All right, Maximov, tell us your story,” Grushenka said.
“There’s not much to tell,” Maximov said, happy to be asked. He started talking about funny names in books and a girl who could dance.
“But why were you beaten?” Kalganov asked.
“For Piron!” said Maximov.
“Who’s Piron?” asked Mitya.
“A famous French writer. I quoted some jokes at a party, and people got angry.”
“They got more angry when I told a story about Piron writing his own funny tombstone.”
“So they beat me,” Maximov finished.
“But why?” someone asked.
“For my education. People get beaten for anything,” Maximov said.
“Enough! That’s boring!” Grushenka said suddenly.
Mitya stopped laughing. The tall Pole stood up, looking bored, and walked around the room.
“He can’t sit still,” Grushenka said, annoyed. Mitya started to worry.
“Let’s have another drink!” Mitya shouted.
He poured three glasses of champagne.
“To Poland!” Mitya toasted.
The Pole with the pipe lifted his glass with pride.
“And you, too!” Mitya urged the tall Pole.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” said the Pole with the pipe.
Pan Vrublevsky, the tall Pole, walked over.
“To Poland! Hurrah!” Mitya shouted, and all three drank.
Mitya poured more.
“Now to Russia! Let’s be friends!”
“Pour for us, too!” Grushenka said.
“Me too,” said Kalganov.
“And me, to Russia, the old grandmother!” Maximov giggled.
“Everyone! More bottles!” Mitya called.
More bottles were put on the table. Mitya filled the glasses again.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted. Everyone drank, except the Poles, who didn’t touch their glasses.
“Why not?” Mitya asked.
Pan Vrublevsky raised his glass, “To Russia as she was before 1772.”
The other Pole agreed, and they both drank.
“You’re fools,” said Mitya suddenly.
The Poles got angry, shouting at Mitya.
“Can’t a man love his country?” Vrublevsky yelled.
“Stop fighting! I won’t have it!” Grushenka cried, stamping her foot. Mitya was scared.
“Sorry, I was wrong!” Mitya said. “Forgive me, panie Vrublevsky.”
“You, be quiet!” Grushenka scolded Mitya.
Everyone sat down quietly.
“I started it,” Mitya said. “Let’s find something fun to do.”
“This is boring,” Kalganov mumbled.
“Let’s play faro again!” Maximov suggested.
“Great!” said Mitya. “If the Poles agree—”
“It’s late,” the Pole with the pipe said.
“Yes, late,” agreed Vrublevsky.
“What does ‘lite’ mean?” Grushenka asked.
“‘Late,’” explained the Pole.
“They’re always late and never want to do anything!” Grushenka complained.
The Pole with the pipe said he was only sad because Grushenka wasn’t nice to him.
“Let’s play,” Mitya said, pulling out his money. “I want to play big.”
“We’ll use the landlord’s cards,” the Pole said.
Vrublevsky agreed.
“Fine, landlord! Bring cards!” Mitya shouted.
The landlord brought a new pack of cards and said the girls and music were coming soon. Mitya ran into the next room to give orders and told them to bring out presents for the girls.
Maximov followed Mitya and whispered, “Give me five roubles so I can play, too!”
“Take ten!” Mitya said, giving him money.
Maximov ran back, happy. Mitya apologized for the wait. The Poles were ready with the cards.
“Let’s start!” Vrublevsky called.
“I won’t play,” Kalganov said. “I lost fifty roubles already.”
“Try again, maybe you’ll win,” the Pole said.
“How much in the bank?” Mitya asked.
“As much as you want to bet,” the Pole replied.
“A million!” Mitya joked.
The little Pole told a story about a man named Podvysotsky winning a million gold pieces in Warsaw, just by giving his word.
“That’s not true,” Kalganov said.
“Don’t say that in polite company,” the Pole snapped.
“A Polish gambler would never give away a million!” Mitya said, but then apologized and started betting.
Maximov put a rouble on the queen card, crossed himself under the table, and won. Mitya won his, too.
They kept playing. Mitya started doubling his bets, but kept losing when he doubled. The small bets kept winning.
“Stop!” Kalganov shouted.
“What’s wrong?” asked Mitya.
“That’s enough! I don’t want you to play anymore.”
“Why?”
“Because I said so. Come away. I won’t let you play.”
Grushenka told Mitya to listen, since he was losing a lot. The Poles stood up angrily.
“Are you joking?” the little Pole said to Kalganov.
“How dare you!” Vrublevsky growled.
“Don’t shout!” Grushenka yelled. Mitya noticed Grushenka looked upset.
Mitya suddenly had an idea. He went up to the little Pole.
“Two words with you, please,” Mitya said.
“What do you want?”
“Let’s go to the next room. I have something good to tell you. Bring Vrublevsky, too.”
The Poles agreed, a bit nervous.
“Where are you going?” Grushenka asked.
“We’ll be right back,” Mitya said, looking braver than before.
Mitya led the Poles into the bedroom. They all sat down. The Poles looked serious.
“What do you want, sir?” the little Pole asked.
“I’ll give you three thousand roubles if you leave and never come back,” Mitya said, showing his money.
The Pole stared at Mitya, then at Vrublevsky.
“Three thousand?” he asked.
“Yes, three! I’ll give you five hundred now, the rest tomorrow. But you must go now and never return.”
The Poles looked at each other again, but the little one looked angry.
“Seven hundred now, not five!” Mitya tried, but the Poles got mad.
“You don’t trust me? I really have the rest in town,” Mitya said, but he felt himself losing hope.
The little Pole stood up proudly. “How dare you!” He spat on the floor. Vrublevsky spat, too.
“You do that because you want more money from Grushenka!” Mitya said, upset.
“This is an insult!” shouted the little Pole, and he stormed out, Vrublevsky following. Mitya felt embarrassed.
The Pole rushed into the main room and said, “Pani Agrippina, I have been insulted!”
Grushenka, very angry now, shouted, “Speak Russian! You used to, so do it now!”
The Pole tried to speak Russian, saying, “I came here to forgive the past, but Mitya offered me money to leave. I spat at him.”
“He offered you money for me?” Grushenka shrieked. “Is it true, Mitya?”
“She’s pure! I never touched her!” Mitya yelled.
“Don’t defend me!” Grushenka cried. She called herself a fool for crying over the Pole all these years. “He’s not the man I loved. He’s old and silly now!”
Grushenka sat down and hid her face. Just then, the girls in the next room started singing.
“This place is a mess!” Vrublevsky shouted. “Landlord, send the girls away!”
The landlord came in, angry. “Why are you yelling? And you, you cheated at cards! I saw you switch the pack. That’s against the law!”
The landlord showed everyone the real pack of cards.
“You’re a cheat!” he said.
“And I saw him change a card, too!” Kalganov said.
Grushenka was very ashamed. “How shameful!”
“I thought so, too!” Mitya said, just as Vrublevsky shouted at Grushenka, calling her a bad name.
Mitya grabbed Vrublevsky, lifted him up, and carried him to the next room.
“He’s on the floor now,” Mitya said, out of breath. “He won’t come back.”
Mitya told the little Pole, “Please leave, too.”
The landlord told Mitya and Kalganov to get their money back, but both refused.
“Keep the money. Let him have it,” Mitya said.
“Good for you, Mitya!” Grushenka cried, still angry.
The little Pole, very angry but proud, told Grushenka, “If you want to come with me, come. If not, good-bye.” He left, still thinking he was important. Mitya slammed the door.
“Lock it,” Kalganov said, but the Poles had already locked it from the other side.
“Good!” Grushenka said. “They deserve it!”

After the fun meal began, Grushenka (a woman Mitya loved) was the first to ask for wine. She wanted everyone to drink and have a good time, just like they did before. Mitya (Dmitri Fyodorovich) was so happy, but Grushenka kept sending him away to enjoy himself and make sure everyone was having fun.

Mitya listened to Grushenka and told the singers to start. The place was small, divided by curtains, with a big bed behind them. Grushenka sat by the door, just like last time, to watch the dancing and singing. All the girls who came before were there, and soon wine and food arrived.

Many people came in to watch, including peasants who remembered the last party. Mitya greeted everyone, poured wine, and made sure the girls had chocolate and tea. The men liked punch or rum. Mitya kept the party going with drinks and snacks for everyone.

The room became noisy and wild, but Mitya loved it. If anyone had asked for money, he might have given it away! The landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, stayed close to Mitya, making sure he didn’t give away too much. He didn’t like the peasant girls drinking and eating too many sweets.

Mitya remembered Andrey, who was outside, and sent him some punch. Kalganov (a friend) didn’t want to drink at first, but after some champagne, he became cheerful and started to enjoy the party. Maximov (an older man) stayed near Kalganov, very drunk. Grushenka started to get drunk, too, and said Kalganov was a charming boy.

Grushenka looked at Mitya with loving eyes but didn’t say much. Suddenly, she pulled him close and asked how he had come in just now, and if he really wanted to give her up to someone else. Mitya said he just wanted her to be happy. Then Grushenka sent him away again to have fun, but called him back soon to talk.

Grushenka asked Mitya how he learned about her coming there the day before. Mitya tried to explain, but he was nervous and kept frowning. Grushenka noticed and asked why. Mitya said he left a sick man and wished he would get well. Grushenka told Mitya not to worry about it and teased him about wanting to shoot himself, calling him silly. She said maybe she’d have something to say to him tomorrow, not today, and sent him away to enjoy the party.

Sometimes Grushenka called Mitya back and asked why he looked sad, even though he was laughing and hugging people. She told him to be happy because she was happy. She said she loved someone there and asked Mitya to guess who. She pointed to Kalganov, who had fallen asleep from drinking.

The girls sang and danced, some dressed as bears, which made the crowd laugh loudly. Grushenka said people should be happy when they get a chance to have fun. Kalganov didn’t like the wild dances and songs and soon fell asleep on the sofa.
Grushenka showed Mitya how nice Kalganov looked asleep and kissed him on the forehead. Kalganov woke up looking for Maximov, who was still having fun with the girls and drinks.

The friends watched Maximov do a silly dance. Mitya was the only one who liked it a lot and hugged Maximov. After, Maximov asked Mitya to help him make friends with one of the girls, but Mitya said no.
