Mitya felt dizzy and went out to the balcony for fresh air. He suddenly thought about ending his life, remembering the shame and trouble he was in, but he also thought things seemed easier before than now. Now, he had hope because Grushenka loved him, but he was still scared about what he had done.
Suddenly, Mitya felt hope and ran back inside to see Grushenka. On the way, he met the landlord, who acted worried and said it was after three o’clock. Mitya told him the party would end soon.

When Mitya came back, Grushenka was missing from the main room. He found her behind the curtain, crying. She told Mitya how she had loved another man for five years, but now that man seemed different. She was ashamed of those years. Grushenka asked Mitya to guess who she really loved now. Smiling through her tears, she said she realized it was Mitya she loved. She asked if he forgave her and if he loved her. Mitya hugged and kissed her, overjoyed.

Grushenka said she had teased Mitya out of spite, but now she wanted to be his slave and love him forever. Then she pulled away, said she wanted to get drunk and dance, and left to join the others. Mitya followed her, feeling like nothing else mattered except this moment.

Grushenka drank more champagne and became even more tipsy. She laughed, called everyone to her, and hugged the girls. Maximov kept dancing and singing, and Grushenka told Mitya to give him money because he was poor. She talked about wanting to be good and maybe going to a nunnery one day, but tonight she just wanted to dance and have fun.

Grushenka decided to dance. She waved a handkerchief and told Mitya to call everyone to watch, even the people who were locked in another room. Mitya went to get the Poles, who yelled back at him angrily. Grushenka danced, but soon felt weak and had to stop, bowing to everyone and saying sorry.

Grushenka asked Mitya to help her, and he carried her to the bed. She told him not to touch her yet, not until they were really together, and not in a place like this. Mitya agreed and knelt by her side. Grushenka said she wanted to be honest and good, and asked Mitya to take her far away. Mitya promised, but worried about the trouble he was in because of the stolen money and the blood he mentioned.

Grushenka said she would help Mitya give the money back to Katya and that money wasn’t important. She wanted them to work together and be honest. She told Mitya not to love Katya anymore, just her. Mitya said he loved Grushenka and would love her even in Siberia. Grushenka didn’t care where they went, as long as they were together.

Grushenka fell asleep for a moment. There was a bell ringing outside, but then everything became quiet. Mitya rested his head on Grushenka. When she woke up, she told Mitya about her dream of being with him in the snowy night.
Suddenly, Grushenka stared past Mitya, looking scared. She whispered, asking who was looking at them. Mitya turned and saw people peeking through the curtains.
Mitya left Grushenka and saw the room was full of new people: the police captain, the deputy prosecutor, the lawyer, and other officials. Kalganov and the landlord were there too.

Mitya realized what was happening and yelled that he understood. The officials told him to sit and explain. The police captain shouted that Mitya’s father’s blood was crying out against him. The lawyer said Mitya was being charged with killing his father that night. Mitya heard them but was so shocked and confused, he could barely understand.

Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin knocked loudly at the locked gate of the widow Morozov’s house. Fenya, the maid, was scared because she thought it might be Dmitri Fyodorovitch (who she was afraid of) coming back. She ran to the house-porter and begged him not to open the gate. But Pyotr Ilyitch said he had very important business with Fenya. The porter let him in. In the kitchen, Fenya asked for the porter to stay with her because she was nervous. Pyotr Ilyitch asked Fenya questions and found out that when Dmitri Fyodorovitch had gone out looking for Grushenka (her mistress), he took a pestle (a heavy tool used for grinding) with him. When he came back, he didn’t have the pestle, and there was blood on his hands.

Fenya said the blood was “dripping” from Dmitri’s hands, but that was just her imagination. Pyotr Ilyitch remembered there really was blood on Dmitri’s hands, because he had helped wash it off. Pyotr Ilyitch wondered if Dmitri had gone to his father Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house with the pestle. He felt sure Dmitri had gone there, which made him very worried.

Fenya told Pyotr Ilyitch that, when Dmitri came back, she asked about the blood. Dmitri said it was human blood and that he had killed someone. Then he ran away like a madman. Fenya thought he might go to Mokroe to hurt her mistress, Grushenka, so she ran out to stop him. She looked at Plotnikov’s shop and saw Dmitri leaving; by then, there was no blood on his hands. Fenya’s grandmother agreed with Fenya’s story. After asking more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house, feeling even more upset.

Pyotr Ilyitch wanted to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house to see if anything had happened. But it was late, the gates were strong, and he didn’t know Fyodor Pavlovitch very well. He worried that if nothing was wrong, Fyodor Pavlovitch would laugh at him for coming at midnight and tell everyone in town. Pyotr Ilyitch really hated scandals.

Even so, Pyotr Ilyitch decided to go to Madame Hohlakov’s house instead. He wanted to find out if she had given Dmitri the three thousand roubles. If she said yes, he would go home. If she said no, he would go to the police captain.

It might have caused more scandal to visit a lady he didn’t know so late at night, but Pyotr Ilyitch couldn’t stop himself. He was very nervous and kept telling himself to get to the bottom of the mystery.
Pyotr Ilyitch arrived at Madame Hohlakov’s house at eleven o’clock. The porter let him in, but didn’t know if the lady was awake.
“Ask at the top of the stairs. If she wants to see you, she will,” the porter said.

Pyotr Ilyitch went upstairs. The footman didn’t want to take his name, but finally called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch asked the maid to tell Madame Hohlakov that someone named Perhotin, an official from town, needed to see her on important business.
The maid told Madame Hohlakov, who was in her bedroom and feeling unwell. At first, Madame Hohlakov didn’t want to see Pyotr Ilyitch, but she was curious.
Pyotr Ilyitch begged the maid to tell Madame Hohlakov it was very important and she might regret not seeing him.
Madame Hohlakov decided to see him. She wrapped a shawl over her shoulders and went to the drawing-room. She looked at Pyotr Ilyitch seriously and said, “What do you want?”
Pyotr Ilyitch explained it was about Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov.

But Madame Hohlakov became upset and shouted that Dmitri had come to her house earlier and tried to murder her. She said she would complain about Pyotr Ilyitch for waking her up and talking about Dmitri.
Pyotr Ilyitch was surprised and asked, “Did he try to murder you, too?”
Madame Hohlakov asked, “Has he killed someone else?”

Pyotr Ilyitch explained quickly: Dmitri had borrowed ten roubles from him at five o’clock, so he knew Dmitri had no money. But at nine o’clock, Dmitri came back with a lot of money and blood on his hands and face. Dmitri said that Madame Hohlakov had given him three thousand roubles to go to the gold-mines.
Madame Hohlakov was shocked. She cried out, “He must have killed his father! I never gave him money! Run to his father! Save him!”
Pyotr Ilyitch asked her again if she was sure she hadn’t given Dmitri any money.
Madame Hohlakov said she had refused to give Dmitri money, and that he got angry and spat at her. She told Pyotr Ilyitch to go save Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Pyotr Ilyitch and Madame Hohlakov sat down. He told her everything he knew about what had happened, including his visit to Fenya and the pestle. Madame Hohlakov became very upset and kept covering her face and shrieking.

Madame Hohlakov said she had always thought Dmitri would kill her, and now she believed it was a miracle she was still alive. She talked about a holy ikon (a religious picture) she had put on Dmitri’s neck, and how maybe that saved her. She asked Pyotr Ilyitch what they should do now.
Pyotr Ilyitch said he was going to the police captain right away to tell him everything.
Madame Hohlakov agreed this was a good idea and said the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch, was an excellent man.
She begged Pyotr Ilyitch to come back and tell her what happened, even if it was in the middle of the night. She wondered if she should go with him.
Pyotr Ilyitch asked her to write a note saying she had not given Dmitri any money, in case it was needed.
Madame Hohlakov was happy to help. She wrote a note saying she had never given Dmitri three thousand roubles.
She gave the note to Pyotr Ilyitch and made the sign of the cross over him three times. She followed him to the door, thanking him and saying how glad she was to have met him.
Pyotr Ilyitch hurried away, but he thought Madame Hohlakov was not as old as he expected and he felt a little better after meeting her.

Madame Hohlakov was very pleased with Pyotr Ilyitch and thought he was very clever for a young man. She almost forgot the whole scary event until she was getting into bed and remembered how close she had come to danger.
But then she fell into a deep, peaceful sleep.
Later, people would remember this meeting as the start of Pyotr Ilyitch’s career. The author says he might tell more about this when he finishes the story of the Brothers Karamazov.

Mihail Makarovitch Makarov was our police captain. He was a retired soldier and a widower (his wife had died). People liked him because he was friendly and always had visitors. He loved having guests for dinner, and there was always plenty of food. The fish-pies were very good and there was lots of wine, even if it wasn’t the best.

The first room in his house was a billiard room with pictures of race horses on the walls. People played cards there every night. Sometimes, even the young ladies and their mothers came to dance at his house. Mihail Makarovitch didn’t live alone. His widowed daughter and her two grown-up daughters lived with him. The girls were cheerful and pretty, even though they didn’t have any money for a dowry. Still, many young men liked to visit them.

Mihail Makarovitch was not the best at his job, but he did his work as well as many others. He didn’t always understand new rules or changes, mostly because he was careless and in a hurry. He liked to say, “I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian.” Even though he owned land, he didn’t really understand the new laws about freeing the serfs. He learned slowly, just by doing his job.

That evening, Pyotr Ilyitch expected to find some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors at the house, but he didn’t know who. The prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, and the district doctor, Varvinsky, were there playing cards. Ippolit Kirillovitch (the prosecutor) was about thirty-five, clever but easily upset, and married to a fat woman. He wished people appreciated him more and sometimes wanted to quit his job and become a lawyer. The Karamazov case made him very excited, since it was very important.

In the next room, Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the new young lawyer, was sitting with the young ladies. Later, people would say it was strange that so many important people were at Mihail Makarovitch’s house that night, but it happened by chance.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was there because his wife had a toothache and he wanted to get away from her. The doctor loved to play cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch wanted to surprise Olga Mihailovna, the oldest granddaughter, because it was her birthday and she was trying to keep it a secret. He liked to tease her in a nice way. He was short, wore shiny rings, and was always very serious at work. He was good at questioning people, especially peasants, and making them wonder about him.

When Pyotr Ilyitch came in, he was shocked. Everyone had stopped playing cards and was talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had joined them, looking ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch learned that old Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov had been murdered and robbed in his own house. The news had just arrived.

Marfa Ignatyevna, Grigory’s wife, was sleeping but woke up when she heard Smerdyakov, the servant, scream from his room. Smerdyakov often had fits, and his screams scared Marfa. She ran to his room, but it was dark and Smerdyakov was struggling. Marfa screamed too, then noticed her husband Grigory wasn’t in bed. She called for him, but got no answer. Then she heard groans coming from the garden.
Marfa thought, “Just like what happened to Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” She went down the steps and saw the gate to the garden was open.
She thought Grigory must be outside. She went to the gate and heard Grigory calling her in a weak voice.
Marfa ran toward Grigory and found him, not by the fence but a little farther away. He was covered in blood. He had crawled there after being knocked down, fainting several times. Marfa screamed.
Grigory mumbled, “He has murdered... his father murdered... Why scream... run... get someone...”

Marfa kept screaming and ran to the window of her master, Fyodor Pavlovitch. She saw him lying on the floor, not moving, with blood all over his clothes. Marfa was so scared she ran out of the garden and rushed to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna, to ask for help. Marya and her daughter woke up, and so did Foma, who was staying with them. They all hurried to help.

Marya remembered that at about eight o’clock she had heard a terrible scream from the garden. It was Grigory’s scream, shouting, “Parricide!” when he grabbed Mitya’s leg. The two women and Foma found Grigory and carried him to the lodge. They gave him water with vinegar, and he woke up.
Grigory asked right away, “Is the master murdered?”

Foma and the women went to the house. They saw the window and the door to the garden were both open, even though Fyodor Pavlovitch had been locking himself in every night. They were too afraid to go in, so they went back to Grigory, who told them to run to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna did, and so the people at the police captain’s house heard about the murder. She arrived just before Pyotr Ilyitch, so his story matched what they already thought.
Everyone decided to act quickly. The deputy police inspector took four witnesses to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house and start the investigation. The district doctor wanted to come too.

They found Fyodor Pavlovitch dead, his head badly hurt, probably with the same brass pestle that had hit Grigory. They found the pestle on the garden path. In the room, they found an empty envelope that had once held three thousand roubles for Grushenka. The money was gone, and the pink ribbon that had tied the envelope was on the floor.

Pyotr Ilyitch’s story made everyone think Dmitri (Mitya) Fyodorovitch was the killer. He had said he would shoot himself before morning, had taken his pistols, loaded them, and written a letter. Pyotr Ilyitch had wanted to warn someone, but Mitya just said, “You’ll be too late.” So, they needed to hurry to Mokroe to find Mitya before he hurt himself.
The prosecutor was excited. “That’s just what madmen do: ‘I’ll kill myself tomorrow, so I’ll have fun until then!’”
The story of Mitya buying lots of food and wine made the prosecutor even more sure.
He remembered another case where a murderer spent the stolen money right away, not even hiding it.

The investigation at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house took a long time. So, two hours before everyone else left, they sent Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, the rural police officer, ahead to Mokroe. He was supposed to watch Mitya secretly and get ready for the arrest. He told only Trifon Borissovitch, the landlord, about his real reason for being there. Mitya didn’t know he was being watched. The pistol box was hidden away by Trifon Borissovitch. Around sunrise, the officials arrived in two carriages. The doctor stayed behind to look at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s body and was very interested in Smerdyakov’s condition.
The doctor said Smerdyakov’s fits were very rare and interesting for science. He also said Smerdyakov might not live through the night.
Now that you know what happened, we can return to our story.

Mitya sat in the room, looking around at all the people. He was confused and didn’t really understand what was happening. Suddenly, he jumped up and shouted, “I’m not guilty! I didn’t kill my father! I wanted to, but I didn’t do it. Not me.”

Right after Mitya spoke, Grushenka (the woman Mitya loved) ran out from behind a curtain and fell at the police captain’s feet. Crying, she said, “It’s my fault! I was bad! I hurt him, and that’s why all this happened. It’s my fault, most of all!”

The police captain got angry at Grushenka and yelled at her, calling her names. But the prosecutor stopped him and told him not to get in the way of the investigation. Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, also told everyone to follow the rules.

Grushenka cried, “Judge us together! Punish us both! I’ll go with him, even if it’s to death!” Mitya hugged her and said, “She’s not guilty of anything!” Then some men pulled Mitya away from her, and Grushenka was led out of the room.

Mitya remembered being dragged away from Grushenka. He sat down at a table. Men with metal badges stood near him. Across the table sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the lawyer. He tried to get Mitya to drink some water. Mitya also noticed the lawyer’s shiny rings and couldn’t stop looking at them. The prosecutor sat on one side, and a young secretary sat on the other, ready to write things down. The police captain stood by the window.
“Drink some water,” said the lawyer again.
Mitya said, “I drank it... but go ahead, judge me, punish me, decide my fate!”
The lawyer asked softly, “Do you say you are not guilty of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, death?”
Mitya answered, “I’m not guilty of my father’s murder. I am guilty of hurting another old man, but not this. Who killed my father if I didn’t? It’s so strange, it doesn’t make sense.”
The prosecutor said, “Don’t worry about Grigory, the old servant. He’s alive and will get better, the doctor says.”
“He’s alive?” Mitya cried, very happy and thankful. He crossed himself and almost couldn’t breathe.
The prosecutor tried to continue, but Mitya jumped up and begged to see Grushenka, to tell her the good news. The lawyer said no, and the men held Mitya back.
Mitya said, “I just wanted to tell her I’m not a murderer now! She is my fiancée! Thank you, gentlemen! Grigory was like a father to me when I was little.”
Mitya asked for a moment to think, saying he felt very upset, and that a man shouldn’t be treated like a drum.

Mitya suddenly felt much better—almost cheerful—like he was meeting with friends. He remembered how he used to visit the police captain, but lately, he hadn’t visited much. He wasn’t as close to the prosecutor, but knew his wife, who liked him for some reason. He barely knew the investigating lawyer, but had talked to him a couple of times.
“You’re a very good lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch!” Mitya said, laughing. “I can help you now. I know there’s a big suspicion about me, but since I’m innocent, we can finish quickly. Can’t we?”
Nikolay Parfenovitch said, “So, for now, we’ll write that you deny the charge.” He told the secretary to write it down.
“Yes, write it down. I agree,” said Mitya. “But write this too: I am guilty of fighting and hurting an old man, but not of killing my father. That’s crazy! I’ll prove it to you soon.”
The lawyer said, “Before we go on, can you say if you disliked your father? You said you wanted to kill him.”
Mitya agreed, “Yes, sadly, I did want to kill him sometimes.”
The lawyer asked, “Can you tell us why you hated him?”

Mitya said, “Everyone knows I hated him. I even said it in public and to Father Zossima. I beat my father and threatened to kill him, and there were many witnesses. But feelings are private, even if I talked about them a lot. I understand why you suspect me, because I said I wanted to kill him, and now he’s dead. But if I didn’t do it, who did? Where and how was he killed?”
The prosecutor answered, “We found him in his study, on the floor, with his head hurt badly.”
“That’s horrible,” said Mitya, putting his face in his hand.
The lawyer continued, “Was your hatred because of jealousy?”
“Yes, jealousy, and other things, too,” said Mitya.
“Money troubles?” asked the lawyer.
“Yes, about money, too,” answered Mitya.
“Was it about three thousand roubles you thought were yours?”
“Three thousand? More!” Mitya shouted. “I needed that money so much. I thought the money under his pillow was mine.”
The lawyer said, “We’ll write down that you thought the money was yours.”
“Yes, write it. I’m not afraid of facts. I’m an honorable man, even if I did bad things. My father was mean, but now that he’s dead, I wish I hadn’t hated him so much,” Mitya said sadly.

Suddenly, Grushenka, who was in another room, ran out crying for Mitya. Mitya rushed to meet her, but the men held them back. They saw each other, but couldn’t touch. Both were crying as they were pulled apart. When it was over, Mitya sat back down and cried, “Why are you hurting her? She didn’t do anything!”
The lawyers tried to calm Mitya down. After a while, Mihail Makarovitch, the police captain, came in and asked if he could talk to Mitya.

The police captain told Mitya that Grushenka was safe downstairs, being cared for by the landlord’s daughters, and that she wanted Mitya to stay calm. He said Grushenka was a good person and not to blame for anything.

Mitya was grateful to the police captain and promised to be calm. He told the lawyers, “Now, I’ll tell you everything. That woman is the queen of my heart. She loves me, even though I’m poor and ugly. I love her so much. Now I feel better.”
Mitya cried happy tears and quickly felt cheerful again. Everyone in the room could tell things were changing.
“Now, gentlemen, I’m ready to answer your questions. Just ask me about the important things, and I’ll tell you everything. Let’s not waste time,” said Mitya.
The questioning started again.

Nikolay Parfenovitch (a young lawyer) looked at Dmitri Fyodorovitch (sometimes called Mitya) with a happy smile. He said, “You are helping us a lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by being ready to answer questions. It’s important to trust each other. We will do our best, and you can see how we are handling things. Right, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He asked this to the prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch.
The prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, agreed but sounded much more serious than Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Nikolay Parfenovitch and Ippolit Kirillovitch worked closely together. Nikolay respected Ippolit very much and believed he was very smart. Ippolit liked Nikolay too. On their way to Mokroe, they talked about the case, and now Nikolay watched Ippolit for any sign of what to do.
Mitya said excitedly, “Let me tell my story my own way without too many small questions, and I’ll tell you everything quickly.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch replied, “Thank you. But before you start, can I ask about the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, using your pistols as security?”
“I gave my pistols as a pledge for ten roubles,” Mitya replied. “That’s all. As soon as I got back to town, I did it.”
“You got back to town? So you had left town before that?” asked the lawyer.
“Yes, I went about forty versts (a Russian distance) into the country. Didn’t you know?”
“Can you please start your story by telling us what you did yesterday, from the morning? When did you leave town, why, and when did you come back?”

“You should’ve asked like that from the start!” Mitya laughed. “I’ll start even earlier, the day before yesterday. I went to a merchant named Samsonov to try and borrow three thousand roubles. I really needed the money.”
The prosecutor asked, “Why did you need exactly three thousand roubles?”
Mitya got a little impatient. “There’s no need to ask so many details about why I needed that much! It would take forever to explain!”
Mitya was friendly but eager to get to the truth.

He quickly said, “Don’t be upset with me, gentlemen. I respect you and know my place. I’m not drunk now. I know I’m in trouble for hurting Grigory, an old man, and I’ll be punished for that. But your questions are so tricky! If you keep asking so many little things, I’ll get confused, and you’ll blame me for it. Please, let’s not start with tiny questions like what I had for breakfast. I know how these tricks work—I’ve been in the service too. Don’t be angry; it’s just how I am.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch laughed, but the prosecutor watched Mitya very closely.
Nikolay Parfenovitch said, “We haven’t asked you any silly questions. We started with important ones.”
Mitya answered, “I see that, and I thank you for being kind to me right now. Can I treat you as my friends? I hope I’m not offending you.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch said, “No offense at all. You said it well.”
Mitya said, “Let’s not have any more of those tricky questions, or who knows where we’ll end up!”
The prosecutor said, “I’ll listen to you, but I still need to know why you needed exactly three thousand roubles.”
“Why? Oh, for one thing and another… I needed to pay a debt.”
“A debt to whom?”
“I won’t answer that, gentlemen. It’s private. It doesn’t matter for the case. I just wanted to pay a debt of honor, but I won’t say to whom.”
The prosecutor said, “Let me write that down.”
“Go ahead. Write that I refuse to say.”
The prosecutor told Mitya, “You don’t have to answer any question you don’t want to. But it might hurt your case if you don’t. Now, please go on.”
Mitya, a little upset, said, “Well, about Samsonov, the man I went to see…”
Mitya told his story, explaining everything in detail. He sometimes got annoyed when the lawyers stopped him to write things down.

Mitya explained how Samsonov fooled him, and how he had to sell his watch for six roubles to pay for the trip. The lawyers wrote this down to show he had almost no money. Mitya got a bit grumpy. He then talked about his trip to see Lyagavy, his night in a hot hut, and coming back to town. He also talked a lot about being jealous over Grushenka.

The lawyers listened and asked about how Mitya watched Grushenka from Marya Kondratyevna’s house and got news from Smerdyakov. They wrote all this down. Mitya felt embarrassed talking about his jealousy, but he kept telling the truth. The way the lawyers stared at him made him uncomfortable.

Mitya thought it was hard to share his personal feelings with these men. When he started talking about his visit to Madame Hohlakov, he felt better but was told to stick to important things. He then told them how desperate he felt after leaving her house, and even said he’d get three thousand roubles “even if he had to murder someone.” The lawyers wrote that down. He then told them how Grushenka had tricked him.

Suddenly, Mitya said, “If I didn’t kill Fenya then, it was only because I didn’t have time.” The lawyers wrote this down too. He started to tell how he ran into his father’s garden, but the lawyer stopped him and took out a brass pestle from a bag.
The lawyer asked, “Do you know this object?” showing Mitya the pestle.
Mitya answered, “Yes, I know it. Let me see it… Oh, never mind.”
The lawyer said, “You forgot to mention it.”
“I didn’t mean to hide it from you,” said Mitya. “I just forgot.”
The lawyer asked, “How did you come to take it with you?”
“I’ll tell you,” said Mitya.
Mitya explained how he grabbed the pestle and ran.
The lawyer asked, “Why did you take it?”
“No reason. I just picked it up and ran.”
“Why, if you had no reason?”
Mitya got angry and gave the lawyer a hard look. He felt embarrassed for telling them about his jealousy.
“Forget the pestle!” he said.
The lawyer kept asking, so Mitya said, “To keep off dogs, maybe. It was dark. Just in case.”
“Have you ever taken a weapon with you at night before?”
Mitya lost his temper. “Write down that I took the pestle to go kill my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, by hitting him on the head! Are you happy now?”
The prosecutor said, “We know you said that because you’re angry at our questions.”
Mitya said, “Yes, I took the pestle. Sometimes you just grab something and run. Let’s move on, or I won’t say any more.”
Mitya sat with his head in his hands, feeling sick and tired of answering questions.

Finally, he said, “You know, listening to you reminds me of a dream I have. In it, someone is chasing me in the dark, hiding from me but always knowing where I am, just to scare me. That’s how I feel right now.”
The prosecutor asked, “You really dream that?”
“Yes. Aren’t you going to write that down?” Mitya said with a twisted smile.
“No need. But your dreams are strange.”
“This isn’t a dream now. This is real! I’m like a wolf and you’re the hunters. Go ahead—hunt me down!”
Nikolay Parfenovitch said softly, “You shouldn’t compare yourself like that…”
“No, I’m not wrong!” Mitya shouted, but then calmed down. “You may not trust someone you think is a criminal, but you should believe in an honest man’s heart.”
“Should I go on?” he asked.
“Yes, please,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Mitya (whose real name is Dmitri) began telling his story carefully, making sure he didn’t miss anything. He explained how he jumped over the fence into his father’s garden, went up to the window, and watched to see if Grushenka (a woman he loved) was with his father. The lawyers listening to him looked very serious and didn’t ask many questions. Mitya couldn’t tell what they were thinking.

When Mitya talked about making a “signal” to his father so he would open the window, the lawyers didn’t seem to care about what the “signal” meant. Mitya noticed this. As he told how he got angry seeing his father at the window, and pulled a heavy pestle from his pocket, he suddenly stopped speaking and looked at the wall.
The lawyer asked, “You pulled out the weapon, and then what happened?”
Mitya replied, “Then I murdered him... hit him on the head and broke his skull. Isn’t that what you want to hear?”
The lawyer asked, “Well, is that your real story?”

Mitya answered quietly, “No. I wanted to kill him, but something stopped me. I ran away from the window and went to the fence. My father saw me, got scared, and jumped back from the window. As I tried to climb the fence, Grigory (the servant) caught me.”
Mitya looked up at the lawyers, feeling angry.
He said, “You’re laughing at me! You don’t believe me because my story sounds strange. I almost killed him, but then I ran away. You think I’m just making it up.”
The prosecutor asked, “When you ran away, did you see if the garden door was open?”
“No, it was shut,” said Mitya.
The prosecutor said, “When we checked, the door was open. The murderer probably went in and out through that door.”

Mitya was shocked. He insisted, “That’s impossible! The door was shut the whole time I was there. Only Smerdyakov (the servant), my father, and I knew the special signals for opening the door. No one else could have gotten inside.”
The prosecutor, now very interested, asked about the signals.
Mitya explained how they used taps on the window as secret signals. He tapped on the table to show what each signal meant, including the one that meant “Grushenka has come.”
The lawyer checked, “So only you, your father, and Smerdyakov knew the signals?”
“Yes. Write that down,” said Mitya.
The prosecutor asked, “If Smerdyakov knew the signals, could he have killed your father?”
Mitya stared at him for a long time, then said, “You want me to blame Smerdyakov, but I won’t.”
Mitya admitted he had thought about Smerdyakov, but didn’t believe he did it. “He’s too weak and scared to kill anyone. He’s not the type.”
The lawyer asked, “Do you suspect anyone else?”
Mitya replied, “No. Maybe it was fate or the devil, but not Smerdyakov.”
Mitya explained, “Smerdyakov is weak and sick. He was always scared of me. He wouldn’t have killed my father, and he didn’t care about money.”
The prosecutor pointed out, “You said you wanted to kill your father, too.”
Mitya got upset, “I told you everything myself. I wanted to kill him, but I didn’t. My guardian angel stopped me.”
Mitya asked, “What did Smerdyakov tell you?”
The prosecutor said, “Smerdyakov was found unconscious in bed with a bad epileptic fit. The doctor said he might not live.”
Mitya said, “Then the devil must have killed him.”
The lawyer said they would come back to this later and asked Mitya to continue.

Mitya rested, then told how he hit Grigory with the pestle when Grigory grabbed his leg as he was climbing the fence. The prosecutor kept interrupting with small questions, like how Mitya was sitting on the wall and where the pestle was.
Mitya explained he was sitting astride the wall with one leg on each side, and the pestle was in his hand.
The prosecutor asked Mitya to show how he struck Grigory.
Mitya sat on the chair like he sat on the wall and swung his arm to show how he hit him.
The lawyer asked, “Why did you jump down after hitting Grigory?”
Mitya said, “I wanted to see if he was okay.”
He explained, “I wiped his face with my handkerchief to see if he was alive.”
He thought he might have killed Grigory, so he ran away.
The lawyer asked why Mitya went to the servant Fedosya with blood on his hands and face.
Mitya said, “I didn’t notice the blood at all.”
Next, they asked about Mitya’s plan. He said, “I was going to kill myself. I had lost everything. Grushenka was gone, and I felt disgraced. I even wrote a note to explain why.”
“And you had a big feast before?”
“Yes, a big feast. I planned to shoot myself at 5 o’clock in the morning. Here’s the note I wrote.”
The lawyers asked if he thought about washing the blood off his hands.
Mitya said, “No. Even if I had, it wouldn’t have changed what happened.”
The prosecutor asked about the large amount of money Mitya had.
They wanted to know where he got it, since earlier that day he didn’t have much.
Mitya refused to say, “I’m not going to tell you.”
Mitya said, “I can’t tell you where I got the money. It would be even more shameful than being accused of murder. So I won’t say.”
The lawyer asked, “Can you at least tell us how much you had when you went to Mr. Perhotin’s?”
“I can’t tell you that,” Mitya answered.
The lawyer asked what Mitya did after he arrived in town.
Mitya told them the rest, but left out details about his feelings. The lawyers didn’t ask much more.
The lawyer asked Mitya to put all the money he had on the table.
Mitya agreed and emptied his pockets.
They counted 836 roubles and 40 copecks.
The lawyers tried to add up how much money Mitya had spent and how much he started with.
They guessed he had about 1,500 roubles at first. Mitya said, “I suppose so.”
The lawyers thought others said it was more. Mitya just replied, “Let them say that.”
Then the lawyer said they needed to search Mitya and his clothes carefully.
Mitya agreed and began turning out his pockets.
The lawyer explained he needed to take off his clothes, too.
Mitya was not happy but agreed, asking to do it behind the curtain.
The lawyer nodded, and they prepared to search him behind the curtains.

Something very surprising happened to Mitya Karamazov. The people in the room, including some peasants and two lawyers (Nikolay Parfenovitch and the prosecutor), told him to take off all his clothes, not just his coat. Mitya felt ashamed and angry, but he did what they said without arguing. The peasants stayed close by, ready in case they needed to use force.

Mitya asked loudly if he had to take off his shirt too, but Nikolay Parfenovitch didn’t answer. He and the prosecutor were busy looking through Mitya’s coat, trousers, waistcoat, and cap, checking for anything hidden inside. Mitya realized they didn’t care about being polite to him at all.

The lawyers found a big dry bloodstain on the back of Mitya’s coat and more blood on his trousers. In front of the peasants, Nikolay Parfenovitch felt all around the clothes, searching in the seams and collars, probably for hidden money. Mitya thought they treated him like a thief, not like an officer.
The secretary, also in the room, reminded the lawyers about a man named Gridyenko who once hid money inside his cap. This made them decide to search Mitya’s cap and clothes even more carefully later.
Suddenly, Nikolay Parfenovitch noticed the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was turned in and covered in blood. He asked Mitya about it.
Mitya explained he got blood on his sleeve while helping Grigory and turned the cuff in when he washed at Perhotin’s.
Nikolay Parfenovitch then told Mitya to take off his shirt too because it was evidence.
Mitya got very angry and asked if he was supposed to stay naked. Nikolay Parfenovitch said they would arrange something, but Mitya had to take off his socks as well.

Mitya sat down and took off his socks, feeling very embarrassed and awkward. Everyone else was dressed, and he felt guilty and ashamed, especially because his socks and underclothes were dirty. He even hated his own feet and big toes. He pulled off his shirt himself and tried to act tough.

The lawyers said he could wrap himself in a quilt while they finished searching his things. After they finished, they left the room, taking all his clothes with them. Mitya waited, cold and upset, feeling like everyone was looking down on him.
At last, Nikolay Parfenovitch came back, but instead of Mitya’s own clothes, he brought other clothes for him. They belonged to Mr. Kalganov, who had left them to help out.

Mitya got mad and refused to wear someone else’s clothes, demanding his own back. The lawyers explained they had to keep his clothes as evidence because of the blood stains. Finally, Mitya agreed and put on the new clothes, which were nicer but didn’t fit well. He complained about looking silly.
Mitya wanted Kalganov to know he didn’t ask for his clothes and felt embarrassed. The lawyers tried to calm him down, saying Kalganov was only trying to help.
Mitya was told to go back to the other room. Dressed in someone else’s tight coat and long trousers, he felt even more ashamed. He thought everyone was laughing at him.
Still angry, Mitya asked if they were going to beat him now. Nikolay Parfenovitch said it was time to question the witnesses.

Nikolay Parfenovitch told Mitya they still didn’t understand where he got the money they found on him, since he refused to explain. Suddenly, Mitya asked about a ring on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s hand, but quickly got upset and started shouting.

Mitya said he would never hide anything if he had killed his father. He said he would have ended his own life if he were guilty. He called the lawyers “scoffers” and said he would say nothing more, even if it would help him. He insisted he was not the killer and wanted them to call their witnesses.

The prosecutor then told Mitya that Grigory, after waking up, said he had seen the door standing wide open when he went into the garden. This was the door Mitya claimed was always shut. Grigory was sure about what he saw and had told them the same story many times.
Mitya jumped up and shouted that this was a lie. He said the door was shut and Grigory was either lying or confused because of his injury.
The prosecutor said Grigory had seen the open door before he was hurt, not after.
Mitya kept shouting that Grigory was wrong and was accusing him out of spite.

The lawyers then showed Mitya an official envelope with three seals. Mitya recognized it as the envelope his father used to keep three thousand roubles. He shouted that Smerdyakov must have stolen it and killed his father, since only Smerdyakov knew where the envelope was hidden.
The lawyers reminded Mitya that he had told them the envelope was under the pillow, so he must have known about it.
Mitya insisted he didn’t know where it was and had only guessed. He said Smerdyakov was the only one who really knew and begged them to arrest Smerdyakov because he must be the real killer.
The prosecutor pointed out that if the door was already open, as Grigory said, Smerdyakov wouldn’t have needed a secret signal to get in. Mitya grew quiet and felt hopeless.

Mitya felt like everything was against him. The prosecutor explained that the evidence looked bad for Mitya: the open door and the mystery of the money he had, even though he had pawned his pistols for just ten roubles earlier that night. He asked Mitya to understand their position.
Mitya was very upset and pale. Suddenly, he announced he would tell them his secret and explain where he got the money, even though it would be shameful for him.
Nikolay Parfenovitch told Mitya that being honest now could help him later. The prosecutor stopped him from saying more, but Mitya hadn’t noticed.
“Gentlemen,” Mitya (Dmitri Fyodorovitch) said, very upset, “I want to tell the truth: that money was mine.” The lawyers were surprised. They didn't expect that.
“What do you mean?” asked Nikolay Parfenovitch. “You said before—”
“Forget what I said before! The money was mine—well, not really mine, but I stole it. It was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it with me all the time.”
“Where did you get it?” they asked.
“I took it off my neck, right here. I sewed it up in a rag and wore it for a month. I'm ashamed of it.”
“Who did you steal it from?”
“You want the truth? I stole it, yes. Last night I spent it all.”
“But you said you got it a month ago?”

“Yes, but not from my father. Not from him. I stole it from Katerina Ivanovna (she used to be my fiancée). She sent for me a month ago, gave me three thousand roubles to send to her sister in Moscow. At that time, I had fallen in love with Grushenka. I took half the money and spent it on fun here in Mokroe, but I kept the other half, fifteen hundred, sewn up in a rag around my neck. Yesterday, I finally took it off and spent it. The eight hundred roubles you found on me is what’s left.”
“But everyone says you spent three thousand, not just fifteen hundred,” said the prosecutor.
“Who counted? I told everyone I spent three thousand, but really I only spent half. I sewed up the rest and kept it with me.”
“This is strange,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said.
The prosecutor asked, “Did you tell anyone about this extra money you kept?”
“No one,” said Mitya.
“Why did you keep it a secret so long? Why was it so hard for you to tell us?” the prosecutor asked.
“It’s not just about the money,” said Mitya. “It’s that I hid part of it. That’s the shameful part.”
“Why did you hide half? Why not spend it all or give it back?”
“That’s the point! I hid it because I was planning. That’s the bad part. I kept it for a whole month.”

“Listen,” Mitya said. “If I’d spent it all and then told Katya (Katerina Ivanovna), I’d be a beast, but not a thief. If I’d spent half and brought the rest back, I’d still have hope to pay her back. But instead, I just kept it and didn’t give it back. That’s what makes me a thief.”
“I see a big difference,” said Mitya. “A scoundrel is bad, but a thief is worse!”
The prosecutor said, “But why did you keep half and not give it back? What did you want to do with it?”

“It was all because of my father,” Mitya explained. “He always bothered Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna), and I was jealous. I thought if she picked me, I’d need money to take her away. So I kept half the money just in case. I didn’t know Grushenka then—I thought she wanted money, and I worried she wouldn’t forgive me for being poor. So I hid the money before I went to get drunk.”
The lawyers laughed. “At least you didn’t spend it all,” they said.

“But that means I stole it!” Mitya said. “Every day I wore that money, I felt like a thief. That’s why I was so angry, why I fought, why I argued with my father. I couldn’t even tell Alyosha, my brother, about it. But sometimes I told myself, ‘Maybe I’m not a thief, because I might still give it back.’ Only yesterday, when I took the money off my neck and spent it, I knew I’d really become a thief. I couldn’t go to Katya and say, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief.’”
“Why did you spend it yesterday?” asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“Because I thought I’d die at dawn anyway. I thought it didn’t matter if I died as a thief or not. But now I see it does. What hurt me most wasn’t being in trouble or going to Siberia, but knowing I’d finally spent that hidden money and become a real thief. I’ve learned a lot tonight. You can’t live or die as a scoundrel—you have to be honest.”
The prosecutor said kindly, “I think this is just your nerves. Why didn’t you just give the money back to Katerina Ivanovna or ask her for help? She might have lent you money if you’d explained.”

Mitya got angry. “You think I should have begged Katya for money, just so I could run away with Grushenka? That would be terrible! I even thought about doing that, but it would have been too shameful. Katya might have given me the money just to get revenge on me. I almost did it, but I couldn’t.”
“I’ve told you everything horrible about myself,” said Mitya sadly. “If you don’t respect that, I’ll be ashamed forever. Are you going to write all this down?”
“Yes, it’s important,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Please, don’t write that part! I’ve told you my secret, and you just poke at my wounds!” Mitya cried, hiding his face.
The prosecutor said, “Don’t worry. You can read everything we write and change what you don’t agree with. But are you sure no one else knew about the money?”
“No one!” Mitya said, upset.
“But many people say you told them you spent three thousand,” the prosecutor said.
“Lots of people heard me say it!” Mitya agreed.
“It means nothing. I lied and everyone repeated it.”
“Why did you lie?” they asked.
“I don’t know. Maybe to show off, or to forget about the money I’d hidden. Once I started, I didn’t want to correct myself.”
“Was the amulet on your neck big?”
“No, about the size of a folded banknote.”
“Show us what’s left of it.”
“I don’t know where it is.”
“When did you take it off?”
“On my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s. I tore it off my neck and took out the money.”
“In the dark?”
“I did it by feel.”
“No scissors?”
“No, it was just an old rag, easy to tear.”
“Where did you put the rag?”
“I dropped it in the marketplace.”
“Where exactly?”
“I don’t know! Somewhere in the marketplace.”
“It’s important. Who helped you sew it?”
“No one, I did it myself. Soldiers know how to sew.”
“Where did you get the rag?”
“I don’t remember. Maybe I tore it from something, or maybe it was an old bit of calico from my landlady’s cap. I took it because it was worthless.”
“Are you certain?”
“I think so, but what does it matter?”
“Will your landlady remember?”
“No, it was just an old rag.”
“Where did you get the needle and thread?”
“I’m done answering! Enough!” said Mitya, frustrated.
“Strange you can’t remember where you dropped the rag,” they said.

“Tell someone to sweep the marketplace. Maybe you’ll find it,” Mitya said bitterly. “You don’t believe me. Why did I even confess? You tricked me into it. Go ahead, celebrate if you want. You torturers!”

Mitya hid his face in his hands. The lawyers were silent. After a while, Mitya looked up, looking hopeless and lost. The lawyers were tired too. It was morning and raining hard outside. Mitya stared out the window.
“Can I look out the window?” he asked.
“Of course,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Mitya walked to the window. He saw the muddy street and some poor dark houses. He remembered wanting to end his life at sunrise, but now he thought, “Maybe this rainy morning is better for that.” He turned back to the lawyers.
“Gentlemen,” he said, “I know I’m in trouble. But what about her? Please tell me—Grushenka is innocent. She didn’t do anything. What will happen to her?”
“Don’t worry,” said the prosecutor. “We have no reason to do anything to her. We’ll do what we can to keep her safe.”
“Thank you,” said Mitya. “You’ve made me feel better. So, what happens now? I’m ready.”
“We need to question the witnesses, and you must be present,” said the prosecutor.
“Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Tea was ready downstairs. They decided to have a glass before continuing. Mitya at first refused, but then he drank some tea. He looked very tired. Even though he was usually strong, he felt weak and dizzy after all that had happened.

The questioning of the witnesses began. The main thing everyone talked about was the money—was it three thousand roubles or fifteen hundred that Mitya (that is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch) spent at Mokroe before, and how much did he spend yesterday? Sadly, every witness spoke against Mitya. Some even told new facts that made things look worse for him.

The first witness was Trifon Borissovitch. He was not nervous at all and seemed angry at Mitya. He spoke little and answered questions clearly. He was sure Mitya had spent at least three thousand roubles a month ago. Many people had heard Mitya say this himself. Trifon said Mitya had wasted about a thousand just on gypsy girls.
Mitya, sitting with his back to the curtains, grumbled, “I don’t think I gave them five hundred. I was drunk and didn’t count.”

Trifon Borissovitch insisted, “It was more than a thousand, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You threw money everywhere, and they picked it up. I saw the money in your hands. It looked like more than fifteen hundred. We know what big amounts look like.”
Trifon also said that yesterday, Mitya told him right away he had brought three thousand roubles.
Mitya asked, “Did I really say that, Trifon Borissovitch?”

Trifon answered, “Yes, you said it in front of Andrey the driver. In the hall, you shouted you would leave your sixth thousand here, counting what you spent before. Stepan, Semyon, and Kalganov heard it too.”
The lawyers were very interested by this “sixth thousand.” They liked how the numbers added up—three thousand before, three thousand now, making six.
They called Andrey, Stepan, Semyon, and Kalganov. The peasants and Andrey agreed with Trifon’s story. Andrey remembered Mitya saying on the road, “Where am I going, to heaven or to hell?”

When Kalganov was called, he was grumpy and said he didn’t know much. He did remember something about the “sixth thousand.” He said he thought the Poles had cheated at cards, and that after they left, Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna) said she loved Mitya. Kalganov answered questions for a long time, then left upset.

The two Polish men were also questioned. The little Pole, Mussyalovitch, was a retired animal doctor, and Pan Vrublevsky was a dentist. They answered politely but kept talking to Mihail Makarovitch instead of Nikolay Parfenovitch, who was in charge. Mussyalovitch talked proudly about Grushenka, which made Mitya angry. Mitya called him a “scoundrel,” and Mussyalovitch asked for that to be written down.

After this, Nikolay Parfenovitch stopped questions about love and asked only about important things. The Poles told how Mitya tried to pay off Mussyalovitch, offering three thousand roubles—seven hundred now, the rest later in the town. Mitya argued, but in the end agreed he might have said it.

The prosecutor liked this. It could mean Mitya hid some of the money somewhere, which explained why only eight hundred roubles were found on him. Mitya said he meant to give a deed to a village instead of money, but the prosecutor didn’t believe him.
The Poles’ story was written down, and then they were let go. The cheating at cards was not discussed much. The two hundred roubles stayed with the Poles.

Next was old Maximov. He came in looking sad and messy. He admitted he borrowed ten roubles from Mitya and wanted to pay it back. When asked how much money Mitya had, Maximov said, “twenty thousand,” but it was clear he was confused.

Then it was Grushenka’s turn. Mitya promised to be calm. Grushenka came in looking pale and serious. She wrapped herself in her shawl because she felt cold and sick. Everyone thought she behaved very well.
Grushenka only glanced at Mitya, but her look made him feel better. Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her about her relationship with Mitya.

She answered that Mitya was just an acquaintance, and she had not loved him. She said she was only laughing at both Mitya and his father because she liked to tease them. She was waiting for another man who had wronged her.
Then they asked about the money. Grushenka said she heard Mitya spent three thousand roubles before at Mokroe. She heard it from Mitya himself, both alone and with others.
The lawyers were pleased. Grushenka also said she knew the money came from Katerina Ivanovna.
She explained that Mitya often told her he was out of money and was hoping to get some from his father.
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly asked, “Did Mitya ever say, even as a joke, that he would hurt his father?”
Grushenka sighed, “Yes, he said it more than once, but only in anger.”
“Did you believe he would do it?”
“No, I trusted his good heart,” she replied.
Mitya stood up and said, “Agrafena Alexandrovna, have faith in God and me. I am not guilty of my father’s murder!”
Grushenka stood, made the sign of the cross, and said, “As he says now, believe him! He is telling the truth.”

Mitya thanked her. Grushenka also said she didn’t know how much Mitya spent yesterday, but she heard him say he had three thousand. She said he told her he had “stolen” the money from Katerina Ivanovna, but she thought he should pay it back. She meant the money spent a month ago.
Grushenka was allowed to leave. She said she would wait downstairs to hear what happened to Mitya.
Mitya felt very tired and soon fell asleep on a chest in the room. The questioning was over.

Mitya had a strange dream. He dreamed he was riding in a cart through snowy fields. A peasant was driving him. They passed a village where many huts had burned down. A row of poor women stood by the road, thin and sad, with one holding a crying baby. The baby was cold, and its arms were bare.
Mitya asked, “Why are they crying?” The driver answered, “It’s the babe weeping. They are poor, burnt out, and have nothing.”
Mitya felt very sorry for the mothers and children. He wondered why people had to be poor and sad, and he wanted to help them right away.
Then, in the dream, Grushenka’s voice said she would not leave him, and Mitya felt happy and full of hope.
Mitya woke up suddenly. Nikolay Parfenovitch stood nearby, asking him to sign the protocol. Mitya noticed someone had put a pillow under his head, but he didn’t know who.
Mitya was very grateful. He said he would sign whatever they wanted.
“I had a good dream, gentlemen,” Mitya said, his face looking bright and joyful.

After the papers were signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned to Mitya (Dmitri Karamazov) and read an official paper. It said that Mitya was accused of serious crimes, he had not convinced them he was innocent, and the witnesses spoke against him. Because of this, they would keep Mitya in prison so he could not escape.
In short, Mitya was told he was now a prisoner and would be taken to the town jail. Mitya listened and only shrugged.
“I don’t blame you, gentlemen. I’m ready. I know you have to do this,” Mitya said.
Nikolay Parfenovitch told Mitya kindly that he would be taken right away by the police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch.

Suddenly, Mitya spoke to everyone in the room. “Gentlemen, we are all cruel sometimes. But I am the worst of all! I always wanted to be better, but I kept making the same mistakes. Now I have been caught, and I accept my punishment. Maybe suffering will make me a better person. But listen—I did not kill my father. I am being punished, not because I did it, but because I wanted to. I will still try to prove I am not guilty. Goodbye, gentlemen. I am sorry for shouting during the questioning. For the last time, as a free man, I shake your hands and say goodbye to all people.”
Mitya held out his hand, but Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly hid his hands behind his back. Mitya saw this and let his hand drop.

Nikolay Parfenovitch, embarrassed, said, “We are not finished yet. We will continue the case in town. I hope you do well in your defense. I have always thought you are more unlucky than bad. You are really an honorable man, but you let your feelings control you too much.”
“You are good people,” Mitya said. “May I see her to say goodbye one last time?”
They agreed, but only if someone would be there to watch.
Grushenka (the woman Mitya loved) came in. The goodbye was short. Grushenka bowed deeply.
“I told you I am yours forever. I will follow you wherever they send you. Goodbye, you are not guilty, but you have hurt yourself,” she said, crying.
“Forgive me, Grusha, for loving you and for causing you pain,” Mitya said. He wanted to say more, but stopped and left.
Mitya was surrounded by guards. Outside, two carts waited. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who looked annoyed, shouted and told Mitya to get in the cart.
Mitya remembered how friendly Mavriky Mavrikyevitch had been before in the tavern. At the gate, many people watched, including Trifon Borissovitch.
“Forgive me, everyone!” Mitya shouted from the cart.
“Forgive us too!” a few people answered.
“Goodbye, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya called.

But Trifon Borissovitch did not answer. He was busy and annoyed because the second cart was not ready. The man supposed to drive it argued it was not his turn, and the right driver, Akim, was missing.
Trifon Borissovitch complained about the peasants causing trouble.
“Why do we need a second cart?” Mitya asked. “I won’t run away.”
Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped, “Don’t call me ‘old fellow’ and keep your advice.”
Mitya went quiet and felt cold. The rain had stopped, but the wind was blowing.
“I think I’m getting sick,” thought Mitya.
Finally, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch got in the cart and squeezed Mitya into the corner. He clearly did not like this job.
“Goodbye, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya called again, this time feeling upset.
Trifon Borissovitch just stared angrily and did not answer.
Suddenly, Kalganov ran out and held out his hand to Mitya.
Mitya shook Kalganov’s hand.
“Goodbye, dear friend. I won’t forget your kindness,” Mitya said.
The cart started moving, and their hands let go. The bell rang, and Mitya was taken away.
Kalganov went back, sat down, hid his face, and cried. Even though he believed Mitya was guilty, he was very sad.
“What kind of people are we?” Kalganov said sadly.
“Is life worth it?” he cried in his grief.

It was the start of November. The weather was very cold and windy. A little snow had fallen, and the wind blew it around the empty streets near the market. The morning was gray, but the snow had stopped.

Near the market, close to Plotnikov's shop, was a small, very clean house. Madame Krassotkin lived there. She was a widow, meaning her husband had died fourteen years ago. She was thirty-two years old and lived quietly with her son, Kolya. She loved Kolya very much and worried about him all the time. She was afraid he would get sick or hurt, and tried hard to help him with his schoolwork. She even tried to be friendly with his teachers and classmates, hoping they would be kind to Kolya. But because of this, some boys teased Kolya and called him a “mother’s darling.”

Kolya could take care of himself. He was strong, brave, and liked by the other boys. He was good at school, and some people said he was even better at arithmetic and history than his teacher, Dardanelov. Kolya was proud, but he was friendly and knew how to behave around teachers. He liked making up fun tricks, mostly to impress others. He liked getting his way, especially with his mother. She was always afraid that Kolya didn’t love her enough, and sometimes she cried about it. Kolya didn’t really like these sad talks, but he did love his mother, even if he didn’t show it much.

There was a bookcase in the house with books that had belonged to Kolya’s father. Kolya liked reading them, even though some were not really for children. His mother didn’t mind, but she sometimes wondered why he read so much instead of playing.
Lately, Kolya had started doing wild and risky things that made his mother very worried. He wasn’t mean, just daring and reckless.

That summer, Kolya and his mother visited a relative who lived at a train station forty-five miles away. Kolya learned all about trains there and made some new friends, boys aged twelve to fifteen. Two boys were from his own town. After a few days, the boys made a crazy bet. Kolya, wanting to prove he was brave, bet he could lie flat between the rails while the eleven o’clock train passed over him at full speed. The boys checked to see if it was possible, and Kolya said he could do it. The older boys teased him, but that only made him want to prove them wrong.

That night, the boys went half a mile from the station so the train would be going fast. It was very dark. Kolya lay down between the rails, and the others hid in the bushes, nervous and scared. Soon, they heard the train coming.

The boys shouted for Kolya to get off the tracks, but it was too late. The train rushed by. When it was gone, the boys ran to Kolya, who was lying still. They pulled at him until he got up and walked away without a word. Later, Kolya said he had pretended not to be scared, but really he had fainted. After this, everyone thought Kolya was very brave. He was pale and had a slight fever the next day, but he was proud of himself. When they got home, people at school heard about the stunt, and even the teachers learned of it. Kolya's mother begged the teachers not to punish him. Dardanelov, a respected teacher, helped him, and the school did not take action.

Dardanelov was a single man who had loved Madame Krassotkin for a long time. A year before, he had asked her to marry him, but she refused because she thought it wouldn’t be fair to Kolya. After Kolya’s dangerous prank, Dardanelov helped Kolya, and Madame Krassotkin started to feel more friendly toward him. Dardanelov was happy with even a little hope. He liked Kolya but was strict with him in class. Kolya was good at his lessons and was second in his class. The boys thought Kolya knew more about history than Dardanelov, because once Kolya asked who founded Troy, and Dardanelov didn’t know. Kolya had read the answer in one of his father’s books, but he wouldn’t tell anyone, which made the other boys respect him even more.

After the train incident, Kolya changed a bit. When his mother heard what he had done, she was so upset that she cried for days. Kolya promised he would never do anything so dangerous again. He even cried and hugged his mother. The next day, Kolya was quiet and serious.

Six weeks later, Kolya got into trouble again, but this time it was just something silly, and he wasn’t the main one involved. Still, his mother worried about him, but now Dardanelov had more hope that she might like him. Kolya understood how Dardanelov felt, and before, he had made fun of him. But after the train incident, Kolya stopped joking about it and spoke more kindly of Dardanelov. Kolya’s mother noticed this and was very thankful. When people mentioned Dardanelov, Madame Krassotkin would blush, and Kolya would look away or call for his dog, Perezvon. Kolya had found Perezvon, a big, shaggy dog, and kept him hidden in the house. He taught Perezvon many tricks, sometimes a bit roughly, but the dog loved Kolya and showed off his tricks whenever Kolya came home.
By the way, Kolya Krassotkin was the boy who had been stabbed with a penknife by Ilusha, Captain Snegiryov’s son. Ilusha was defending his father when the other boys teased him and called him names.

On a cold and snowy November day, Kolya Krassotkin was at home. It was Sunday, so there was no school. Kolya wanted to go outside on some important business, but he had to stay home because all the adults were gone. Madame Krassotkin had rented two small rooms in their house to a doctor's wife and her two children. The doctor had left a year ago and hadn’t written in six months. The doctor's wife was very sad and only felt better because she was friends with Madame Krassotkin. Now, her only servant, Katerina, suddenly needed to go to the hospital to have a baby. The doctor's wife took care of Katerina, and Madame Krassotkin helped her. That morning, both ladies were busy helping Katerina, so they were not at home.

Because the ladies were away and the Krassotkins' servant, Agafya, had gone to the market, Kolya had to look after the “kids,” meaning the doctor's children. Kolya wasn’t worried about this, and he had his dog, Perezvon, with him. Perezvon had to stay under the bench in the hall until Kolya was ready to leave. Kolya liked the children, Nastya and Kostya, and sometimes played games with them, though he said he only did it because they were small. The children loved Kolya.

But today Kolya wasn’t in the mood to play. He had something very important to do and was waiting for Agafya to return so he could go out. He kept checking on the kids, who sat together reading a book. Every time Kolya looked in, they smiled at him, hoping he would play with them, but he was too busy.

When it was almost eleven o’clock, Kolya decided that if Agafya didn’t come back soon, he would leave anyway. He planned to tell the kids to be brave, not to be naughty, and not to be scared. He put on his warm coat, picked up his satchel, and ignored his mother’s rule about wearing boots instead of galoshes. Perezvon wanted to go out too, but Kolya made him wait until he opened the door and whistled for him. Then Perezvon ran out, very happy.

Kolya opened the door to check on the kids again. They were arguing about something. Nastya, who was eight, always won arguments with Kostya, who was seven. If Kostya didn’t agree, he asked Kolya for the answer, and both children believed Kolya was always right. Kolya listened to their talk.
“I don’t believe babies come from cabbages,” said Nastya. “It’s winter, so there are no cabbages. The old woman couldn’t have brought Katerina a baby.”
“Maybe babies only come to people who are married,” Nastya added.
“How can Katerina have a baby if she isn’t married?” asked Kostya.
“Maybe she has a husband who is in prison,” said Nastya.
“Is her husband in prison?” Kostya asked.
“No, she doesn’t have a husband. Maybe she wanted to get married so much that now she has a baby,” Nastya guessed.
“Maybe,” said Kostya, giving up.
Kolya came in and said, “You two are funny!”
“And Perezvon is with you!” said Kostya, calling to the dog.
Kolya told them, “I need your help. Agafya must be hurt, since she’s not back. I have to go out. Will you be all right?”
“You won’t be naughty or scared while I’m gone?” Kolya asked.
The children looked sad and worried.
“If you’re brave, I’ll show you something special—a little copper cannon that really shoots.”
The children smiled. “Show us!” said Kostya.
Kolya took a small bronze cannon out of his satchel and put it on the table.
“It has wheels,” Kolya said, rolling it. “It really fires, too.”
“Can it hurt someone?” they asked.
“Yes, if you aim at someone,” Kolya explained, showing them how to load it. He told them the cannon would “kick” when fired.
The children were amazed that the cannon could kick back.
“Do you have any gunpowder?” Nastya asked.
“Yes,” Kolya said.
“Show us!” asked Nastya.
Kolya took out a small flask with real gunpowder and some shot in a paper. He showed a little powder in his hand.
“Be careful—if there’s fire, it could blow up!” Kolya warned.
The children were both scared and excited. Kostya liked the shot best.
“Does the shot burn?” he asked.
“No,” said Kolya.
“Can I have some?” Kostya begged.
“Here, but don’t show your mother until I’m back, or she’ll think it’s gunpowder and be scared.”
“Mother never whips us,” Nastya said.
“I know. Don’t trick your mother except this once. Now, can I go out? Will you be brave?”
“We’ll cry,” said Kostya, already about to cry.
“We’ll both cry,” said Nastya.
“Oh, children! It’s so hard to be your age,” Kolya said. “I guess I’ll have to stay with you, even though I want to go.”
“Tell Perezvon to pretend to be dead!” asked Kostya.

Kolya told Perezvon to do tricks. The dog whined, jumped, stood on two legs, and even lay on his back pretending to be dead. Just then, Agafya, the servant, came back from the market with food. She watched as Perezvon finished his trick and jumped up, happy.
“What a dog!” said Agafya.
“Why are you late?” Kolya asked her.
“Don’t call me that, you brat,” Agafya replied, but she wasn’t really angry.
“Agafya, will you promise to look after the kids while I’m out?” Kolya asked.
“You don’t need me to promise. I’ll watch them,” Agafya said.
“Promise on your honor!” Kolya insisted.
“Don’t go out, it’s cold,” said Agafya.
Kolya told the children, “Agafya will stay with you until I come back or your mother returns. She’ll give you lunch, too.”
“Goodbye, kids, I feel better now,” Kolya said. He whispered to Agafya, “Don’t tell them silly stories about Katerina.”
“Go on, silly boy! You need a good scolding!” Agafya said, shaking her head.

Kolya finally left the house and went outside. He noticed how cold it was and said, “It is freezing.” He walked down the street toward the market-place. When he got near the market, he stopped at a gate, took out a whistle, and blew it loudly. Soon, a boy named Smurov came running out. Smurov was about eleven, wore a nice coat, and was in a lower class than Kolya. Smurov was not really supposed to play with Kolya because Kolya was known for being naughty, so Smurov was sneaking out. Smurov was one of the boys who, two months earlier, had thrown stones at Ilusha and had told Alyosha Karamazov about it.

“I've been waiting for you for an hour, Kolya,” said Smurov. They started walking toward the market together. Kolya said he was late because something held him up and asked if Smurov would get in trouble for being with him. Smurov said he wouldn’t get punished and asked if Kolya brought Perezvon (Kolya’s dog). Kolya said yes. Smurov wished it was Zhutchka, Ilusha’s old dog, but Kolya said Zhutchka was gone. Smurov suggested pretending Perezvon was Zhutchka, but Kolya said it’s not good to lie, even for a good reason. He also told Smurov not to tell anyone Kolya was coming. Smurov promised he hadn’t told anyone.

Smurov said Perezvon wouldn’t comfort Ilusha because Ilusha’s father promised to bring him a mastiff puppy to make him feel better, but he doubted it would help. Kolya asked how Ilusha was. Smurov answered that Ilusha was very sick and could hardly breathe. He tried to walk but was too weak and blamed his boots, but really, he was just too ill. The doctor Herzenstube was caring for him, and now their family had money again.

Kolya called the doctors and quacks “rogues” and said he didn’t believe in medicine. He also asked why so many boys visited Ilusha. Smurov said only ten boys visited, not the whole class. Kolya wondered why Alyosha Karamazov spent so much time with them, especially since his brother was about to be on trial. Smurov said Alyosha wasn’t being sentimental; the boys went to see Ilusha because they wanted to.

Kolya insisted he was going to see Ilusha on his own, not because Alyosha told him to, and he didn’t want anyone to analyze his actions. Smurov said Ilusha would be happy to see Kolya and asked why Kolya hadn’t visited before. Kolya said it was his own business. Smurov explained that Ilusha’s father would be very upset if Ilusha died and that the boys’ visits made him happy. They used to think badly of Ilusha’s father, but now they knew he was a good man and that the real problem was the man who beat Ilusha’s father before.

Kolya and Smurov walked in silence for a while. Smurov looked up to Kolya and wondered why Kolya had chosen this day to visit Ilusha. The market was busy with wagons and people selling things. Perezvon ran around happily, sniffing other dogs.

Kolya said he liked watching how dogs greet each other. Smurov replied it was funny, but Kolya said it wasn’t; to dogs, people would look just as silly. Kolya said he was a Socialist, meaning everyone is equal and shares everything, but told Smurov he was too young to understand. They talked about how the cold felt worse at the start of winter because people weren’t used to it yet.

Kolya pointed out a peasant with a frozen beard and teased him. The peasant replied calmly. Smurov told Kolya not to annoy him, but Kolya said the peasant wouldn’t mind and guessed his name was Matvey, which turned out to be right.

Kolya and the peasant joked about getting whipped at school. Kolya said it didn’t hurt much. The peasant sighed about how hard life was. The boys said goodbye to him. Kolya told Smurov he liked talking to peasants and wanted to be fair to them. Smurov asked why Kolya lied about being whipped, and Kolya explained that peasants expect schoolboys to get whipped, so he just told him what he wanted to hear.

Smurov asked Kolya not to tease people or get into trouble like he did with the goose before. Smurov admitted he was scared because his father didn’t want him with Kolya. Kolya said nothing bad would happen. Kolya then teased a market woman by calling her the wrong name, and they joked back and forth. Other market women laughed.

Suddenly, a young man got very angry at Kolya. He shouted that he knew Kolya and accused him of being naughty again. Kolya didn’t remember this man but answered back boldly. The man repeated that he knew Kolya and kept shouting. Kolya told him it was none of his business, then tried to confuse him by mentioning people he didn’t know, like Trifon Nikititch and Sabaneyev. The man got even more confused and turned to the women for help, but they just laughed and tried to guess who Kolya was talking about. The man got frustrated and threatened to beat someone up, but the women teased him.
By now, Kolya and Smurov were far away. They felt cheerful. Smurov asked Kolya who Sabaneyev was, and Kolya said he didn’t know—he just liked confusing silly people.
Kolya then called out to another peasant, who answered in a friendly way. Kolya joked with him, and the peasant said he was cleverer than Kolya. Kolya admitted maybe he was, and they said goodbye.

After this, Kolya told Smurov he liked recognizing clever peasants. Soon, the church clock struck half-past eleven. The boys hurried to Captain Snegiryov’s house, where Ilusha lived. When they were close, Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go get Alyosha Karamazov to come outside first. Smurov wanted Kolya to go in with him, but Kolya insisted on waiting outside. Smurov ran to do what Kolya asked.

Kolya leaned against the fence, trying to look important while he waited for Alyosha. He had always wanted to meet Alyosha. The other boys talked about him a lot, but Kolya pretended not to care. Secretly, he liked what he heard about Alyosha and wanted to get to know him. Kolya thought, “I have to act grown up, or he’ll just think I’m a little kid. I wish I was taller. Tuzikov is younger but much taller than me. At least I have a clever face. I’m not handsome, but I look smart. I shouldn’t be too friendly right away, or he might think I’m silly.”

Kolya tried hard to look independent. He was upset most about being short, not his face. At home, he measured his height every two months, hoping he would grow, but he grew very slowly. Really, Kolya’s face was not ugly; he had fair skin with freckles, bright gray eyes, and a small nose that turned up. He sometimes worried he didn’t even look clever. But Kolya didn’t think about his looks all the time. Most of the time, he forgot about it and focused on other things.

Alyosha came out quickly and smiled at Kolya. Kolya noticed that Alyosha looked glad to see him, and this made Kolya happy. Alyosha looked different now; he was wearing nice clothes instead of his old cassock, a round hat, and had short hair. He looked kind and handsome. Alyosha came out without an overcoat, in a hurry, and shook Kolya’s hand right away.
“Here you are at last! We’ve been waiting for you!” Alyosha said.
Kolya answered, “There were reasons I couldn’t come before. But I’m glad to meet you. I’ve wanted to for a long time and heard a lot about you,” he said, a little out of breath.
Alyosha replied, “We would have met anyway. I’ve heard a lot about you, too, but you took a long time to come.”
Kolya asked, “How is everything?”
Alyosha said sadly, “Ilusha is very sick. He’s dying.”
“How terrible! Medicine doesn’t work, Karamazov,” Kolya said, upset.
Alyosha told him, “Ilusha talks about you all the time, even in his sleep. You were very important to him, before the knife incident. Is that your dog?”
“Yes, his name is Perezvon,” Kolya answered.
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha asked hopefully. “Is Zhutchka gone forever?”

Kolya smiled a little and said, “Everyone wants it to be Zhutchka. I’ll tell you everything. That’s why I wanted to talk to you before we go in.” Kolya explained that last spring, Ilusha joined the preparatory class. The younger boys teased him because he was small and poorly dressed. Kolya was in a higher class and saw that Ilusha was proud and brave, even when teased. Kolya stood up for him and protected him. Soon, Ilusha became very devoted to Kolya, always following him. Kolya liked teaching and spending time with younger kids. But Kolya noticed Ilusha was sometimes too soft and sensitive, and sometimes argued back when Kolya was cold to him. Kolya tried to make Ilusha stronger by acting colder when Ilusha was more tender. Then, for three days, Ilusha seemed very sad. Kolya found out that Smerdyakov (the servant of Alyosha’s late father) had taught Ilusha a mean trick: to put a pin in some bread and feed it to a hungry dog, Zhutchka. The dog ate the bread, got hurt, and ran away crying. Ilusha felt very guilty and told Kolya, crying. Kolya decided to teach him a lesson and pretended to be angry. He told Ilusha he didn’t want to be friends for a while and sent Smurov (another boy) to tell him. Ilusha got angry and said, “Tell Krassotkin I’ll throw bread with pins to all the dogs!” Kolya then ignored Ilusha, and the other boys started bullying him too. One day, Ilusha attacked them after school and then tried to stab Kolya with a penknife, but only gave him a scratch. Ilusha ran away crying. Kolya didn’t tell on him. Later, Kolya heard Ilusha had bitten Alyosha too. Kolya wished he had forgiven Ilusha when he got sick, but he hadn’t. Now Kolya explained it all to Alyosha and said maybe he had been stupid.

“Oh, I wish I had known all this before!” Alyosha said sadly. “When Ilusha was sick, he talked about you all the time. If we could find Zhutchka, it might make him better. He thinks he’s sick because he hurt the dog. We’re hoping you can help.”
Kolya asked, “Why did you think I could find the dog?”

Alyosha explained, “There were rumors you were looking for Zhutchka. Smurov said so. We’ve tried to tell Ilusha the dog is alive. The boys even brought him a live hare, but he just wanted it set free. His father got him a mastiff puppy, but it doesn’t help.”
Kolya then asked, “What do you think of Ilusha’s father?”

Alyosha replied, “He’s not just a clown. Sometimes people act silly because they’ve been hurt and can’t speak the truth. Ilusha means everything to his father, and if Ilusha dies, his father may go mad or worse.”
“I see you understand people, Karamazov,” Kolya said, impressed.
Alyosha said, “When I saw you with a dog, I hoped it was Zhutchka.”

Kolya replied, “Maybe we’ll find Zhutchka later, but this is Perezvon. I’ll let him in soon. Maybe he’ll cheer Ilusha up more than the puppy. Wait, I’m keeping you outside in the cold! I’m selfish. We’re all selfish, Karamazov!”
