Alyosha smiled, “It’s cold, but I don’t mind. Let’s go inside. By the way, what’s your full name?”
“Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin—‘Krassotkin son’ in official papers,” Kolya answered, laughing. “But I don’t like the name Nikolay.”
“Why not?” Alyosha asked.
“It’s too ordinary.”
“You’re thirteen?” Alyosha asked.

“No, almost fourteen, in two weeks. I don’t like being asked my age. People say I played robbers with the younger boys last week, but I only did it to help them, not for fun. This town gossips a lot.”
Alyosha said, “But even if you played for fun, what’s wrong with that?”
“Play for fun? You don’t play horses, do you?” Kolya asked.

Alyosha said, “Look at it this way—grown-ups go to the theater to watch heroes and robbers. When kids play soldiers or robbers, it’s just their way of acting. It’s like art, only they are the actors.”
Kolya looked interested. “Really? That’s an interesting idea. I wanted to learn from you, Karamazov.”
Alyosha smiled and shook his hand. “And I want to learn from you.”
Kolya was very pleased that Alyosha treated him like an equal, not like a little boy.
“I’ll show you something soon, Karamazov. It’s a show, too. That’s why I came,” Kolya said, nervous but excited.
“Let’s go to the house. The boys leave their coats there because the room is small and hot,” Alyosha suggested.

Kolya said, “I’ll just come in for a minute and keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the hall and pretend to be dead. Watch—Perezvon, lie down and be dead!” The dog lay down. “I’ll go in first, then whistle, and you’ll see Perezvon rush in. Smurov must open the door at just the right moment. I’ll arrange everything. Watch and see!”

The Snegiryov family's small room was crowded. Several boys sat with Ilusha. They were all there because Alyosha had brought them, even if they said otherwise. Alyosha had carefully talked to each boy and brought him to Ilusha without making a fuss. This made Ilusha very happy, because these boys had once been his enemies. Only Krassotkin was missing, and Ilusha felt sad about that. He remembered with pain that he had stabbed Krassotkin, who had been his best friend. Smurov, the first boy to make up with Ilusha, thought this was the reason Krassotkin stayed away. When Smurov tried to invite Krassotkin, Krassotkin told him to say he didn’t need anyone’s help and would visit Ilusha if he wanted, for his own reasons.

This happened two weeks before Sunday. That’s why Alyosha hadn’t visited Krassotkin, even though he wanted to. Alyosha sent Smurov to Krassotkin two more times, but Krassotkin refused both times and said not to bother him again. Smurov didn’t even know Kolya (Krassotkin) would visit Ilusha until the night before, when Kolya told him to wait at home so they could go together, but not to tell anyone he was coming. Smurov hoped Kolya would bring back Ilusha’s lost dog, because Kolya had said it shouldn’t be hard to find if it was alive. When Smurov guessed this out loud, Kolya got angry and said he wasn’t going to search for other people’s dogs, and anyway, a dog wouldn’t live after swallowing a pin.

For two weeks, Ilusha hadn’t left his bed in the corner under the icons. He hadn’t been to school since biting Alyosha’s finger. He got sick that day. At first, he could still walk around a little, but now he was so weak he couldn’t move without his father’s help. His father was very worried, stopped drinking, and cried in secret because he was afraid Ilusha would die.

After crying, the captain would try to cheer up Ilusha by telling stories or acting silly. But Ilusha didn’t like seeing his father act like a clown. It hurt him, and he remembered the “wisp of tow” and that terrible day.

Ilusha’s gentle sister Nina, who was crippled, didn’t like the silly jokes either. Their older sister Varvara was away at school. The mother, who wasn’t very well, laughed at her husband’s clowning, though most of the time she complained that everyone ignored her. Lately, she had become quieter and spent a lot of time watching Ilusha. At first, she didn’t like the boys visiting, but later their games and stories made her happy, and she even kissed some of them, especially Smurov.
The captain loved having the children visit. He thought their visits would help Ilusha get better and didn’t doubt his son would recover.

He treated the boys very kindly, sometimes even letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha didn’t like that, so the game stopped. The captain bought them snacks and gave them tea. He had enough money because Katerina Ivanovna had given him two hundred roubles. Later, when she learned more about their troubles, Katerina Ivanovna visited herself and helped the family a lot. The captain, scared for Ilusha, accepted her help.

Doctor Herzenstube visited every other day, but Ilusha didn’t get better. On that Sunday, a famous doctor from Moscow was coming, sent by Katerina Ivanovna. The captain didn’t know Kolya was coming, though he wished he would, since Ilusha missed him.

When Kolya Krassotkin opened the door, everyone was gathered around Ilusha’s bed, looking at a tiny mastiff puppy. The captain had got this puppy to cheer up Ilusha, who still missed his lost dog Zhutchka. Ilusha tried to seem happy about the puppy, but everyone saw it just reminded him of Zhutchka. He stroked the puppy sadly. He would have been happiest if he had both dogs.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys shouted when he saw Kolya enter.
Kolya’s arrival made everyone excited. The boys stood aside so Kolya could see Ilusha. The captain hurried to greet him.
“Please come in! Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!” he said.
Kolya quickly shook the captain’s hand, then politely bowed to Ilusha’s mother and sister Nina. The mother was pleased with his good manners.
“See, he’s a well-brought-up boy,” she said, happy.

Kolya went to Ilusha’s bed. Ilusha looked very pale and stared at Kolya. Kolya hadn’t seen Ilusha for two months and was shocked at how thin and sick he looked. Kolya tried to act normal, but his voice shook as he said, “Well, old man, how are you?” Ilusha just smiled a little, but couldn’t talk. Kolya gently patted his hair and whispered, “Never mind!” trying to cheer him up. They were quiet for a moment.
Kolya tried to sound casual. “Hey, you got a new puppy?” he said.
“Ye—es,” Ilusha whispered weakly.

Kolya talked about the puppy, trying to sound interested, but inside he was trying not to cry. The other boys started talking about how big the puppy would get. The captain joined in, talking about how fierce it would be.
Kolya sat at the foot of the bed. He had wanted to say something clever, but now he forgot what it was.
“No ... I came with Perezvon. I have a dog now, called Perezvon. He’s outside. I brought him to show you,” Kolya said, turning to Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he asked suddenly.
Ilusha’s face shook. He looked at Kolya with pain. Alyosha, standing by the door, frowned and tried to tell Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya kept going.
“Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked, his voice breaking.
“Oh, your Zhutchka’s lost and gone,” Kolya said.
“It must have died after eating what you gave it,” Kolya went on, but he was breathing hard. “But I have a dog, Perezvon. I brought him to show you.”
“I don’t want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.
“No, you have to see him, he’ll amuse you. He’s shaggy, like Zhutchka. May I bring him in, madam?” Kolya asked Ilusha’s mother, looking very excited.
“I don’t want him, I don’t want him!” cried Ilusha, almost in tears.
The captain tried to stop Kolya, but Kolya couldn’t wait. He told Smurov to open the door and blew his whistle. Perezvon the dog ran into the room.
Kolya made Perezvon stand up and do tricks. Ilusha stared at the dog, hardly able to breathe.
“It’s ... Zhutchka!” Ilusha suddenly cried, his voice full of surprise and happiness.
“Who did you think it was?” Kolya shouted with joy, picking up the dog and holding him up to Ilusha.

Kolya explained that he had found Zhutchka by the marks Ilusha had described: blind in one eye and a torn ear. The dog had been living as a stray. Kolya said the dog hadn’t swallowed the pin after all, just got pricked and ran away. That’s why he squealed. Ilusha was so happy and surprised he couldn’t speak. The captain started crying with joy, and the other boys cheered Kolya for finding the dog.
Kolya told everyone how he found Zhutchka and hid him at home, teaching him tricks so he could bring him back as a surprise. He asked for some meat to show a trick.
The captain ran to get cooked beef. While waiting, Kolya made Perezvon play dead. The boys laughed and Ilusha smiled, but Ilusha’s mother was the happiest and clapped for the dog.
Kolya said nothing could make the dog move except his own call. He called Perezvon, who jumped up and wagged his tail. The captain brought the beef.
Kolya checked if the meat was hot, then made the dog stand still with a piece of meat on his nose. Everyone watched as the dog didn’t move.
Kolya shouted, “Paid for!” and the dog flipped the meat into his mouth. Everyone cheered and clapped.
Alyosha asked, a little sad, “Did you really stay away all this time just to train the dog?”
“Yes,” said Kolya. “I wanted to show him at his best.”
Ilusha called Perezvon over. Kolya let the dog jump on the bed. Ilusha hugged the dog and buried his face in its fur, so happy.

Kolya said, “Ilusha, I brought you something else—a little cannon I told you about.” He took the toy cannon from his bag and gave it to Ilusha, who was delighted. Kolya also brought gunpowder so they could fire it.

The captain, as a soldier, loaded the cannon with just a little powder. They set it off, and it exploded with a loud bang. Ilusha’s mother was startled, then laughed. Kolya gave Ilusha the cannon as a present.

Ilusha’s mother wanted the cannon for herself and started to beg for it. Ilusha said she could have it, but wanted Kolya’s permission first. Kolya agreed and handed it to her politely. She was so happy she cried and played with the cannon, rolling it on her lap.

Kolya promised Ilusha he would bring more powder and explained how to make it. The boys talked about making powder and getting in trouble for it. Kolya said he had a bad reputation now because of these adventures.

Kolya talked about being punished for making powder, and then told the story about the goose—how he and another boy made a goose stick its head under a cart wheel and broke its neck. They got in trouble, and Kolya had to pay for the goose. The story made everyone laugh except for Alyosha, who listened seriously.

Kolya went on, acting important. He boasted about knowing history and languages, but then said he didn’t care much for them. Another boy, Kartashov, said he knew who founded Troy, and named the people. Kolya teased him, asking what “founding” meant, making the boy embarrassed. Kolya said history is full of foolishness and only science and math are important, but he studied Latin because he promised his mother. Alyosha gently disagreed, but Kolya insisted.

Suddenly, Nina said, “The doctor has come!” A carriage stopped outside. The captain rushed out to meet the important doctor from Moscow. The mother sat up straight, and Alyosha fixed Ilusha’s pillows. The boys got ready to leave. Kolya said he would wait in the hall and come back after the doctor left, with Perezvon.
The doctor entered, looking surprised at the crowded, poor room. The captain bowed and showed him in.
“Where is the patient?” the doctor asked.
Kolya asked Alyosha, “What do you think the doctor will say to him? That doctor looks strange. I don't like medicine at all!” Alyosha answered sadly, “Ilusha is dying. I think that is certain.”

Kolya said, “Doctors are cheats! Medicine is fake! But I'm glad I finally met you, Karamazov. I wanted to know you for a long time, but it's sad we meet like this.” Kolya wanted to say something nicer but felt awkward. Alyosha noticed and smiled, squeezing his hand.

Kolya mumbled, “I've always respected you. I know you're a mystic and went to the monastery, but that doesn't bother me. Real life will help you change.” Alyosha was surprised and asked, “What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?” Kolya replied, “Oh, God and all that stuff.” Alyosha asked, “Don’t you believe in God?” Kolya said, “I don’t mind God. He’s only an idea, but maybe the world needs Him. If there was no God, someone would invent Him.” Kolya started to blush, worrying Alyosha might think he was trying to act smart.

Kolya quickly added, “I don't like talking about this. You can still love people even if you don't believe in God, right? Voltaire didn’t believe in God and loved people!” Alyosha replied gently, “Voltaire believed in God a little, but I don’t think he loved people much.” Then Alyosha asked, “Have you read Voltaire?” Kolya said, “Not really. I read Candide, but only in an old Russian translation.” Alyosha asked, “Did you understand it?” Kolya answered, “Yes, I think so. There’s a lot of bad stuff in it, but it’s a book with ideas.” Then Kolya suddenly said, “I am a Socialist, Karamazov, I can’t help it.”

Alyosha laughed, “But when did you become a Socialist? Aren’t you only thirteen?” Kolya said, “I’ll be fourteen soon! My age doesn’t matter, it’s what I believe that matters.” Alyosha answered, “When you are older, you’ll see how age matters. I also think you are repeating other people’s ideas.” Kolya interrupted, “You want obedience and mysticism, but Christianity just helps rich people keep poor people down. Isn’t that true?” Alyosha said, “I know where you read that. Someone told you!” Kolya argued, “No one told me. I can think for myself. I’m not against Christ. He was very kind, and if He lived now, He would join the revolution.” Alyosha was surprised, “Who told you that?” Kolya said, “I talked to Mr. Rakitin, but I also heard Byelinsky said it.” Alyosha asked, “Have you read Byelinsky?” Kolya replied, “Not really, but I read the part about Tatyana and Onyegin.” Alyosha asked, “Do you understand that?” Kolya said, “You think I’m like little Smurov! But I’m not a big revolutionist. I argue with Mr. Rakitin. I think women should obey, like Napoleon said. I also think leaving Russia for America is silly. We can help people here. That’s what I answered when someone asked me to go.” Alyosha asked, “Who? Did someone really ask you to go to America?” Kolya said, “Yes, but I said no. Don’t tell anyone! I don’t want trouble with the secret police.”

Alyosha changed the topic, “Have you read Pushkin—Onyegin? You mentioned Tatyana.” Kolya said, “No, but I want to. I’m not against reading both sides.” Then Kolya asked, “Karamazov, do you look down on me?” Alyosha said, “No. I just feel sad that your good nature is getting mixed up with silly ideas.” Kolya said, “Don’t worry about me. I know I am sensitive. You smiled before, and I thought it was at me.” Alyosha said, “No, I smiled because I read something funny by a German. He said Russian kids will correct a star map they don’t know about. He meant Russian kids are proud even when they don’t know things.” Kolya laughed, “That’s true! But Russian kids are also bold and independent. Still, the German was right. But Germans are annoying, even if they are smart.”

Kolya added, “Anyway, we’re talking too much. The doctor is taking a long time. Maybe he’s with Nina. I liked Nina. She asked me, ‘Why didn’t you come before?’ She sounded so sad. She seems very nice.” Alyosha said, “You’ll visit more and see what she’s like. It will help you to know people like that.” Kolya said, “I feel bad for not coming sooner!” Alyosha said, “Yes, Ilusha was so happy to see you. He waited for you.” Kolya said, “Don’t remind me! It’s my own fault. I was proud and stubborn. I see that now. I’m a beast sometimes!” Alyosha replied, “No, you have a good heart, even if it’s confused. That’s why Ilusha likes you.” Kolya said, “And you say that! I thought you despised me, but I care about what you think.” Alyosha said, “Are you really this sensitive?” Kolya said, “You noticed? When I talked about the goose, I thought you thought I was showing off. And when I said if there was no God, someone would invent Him, I was copying a book. But I wasn’t trying to show off. I just felt happy. Oh, Karamazov, I feel unhappy sometimes. I think everyone is laughing at me, and then I want to change everything.”

Alyosha smiled, “And you worry everyone around you.” Kolya agreed, “Yes, especially my mother. Am I very silly now?” Alyosha said, “Don’t think about that! Everyone seems silly sometimes. Lots of smart people are afraid of looking silly, and that makes them sad. It’s strange to feel this way so young, but it’s common now. But you shouldn’t be like everyone else.” Kolya asked, “Even if everyone is like that?” Alyosha said, “Yes, even then. Be different. You’re not afraid to admit mistakes, and that’s rare.” Kolya said, “You know how to make me feel better. I wanted to meet you for so long. Did you think of me too?” Alyosha said, “Yes, I did. And if you asked because of pride, that’s okay.”

Kolya said, “Our talk is like a love letter! That’s not silly, is it?” Alyosha smiled, “Not at all. And even if it is, it’s good.” Kolya teased, “You’re a little embarrassed now, aren’t you?” Alyosha laughed, “Maybe, I don’t know why.” Kolya said happily, “I like you even more now because you’re like me!” Alyosha suddenly said, “You will be unhappy in life, Kolya.” Kolya agreed, “I know.” Alyosha said, “But you will still love life.” Kolya cheered, “Yes! You know everything! I’m glad we are friends. All this month, I thought either we’d be friends forever or enemies forever.” Alyosha laughed, “That means you liked me.” Kolya said, “I did! I dreamed of being your friend. Oh, here’s the doctor! What will he say? Look at his face!”

The doctor came out of the room, wearing his warm coat and hat. He looked upset and like he didn’t want to be there. He glanced at Alyosha and Kolya, looking serious. Alyosha waved to the coachman, and the carriage came. The captain hurried after the doctor, looking very sad and scared.
“Your Excellency, is it possible?” the captain asked the doctor, but he was too upset to finish. He looked at the doctor, hoping for good news.
“I can’t help it, I am not God!” the doctor said quickly.
“Doctor, will it be soon?” the captain asked, very worried.
“You must be ready for anything,” the doctor answered, looking down and getting ready to leave.
“But is there nothing that can help him?” the captain begged.
“It’s not up to me now,” the doctor said. Then he added, “If you could send your patient right away to Syracuse, maybe the new climate would help—”
“To Syracuse?” the captain asked, confused.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya said quickly. The doctor looked at him.
“Sicily, your Excellency,” the captain said sadly, pointing to his poor home. “But you’ve seen my family?”

“No, Sicily is not for the family. Your family should go to the Caucasus in spring. Your daughter should go there, and your wife should go to Paris to see a doctor for her illness. I could give you a note.”
“Doctor, you see we can’t do that,” the captain said, showing the plain walls.
“That’s not my business,” the doctor said, smiling a little. “I told you what medical science says. The rest is not up to me.”
Kolya said loudly, “Don’t be afraid, apothecary, my dog won’t bite you.” He called the doctor “apothecary” on purpose to annoy him.
“What’s that?” the doctor asked, surprised, looking at Kolya. “Who is this?” he asked Alyosha.
“I’m Perezvon’s master, don’t worry about me,” Kolya said.
“He’s just a schoolboy, doctor. Don’t pay attention to him,” Alyosha said quickly, frowning at Kolya. “Kolya, be quiet!”
“He needs a good scolding!” the doctor shouted, getting very mad.
“And you know, apothecary, maybe my Perezvon will bite!” Kolya said, getting upset.
“Kolya, if you say another word, I won’t talk to you anymore,” Alyosha said firmly.
Kolya pointed at Alyosha. “Only Alyosha can tell Nikolay Krassotkin what to do. I obey him. Good-bye!”

Kolya went into the room, and Perezvon followed. The doctor stood shocked, then left in a hurry, still angry. The captain helped him to the carriage. Alyosha went after Kolya into the room, where Ilusha was calling for his father and holding his hand. Soon, the captain came in too.
“Father, come ... we ...” Ilusha tried to say, but he was too excited. He hugged his father and Kolya together.
“Father, I feel so sorry for you,” Ilusha moaned.
“Ilusha, the doctor said you will get better ... we’ll be happy ...” the captain said, trying to smile.
“Father, I know what the doctor really said about me. I saw,” Ilusha cried, hugging them both.
“Father, don’t cry. When I die, find a good boy and name him Ilusha. Love him like you loved me.”
“Stop it, old man, you’ll get well,” Kolya said, sounding angry to hide his sadness.
“But don’t forget me, father. Visit my grave by the big stone where we used to walk. Come with Kolya and Perezvon. I will wait for you,” Ilusha said.
Kolya ran out to the hall. He tried not to cry, but tears came. Alyosha found him crying.
“Kolya, you must come back. Ilusha will be so sad if you don’t,” Alyosha said.
“I will! I feel so bad for not coming sooner!” Kolya said, crying.
Kolya ran outside.
“Good-bye, Karamazov! Will you come?” Kolya shouted to Alyosha.
“I will come in the evening,” Alyosha replied.
“It’s from the Bible. It means if he forgets what’s most precious to him, he wishes something bad would happen to him,” Alyosha explained.
“I understand! Be sure to come! Come on, Perezvon!” Kolya called, and hurried home.

Alyosha walked to the widow Morozov's house to visit Grushenka, who had sent her maid Fenya to ask him to come quickly. Alyosha found out from Fenya that Grushenka had been very upset since yesterday. Ever since Mitya was arrested two months ago, Alyosha often visited Grushenka, bringing her news and messages from Mitya. Soon after Mitya's arrest, Grushenka had become very sick, even falling unconscious for a whole week. She had only gotten better in the last two weeks and could go outside again. Alyosha noticed that Grushenka looked different now—she was thinner and seemed more serious, but he thought her face was even kinder and stronger than before. She didn’t act silly like she used to.

Alyosha thought it was strange that, even though Grushenka was engaged to Mitya, who was in jail for a terrible crime, and even though she had been so sick, Grushenka was still cheerful sometimes. Her eyes were softer now, but sometimes she looked jealous when she talked about Katerina Ivanovna. Grushenka was jealous of Katerina Ivanovna, even though Katerina never visited Mitya in prison. Grushenka told Alyosha all her worries, and sometimes he didn’t know what to say.

Alyosha went into Grushenka’s home, feeling worried. Grushenka had just come back from seeing Mitya and jumped up happily when she saw Alyosha. There were cards on the table for a game, and on the sofa, old Maximov was lying down. He was sick but smiling. Maximov had come with Grushenka from Mokroe two months ago and had nowhere else to go, so Grushenka let him stay. She gave him food and a bed on the sofa, and soon he became important to her, especially when she was sad. Grushenka didn’t see many people except Alyosha, who visited sometimes, and Maximov, who stayed all the time.

When Grushenka came home after seeing Mitya, she would sit and talk to Maximov about little things to distract herself from her sadness. Maximov was a good storyteller, and he cheered her up. Grushenka’s old merchant friend was very sick and didn't want to see her, but Grushenka still sent people to ask about him every day.
“You’ve come at last!” Grushenka cried happily to Alyosha. “Maximushka kept saying maybe you wouldn't come. I really need you! Sit down. Want some coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha. “I’m very hungry.”

“Good! Fenya, bring coffee and hot little pies. I had trouble over those pies today—I brought them to Mitya in prison, but he wouldn’t eat them. He even stomped on one! We quarreled again. Every time I visit, we end up arguing.”
“What did you argue about?” Alyosha asked.
“He was jealous of the Pole. He asked, ‘Why are you keeping him?’ He’s always jealous, even of Kuzma last week!”
“But he already knew about the Pole?”
“Yes, but today he suddenly got angry about it. Rakitin went in after me. Maybe Rakitin is making it worse. What do you think?”
“He just loves you very much, and he’s scared,” Alyosha said.
“Maybe he is, with the trial tomorrow. I went to talk to him about that, but he only wants to talk about the Pole. He’s silly! At least he’s not jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was very jealous, too,” said Maximov.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka laughed.
“Of the servant girls.”
“Be quiet, Maximushka. I’m not in the mood for jokes,” Grushenka said, but she smiled a little.
“I don’t deserve your kindness,” Maximov said sadly.

“Everyone matters, Maximushka. And now the Pole is sick, too. I’ll send him some pies as well, since Mitya is accusing me of it anyway. Ah, here’s Fenya with a letter. It’s from the Poles—asking for money again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch, the Pole, had sent Grushenka another long letter asking to borrow three roubles, saying he would pay her back soon. Grushenka had gotten many letters like this during her illness, each asking for less and less money. At first, they asked for two thousand roubles, but now they only wanted one rouble. Grushenka knew they were poor, so she sometimes sent them small amounts.

One evening, Grushenka visited the Poles herself and saw they were very poor with no food or fuel. Still, they acted very proud. Grushenka laughed and gave her old admirer ten roubles. She told Mitya about it, and he wasn’t jealous then. But now, the Poles kept asking for more money, and today Mitya was very jealous.

“Like a fool, I visited the Pole for a minute on my way to see Mitya. My Pole even tried to sing sad songs to me, hoping I would marry him!” Grushenka said quickly. “Mitya got so angry! Anyway, Fenya, give the Pole’s girl three roubles and a dozen pies. And Alyosha, tell Mitya I did send the pies.”
“I won’t tell him,” Alyosha smiled.
“You think he’s really upset about it? He’s jealous on purpose. He doesn’t care!” Grushenka said angrily.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“You wouldn’t understand, Alyosha. I’d be upset if he wasn’t jealous! But what hurts is that he doesn’t love me. He’s pretending to be jealous so he can blame me. He even praised Katerina to my face, saying she’s done so much for him. He wants to blame me for everything. He does it on purpose!” Grushenka began to cry.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.
“Well, I’ll find out!” Grushenka snapped, wiping her eyes. Her face looked sad and angry.
“Enough of this. Alyosha, what will happen tomorrow at the trial? I’m the only one who cares! Will they blame Mitya for what the valet did? No one is standing up for him!”
“They questioned the valet a lot,” Alyosha said. “But everyone thinks it wasn’t him. Now he’s very sick.”
“Can’t you go talk to Mitya’s lawyer yourself? He was brought from Petersburg for a lot of money.”
“Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna, and I paid the money together. But Katerina paid for the doctor herself. The lawyer, Fetyukovitch, came because the case is famous now. I saw him yesterday.”
“Did you talk to him?” Grushenka asked.
“He listened but didn’t say much. He said he’d think about what I told him.”
“They are all cheats! And why did Katerina send for the doctor?”
“To prove Mitya is mad, so maybe he won’t get in so much trouble. But Mitya doesn’t like that idea.”
“If he did kill someone, he was crazy then, and it was my fault! But he didn’t do it! Still, everyone is against him.”
“Yes, there is a lot of evidence,” Alyosha said.
“Grigory insists he saw the door open and won’t change his mind. He’s rude about it, too.”
“That’s the strongest evidence,” Alyosha agreed.
“And Mitya seems crazy now,” Grushenka said worriedly. “He keeps talking to me about a poor baby and says, ‘It’s for that baby I’m going to Siberia.’ What does he mean, Alyosha?”
“Maybe Rakitin has been talking to him,” Alyosha said kindly. “But I’ll see Mitya today.”
“It’s not Rakitin. It’s Ivan Fyodorovitch. Ivan has been to see him, that’s what it is,” Grushenka said, then stopped suddenly, looking embarrassed.
“Ivan? Mitya told me Ivan hasn’t visited him at all.”
“Well, I’ve said this much, so I’ll tell you the truth. Ivan visited Mitya twice, but he told Mitya not to tell anyone. He came secretly.”

Alyosha thought about this news. “Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case. He seems upset when I visit, so I haven’t seen him for three weeks. If he visited Mitya last week, maybe that’s why Mitya is different now.”

“There’s a secret between them!” Grushenka said. “Mitya said there was a secret he couldn’t tell me, and now he’s acting strange—sometimes happy, sometimes worried. He keeps pulling at his hair when he’s upset.”
“But you said he was worried.”
“Yes, he is, but sometimes he laughs like a little kid too.”
“Did he really tell you not to tell me about Ivan?”
“Yes. He’s most afraid of you, Alyosha, because of the secret. Please, go find out what it is and come tell me. That’s why I asked you to come.”
“You think it’s about you? If it was, he wouldn’t say there was a secret,” Alyosha said.
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me but doesn’t dare.”
“What do I think?” Grushenka said. “I think they are all planning to leave me—Mitya, Katerina, and Ivan. Mitya said Ivan loves Katerina. Is that true, Alyosha? Tell me, please.”
“I don’t think Ivan loves Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha answered honestly.
“I knew it! Mitya is lying to me. He’s jealous just to blame me later. He even said I believed he did the terrible thing. I’ll show them all at the trial!” Grushenka cried and started crying again.

“Grushenka, I know Mitya loves you more than anyone,” Alyosha said, standing up. “If Mitya tells me his secret today, I’ll tell him I promised to tell you, and then I’ll come back and tell you. But I don’t think the secret is about Katerina. Goodbye for now.”
Alyosha shook hands with Grushenka. She was still crying, but Alyosha saw she felt a little better after talking. He was sorry to leave her sad, but he had many things to do.

Alyosha went to visit Madame Hohlakov's house. She had been sick for three weeks because her foot was swollen. She spent her days lying on her couch, wearing fancy clothes. Alyosha noticed she had started to dress up more, maybe because a young official named Perhotin often visited her.

Alyosha hadn't visited for four days and wanted to see Lise (Madame Hohlakov's daughter) because Lise had sent a message saying she needed to talk to him about something important. When Alyosha arrived, the maid went to tell Lise, but Madame Hohlakov sent for Alyosha first. Madame Hohlakov was excited to see him, lying on her couch in nice clothes. She greeted him happily and started talking a lot.

Madame Hohlakov said it felt like ages since Alyosha had visited, even though it was only four days. She guessed he wanted to see Lise and said she trusted him with her daughter. She called him a monk since Father Zossima died, even though Alyosha was wearing a nice new suit. She talked quickly, mixing up her thoughts, and kept changing the subject. She worried about Lise, about Alyosha’s brothers, and about the upcoming trial. She even called for coffee.
Alyosha thanked her and said he had already had coffee.
Madame Hohlakov asked where he had coffee, and Alyosha said it was at Agrafena Alexandrovna’s house.

Madame Hohlakov didn’t like this and said Agrafena had caused a lot of trouble, but then she changed the subject again. She said she would attend the trial even though she was sick, because she was a witness. She worried about what she would say.
Alyosha said he didn’t think she’d be able to go because she wasn’t well enough to sit up.

Madame Hohlakov insisted she could sit up and started worrying again about the trial, about people going to Siberia, and about all the changes happening so quickly. She was upset that people were writing about the case in newspapers. She said there was even a rumor that she was a “dear friend” of Alyosha’s brother, which made her very upset.
Alyosha asked where the rumor was printed. Madame Hohlakov showed him a newspaper called Gossip and told him to read the article.
Madame Hohlakov seemed very upset about the newspaper. She couldn’t focus well and kept jumping from one idea to another.

Alyosha knew there were many wild stories about the Karamazovs in the papers. The article he read didn’t use names but said a certain lady wanted to run away with Alyosha’s brother and offered him money, but instead, he stayed and was accused of murder.

Madame Hohlakov quickly said she was the lady in the article. She was upset the writer called her “middle-aged charms.” She thought Rakitin, Alyosha’s friend, had written the article because she had turned him out of her house.
Alyosha said maybe it was Rakitin, but he didn’t know. Madame Hohlakov was sure it was Rakitin and started to explain why she had sent him away.

Madame Hohlakov told Alyosha that Rakitin seemed to have fallen in love with her and visited often. She liked young people like Perhotin, who was polite and clever, but Rakitin got jealous. One day, Rakitin gave her a poem about her foot. Soon after, Perhotin visited, and Madame Hohlakov showed him the poem. Perhotin made fun of it, which made Rakitin angry. They argued, and Madame Hohlakov fainted from all the excitement. When she woke up, she asked Rakitin not to visit her again. She felt bad about it but thought it would be a dramatic scene. Now she wondered if Rakitin had written the gossip article about her.
Alyosha said he really needed to see his brother today.
Madame Hohlakov asked Alyosha what “aberration” meant in court, thinking it meant someone could be forgiven for a crime if they were not in their right mind.

Madame Hohlakov talked about the new doctor who came to town. She thought Dmitri (Mitya) might be acquitted of murder because he was in a state of “aberration,” meaning he didn’t know what he was doing. She believed the new laws would help him.
Alyosha said sharply that Dmitri did not kill his father.
Madame Hohlakov said she thought Grigory (the old servant) had done it instead.
Alyosha was shocked.

Madame Hohlakov explained her idea: after Dmitri hit Grigory, Grigory got up, went inside, and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch while confused from the blow. But then she changed her mind again, saying it would be better if Dmitri had done it, because then he could be found not guilty due to “aberration.” She rambled about how everyone seems confused nowadays.
Alyosha said again that he needed to go see Lise.

Madame Hohlakov suddenly started crying and said she trusted Alyosha with Lise, but not Ivan (Alyosha’s other brother). She was upset because Ivan had visited Lise secretly. Lise had also been acting strange, having fits and being rude to their maid Yulia but then apologizing and hugging her. Madame Hohlakov begged Alyosha to talk to Lise and find out what was wrong.
Alyosha said he would go to Lise.
Madame Hohlakov told Alyosha not to forget to come back and tell her what he learned from Lise, because it was very important.
Alyosha said he would try, but he was in a hurry.
Madame Hohlakov begged him to promise, but Alyosha had already left the room.

Alyosha went in to see Lise (a girl who was sick and couldn't walk). She sat in her chair and stared at him. Her face looked pale and thin. Alyosha was surprised at how much she had changed. He touched her hand, but she didn't move. He sat down in front of her.
“I know you want to go to the prison, and Mama kept you here talking about me and Yulia,” Lise said quickly.
“How did you know that?” Alyosha asked.
“I listened at the door. Why do you look at me like that? I like to listen. I’m not sorry.”
“Are you upset?” Alyosha asked.

“No, I’m happy. I keep thinking it’s good I said no to marrying you. You wouldn’t be a good husband. If I loved someone else and asked you to take him a letter, you would do it, even if you were old. You’d always run my errands.” She laughed.
Alyosha smiled. “You are mean but honest.”
“I’m honest because I’m not embarrassed with you. I don’t respect you, Alyosha. I like you, but I don’t respect you. If I did, I’d be embarrassed.”
“No,” Alyosha agreed.
“Do you believe I’m not embarrassed with you?”
“No, I don’t believe it.”
Lise laughed nervously and started talking fast.
“I sent Dmitri (your brother) some candy in prison. You’re actually pretty, Alyosha! I’ll love you for letting me not love you.”
“Why did you want to see me today, Lise?”
“I want someone to hurt me, to marry me, and then go away. I don’t want to be happy.”
“You like trouble?”
“Yes, I want trouble. I keep thinking about setting the house on fire in secret, and watching it burn. But it’s just silly. I’m bored.”
“It’s because you have an easy life,” Alyosha said softly.
“Is it better to be poor?”
“Yes, it’s better.”

“That’s what your monk taught you. I don’t believe it. If I’m rich, I’ll eat sweets and not share. If I’m ever poor, I might hurt someone. Maybe even if I’m rich, too. But sometimes I want to do farm work and be a peasant. I’ll marry you and we’ll live on a farm. Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”
“He always dreams. He says, ‘Why live real life? Dreaming is better.’ But he wants to get married. He likes me. Can you spin tops, Alyosha?”
“Yes.”
“Kalganov is like a top, he needs someone to wind him up. If I marry him, I’ll keep him spinning forever. Are you embarrassed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You’re mad I don’t talk about holy things. I don’t want to be holy. What happens to the biggest sinner in the next world?”
“God will scold you,” Alyosha said.
“I’d like that! I’d laugh. I still want to burn our house, Alyosha. Don’t you believe me?”
“Kids sometimes want to burn things, it’s like a sickness.”
“That’s not what I mean.”
“You think bad is good. Maybe you’re sick.”
“You despise me! I just want to do bad things, not good ones.”
“Why?”
“So everything will be destroyed. I think about doing awful things in secret, and then everyone would know and point at me. That would be fun. Why, Alyosha?”
“I don’t know. Sometimes people want to destroy things.”
“I don’t just say it. I’ll do it.”
“I believe you.”
“I love you for believing me. You’re not lying. You think I’m just saying this to annoy you?”
“No, but maybe a little.”
“Maybe a little. I never lie to you.”
Alyosha noticed she was very serious now, not joking like before.
“Sometimes people love doing wrong,” Alyosha said.
“Yes! Everyone loves doing wrong, all the time. People pretend they hate evil, but they really love it.”
“Are you still reading bad books?”
“Yes. Mama reads them and hides them, but I find them.”
“Aren’t you ashamed to hurt yourself?”
“I want to hurt myself. There’s a boy here who lay down on the train tracks. Your brother is on trial for killing your father, and everyone loves it really.”
“Loves it?”
“Yes, they do. They say it’s bad but secretly they like it. I like it.”
“Maybe you’re right about people,” Alyosha said.

“You have funny ideas, Alyosha! And you’re a monk! I respect you for not lying. I’ll tell you a dream. I dream about devils coming into my room at night. They try to grab me, but if I cross myself, they back away. But then I want to say mean things about God, and if I do, the devils rush at me again. Crossing myself keeps them back. It’s scary but fun.”
“I’ve had that dream too,” Alyosha said.
“Really?” Lise cried. “That’s important! Can two people have the same dream?”
“I guess they can.”
“Alyosha, it’s important! Is it true? Are you joking?”
“It’s true.”
Lise was quiet for a moment, very surprised.
“Alyosha, come see me more often.”
“I’ll always come see you,” Alyosha promised.
“You’re the only person I can talk to. Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don’t know.”
“I read a book about a Jew who hurt a little child and crucified him. He said the child died in four hours and he liked to watch. Isn’t that nice?”
“Nice?”
“Yes, I imagine I did it, and I’m eating pineapple compote while watching. I love pineapple compote. Do you like it?”
Alyosha just looked at her. Her face twisted and her eyes glowed.

“When I read about the child, I cried all night. I imagined his pain, and thought about pineapple compote. In the morning, I wrote to someone and asked him to visit. When he came, I told him about the child and the pineapple compote. He laughed and left. Was he laughing at me, Alyosha?”
“Did you really send for that person?”
“Yes.”
“Did you write to him?”
“Yes.”
“To ask about the child?”
“No, I just asked him to come. Then I asked about the child when he arrived. He laughed and left.”
“He acted properly,” Alyosha said quietly.
“But did he despise me?”
“No. Maybe he even believes in the pineapple compote idea. He is very sick, Lise.”
“Yes, he believes it,” Lise said, eyes flashing.
“He doesn’t hate anyone, but he doesn’t trust anyone, so maybe he does despise people.”
“So he despises me?”
“Yes, you too.”
“Good,” said Lise, grinding her teeth. “It’s nice to be despised. The child’s pain is nice, and being despised is nice.” She laughed at Alyosha.
Suddenly, Lise jumped up and grabbed Alyosha. “Save me! I told you the truth! I want to die because I hate everything! Alyosha, why don’t you love me?”
“But I do love you!” Alyosha said.
“Will you cry for me?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won’t marry you, but just cry for me?”
“Yes.”
“Thank you! I only want your tears. Everyone else can hate me; I don’t love anyone. I hate everyone! Go, Alyosha, you need to see your brother,” she said and pulled away.
“How can I leave you like this?” Alyosha asked.
“Go to your brother, or you’ll miss seeing him. Here’s your hat. Tell Mitya I send my love. Go!”
She pushed Alyosha out. He looked at her in surprise and noticed a small, sealed letter in his hand. It was for Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov. He looked at Lise. Her face looked angry.
“Give it to him! Today, or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I called you,” she ordered.

She slammed the door and locked it. Alyosha put the letter in his pocket and went downstairs, forgetting all about Madame Hohlakov. After he left, Lise opened the door a little and slammed it shut on her own finger, hurting herself. Then she sat in her chair, looked at her bleeding finger, and whispered to herself, “I am

Alyosha went to the prison very late in the day. It was already getting dark outside because it was November, and the days were short. But Alyosha was not worried; he knew he would be let in easily. Usually, people had to follow special rules to visit Mitya (his brother Dmitri), but some people—like Grushenka, Alyosha, and Rakitin—were allowed to visit more freely. Everyone in the prison liked Alyosha, so even if he was late, they let him in.

Mitya always came down from his cell to meet visitors. When Alyosha came in, he saw Rakitin leaving and Mitya laughing loudly. Rakitin looked annoyed and didn’t even say hello to Alyosha. Mitya joked with Rakitin, but Rakitin got angry and said something mean about Mitya’s family before leaving. Mitya told Alyosha he had been waiting for him all morning.

Alyosha asked Mitya why Rakitin visited so often, since they didn’t seem to be close friends. Mitya said Rakitin was clever but didn’t really understand him or jokes. Then Mitya said, “It’s all over with me now,” and sat beside Alyosha.

Alyosha asked, “Is it because your trial is tomorrow?” But Mitya said it wasn’t just the trial. He started talking about “ethics” and philosophy, saying he learned some things from Rakitin. Mitya felt sad about losing his faith in God because of ideas he didn’t fully understand. Rakitin liked to talk about science and wrote articles, even poems, for newspapers and tried to start his writing career by writing about Mitya’s case.

Mitya explained that Rakitin wanted to write an article saying Mitya was not to blame for what happened, but that his environment made him do it. Mitya didn’t care much about Rakitin’s opinions but thought he was smart. He told Alyosha about Rakitin’s plans to get rich and marry Madame Hohlakov, but Rakitin was thrown out of her house after writing a silly poem. Mitya laughed about it, but also called Rakitin vain and mean.

Alyosha said he couldn’t stay long because tomorrow would be a very important day for Mitya—the day of his trial. Mitya said he didn’t want to talk about the murder anymore and became very excited. He hugged Alyosha and told him that even if he went to prison for many years, he was not afraid anymore. He had become a new person inside and wanted to help others, even in prison. He believed that if he had God, he could survive anything, and that people must care for one another.

Mitya said he now really wanted to live and was no longer afraid of suffering. He said, “I exist!” and that was enough for him to be strong. He talked about Ivan (their brother), saying Ivan was different from Rakitin because Ivan had his own ideas and was always quiet. Mitya was worried about what life would mean if there was no God. He wondered how people could be good without God, and who would they thank or love if God did not exist.

Mitya said he would tell Alyosha more about Ivan after the trial. For now, he was worried about the trial, and about people like Katerina Ivanovna and Grigory, who would testify against him. He was also very sad about Grushenka, the woman he loved, and how she was suffering because of him.

Alyosha told Mitya that Grushenka was sad because of him. Mitya said he was jealous and hadn’t asked her for forgiveness. He warned Alyosha never to ask a woman for forgiveness because, in his opinion, it only made things worse. Still, he loved Grushenka very much and wished they could get married, even if he was sent away to Siberia.

Mitya suddenly remembered a secret that Grushenka had told Alyosha about. He whispered to Alyosha that Ivan wanted to help him escape from prison and go to America with Grushenka. Ivan would pay for everything. But Mitya wasn’t sure if it was right to run away from punishment, and he didn’t want to decide until after the trial. He asked Alyosha not to say anything to Ivan and not to decide anything yet.

Alyosha asked if Ivan was really serious about the escape plan. Mitya said Ivan was very serious and had arranged everything, but told him not to tell anyone, especially Alyosha, because Ivan thought Alyosha would act like Mitya’s conscience.
Alyosha said they should wait until after the trial to decide. Mitya agreed, but joked that maybe he was just a foolish person after all.

Alyosha asked if Mitya thought he could be found not guilty. Mitya didn’t think it was likely and hurriedly told Alyosha to go because the prison superintendent was coming. They hugged, and Mitya told Alyosha to bless him for the hard day to come.

Mitya told Alyosha that Ivan had suggested the escape plan but probably thought Mitya was guilty. Alyosha asked if Mitya had ever asked Ivan if he believed he was guilty, but Mitya said he hadn’t dared.

As Alyosha was leaving, Mitya suddenly called him back and looked at him very seriously. He asked Alyosha if he, deep inside, believed that Mitya was the murderer. Alyosha answered right away that he never believed it, not even for a moment, and raised his hand as if swearing to God. Mitya looked very happy and relieved. He thanked Alyosha and said he had given him new hope and strength.

Alyosha left the prison in tears, feeling sad that Mitya had been so full of doubt and worry, even about his own brother. Alyosha’s heart hurt with compassion for Mitya, and now he also wanted to see Ivan, as he was worried about him too.

Alyosha was walking to see Ivan. On the way, he passed by Katerina Ivanovna’s house. He saw lights in her windows and decided to visit her. He hadn’t seen Katerina Ivanovna for over a week. He thought Ivan might be there too, since tomorrow was going to be a very important day. As Alyosha went up the stairs, he saw Ivan coming down. Ivan had just been with Katerina Ivanovna.
“Oh, it’s you,” Ivan said in a cold voice. “Goodbye! Are you going to see her?”
Alyosha answered, “Yes.”
Ivan warned, “I don’t think you should. She’s upset, and you’ll only make it worse.”
Suddenly Katerina Ivanovna opened the door upstairs and called, “Alexey Fyodorovitch (that’s Alyosha), have you come from him?”
Alyosha replied, “Yes, I have been with him.”
She asked quickly, “Did he send any message? Come up, Alyosha. Ivan, you must come back too!”
Katerina Ivanovna sounded so firm that Ivan decided to go back with Alyosha, though he muttered angrily that she was listening to them.
Ivan kept his coat on and said he wouldn’t stay long. Katerina Ivanovna told Alyosha to sit, but she stayed standing. She looked serious and a little angry.
She asked, “What did he want you to tell me?”
Alyosha said, “He asked that you would protect yourself and not talk at the trial about what happened when you first met, in that town.”
Katerina Ivanovna laughed bitterly. She asked if he wanted her to protect herself or him.
Alyosha answered gently, “Both yourself and him.”
Katerina Ivanovna said Alyosha didn’t really know her, and that maybe he would hate her after her testimony tomorrow.
Alyosha told her she would speak honestly at the trial, and that was all that mattered.

Katerina Ivanovna said sometimes women can be unfair. She said she was afraid of “that monster”—then suddenly asked Ivan if he thought Mitya (Dmitri) was the murderer. Alyosha could tell she and Ivan had argued about this before.
Katerina Ivanovna told Ivan that he was the one who made her believe Smerdyakov killed Fyodor Pavlovitch (their father). Ivan just gave a tense smile. Alyosha was surprised they talked so closely.
Ivan said he was leaving and would come back tomorrow. He left the room quickly.
Katerina Ivanovna grabbed Alyosha’s hands and told him to follow Ivan and not leave him alone. She said Ivan was ill and the doctor had said so.
Alyosha ran after Ivan, who was a short distance ahead.
Ivan saw Alyosha and guessed Katerina Ivanovna had sent him, saying he knew the routine.
Alyosha said Katerina Ivanovna was mistaken, but Ivan really did look sick.
Ivan kept walking, and Alyosha followed.
Ivan asked calmly if people know when they are losing their minds.
Alyosha said he didn’t know, and maybe people can’t see it in themselves.
Ivan told Alyosha to change the subject if he wanted to talk.
Alyosha remembered he had a letter for Ivan, from Lise (a young girl who liked Ivan). Ivan saw the letter, laughed meanly, tore it up, and threw the pieces in the wind.
Ivan said Lise was acting like grown-up women, even though she was only a child.
Alyosha was upset and told Ivan not to be mean to Lise. She was just a sick, sad child.
Ivan said he didn’t care and didn’t want to talk about her.

Ivan then talked sharply about Katerina Ivanovna. He said she would pray all night for help to decide what to say at the trial—whether to help or hurt Mitya. Ivan said Katerina Ivanovna wanted him to comfort her like a nurse.
Alyosha said softly that Katerina Ivanovna loved Ivan.
Ivan answered that he didn’t really care for her.
Alyosha asked why Ivan sometimes gave her hope, if he didn’t love her.
Ivan said he couldn’t break up with her now because she might get back at him by saying bad things about Mitya in court. So he just waited for the trial to end.
Alyosha asked what Katerina Ivanovna could say that would hurt Mitya.
Ivan replied she had a letter written by Mitya that could prove he killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Alyosha said that was impossible, because Mitya didn’t do it.
Ivan said he had read the letter himself.
Alyosha insisted Mitya didn’t kill their father.
Ivan stopped. He asked Alyosha who he thought the real murderer was.
Alyosha quietly said, “You know who.”
Ivan guessed Alyosha meant Smerdyakov.
Alyosha started trembling.
Alyosha repeated, “You know who.”
Ivan grew upset and demanded to know more.
Alyosha said one thing he knew for sure: “You didn’t kill father.” Alyosha said it again and again.
Ivan was shocked. “I know I didn’t. Are you crazy?” he said, but he looked pale and nervous.
Alyosha said Ivan had blamed himself many times in his mind.
Ivan asked when he had ever said such a thing.
Alyosha explained that Ivan had thought it to himself over the past months, blaming himself, but he was wrong. Alyosha said God had sent him to tell Ivan he was not the murderer.
Ivan began shaking and grabbed Alyosha’s shoulder. He whispered, “You’ve been in my room! You saw him, didn’t you?”
Alyosha asked, confused, if Ivan meant Mitya.
Ivan shouted it wasn’t Mitya. He wanted to know if Alyosha knew about a strange visitor.
Alyosha said he didn’t know who Ivan meant.
Ivan stopped and thought, then made a strange grin.
Alyosha, his voice shaking, repeated that Ivan was not the murderer and God wanted him to say this, even if Ivan hated him for it.
Ivan became calm again. He told Alyosha coldly he didn’t want prophets or messengers from God in his life. He said he was breaking off with Alyosha and not to come see him anymore.
Ivan walked away without looking back.

Alyosha called to him, “If anything happens to you today, come to me first!” But Ivan didn’t answer. Alyosha watched Ivan disappear into the dark, then went home sadly. Alyosha and Ivan both lived in rented rooms, not in their old house. Alyosha stayed with working people, Ivan lived alone in a nicer place. Ivan did everything for himself and liked being alone these days.

Ivan reached his house but stopped at the door, shaking with anger. Suddenly he turned away and walked quickly in the other direction. He walked a long way to a small wooden house where Marya Kondratyevna lived with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was very sick, stayed with them after Fyodor Pavlovitch’s death. Ivan was now going to see Smerdyakov, feeling like he had to do it.

Ivan had visited Smerdyakov three times since coming back from Moscow. First, he saw him the day he arrived. He visited again two weeks later. After that, he did not see Smerdyakov for over a month, and hardly heard about him.

Ivan came back five days after his father died, so he missed the funeral. Alyosha did not know Ivan’s address, so he asked Katerina Ivanovna, and she asked her family to send a telegram. Ivan got the message late, then hurried home. Alyosha met him and surprised Ivan by saying he did not think Dmitri (Mitya) was guilty, but instead said Smerdyakov was the murderer. Even after meeting with the police, Ivan thought Alyosha only took Mitya’s side because they were close brothers.

Ivan did not like his brother Mitya much. Sometimes he felt sorry for him, but also looked down on him. Ivan did not like that Katerina Ivanovna loved Mitya. When Ivan visited Mitya, this only made Ivan more sure that Mitya was guilty. Mitya was upset, spoke wildly, and said his father had “stolen” three thousand roubles from him.
“The money was mine. Even if I stole it, I had the right,” Mitya kept saying.

Mitya did not try hard to fight the evidence against him. He got angry and insulted Ivan, saying people who believe “everything is lawful” shouldn’t judge him. After talking to Mitya, Ivan went to visit Smerdyakov for the first time.

On the train, Ivan thought a lot about Smerdyakov and their last talk. Some things seemed strange, but Ivan did not tell the police about this yet. He wanted to see Smerdyakov first, who was in the hospital.

The doctors—Herzenstube and Varvinsky—told Ivan that Smerdyakov’s seizure was real and serious, not fake. They said his life had been in danger, but now he would survive, though his mind might be weak for a while. Ivan wanted to see for himself.

Ivan was allowed to visit Smerdyakov in the hospital. Smerdyakov looked very sick and weak and spoke slowly. He complained about pain and headaches, but one of his eyes looked clever as always. Ivan sat down, but Smerdyakov waited quietly.
“Can you talk to me?” Ivan asked. “I won’t tire you.”
“Of course,” Smerdyakov said softly. “Have you been back long?”
“I just arrived today,” Ivan said. Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why do you sigh? You knew this would happen,” Ivan said.
“How could I help knowing? But I didn’t know it would turn out like this,” Smerdyakov answered.
Ivan asked, “You told me before you left you might have a fit in the cellar. How did you know?”
“Have you told the police about that?” Smerdyakov asked calmly.
Ivan got angry and said, “I will! You have to explain a lot to me.”
“Why would I play games with you? I trust you,” Smerdyakov replied.
Ivan said, “You can’t know when a fit will happen. How did you know when and where you’d have one?”
Smerdyakov answered, “You can’t know exactly, but you can feel it coming sometimes. I had to go to the cellar often, and I was scared.”
“But you did say the exact time and place!” Ivan said.
“Ask the doctors if it was a real fit or not,” Smerdyakov replied.
Smerdyakov explained he was afraid and thought the fear brought on the fit. He said he had told the doctors and the lawyers everything, and they wrote it down.
Ivan was surprised Smerdyakov already told this to the police.
“What do I have to fear? Let them write the truth,” Smerdyakov said.
Ivan asked if he had told the police he could fake fits, as he once bragged. Smerdyakov said, “No, I didn’t tell them that.”
Ivan asked, “Why did you send me to Tchermashnya?” Smerdyakov said he was afraid Ivan would go far away to Moscow.
Ivan said, “You told me to leave because you wanted me gone.”
Smerdyakov answered, “I wanted to protect you, and myself. I thought there would be trouble about the money, and I was afraid.”
“You could have said it more clearly!” Ivan snapped.
Smerdyakov said, “I was scared and worried Mitya would take the money. But I didn’t know anyone would be killed! I thought he might just take the money, not murder.”
Ivan said, “But you just said you couldn’t know. How could I have guessed and stayed home?”

Smerdyakov explained, “I asked you to go to Tchermashnya, not Moscow, so you’d be closer in case something happened. I warned you about Grigory being sick and about the knocks on the gate, so maybe you would guess Mitya would do something and stay at home.”
“You are tricky!” Ivan said.
“I thought you did guess,” Smerdyakov replied.
“No, if I had guessed, I would have stayed,” Ivan said.
“I thought maybe you left because you were scared and wanted to save yourself,” Smerdyakov said.
Ivan remembered Smerdyakov telling him, “It’s always worth speaking to a clever man,” when he left. Ivan asked, “Were you glad I left?”
Smerdyakov said, “I was glad you went to Tchermashnya, because it’s closer. But I felt you were leaving us when we needed help.”
“You left your father and didn’t protect us,” Smerdyakov said.
Ivan asked if Smerdyakov told the police about the knocks. Smerdyakov said he told them everything.
Ivan said he had expected Smerdyakov might do something bad, because he had bragged he could fake a fit. Smerdyakov said he never really faked a fit, he just wanted to impress Ivan.
“My brother accuses you of murder and stealing,” Ivan said.
Smerdyakov replied, “What else can he do? No one will believe him after seeing all the proof.”
Smerdyakov said, “If I really planned such a crime, would I have told you I could fake fits? That would have been stupid. If you tell the police about our talk, it would actually help me.”
Ivan stood up and said, “I don’t suspect you. Thank you for clearing things up. I’ll come again. Is there anything you need?”
“No, Marfa Ignatyevna takes care of me. Good people visit me,” Smerdyakov answered.
Ivan said, “I won’t tell anyone that you can fake fits, and you shouldn’t, either.”
Smerdyakov replied, “I understand. If you don’t talk, I won’t mention our talk at the gate.”
Ivan left, feeling a little insulted by Smerdyakov’s last words, but he walked out of the hospital.

Ivan felt relieved that it was Mitya, not Smerdyakov, who did the murder, though he didn’t know why. The evidence against Mitya was strong. Many witnesses said things that made it look bad for Mitya. Marfa, Grigory’s wife, said Smerdyakov was moaning all night and couldn’t have left his bed.
Ivan told Doctor Herzenstube that Smerdyakov wasn’t mad, just weak. The doctor only smiled.
Doctor Herzenstube said Smerdyakov spent his time learning French words, with a notebook under his pillow.

Ivan decided Mitya was guilty and didn’t like thinking about him. But Alyosha still believed Mitya was innocent and said Smerdyakov was probably guilty. Ivan was surprised that Alyosha never tried to talk with him about Mitya, only answering questions.

Ivan was also busy thinking about Katerina Ivanovna. He loved her very much, but sometimes felt angry at her too. Katerina was upset and hurt after what happened with Mitya, and when Ivan returned, she turned to him for help. But she did not give herself fully to Ivan, and sometimes told him she felt bad for leaving Mitya. This made Ivan angry, but that is another story.

For a while, Ivan almost forgot about Smerdyakov. But two weeks later, he started to worry again. He wondered why, on the last night, he had sneaked onto the stairs in his father’s house. Why did he feel so bad afterward? Why did he call himself a scoundrel? These thoughts bothered him more and more. One day, he met Alyosha in the street and asked:
“Do you remember when Mitya beat father, and I told you I reserved ‘the right to desire’? Did you think I wanted father to die?”
“I did think so,” Alyosha answered softly.
Ivan asked, “Did you think I wanted Mitya to kill father, and maybe even help make it happen?”
Alyosha turned pale and looked at Ivan.
Finally Alyosha said, “I did think that, too.”
“Thanks,” Ivan said quickly and walked away. After that, Ivan avoided Alyosha, and Alyosha stopped visiting him. Right after this meeting, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov again.

Smerdyakov had left the hospital and now lived in a small, old wooden house. The house was split by a hallway. On one side lived Marya Kondratyevna (a woman) and her mother, and on the other side lived Smerdyakov. Some people thought Smerdyakov was going to marry Marya Kondratyevna, and that was why he stayed there for free. Marya and her mother respected him and thought he was very smart.

Ivan went to visit Smerdyakov. He followed Marya Kondratyevna’s directions and went straight to Smerdyakov’s room. The room was hot, with blue wallpaper and lots of cockroaches. There were only a few benches, two chairs, a table with a pink cloth, and some potted plants. Smerdyakov sat at the table wearing a dirty dressing-gown and new glasses. He was writing in an exercise-book. Ivan could see that Smerdyakov was healthy again, and seeing him with glasses made Ivan even more angry.

Smerdyakov looked at Ivan through his glasses, took them off slowly, and stood up lazily. He did not act very polite. Ivan felt Smerdyakov was looking at him in a mean way, as if asking, “Why are you here again?” Ivan tried to stay calm.
Ivan asked, “Are we alone? Can anyone hear us?” Smerdyakov said no one could hear them.

Ivan got angry and asked Smerdyakov what he meant when he spoke in the hospital about not telling the police their talks, if Ivan kept quiet about Smerdyakov faking his fits. Ivan wanted to know if Smerdyakov was threatening him.
Smerdyakov answered calmly, saying that he meant Ivan knew about the murder before it happened and let it happen. Smerdyakov promised not to tell this to the police.
Ivan was shocked and asked, “Are you crazy? Do you think I knew about the murder?”
Smerdyakov said he thought Ivan wanted his father dead.
Ivan got so angry he hit Smerdyakov on the shoulder, making him cry. Smerdyakov said, “It’s a shame to hit a sick man,” and wiped his eyes.
Ivan told him to stop crying and not to make him lose his patience.
Ivan asked if Smerdyakov thought he and Dmitri planned to kill their father together. Smerdyakov said he suspected everyone because he was scared.
Ivan suddenly yelled, “It was you who killed him!” Smerdyakov just smiled and said Ivan knew he didn’t do it.

Ivan wanted to know why Smerdyakov thought he might want his father dead. Smerdyakov said it was about the inheritance. If their father married Agrafena Alexandrovna (Grushenka), she would get all the money. But if he died before marrying, Ivan and his brothers would get lots of money.

Ivan asked if Smerdyakov thought he had planned for Dmitri to do the murder. Smerdyakov said yes, because if Dmitri killed their father, Dmitri would go to prison, and Ivan and Alyosha would get more money.

Ivan said that if he had planned on anyone, it would have been Smerdyakov, not Dmitri. Smerdyakov replied that Ivan leaving for Tchermashnya after Smerdyakov suggested it showed Ivan was letting him do whatever he wanted.
Smerdyakov pointed out that Ivan agreed to go to Tchermashnya only because Smerdyakov mentioned it, and that showed Ivan expected something from him.
Ivan shouted that it wasn’t true. Smerdyakov said Ivan should have been angry and stopped him, but instead he went away, which looked suspicious.
Ivan sat, upset, and said he was sorry he hadn’t hit Smerdyakov in the face before. Smerdyakov talked about how people still hit each other in special situations, but Ivan hadn’t dared.
Ivan noticed Smerdyakov’s exercise-book and asked why he was learning French. Smerdyakov said maybe he would go to Europe one day.

Ivan called Smerdyakov a monster and said he would try to bring him to justice for the murder. Smerdyakov said Ivan had nothing to accuse him of, and if Ivan started talking, Smerdyakov would tell everything too.
Ivan asked if Smerdyakov thought he was scared now. Smerdyakov said people would believe him, and Ivan would be ashamed.

Ivan left, very upset. Outside, he wondered if he should go to the police about Smerdyakov, but he realized he had no proof. Ivan remembered how, before the murder, he had left when Smerdyakov suggested it, and he wondered if maybe he had wanted the murder to happen. Ivan felt terrible and thought, “If I don’t dare to stop Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!”

Ivan went to see Katerina Ivanovna. He told her everything Smerdyakov had said. Ivan was very upset and paced the room. Finally, he said, “If Smerdyakov is the murderer, then I share the blame, because I let it happen.”

Katerina Ivanovna got a letter from her desk and gave it to Ivan. It was a letter Dmitri had written to her when he was drunk. In the letter, Dmitri (also called Mitya) said he would pay back money he owed her. He also wrote he would break his father’s skull to get money if Ivan was gone, and that he loved another woman.

Dmitri’s letter said if he could not borrow money, he would get it from his father, even if he had to go to Siberia. He begged Katerina to forgive him, but said she would be happier if she didn’t. He wrote he would rather go to Siberia than be with her, and that he might even kill the person who had robbed him.
At the end, Dmitri wrote that the money was under his father’s mattress, tied with pink ribbon. He said he was not a thief, but a murderer, and he had ruined himself.
After reading the letter, Ivan was sure Dmitri was guilty. He stopped worrying about Smerdyakov and thought only about Dmitri. A month went by. Ivan heard Smerdyakov was very sick and going mad.

Ivan also became ill. He visited a Moscow doctor. His relationship with Katerina Ivanovna was tense. Even though she sometimes defended Dmitri, Ivan hated Dmitri more and more, because he believed Dmitri had killed their father.

Ivan visited Dmitri ten days before the trial and offered to help him escape, even though it would cost Ivan a lot of money. Ivan partly did this because he felt guilty after what Smerdyakov had said about the inheritance. Ivan wondered if he wanted Dmitri to escape because he was guilty at heart, too.

Later, Ivan remembered Katerina accusing him of making her believe Dmitri was guilty, even though she had shown Ivan the letter herself. She also said she had visited Smerdyakov, and Ivan wondered what Smerdyakov had told her. Ivan became very angry and rushed off to see Smerdyakov again, thinking, “Maybe I will kill him this time.”

Ivan walked alone to Smerdyakov’s house. The wind blew hard, and dry snow whirled in the dark. Ivan’s head hurt and his hands shook. Near Marya Kondratyevna’s cottage, Ivan bumped into a drunken peasant who was singing and swearing. Ivan felt angry and pushed him hard. The peasant fell and didn’t move. Ivan thought, “He’ll freeze,” but kept walking to Smerdyakov’s.

Marya Kondratyevna met Ivan at the door. She whispered that Smerdyakov was very sick and didn’t want tea. Ivan asked if Smerdyakov was making trouble. She said no, he was very quiet, but begged Ivan not to stay long.

Ivan entered. The room was hot. Smerdyakov sat on a sofa, looking thinner and paler. He stared at Ivan with tired eyes. Ivan asked where to sit and sat at the table. He wanted to know if Katerina Ivanovna had visited Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov finally said yes, but told Ivan to leave him alone.

Smerdyakov said Ivan looked sick too. Ivan said that didn’t matter, just answer his question. Smerdyakov teased Ivan about his yellow eyes and shaky hands. Ivan grew angry and demanded answers, but Smerdyakov at first refused.

Smerdyakov told Ivan not to worry about the trial tomorrow, saying nothing would happen to him. Ivan was surprised and a little scared. Smerdyakov hinted that Ivan already understood everything about the murder. Ivan insisted he did not.

Smerdyakov told Ivan, “You didn’t kill him.” Ivan remembered Alyosha and said, “I know it wasn’t me.” Smerdyakov just asked, “Do you?” Ivan grabbed Smerdyakov and shouted for the truth. Smerdyakov glared at Ivan and whispered, “You killed him, if that’s it.”
Ivan laughed bitterly. He asked Smerdyakov if he meant the murder happened because Ivan went away. Smerdyakov said Ivan understood everything.

Smerdyakov said, “You are the real murderer. I was only your servant and followed your words.” Ivan became very cold and shivered. Smerdyakov was surprised Ivan didn’t seem to know. Ivan stared at him, unable to speak.

Ivan muttered, “Are you real, or am I dreaming?” Smerdyakov answered, “There’s no phantom, just us—and God sees us.” Ivan shouted that Smerdyakov was lying. Smerdyakov calmly watched Ivan, thinking he was pretending not to know.

Smerdyakov slowly pulled a bundle of money from his stocking and put it on the table. Ivan was scared but Smerdyakov told him to look at the money. There were three packets of hundred-rouble notes—three thousand roubles.

Smerdyakov told Ivan to take the money. Ivan was pale and joked about being scared by the stocking. Smerdyakov asked if Ivan really hadn’t known until now. Ivan said he kept thinking Dmitri was the killer and grabbed his head in distress. Then he asked Smerdyakov, “Did you kill him alone?”
Smerdyakov answered, “I did it with your help. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is innocent.” Ivan trembled and said he couldn’t speak right.
Smerdyakov offered lemonade but hid the money first, covering it with a big yellow book. Ivan refused lemonade and asked Smerdyakov to tell him exactly how the murder happened.
Smerdyakov said he pretended to fall ill and went down to the cellar faking a fit. He screamed until they carried him inside. That night, he expected Dmitri to come and try to get into the house.
Smerdyakov explained he had told Dmitri about the secret knocks. He believed Dmitri would come, and was ready for it.

Ivan interrupted, wondering why Smerdyakov would take the money if Dmitri killed their father. Smerdyakov said he hid the money behind the ikons, not under the mattress as everyone thought. If Dmitri killed their father, Smerdyakov would get the money later and blame Dmitri. If Dmitri didn’t kill him, Smerdyakov wouldn’t take the money.

Ivan got confused and asked if Dmitri killed their father and Smerdyakov only took the money. Smerdyakov said no, Dmitri did not kill him. Smerdyakov wanted Ivan to know he was only able to do it because Ivan let it happen and went away.

Ivan told Smerdyakov to go on and tell what happened that night. Smerdyakov said he heard a shout, then Grigory came out and was attacked. Smerdyakov waited, then went to see Grigory lying hurt. He decided to finish the plan since Grigory wouldn’t see anything. He tricked his master, Fyodor Pavlovitch, by saying Grushenka had come. When his father leaned out the window to look, Smerdyakov hit him with a heavy paper-weight and killed him. He wiped the paper-weight, took the money from behind the ikons, and hid it in the garden. He went back to bed and waited for Marfa Ignatyevna to wake up. When she did, everything happened as expected.
Ivan listened in silence. Smerdyakov was sweating and looked upset, but it was hard to tell what he felt.
Ivan asked about the door—how could Grigory have seen it open if Smerdyakov only opened it later? Smerdyakov said Grigory must have imagined it, but now everyone believed Dmitri was guilty.

Ivan, confused, asked why Smerdyakov opened the envelope with the money and left it on the floor. Smerdyakov explained it would look more like Dmitri did it, since he would want to check inside, not just take the envelope.
Ivan was shocked Smerdyakov had planned all this. Smerdyakov said he thought it all out long ago.
Ivan shouted that he would tell the truth at the trial tomorrow. “We’ll go together! I will confess everything!” Smerdyakov said Ivan was sick and wouldn’t really do it.

Smerdyakov told Ivan he wouldn’t confess, because he would be too ashamed and had no proof. He said Ivan cared most about comfort and being respected, and was more like Fyodor Pavlovitch than anyone else.
Ivan took the money and said he would show it in court. Smerdyakov said no one would believe him, since Ivan had plenty of money already.
Ivan warned Smerdyakov he only stayed alive because Ivan needed him for the trial. Smerdyakov dared Ivan to kill him, but Ivan left, saying, “Till tomorrow!”

Outside, the snowstorm was still strong. Ivan almost stumbled over the same peasant he had knocked down. The peasant was nearly buried in snow. Ivan carried him to a nearby house and got help to take him to the police station and fetch a doctor. This took an hour, but Ivan was glad he helped.
Almost home, Ivan wondered if he should go straight to the prosecutor, but decided to wait until tomorrow.

In his room, Ivan felt cold and troubled. He tried to make tea but didn’t drink it. He felt sick and restless, and kept staring at the sofa across the room, as if something there upset and worried him.

Ivan was feeling very sick, but he did not want to admit it. He knew he needed to stay strong because an important moment in his life was coming. He wanted to defend himself and needed all his strength.

Ivan did see a doctor, who said his brain was not well and that he might have hallucinations. The doctor told him to rest right away, or things would get worse. But Ivan did not listen. He said he would only rest if he could not walk anymore.

Ivan sat in his room and stared at the sofa. Suddenly, he noticed a man sitting there. The man looked like a Russian gentleman, not young, with dark hair and a beard. He wore clothes that were old-fashioned and a little shabby. His scarf was worn out, and his trousers were too tight for the current style.

This man looked like someone who used to be rich but was now poor. He seemed like a friendly guest who stayed with people because he was good company. He was the sort of person who liked to tell stories and play cards but did not like to do any work.
The man’s face looked friendly, but he could change his look easily. He wore a gold ring with a fake opal and had a lorgnette (a kind of glasses) on a ribbon.
Ivan did not want to talk. The man sat quietly, waiting for Ivan to speak first, but soon he started the conversation.
“You went to see Smerdyakov about Katerina Ivanovna, but you forgot to ask about her,” the man reminded Ivan.
Ivan remembered and felt upset. He told the man not to act like he was helping, because Ivan would have remembered on his own.

The man smiled and said it didn’t matter if Ivan believed him. He started talking about believing in things and how some people need proof to believe in something. He joked about ghosts and devils and said he wanted to join a club just to argue.
Ivan got up and said he must be sick and was probably seeing things. He said he would put a wet towel on his head to see if the visitor would go away.
Ivan put a wet towel on his head and walked around the room.
The visitor said he was glad Ivan was treating him like an old friend.
Ivan laughed and called him a fool. He said he wasn’t afraid of the visitor and would not go crazy.
The visitor teased Ivan, saying Ivan was starting to believe he was real.
Ivan got angry and said the man was not real. He was just Ivan’s sickness, just a part of Ivan’s own thoughts, and not even the best part.
The visitor reminded Ivan about a moment when Ivan thought of him, proving Ivan believed in him for just a second.
Ivan said maybe he was dreaming last time and had not really seen the visitor.
The visitor brought up Alyosha, but Ivan told him not to talk about his brother.
Ivan laughed and told the visitor not to mention Alyosha.
The visitor said Ivan was being nicer than last time and thought he knew why.
Ivan shouted at him to stop talking about his plans.
The visitor guessed Ivan’s plan was to help his brother and called it noble.
Ivan threatened to kick him.
The visitor joked that if Ivan kicked him, it would mean Ivan believed he was real, because no one kicks a ghost.
Ivan said he was really only scolding himself, since the visitor was just part of him.
Ivan complained that the visitor only said his worst and stupidest thoughts.

The visitor started telling Ivan about himself. He said he used to be called an angel, but now he just wants to be thought of as a gentleman. He liked being on earth, dreaming and doing normal things. He asked Ivan about his health.
Ivan called him a fool again.
The visitor kept talking about being sick and how doctors could not help him.
Ivan said, “The devil can have rheumatism!”
The visitor joked that if he took on a human shape, he could get sick too.
The visitor talked about dreams and how sometimes people see amazing things in nightmares. He said that even though he was part of Ivan’s mind, he could still say surprising things.
Ivan said the visitor was just trying to trick him into thinking he was real.
Ivan asked the visitor to leave. He took off the wet towel and sat down, feeling desperate.
The visitor talked about how he once went to a fancy party and caught a cold, even though he was in a spirit form.
Ivan, not believing, asked if there could be an ax floating in space.
The visitor joked about what would happen to an ax if it floated in space.
Ivan complained that the visitor was being silly and just trying to confuse him.
The visitor talked about doctors and how hard it was to get help, telling a long story about being sick and trying different cures.

The visitor said he is always blamed for things and that he did not choose his job. He wished he could just be a simple person who could go to church and be happy, instead of being forced to cause trouble.
Ivan asked, “Don’t you believe in God?”
The visitor said he did not know if God was real.
Ivan said, “You see! You are just me, just my own thoughts!”
The visitor agreed, saying he only knew he existed, but was not sure about anything else.
Ivan asked for a story.
