The visitor told a legend. He said there was once a man who did not believe in anything. When the man died, he found out there was life after death and was so angry that he was punished. He was told to walk a long, long way—more than a billion kilometers—in the dark. When he finished, he would be let into heaven.
Ivan asked about the punishments in the other world. The visitor said that now punishments were more about feeling bad inside instead of physical pain.
Ivan asked if the man was still walking. The visitor said, “No, after almost a thousand years, he got up and walked the whole way.”
Ivan laughed at the story, asking, “Does it matter if he lies there forever or walks forever?”
The visitor said the world could have ended and started again many times, so maybe the man had enough time to finish his walk.
Ivan asked what happened when the man got to heaven.
The visitor said that as soon as he entered, the man was so happy, he said walking all that way was worth it.
Ivan suddenly remembered that he had made up that story himself when he was a boy. He realized the visitor was just part of his own dream.
The visitor laughed and said Ivan must believe in him a little, since he argued so much.
Ivan shouted that he didn’t believe, but then admitted he kind of wanted to.
The visitor teased Ivan, saying he was just helping Ivan stop believing in him by telling the old story.
Ivan said the visitor was just trying to prove he was real.
The visitor explained he wanted Ivan to go back and forth between believing and not believing, so that in the end, Ivan would have a tiny bit of faith, which would grow.
Ivan asked if the visitor was trying to save his soul.
The visitor said he often tried to tempt holy people, because their souls were very valuable.

The visitor told a silly story about a man who lost his nose and went to confession. The priest tried to comfort him, but the man said he would rather have his nose back, even if it meant people could pull it.
The visitor told another story about a girl and a priest.
Ivan begged the visitor to leave him alone, saying he felt terrible.

The visitor said Ivan was upset because the visitor did not look special or scary, just like an ordinary person. The visitor said he had once wanted to sing with the angels but stopped himself, because if he did, everything on earth would end. He was stuck doing his bad job and did not know the final secret of why.
Ivan complained that the visitor was just repeating old thoughts he had already decided were useless.
The visitor joked about his own storytelling style.
Ivan said he could not believe he had created such a silly part of himself.
The visitor said he knew a smart young Russian man who had written a poem called The Grand Inquisitor.
Ivan angrily told him not to talk about it.
The visitor mentioned another poem Ivan had written.
Ivan threatened to hurt him.
But the visitor kept talking, repeating ideas Ivan had thought before about how, if people stopped believing in God, they could make their own rules and live for happiness on earth.
Ivan pressed his hands to his ears and trembled, but the visitor’s voice went on.
The visitor said that if people realized there was no God or life after death, they could do whatever they wanted, because “all things are lawful.”
The visitor talked more and more, but Ivan finally threw a glass at him to make him stop.
The visitor jumped up, shook himself, and teased Ivan for trying to throw something at a dream.
Suddenly, someone started knocking loudly at the window. Ivan jumped up.
The visitor said it was Ivan’s brother, Alyosha, bringing important news.
Ivan said he already knew Alyosha was coming and that it must be serious.
The visitor told Ivan to let his brother in because it was snowing outside.

Ivan wanted to go to the window, but he felt like he couldn’t move. Finally, he broke free and looked around. The visitor was gone. The glass was still on the table. The knocking at the window was quieter now.
Ivan said, “It was not a dream! It all really happened just now!” and ran to the window.
Ivan opened the window and shouted, “Alyosha, what do you want? Tell me in two words!”
Alyosha said, “An hour ago, Smerdyakov hanged himself.”
Ivan told Alyosha to come to the door, and he went to let him in.

Alyosha came in and told Ivan some sad news. He said that about an hour ago, Marya Kondratyevna (the lady who looked after Smerdyakov) had rushed to him and cried that Smerdyakov had taken his own life. “I went to tidy up and found him hanging on a nail in the wall,” she had said. Alyosha asked if she had told the police, but she said no, she came straight to Alyosha instead, running all the way. She was shaking and very scared. Alyosha went with her to Smerdyakov’s cottage. Smerdyakov was still there. On the table, there was a note: “I destroy my life of my own will and desire, so as to throw no blame on any one.” Alyosha left the note and went at once to tell the police captain. Then he came straight to Ivan and told him everything. Alyosha watched Ivan closely while telling the story.
Suddenly Alyosha cried, “Brother, you must be very sick. You look like you don’t even understand me.”
Ivan said, “It’s good you came. I already knew he had hanged himself.”
“How did you know?” asked Alyosha.
“I don’t know. But I knew. Did I know? Yes, he told me. He told me just now.”
Ivan stood in the middle of the room, looking at the ground and sounding lost.
Alyosha looked around and asked, “Who is he?”
“He’s gone now,” Ivan said, then looked up and smiled a little.

Ivan said, “He was afraid of you, Alyosha. Dmitri calls you a cherub. Do you know what seraphim are? Maybe they’re just something in the sky, or maybe just a bunch of little things. Anyway, there’s a constellation called the Lion and the Sun. Do you know it?”
Alyosha was worried. “Brother, please sit down on the sofa,” he said. “You are sick. Put your head on the pillow. Would you like a wet towel for your head?”
“Yes, give me the towel. It’s on the chair. I just threw it there,” Ivan said.
“It’s not here. Don’t worry, I’ll find it,” said Alyosha. He found a clean towel by Ivan’s dressing-table. Ivan stared at it, thinking hard.
“Wait,” Ivan said, “An hour ago I took that towel, made it wet, and put it on my head. Then I threw it here. Why is it dry now? There was no other.”
“You put that towel on your head?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, and walked around the room an hour ago. Why are the candles so low? What time is it?”
“Almost twelve,” Alyosha replied.

Suddenly Ivan shouted, “No! It wasn’t a dream. He was here, sitting on that sofa. When you knocked, I threw a glass at him. Wait, maybe I was asleep last time, but this was real. I have dreams that feel real. But he was here. He is very stupid, Alyosha, very stupid.” Ivan laughed and walked around the room.
“Who is stupid? Who are you talking about?” Alyosha asked, worried.

“The devil! He’s been visiting me. He has come here two or three times. He teases me for thinking he’s just a small devil, not the big scary Satan. But he’s not Satan, he’s just a silly devil. If you saw him, you’d see he has a tail like a dog’s. Alyosha, you look cold. Do you want some tea? Is it cold out? Should I tell someone to bring tea?”
Alyosha quickly got the towel wet and persuaded Ivan to sit down. He put the wet towel on Ivan’s head and sat beside him.

Ivan started talking again. “What were you saying about Lise? I like Lise. I said something mean about her, but I like her. I’m scared for Katya tomorrow. She’ll throw me away and think I’m hurting Mitya because I’m jealous. But that’s not true. Tomorrow, something hard will happen, but I will not hang myself. I could never take my own life, Alyosha. How did I know Smerdyakov hanged himself? He told me.”
“Are you sure someone was really here?” Alyosha asked.

“Yes, on that sofa. You would have made him leave. You did, in fact, when you came. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know that? And he is myself, Alyosha. All that is bad in me, he guessed it. He’s stupid but clever. He made me listen to him. He told me true things about myself that I never wanted to admit. Alyosha, I wish it was him, not me.”
“He has worn you out,” said Alyosha, looking kindly at Ivan.
“He keeps teasing me, saying things like, ‘What is conscience? Why should I feel bad? Let’s give up on that and be like gods.’ That’s what he said!”
“No, you said that, not him,” Alyosha cried. “Don’t listen to him. Forget him. Let him go away forever!”
“But he’s mean. He laughed at me and told lies about me. He said, ‘You want to be a hero. You want to confess that you made the valet kill your father.’ ”
“Brother,” Alyosha said quickly, “you didn’t do it. That’s not true!”
“That’s what he says. He says, ‘You want to be a hero, but you don’t really believe in being good. That makes you mad and mean.’ He said that about me.”
“It’s just you saying that, not him,” Alyosha said sadly. “You’re sick and making yourself upset.”

“No, he knows what he’s saying. He says, ‘You’re just proud. You’ll say you did it, and you want people to praise you as a kind person. But that’s not true! You want people to say, “He’s a criminal, but he wanted to save his brother.” ’ That’s not true, Alyosha!” Ivan shouted. “I don’t want people to praise me! That’s a lie! That’s why I threw the glass at him.”
“Brother, calm down, please stop,” Alyosha begged.

Ivan kept going. “He knows how to hurt me. He said, ‘You hoped Smerdyakov would get sent away and Mitya would be freed, and you would only get blamed a little. But now Smerdyakov is dead, who will believe you?’ That’s horrible, Alyosha. Who can ask me that?”
Alyosha was frightened but tried to help. “How could he tell you Smerdyakov died before I came? No one knew before me.”

“He told me,” Ivan insisted. “That’s what we talked about. He said, ‘If you believed in being good, it wouldn’t matter if people doubted you. But you’re just like our father. Why do you want to interfere? You don’t even know why you’re doing this! You’ll think about it all night, but you’ll still go. You’ll go because you’re scared not to. Guess why!’ Then he left. When you came in, he left. He called me a coward, Alyosha! He said I can’t be great. Smerdyakov said the same. Katya despises me. Even Lise will despise me. ‘You want to be praised.’ That’s a mean lie! And you despise me too, Alyosha. Now I’ll hate you! And I hate the monster too! I don’t want to save the monster. Let him rot! I’ll go tomorrow and shout at them all!”

Ivan jumped up, threw off the towel, and walked quickly around the room. Alyosha remembered Ivan had said he felt like he was awake and asleep at the same time. Now it seemed just like that. Alyosha wanted to get a doctor but didn’t want to leave Ivan alone. Soon Ivan was so sick he couldn’t speak clearly. Suddenly he nearly fell, but Alyosha caught him. Alyosha helped Ivan into bed and undressed him. Ivan slept soundly. Alyosha lay down on the sofa and watched over him.

As Alyosha fell asleep, he prayed for Mitya and Ivan. He began to understand why Ivan was so sick. Ivan was fighting inside between doing what’s right and not believing in it. Alyosha thought, “If Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan, but he will still tell the truth.” Alyosha smiled softly. “God will win,” he thought. “Ivan will either do what’s right and find the truth, or he will be lost in hate.” Alyosha prayed again for Ivan.
At ten o'clock in the morning, Dmitri Karamazov's (people called him Mitya) trial started at the district court.

Something surprised everyone that day. People had talked about the case for two months, but no one expected so much excitement. The whole town, and even people from other cities in Russia, were interested in Mitya’s trial.

Many visitors came from different places, even from Moscow and Petersburg. There were lots of lawyers and important people. All the tickets were taken quickly. There were so many lawyers that some had to stand behind a special wall at the back. The courtroom was crowded, and people stood close together.

Some ladies wore fancy clothes, but most didn’t care how they looked—they just wanted to see what happened. Many ladies wanted Mitya to be found not guilty, maybe because he was known to be charming. Two women, Katerina Ivanovna and Grushenka, were rivals for Mitya’s love, and people were excited to see them at the trial. Katerina was proud and came from a rich family. Some said she wanted to marry Mitya even if he went to Siberia. Grushenka was well-known in town, but many wondered why Mitya and his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, liked her so much.

Everyone talked about the case. Some families even argued about Mitya. Most men in the crowd wanted Mitya to be found guilty. Some men were angry with him for things he had done in town. But everyone was interested in the trial, and the lawyers cared most about the law.

The famous lawyer Fetyukovitch was there to defend Mitya. People said he always made cases famous. The prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, was nervous because he and Fetyukovitch didn’t get along. Ippolit worked very hard on his cases, which made some people laugh at him.
The President of the court was a kind and smart man. He wanted to be fair and looked at the case as something important for the whole society, not just about the people involved.

The courtroom was full before the judges came in. There was a table with evidence—like Fyodor Pavlovitch’s bloody dressing-gown, the brass pestle (the weapon), Mitya’s clothes, the gun, and the envelope with three thousand roubles for Grushenka. Chairs for witnesses were up front, and seats for the public were farther back.
At ten o’clock, the three judges arrived, along with the prosecutor. The President was a short, heavy man. The prosecutor looked tired and pale. The President checked that all the jury were present.

I can’t remember every detail, but I do know the jury was made up of four town officials, two merchants, and six peasants or workers. People wondered if these men could understand such a complicated case. The officials were not important people, and the peasants looked very serious and strict.

The President began the case about the murder of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. Mitya was brought in. The room went quiet. Mitya looked very fancy in his new coat and gloves. He walked in straight and sat down calmly.
At the same time, the famous lawyer Fetyukovitch came in. He was tall and thin, with long fingers and a sharp face. He wore a fancy suit and white tie.

The President asked Mitya questions about his name and work. Mitya answered loudly, surprising everyone. Then they read the names of the witnesses. Four witnesses were missing: Miüsov (in Paris), Madame Hohlakov and Maximov (sick), and Smerdyakov (who had died). When they announced Smerdyakov’s death, people whispered, and Mitya shouted out:
“He was a dog and died like a dog!”
Mitya’s lawyer hurried to him, and the President warned Mitya not to shout again.
Mitya said quietly to his lawyer, “I won’t again. It escaped me.”
This didn’t help Mitya look good to the jury. Then the clerk read the main points of the case: why Mitya was arrested and why he was on trial. After this, the President asked:
“Prisoner, do you plead guilty?”
Mitya stood up.
He shouted, “I’m guilty of being lazy and wild, but I didn’t kill my father! I didn’t steal from him! I’m not a thief.”

Mitya sat down, shaking. The President told him to answer only the questions. The witnesses took an oath. Mitya’s brothers could speak without swearing an oath. After a speech from the priest and President, the witnesses sat apart, and the trial began.

The trial started with the witnesses for the prosecution. I won’t write down every question and answer, because later, the lawyers’ speeches summed up everything that happened. There was even a big surprise before the end, which changed the whole trial.

Right from the start, everyone noticed that the prosecution’s case was very strong. All the facts seemed to prove that Dmitri (also called Mitya) was guilty of the crime. Even the ladies in the court, who secretly hoped he would go free, still thought he had done it. The men were excited to see if Fetyukovitch, the famous defense lawyer, could save Mitya from such a difficult case.

Fetyukovitch seemed very confident. People guessed he had a secret plan, but no one knew what it was. He had learned all the details of the case in just a few days and was very clever when questioning the witnesses. He tried to confuse them and show that their stories weren’t perfect. But most people thought he was just showing off, because they believed it wouldn’t help Mitya much.

When Grigory, the old servant of Fyodor Pavlovitch, was questioned, he walked in calmly and answered with confidence. He said the father had been unfair to Mitya about money and didn’t bring up his children well. Grigory described how Mitya had once burst into the house and beaten his father. He said he had forgiven Mitya for hitting him. Grigory talked about Smerdyakov, another servant, saying he was clever but not honest in his beliefs, though he did return lost money once.

Grigory insisted the garden door had been open, which was important for the case. But when asked for proof about Mitya’s lost inheritance, Grigory had none. No one, not even Alyosha or Ivan, could give clear evidence about the money.

Fetyukovitch asked Grigory about the special envelope where Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have hidden three thousand roubles. Grigory said he never saw such an envelope and only heard about it later. Fetyukovitch asked every witness this same question, but none had seen the envelope.
Suddenly, Fetyukovitch asked Grigory about the medicine he used for his back pain that night. Grigory said it was made with saffron, milfoil, pepper, and spirit.

Fetyukovitch joked that with so much spirit, Grigory might have been seeing things, like the open garden door, because he was drunk. People laughed, and even the President of the court had to remind Fetyukovitch to ask better questions.

Then, the President asked Mitya if he wanted to say anything. Mitya thanked Grigory for caring for him as a child and forgiving him for his anger. Mitya called himself a poodle, joking about loyalty, but the President told him to watch his words.

Next, it was Rakitin’s turn. Rakitin was an important witness. He knew a lot about the Karamazovs and told stories about Mitya’s wild behavior. But he didn’t have clear proof about Mitya’s inheritance either.
Rakitin blamed the crime on the family’s bad habits and Russia’s problems. His speech was long and gloomy, but some people even clapped when he talked about how hard life was for poor people.
But then Rakitin made a mistake. He spoke badly about Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna), calling her a “kept mistress,” which Fetyukovitch quickly used against him.
Fetyukovitch asked Rakitin if he was the same person who wrote a religious pamphlet. Rakitin was embarrassed and said he didn’t mean for it to be published.
Fetyukovitch then asked if Rakitin had brought Alyosha (Alexey Fyodorovitch) to meet Grushenka for twenty-five roubles. Rakitin said it was a joke and he planned to give the money back.
After this, Rakitin left the stand looking bad. Mitya shouted angrily that Rakitin had borrowed money from him and didn’t believe in God. The President scolded Mitya for speaking out.

Captain Snegiryov was the next witness, but he was drunk and wearing dirty clothes. When asked about Mitya attacking him, he refused to answer and said his son Ilusha had told him not to talk about it. The captain began to cry and was taken away, which made the crowd laugh.

Fetyukovitch kept showing how much he knew about the case. Trifon Borissovitch, who ran the inn at Mokroe, said Mitya had spent almost all his money, giving gifts to everyone. He said he saw three thousand roubles in Mitya’s hands.

Fetyukovitch didn’t really argue with Trifon Borissovitch, but asked about a time when some peasants found a hundred roubles that Mitya dropped. Trifon first denied it but later had to admit it after the peasants told the story. This made people doubt his honesty.

The Polish witnesses acted proud and said Mitya had tried to buy their honor with three thousand roubles. But Fetyukovitch proved that they had cheated at cards, and even Trifon had to admit it. Kalganov also confirmed the Poles had cheated. The crowd laughed, and the Poles lost their good reputation.

Fetyukovitch did the same with almost all the prosecution’s witnesses. He made people doubt their stories, even though everyone still thought the case against Mitya was very strong. But people wondered what Fetyukovitch’s secret plan was, because he seemed sure of himself, and they waited to see what would happen next.

The doctors came to talk about Mitya (Dmitri Karamazov), but their words did not help him much. Fetyukovitch, Mitya’s lawyer, did not really count on their help anyway. He only brought in the famous doctor from Moscow because Katerina Ivanovna wanted him to. There were three doctors: the famous one from Moscow, Doctor Herzenstube, and the young Doctor Varvinsky. Herzenstube and Varvinsky also spoke for the other side.

Doctor Herzenstube was an old man with gray hair. He was kind to everyone, and helped poor people for free. He was stubborn and did not change his mind easily. The famous Moscow doctor had made rude jokes about him, which people knew about. Still, all three doctors came to court to give their opinions.

Doctor Herzenstube said right away that Mitya’s mind was not normal. He thought Mitya acted strange in the past and even now. For example, when Mitya walked into the court, he marched in like a soldier, looking straight ahead. Doctor Herzenstube thought Mitya should have looked at the ladies, because Mitya usually liked ladies and might wonder what they were saying about him.

The Moscow doctor also said that Mitya’s mind was not normal. He talked a lot about “madness” and “mania” and said that, if Mitya did the crime, it must have been because he couldn’t stop himself. The doctor noticed that Mitya got very upset if someone talked about the three thousand roubles he thought he had lost. But he could talk calmly about other things.

The Moscow doctor disagreed with Doctor Herzenstube about looking at the ladies. He said that, if Mitya was going to look anywhere, he would look for his lawyer for help, not at the ladies. But he still thought Mitya’s mind was not normal.

Doctor Varvinsky, the youngest doctor, surprised everyone. He said Mitya’s mind was normal now and before. He thought Mitya was just nervous and excited, maybe from jealousy or drinking, but not crazy. He also said it made sense for Mitya to look straight ahead at the judges, not at the ladies or the lawyer.
“Bravo, doctor!” Mitya shouted from his seat, happy about Varvinsky’s answer.

Mitya was told to be quiet, but many people in the court agreed with the young doctor. His words helped Mitya. Then Doctor Herzenstube was called as a witness. He had known the Karamazov family for many years, so he shared some stories.
“Mitya could have had a different life,” Doctor Herzenstube said. “He had a good heart when he was a boy.” He shared a Russian saying: “One head is good, but two are better.”

The doctor explained that Mitya did not find someone else to help him think, so his “wits went wandering” and he got lost in life. He remembered Mitya as a small, poor boy with no shoes, running around the yard.
The doctor remembered when he was younger and saw Mitya as a little boy. He wanted to buy him something children like to eat.
After some guessing, someone said, “Nuts?” and the doctor agreed.

The doctor told how he bought Mitya a pound of nuts, and taught him to say some German words. Years later, Mitya came back as a grown man and thanked him for the nuts, saying he never forgot it. Both laughed and cried together.
Mitya, hearing this story in court, cried out that he was crying now too for the kind doctor.

The story made people in the court feel sorry for Mitya. But the biggest help for Mitya came from Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence, which would be told soon. Before that, Alyosha (Mitya’s brother) was called to say something important that might help Mitya’s case.

Alyosha was called as a witness. Everyone treated him kindly because they knew he was good. Alyosha answered questions quietly, showing he cared for his brother, Dmitri (Mitya). He said Mitya could get angry and act wild, but he was also proud and could be generous and do good things. Alyosha admitted that Mitya was upset about Grushenka and fighting with their father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, which made things hard for him. But Alyosha strongly said he did not believe Mitya killed their father for money, even though Mitya was obsessed with the three thousand roubles he thought was his by right. Alyosha didn’t want to talk much about Mitya’s troubles with Grushenka and Katya.
The prosecutor asked, “Did your brother ever tell you he wanted to kill your father? You don’t have to answer if you don’t want to.”
Alyosha replied, “He never told me that straight out.”
“Did he hint at it?” the prosecutor pressed.
Alyosha explained, “He once told me he hated our father and was afraid that if he lost control, he might do something terrible, maybe even kill him.”
“Did you believe him?” the prosecutor asked.
Alyosha said, “I was afraid it could happen, but I always believed something would stop him. He didn’t kill our father,” Alyosha said loudly.
The prosecutor was surprised.

The prosecutor said he thought Alyosha truly believed Mitya was innocent, but he said this idea was different from the other evidence. He asked Alyosha why he was so sure Mitya was innocent and if he had proof someone else, like Smerdyakov, was guilty.
Alyosha said quietly, “I only answered questions before. I did not accuse Smerdyakov on my own.”
“But you spoke against him?”
“I did, because Mitya said things about him after he was arrested. I truly believe my brother is innocent, so if he didn’t do it, then—”
“Then Smerdyakov? Why do you believe that? Why do you trust your brother so much?”
“Because I know my brother. He wouldn’t lie to me. I could see it in his face.”
“That’s your only proof?”
“Yes, I have no other proof.”
“And you have nothing against Smerdyakov except what your brother said?”
“No, nothing else.”
The prosecutor stopped the questions. Many people listening were disappointed because they had hoped Alyosha would have proof, but all he had was his feelings as Mitya’s brother.

Now Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, asked Alyosha when Mitya talked about hating his father and maybe wanting to kill him. Did Alyosha hear it during their last meeting before the murder? Alyosha suddenly remembered something.
Alyosha said, “I just remembered something I had forgotten. It didn’t make sense to me before, but now—”

Alyosha told the court how, when he last saw Mitya that evening near the monastery, Mitya hit his own upper chest and said he had a way to save his honor. Alyosha thought maybe Mitya meant he had the strength in his heart not to do something bad, like hurting their father. But Mitya kept pointing to a spot high on his chest, not where the heart is. Alyosha realized now that Mitya might have been pointing to the little bag where he kept fifteen hundred roubles!
Mitya shouted from his seat, “That’s right, Alyosha! It was the little bag I was hitting.”

The lawyer told Mitya to be quiet, then asked Alyosha more questions. Alyosha explained that the disgrace Mitya felt was about the fifteen hundred roubles — money he owed Katerina Ivanovna (Katya) but planned to use for running away with Grushenka instead.
Alyosha said, “My brother cried that he could solve half the disgrace right away, but he was too weak to do it. He knew he wouldn’t give the money back.”
Fetyukovitch asked, “Are you sure he pointed to that part of his chest?”

“Yes,” Alyosha said, “I wondered at the time why he pointed so high. Now I know it was the bag of money. When Mitya was arrested, he said the most shameful thing was not paying Katya back when he could have. That debt made him miserable.”
The prosecutor interrupted and asked Alyosha to explain again. He wanted to know if Mitya had really pointed to something on his chest.
Alyosha said, “He pointed with his fingers, not his fist, very high up. I can’t believe I forgot it until now.”
The judge asked Mitya if this was true. Mitya agreed and said the disgrace was not paying Katya back. He said, “I knew I wouldn’t do it, and that’s the most shameful part. Thank you, Alyosha!”

Alyosha’s cross-examination ended. The most important thing was that he remembered Mitya really had a bag with fifteen hundred roubles, which helped show that Mitya might have been telling the truth about the money. Alyosha felt relieved, but wondered why he had forgotten it until now.

Next, Katerina Ivanovna (Katya) was called as a witness. People in the court were excited to see her. She looked calm and beautiful, though her eyes were serious. She spoke clearly. The judge was very polite to her. Katya said she used to be engaged to Mitya, but he left her. When they asked about the three thousand roubles she gave Mitya to send to her family, she said she gave it because Mitya needed money. She told him to send it if he wanted, and he didn’t have to worry about paying her back.
The rest of Katya’s answers were similar.

Katya said she believed Mitya would send the money when he got money from his father. She trusted him to be honest about money. She knew Mitya argued with his father and thought his father treated him unfairly. She never heard Mitya threaten his father. If Mitya had come to her, she would have told him not to worry about the three thousand. But he stopped visiting her, and she could not invite him. She also said she once borrowed more than three thousand from him before, and she couldn’t pay him back then.
Katya sounded brave. Now Fetyukovitch, her own lawyer, started questioning her.

He asked if her borrowing money from Mitya happened when they first met. Fetyukovitch didn’t know about the story of the four thousand roubles Mitya gave her, or about her bowing to him in thanks. Katya had never told him and might not have planned to say it in court.

Katya decided to tell the whole story. She explained how she went to Mitya to ask for money to save her father and how she thanked him deeply. She didn’t say that Mitya, or her sister, told her to go — she made it sound like her own idea. The story made everyone in the court silent and amazed, because it showed Katya was brave to talk about something so embarrassing just to help Mitya. Some people later whispered mean things, saying maybe she wasn’t telling the whole truth.
Some people in town said, “Even if nothing bad happened, it’s still strange for a young girl to go ask a man for money like that.”

Katya must have known people would gossip, but she told her story anyway. While some people doubted her later, at the time everyone respected her honesty. The prosecutor didn’t ask any questions, and Fetyukovitch was happy because now it seemed silly to think Mitya would kill his father for money when he once gave away all he had. During Katya’s story, Mitya hid his face and cried out:
“Katya, why have you ruined me?” and sobbed so everyone could hear.
Then he said, “Now I am condemned!”
He sat very still, and Katya sat down, looking pale and shaking. Then Grushenka was called.
Something big was about to happen that would hurt Mitya’s chances. Everyone later agreed that if it hadn’t happened, Mitya might have gotten mercy. First, a few words about Grushenka.

Grushenka wore all black and walked quietly to the witness stand. She looked strong and proud, but also a little nervous. Sometimes she sounded angry or ashamed. She said it wasn’t her fault Fyodor Pavlovitch bothered her. Then she admitted, “It was all my fault. I laughed at both him and Mitya, and I caused this.”

When Samsonov’s name was mentioned, Grushenka snapped, “That’s nobody’s business. He helped me when I had nothing.” The judge told her to answer only the questions. Grushenka blushed and looked upset.

She said she never saw the envelope with the three thousand roubles, but only heard from “that wicked wretch” (Smerdyakov) that Fyodor Pavlovitch had it. She said, “I was only joking. I wouldn’t have taken it.”
The prosecutor asked, “Who is ‘that wicked wretch’?”
“Smerdyakov, who murdered his master and hanged himself last night,” she replied.
They asked her if she had proof, but Grushenka had none.
She said, “Dmitri Fyodorovitch told me Smerdyakov did it. The woman who came between us ruined him; she is the cause of it all,” meaning Katya. She was angry.
They asked again, “Who do you mean?”
“Katerina Ivanovna. She tried to charm me. She’s not as innocent as she looks,” Grushenka said.
The judge told her to calm down, but Grushenka was too upset.
The prosecutor asked, “When Mitya was arrested, you ran out and shouted, ‘It’s my fault, we’ll go to Siberia together!’ Did you believe he killed his father?”
Grushenka said, “I don’t remember. Everyone said he did it, and I felt guilty. But when he said he was innocent, I believed him and always will. He does not lie.”
Fetyukovitch asked about Rakitin, who took twenty-five roubles from her for bringing Alyosha to see her.
Grushenka replied, “It’s not strange. Rakitin always came to me for money, even though he didn’t need it.”
“Why did you give him money?” asked Fetyukovitch.
“He is my cousin. His mother and mine were sisters. But he asked me not to tell anyone—he’s ashamed of me.”

This was a surprise to everyone. No one knew Rakitin was related to Grushenka, not even Mitya. Grushenka was angry because she heard Rakitin gave evidence against Mitya. Now Rakitin’s speech in court was ruined. Grushenka’s testimony didn’t last long and didn’t help Mitya. Most people in the court looked at her with dislike. Mitya sat quietly, staring at the floor.
Now it was Ivan’s turn to give evidence.
Ivan was supposed to speak in court before Alyosha, but when it was his turn, the court usher said Ivan was sick and couldn’t testify yet. No one paid much attention, and the reason came out later.

When Ivan finally came in, most people didn’t notice at first. The important witnesses, especially the two women who didn’t like each other, had already been questioned. People were tired and not very interested anymore. Ivan walked very slowly, looking sad and sick. He didn’t look at anyone. Alyosha, his brother, jumped up and made a noise, but hardly anyone noticed.

The President of the court told Ivan he didn’t have to answer the questions if he didn’t want to, but he should tell the truth. Ivan listened with a blank face, then started to smile and finally laughed.
Ivan said, “Well, what else?”
The whole room became quiet because Ivan was acting strangely. The President looked worried.
The President asked, “Are you still sick?”
Ivan replied, “Don’t worry, I’m well enough and have something interesting to say.”
The President asked, “Do you have something special to tell us?”
Ivan looked down, waited a little, then said, almost stuttering,
“No, I don’t. Nothing special.”

They started asking Ivan questions. He answered quickly and seemed like he didn’t want to be there. He said he didn’t know about his father’s money with Dmitri and wasn’t interested. He said he had heard threats from Dmitri and had heard about the envelope full of money from Smerdyakov.
Suddenly Ivan said, “The same thing again and again. I have nothing special to tell.”
The President tried to be kind and said he understood Ivan was sick.
The President turned to the lawyers to ask if they wanted to question Ivan more, but Ivan suddenly said in a tired voice,
“Let me go, I feel very ill.”
Ivan started to leave without waiting for permission, but after a few steps, he stopped, smiled, and came back.
Ivan said, “I am like the peasant girl in the story: ‘I’ll stand up if I like, and I won’t if I don’t.’”
The President asked, “What do you mean?”
Ivan pulled out a bunch of money and said, “Here’s the money from the envelope—the money for which our father was killed. Where should I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it.”
The usher took the money and gave it to the President.
The President asked, “How did you get this money, if it’s the same money?”

Ivan said, “I got it from Smerdyakov, the real killer, yesterday. I was with him before he hanged himself. He killed our father, not my brother. I made him do it... Who doesn’t wish their father would die?”
The President asked, “Are you in your right mind?”

Ivan answered, “I think I am, just like all of you.” He turned to the people watching and shouted that everyone wishes their father would die, and they just wanted a show. He asked for water and grabbed his head.
The usher came to help. Alyosha cried out that Ivan was sick. Katerina Ivanovna, another lady, stood up in horror. Mitya (Dmitri) listened with a strange smile.
Ivan said, “Don’t worry. I’m not crazy, just a murderer. You can’t expect good speech from a murderer,” then laughed oddly.
The judges and lawyers whispered to each other. The room was tense. The President tried to calm down.
He told Ivan his words didn’t make sense and asked if he could explain what he meant.
Ivan said, “I have no proof. Smerdyakov won’t send proof from the grave. You only care about envelopes. I have no witnesses... except maybe one.” He smiled.
The President asked, “Who is your witness?”

Ivan said, “He has a tail—he’s the devil! But never mind. He’s probably under that table. I told him I didn’t want to be quiet, and he talked nonsense. Everything is so stupid! Take me instead of Mitya! Why is everything so stupid?”
Ivan looked around the room again. Alyosha ran to him, but the usher already grabbed Ivan’s arm.
Ivan yelled, grabbed the usher, and threw him to the floor. The police quickly caught Ivan. He shouted and screamed as they took him away.

The whole court was in confusion. Later, when things were calm again, the usher was scolded, but he explained Ivan had seemed fine earlier and insisted on testifying. Before everyone could calm down, something else happened. Katerina Ivanovna had a fit. She cried loudly and didn’t want to leave. She shouted to the President,
“I have more evidence! Here is a letter from Mitya. He wrote that he would kill his father! But Ivan is sick, he’s not well!”

The usher took the letter to the President. Katerina Ivanovna sat down, crying quietly. The letter was from Mitya, written at the tavern, and it was strong proof against him. If it wasn’t for that letter, things might have gone better for Mitya. The President gave the letter to the judges and lawyers. Katerina Ivanovna was asked if she was ready to answer questions.
She said, “I am ready!” She was asked to explain the letter.

She said she got the letter the day before the crime, and it was written two days before, when Mitya was drunk. She told how she gave Mitya money even though she knew he would use it badly. She wanted to test him, and he took the money and spent it. She said he wrote in the letter about killing his father, and the court should read it carefully.
Mitya shouted, “That’s true, Katya! I saw you were testing me, and I took your money. Hate me if you want, I deserve it!”
The President warned Mitya to be quiet.

Katya kept talking fast. She said the money made Mitya feel bad, and he wanted to pay her back. She said he killed his father, didn’t pay her back, and went to the village with Grushenka. She said he wrote the letter while drunk, never thinking she would show it to anyone. She told everyone to read it to see how Mitya planned everything.
Katya seemed to have planned to show the letter for a long time. The letter was read aloud and everyone was shocked. Mitya was asked if he wrote it.
Mitya cried, “It’s mine! I wouldn’t have written it if I wasn’t drunk! We hated each other, Katya, but I loved you even when I hated you, and you didn’t love me!”
Mitya sat down, very upset. The lawyers began asking Katya why she hid the letter and why she lied before.

Katya cried out, “Yes, I lied! I wanted to save him, even though he hated me! He despised me from the moment I bowed down to him. He only wanted to marry me because I had money! I tried to win him with my love, but he didn’t understand. I got the letter the next evening. That morning I wanted to forgive him everything.”
The President and prosecutor tried to calm her. But she kept talking, even more clearly, about how Ivan had been troubled for two months trying to save Mitya.

Katya said, “Ivan was always trying to make Mitya’s guilt seem less. He told me he never loved his father and maybe wished him dead. He told me everything! He even said if Smerdyakov did it, maybe it was partly his own fault, because Smerdyakov knew he didn’t like his father. When I showed Ivan the letter, he was sure Mitya did it and became very upset. He grew sick and confused. The doctor said Ivan was about to have brain fever. Last night, Ivan learned Smerdyakov was dead, and that made him even worse—all because he tried to save Mitya!”
Katya’s words were very emotional. She had once begged Mitya for help to save her father, and now she was trying to save Ivan’s reputation.

Some people wondered if Katya was telling the truth about her feelings for Mitya, but she believed it. She loved him in a hurt and angry way, but couldn’t forgive him. After saying everything, she became ashamed and started crying and screaming. She was carried out. Then Grushenka ran to Mitya.
Grushenka cried, “Mitya, Katya has ruined you! See what she is!” The guards tried to take her out, but she fought to stay. Mitya also tried to get to her, but was stopped.

The people watching had plenty of drama to see. Then the doctor from Moscow came and said Ivan was very sick with brain fever and must be taken away. The doctor said Ivan had visited him before and talked about seeing things that weren’t real. The letter from Katya was added as evidence. The judges decided to keep going and add both new pieces of evidence to the official record.

The other witnesses didn’t add anything new. Everyone waited for the speeches from the lawyers. Fetyukovitch, Mitya’s lawyer, looked worried after Katya’s evidence, but the prosecutor was happy. When all the evidence was finished, the court took a break until the prosecutor was ready to make his speech.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was very nervous as he began his speech. He felt hot and cold at the same time and even sweated. He believed this speech was the best thing he would ever do. Later, people said he put his whole heart and mind into it. Ippolit Kirillovitch truly thought that the prisoner, Dmitri Karamazov, was guilty. He wanted to protect society and was honest in his words. Even people who did not like him admitted his speech made a big impression. At first, his voice shook, but soon he spoke loudly and clearly. When he finished, he was so tired he almost fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” began Ippolit Kirillovitch, “this case is famous all over Russia. But why are we so shocked? Terrible crimes happen so often that we are used to them. That is what is really scary–that we are not horrified anymore. Why don’t we care? Is it because people don’t believe in right and wrong anymore? I don’t know, but these questions should bother all of us. Thanks to newspapers, we hear about many terrible things, sometimes even worse than this case. Most crimes show there is a big problem in our country, a problem that is very hard to fix.”

“For example, sometimes a young officer kills someone who helped him, just to steal money. Another person kills a woman he knows just to get what he wants. Even if some people don’t kill, they think like that and wonder if things like honor or not killing really matter. This is a sad thing to see.”

“Maybe you think I am too negative, but even if only a little of what I say is true, it is still awful. Look at how many young people even hurt themselves, not caring what happens after death. There are many people doing bad things. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the man who died in this case, was almost innocent compared to some others. Yet we all knew what he was like.”

“Maybe one day, smart people will study why crimes like this happen in Russia. But for now, we sometimes act shocked, but deep down we like to hear about exciting or strange things. Or we just pretend it didn’t happen. But sooner or later, we must be honest with ourselves and try to understand what is happening in our society.”

“A famous writer once wrote about Russia being like a fast troika (a carriage with three horses) racing to an unknown place. People move aside to let it pass. But I think the writer was either too hopeful or just afraid to say the truth. If the troika was led by people like the ones in the old story, it would never reach a good place. And now, our people are even worse.”
At this point, some people in the court clapped. Ippolit Kirillovitch felt better after hearing the applause. He was glad that people were listening to him.

“Now, what about the Karamazov family, which everyone is talking about?” he continued. “I think this family shows, in a small way, what is happening in our society. Think about the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch. He was born noble but poor, then got some money after marrying. He became greedy and cared only about himself and his own pleasure. He didn’t care about being a good father, left his children to the servants, and only wanted to enjoy life. He even tried to take his son’s money and girlfriend. I understand why his son, Dmitri, was so angry with him.”

“But enough about the old man. He has died and paid for his actions. Still, we should remember that there are other fathers like him today. They may hide it better, but they think the same way. Maybe I am being too negative, but let me say what I think.”
“Now let’s talk about his children. The prisoner here is Dmitri Karamazov, and I will talk mostly about him. But I will mention the other two sons quickly.”

“The oldest son is Ivan Karamazov. He is very smart and well-educated, but he doesn’t believe in anything. He is a lot like his father. We heard from Smerdyakov, the servant who died, that Ivan taught him that anything is allowed and nothing should be forbidden. Smerdyakov said Ivan was the most like Fyodor Pavlovitch.”

“The third son is Alexey, or Alyosha. He is kind and religious, not like Ivan. He wanted to join a monastery and be a monk. He tries to hold on to good ideas and stay away from the bad things in society.”

Some people clapped again when Ippolit Kirillovitch talked about these ideas. He was very excited to explain his thoughts, even if they were not all about the case. Some people said he was being mean to Ivan because Ivan had beaten him in arguments before, but we don’t know if that’s true. Now he would focus more on the case itself.

“Let’s go back to the oldest son, Dmitri Karamazov, who is on trial,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “His life is full of ups and downs. He loves learning and good things, but he also gets into fights and spends too much money. He can be good and noble, but only if things are easy for him. If he gets what he wants, he can be very generous. But if he doesn’t have money, he will do almost anything to get it. Let’s look at his story step by step.”

“First, Dmitri was a poor child and ran around without shoes. I know how hard childhood can affect someone. But he grew up and became an officer. He got into trouble and was sent far away. He needed money and argued with his father about his inheritance. Finally, his father sent him six thousand roubles and they agreed that Dmitri would not ask for more.”

“Then Dmitri met a smart and good young woman. He did something noble for her, but later, she said he had hurt her feelings and made fun of her, even though she tried to help him. She offered him three thousand roubles, hoping he would not accept it, but he did. He then spent the money quickly on someone else.”

“So what should we believe? Was Dmitri really noble, or really bad? I think he can be both at different times. That is the kind of person he is. Sometimes he is generous, sometimes he is very selfish. He is a person of extremes.”

“Now, about the three thousand roubles. After Dmitri took the money, could he have really saved half of it in a little bag for a whole month, even when he needed it? He didn’t use it, even when he needed money for his girlfriend. That does not seem like something Dmitri would do.”

“Dmitri said he kept the money so that if his fiancée forgave him, he could return half to her and say, ‘I am a scoundrel, but not a thief.’ He thought this made him better than a thief. But can we really believe that? Dmitri did not have much self-control. Wouldn’t he have opened the bag and taken some money when he needed it?”

“I think the real Dmitri would have opened the bag and taken some money whenever he wanted. Maybe at first he would only take a little, but soon he would have spent it all. That is more like the Dmitri we know. The story of saving the money doesn’t fit his character. But we will talk more about this later.”

Then Ippolit Kirillovitch talked about the money problems between Dmitri and his father, and what the doctors said about Dmitri always thinking about the three thousand roubles he thought he was owed.

The prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, told everyone that some doctors said the prisoner, Mitya (Dmitri), was crazy. But he didn’t agree. He said Mitya was angry and jealous, not insane. The main reason for Mitya’s anger, he explained, was jealousy.

Ippolit Kirillovitch explained how Mitya fell in love with Grushenka (a young woman), starting from the night he went to her house to hurt her, but instead, he ended up begging at her feet. At the same time, Mitya’s father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, also fell in love with Grushenka. Both father and son wanted her, and Grushenka liked to tease them. Fyodor even offered her three thousand roubles to visit him, and was ready to marry her. Grushenka played with their feelings, and Mitya was finally arrested while begging her to go with him. Grushenka felt sorry, blaming herself for what happened.

The prosecutor repeated what Mr. Rakitin said about Grushenka: she had been hurt before, was left poor, and protected by a rich old man. She became careful and sometimes mean to people. This explained why she played tricks on both Mitya and his father.

Mitya loved Grushenka but was jealous, especially of his own father. He thought his father was using the three thousand roubles—money Mitya believed should be his—to win Grushenka. This made Mitya furious and desperate.
The prosecutor then said that the idea of killing his father came to Mitya’s mind, and he shared evidence for this.

At first, Mitya talked in taverns about killing his father. He liked to tell people everything, even dangerous things. If people didn’t agree with him, he got angry and caused trouble. People started to think he might really do what he said.
The prosecutor talked about the family meeting at the monastery, and how Mitya had a violent fight at his father’s house after dinner.

The prosecutor said he wasn’t sure if Mitya planned the murder from the start, but he knew Mitya had thought about it many times. Mitya had imagined killing his father, but maybe hadn’t decided when or how.

But today, a letter written by Mitya proved he had planned it. Two days before the murder, Mitya wrote that if he couldn’t get the money, he would kill his father and take it. The letter was signed by Mitya, and he didn’t deny writing it.

Some said Mitya was drunk when he wrote the letter, but the prosecutor said he must have planned it while sober. Mitya had talked about killing his father before he made a plan, but after deciding, he became quiet and acted differently. Mitya still tried to borrow money to avoid killing his father.

The prosecutor described how Mitya tried to get money. He visited Samsonov, traveled to see Lyagavy, sold his watch, and was very jealous and worried about Grushenka. He finally came back to town and was glad Grushenka hadn’t visited his father. He took her to Samsonov, then hurried to hide in the garden, learning that the servants were gone and he could get into the house. Still, he tried to borrow money from Madame Hohlakov, who told him to change his life and go to work in Siberia instead.

After this, the prosecutor said that when Mitya heard Grushenka wasn’t at Samsonov’s, he went wild with jealousy, thinking she was with his father. If the maid had told him the truth, things might have been different, but she didn’t know.

Even though Mitya was upset, he grabbed a brass pestle as a weapon. He had thought about using any object as a weapon for a long time, so he took the pestle on purpose. He went to his father’s garden, thinking Grushenka was inside. He believed she was with his father, laughing at him, and he couldn’t stand it. The prosecutor then talked about Smerdyakov, the servant, and said it was important to consider if he was part of the murder, even though he acted like it wasn’t.

Ippolit Kirillovitch started his speech. He asked where the idea came from that Smerdyakov was the murderer. Dmitri Karamazov, the prisoner, was the first to say Smerdyakov did it, but he never gave any proof. Only Dmitri’s two brothers, Ivan and Alyosha, and Madame Svyetlov agreed, but they also had no real evidence. Ivan only said it today when he was very sick. Alyosha just guessed because of how Smerdyakov acted. Madame Svyetlov said to trust what Dmitri said. That was all the proof they had. Still, people kept saying Smerdyakov was guilty. Ippolit Kirillovitch wondered if that made sense.

Then, Ippolit Kirillovitch talked about Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov was not very smart and had learned a little in school. He often talked about big ideas he didn’t really understand, and sometimes he felt bad or confused because of what his master, Fyodor Pavlovitch, did or what Ivan Karamazov said. Smerdyakov had epilepsy, which made him weak, and everyone agreed he was not brave.

Smerdyakov was so scared of Dmitri that he did whatever Dmitri asked. He told Dmitri about the money envelope and the secret signals to get into the house because he was afraid Dmitri would hurt him. Smerdyakov once said, "He would have killed me." He was always nervous and tried to please Dmitri so he would be safe.

Smerdyakov had always been an honest servant, and his master trusted him, especially after Smerdyakov once found and returned some lost money. But because he had lied to his master this time, Smerdyakov felt very guilty. People with epilepsy, like Smerdyakov, often worry a lot and feel bad even when they shouldn’t, and Smerdyakov really was scared and upset by what was happening in the house.

Smerdyakov felt that something terrible was going to happen. Right before the murder, when Ivan was leaving for Moscow, Smerdyakov asked him to stay, but he was too shy to say why. He just gave hints, but Ivan did not understand.
Smerdyakov thought Ivan could keep everyone safe. Even in a letter, Dmitri wrote he might do something bad if Ivan left. So, Ivan staying seemed to mean the house would be peaceful.

But Ivan left, and soon after, Smerdyakov had an epileptic fit. This was not strange, because Smerdyakov had felt one coming for days. He went to the cellar, worried he might have a fit, and then it happened. Some people thought he was pretending, but Ippolit Kirillovitch asked why Smerdyakov would fake it. What would he gain? Even the doctors could not say for sure if the fit was real or fake.

On the night of the murder, only five people were at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house: Fyodor Pavlovitch, Grigory, Marfa Ignatyevna, Dmitri, and Smerdyakov. Fyodor could not have killed himself, Grigory was hurt, and Marfa would never do such a thing. That only left Dmitri and Smerdyakov. Dmitri says he didn’t do it, so people blame Smerdyakov, but Ippolit Kirillovitch said that blaming Smerdyakov made no sense.

Ippolit Kirillovitch asked everyone to look at the facts. If Smerdyakov killed Fyodor Pavlovitch by himself, it must have been for the money. But Smerdyakov told Dmitri about the money, the envelope, and the secret signals. Why would he do that if he planned to steal it himself? Even if he was afraid, it did not make sense for him to tell someone else everything that could get him caught.

If Smerdyakov wanted to kill and rob his master, he would have kept quiet about the money and the signals. No one else knew about the envelope, so if Smerdyakov had killed Fyodor and taken the money, no one could have blamed him unless they knew the money was there. But Smerdyakov told Dmitri all about it. That would be a silly thing for a robber to do.

On the day of the murder, Smerdyakov had a fit and was moved to Grigory’s room, as usual. If he was pretending, it would only make people watch the house more carefully. Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it was hard to believe Smerdyakov would fake a fit just to make it easier to murder his master.

Some people might think Smerdyakov faked being sick to avoid suspicion and told Dmitri about the money so Dmitri would do the crime. But then, after Dmitri left and made a lot of noise, Smerdyakov would have to go in and kill Fyodor a second time and steal money that was already gone. That did not make sense either.

Maybe, someone could say, Smerdyakov really had a fit, woke up, heard something, and decided to kill his master. But how would he know what happened while he was unconscious? That idea didn’t make sense, either.

Some people wondered if Dmitri and Smerdyakov worked together. But if that were true, why would one pretend to be sick while the other did all the work? Ippolit Kirillovitch could not find a good reason for such a strange plan.
Maybe Smerdyakov just agreed not to stop Dmitri out of fear, but that would still mean Dmitri was the murderer, and Smerdyakov only let it happen because he was scared.

But when Dmitri was arrested, he quickly blamed Smerdyakov alone, not as an accomplice, but as the only murderer. If they had planned it together, Smerdyakov could have told the truth to protect himself, but he never did.

In fact, Smerdyakov told everyone he gave Dmitri information about the money and signals, which would make him look suspicious. If he were guilty, he would have hidden that. But Smerdyakov did not hide anything, and then he killed himself, leaving a note that said he died by his own choice and did not blame anyone. If he was guilty, he could have written a confession, but he didn’t.

Then, the court saw the three thousand roubles, which were said to be the stolen money. Ivan Karamazov said Smerdyakov gave them to him before he died. But if Smerdyakov had really confessed to Ivan, why didn’t he write it in his last letter?
Just having the money is not proof. Ivan had other money, too, so they could not be sure it was the same money from the envelope.

Ivan didn’t tell anyone about Smerdyakov’s confession right away. Ippolit Kirillovitch thought maybe Ivan waited because he was sick, having hallucinations, and maybe confused by Smerdyakov’s death. Maybe Ivan truly believed Smerdyakov was guilty, even if it wasn’t true, because of his illness.

Next, Ippolit Kirillovitch pointed to Dmitri’s letter, written before the murder, where Dmitri described exactly how he could kill his father. The crime happened just as Dmitri had written. Ippolit Kirillovitch said this showed Dmitri was the murderer. Dmitri probably killed Fyodor in anger, then took the envelope with the money.

Ippolit Kirillovitch said that if a thief like Smerdyakov had done it, he would have taken the whole envelope and not left the torn cover on the floor. But Dmitri, who had never stolen before, was so upset that he tore open the envelope right there and left it behind.

Dmitri acted like the money was his, not like a thief. He was so angry and confused he didn’t think about hiding evidence. He ran away, and Grigory, the servant, tried to stop him, but Dmitri hit Grigory with a brass pestle.

Dmitri says he checked on Grigory because he felt sorry for him. But Ippolit Kirillovitch said Dmitri wanted to make sure Grigory was dead and could not tell anyone what happened. Dmitri tried to help Grigory, but when he thought Grigory was dead, he ran to see his girlfriend, still covered in blood. He didn’t even notice the blood, because sometimes criminals do not notice such things when they are upset. Dmitri wanted to find his girlfriend, but when he got to her place, he learned she had gone to Mokroe to see her first lover.

Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, began his speech about the case. He liked to tell stories to explain things. He started talking about Grushenka’s first boyfriend and shared some thoughts about it.

Kirillovitch said that Mitya Karamazov (also called Dmitri) had always been jealous of everyone, but when he learned about Grushenka’s old boyfriend, he just gave up. Mitya realized Grushenka cared a lot about this man and had hidden him from Mitya. Mitya felt very sad and thought he had no hope.

The prosecutor told the jury that Mitya suddenly wanted to be fair. Even though he had just done something terrible—killed his father—he respected Grushenka’s right to love someone else. But now he wondered what he could give her, since her old boyfriend had come back, saying he was sorry and promising her a good life.

Mitya understood he had no future because of his crime. He thought about killing himself. He ran to get the pistols he had left with his friend Perhotin, and took the money he had stolen. He dreamed of throwing a big party, making everyone remember him, and then ending his life in front of Grushenka so she would know how much he loved her.

Kirillovitch described what Mitya did next. He went to Perhotin’s, then to a shop, and then got a driver. Witnesses told what he said and did. It seemed clear that Mitya was feeling very desperate and guilty.

The prosecutor said Mitya didn’t try to hide what he had done. He almost confessed to people around him, even saying to the driver, “You are driving a murderer!” But he wanted to reach Mokroe first to see how things would turn out. When he got there, he saw that maybe Grushenka didn’t really want to celebrate with her old boyfriend. Mitya felt like he had won, but it was a terrible feeling.

The prosecutor said that sometimes, being punished by the law is better for people who have done something wrong. Mitya found out Grushenka loved him and had chosen him over her first boyfriend, but it was too late for him to have a happy life.

Kirillovitch explained that Grushenka had always seemed out of reach to Mitya, but now she was close. That’s why he didn’t go through with shooting himself. Instead, he stayed by her side at the party, forgetting everything else.

Mitya was confused and scared, but he was also excited by the party, the music, and Grushenka’s laughter. He hoped he had a little more time before being caught—maybe until morning. He tried to enjoy his last hours.

Even with all this going on, Mitya hid half of his money somewhere in the house at Mokroe. He had been there before and knew the place. He might have hidden the money in case something happened and he needed it later.
The police searched but didn’t find the money. Mitya was caught by surprise while he was with Grushenka. He didn’t have a plan to defend himself.
The prosecutor said it was hard to watch someone realize they were trapped. Mitya was scared and tried to think of ways out, but he was confused and didn’t know what to say.

At first, Mitya said some things that made him look guilty, like, “Blood! I’ve deserved it!” But then he tried to say he wasn’t guilty of killing his father, only of hurting Grigory, the servant. Mitya said, “Who killed my father, if not me?” and admitted he had wanted to kill him, but said he didn’t do it.

When someone asked if Smerdyakov could have killed his father, Mitya got angry and said Smerdyakov wasn’t able to do something like that. But the prosecutor thought Mitya would try to blame Smerdyakov later. For now, Mitya just denied everything.

The police only found half the money on Mitya. That’s when Mitya started talking about a little bag where he said he hid the rest. The prosecutor thought Mitya made up the story about the bag, hoping it sounded true.
When the police mentioned Grigory’s story about the open door, Mitya was shocked and suddenly shouted that Smerdyakov must have done it. He then told the story about the little bag.

The prosecutor thought Mitya’s story about the bag was silly and impossible. He asked Mitya questions about how he made the bag, but Mitya kept changing his answers and couldn’t remember the details, which made it seem like he was lying.

Kirillovitch told the jury that Mitya’s whole story was unbelievable and hadn’t changed at all since his arrest. He said if there was any real proof that Mitya was innocent, he would be happy to accept it, but there was none.
The prosecutor finished his speech passionately, talking about the father’s blood crying out for justice and how all the facts pointed to Mitya’s guilt.
He told the jury to remember their job was to protect justice in Russia and not to let people think it was okay for a son to kill his father.

When Kirillovitch finished, he left the room quickly and almost fainted. The serious people in the audience thought his speech was good, but some ladies were not sure. They trusted the defense lawyer, Fetyukovitch, to speak next.

Everyone looked at Mitya. He sat quietly, sometimes lifting his head when Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor spoke about Rakitin’s opinion of Grushenka, Mitya looked upset. When the prosecutor talked about the police questioning him, Mitya seemed like he wanted to shout but kept quiet. People later made fun of the prosecutor for bragging too much.
The court took a short break. People in the audience talked about the speech.
Some people thought the speech was important.
Others said it had too much psychology.
Some thought it was all true.
Others said the prosecutor was very good at this.
People agreed he summed up the case well.
Someone joked that the prosecutor summed up the people in the audience, too.
Others thought some parts were silly.
Some said it was hard to understand.
Others thought the prosecutor got carried away.
Some people said the speech was unfair.
Others said it was clever and the prosecutor finally got his chance to speak.
People wondered what the defense lawyer would say.
In another group, people talked about how the prosecutor had made fun of the lawyer from Petersburg.
Some thought that was a mistake.
Others said he was in too much of a hurry.
People said the prosecutor was nervous.
Some wondered what Mitya must be feeling.
They felt sorry for Mitya.
In another group, people talked about the ladies in the courtroom.
One lady had a lorgnette (a kind of glasses).
Someone said she was a general’s ex-wife.
Others joked about her.
People talked about how the police caught Mitya at Mokroe.
They said they had heard the story before.
Some thought the prosecutor liked to brag.
Others said he got offended easily.
Some said the speech had too many long sentences.
Others remembered the part about “Hamlets” and “Karamazovs.”
Someone said the prosecutor was trying to please the liberals.
Others thought he was scared of the defense lawyer.
People wondered what Fetyukovitch would say.
Some thought the jury (the peasants) would be hard to convince.
In another group, people talked about the speech’s part about other countries.
They thought it was true that other countries might not put up with such things.
Someone mentioned that in England, people were talking about Russia.
Others said it would be hard for other countries to do anything.
Someone said Russia could get food from America.
The bell rang, and everyone hurried to their seats. Fetyukovitch, the defense lawyer, got up to speak.

The room was very quiet as the famous lawyer began to speak. Everyone looked at him. He talked in a calm, simple way. He did not try to impress people or use fancy words. He sounded friendly, like he was talking to friends. His voice was nice and strong. People could see he might become very emotional later. His words were clear, though his way of speaking was not always perfect. Some ladies did not like that he kept bending forward, almost as if he would jump at the listeners.

At first, the lawyer spoke in a way that seemed a little mixed up. He talked about different facts one by one. Later, all the facts would fit together. His speech had two parts: first, he argued against what the other lawyer said, sometimes making jokes. In the second part, he became more serious and emotional, which excited the audience.

He got right to the point. He said that even though he worked in Petersburg, he often came to smaller towns to help people he thought might be innocent. He felt this way about the prisoner now. When he first read about the case in the newspapers, something made him believe the prisoner might not be guilty. He noticed there were many pieces of evidence against the prisoner, but none of them seemed strong if you looked at them one at a time. When the prisoner’s family asked him to help, he came quickly. He believed his job was to show that each piece of evidence was weak if you checked it carefully.

Fetyukovitch, the lawyer, told the jury he was new to the town and had no opinion about the prisoner, Dmitri (sometimes called Mitya). He knew Dmitri could be wild and rude, and many people in town did not like him. Still, Dmitri had been welcomed in the prosecutor’s family, mostly because the prosecutor’s wife liked him. Fetyukovitch said the prosecutor might be a little unfair to Dmitri because of his bad behavior, even if he tried to be just. He warned that sometimes smart people, like the prosecutor, can make mistakes when they try too hard to understand people’s feelings. He joked that psychology (trying to understand why people do things) can be dangerous if used the wrong way, which made people in the audience laugh.

He gave an example. The prosecutor said that when Dmitri ran away in the dark garden, he climbed the fence and hit the servant, Grigory, with a brass pestle. Then Dmitri came back and spent time with Grigory, checking if he was alive. The prosecutor thought Dmitri did this to make sure the only witness against him was dead, not because he cared.

Fetyukovitch said you could look at it another way. If Dmitri was really trying to hide his crime, why did he leave the envelope with the money in his father’s study? If he had taken it, no one would have known about the money. The prosecutor said Dmitri acted without thinking when he left the envelope, but acted very carefully when he checked on Grigory. That makes no sense. If Dmitri was so clever, why did he risk being seen while helping Grigory? Why did he wipe Grigory’s blood with his own handkerchief, which could be used as evidence? Why didn’t he try harder to hide what he did? If he was so cold and mean, why not just hurt Grigory more to make sure he could not talk? If Dmitri really cared for Grigory, maybe he was not guilty of his father’s murder. If he had killed his father, he would only think about saving himself, not about helping Grigory. Fetyukovitch wanted to show that psychology could be used to prove anything, so people should be careful with it.
People laughed and agreed with Fetyukovitch. The rest of his speech had more points like this, but I will only tell you the most important ones.
Fetyukovitch made everyone pay attention when he spoke. He said there might not have even been any three thousand roubles, so maybe nothing was stolen at all.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” Fetyukovitch began, “Think about this: they say there was a robbery, but is there any proof that the money was really there? The only person who actually saw the notes was Smerdyakov (the servant). He told the prisoner, Dmitri Fyodorovich, and his brother Ivan Fyodorovich about it, and also Madame Svyetlov (Grushenka). But really, only Smerdyakov saw the money himself.

If Smerdyakov saw the money, when was the last time? Maybe Fyodor Pavlovitch (the father) took the notes out from under his bed and put them somewhere else. Smerdyakov said the money was under the mattress, but when people looked, the bed was neat and clean, not messed up at all. How could Dmitri have taken the money without messing up the bed or leaving blood stains?

What about the envelope found on the floor? The prosecutor said that without that envelope, no one would know about the money or the robbery. But just because an envelope was there doesn’t prove there was money inside or that it was stolen. Smerdyakov said he saw the money, but that was two days before everything happened. Maybe Fyodor Pavlovitch got bored waiting for Grushenka, opened the envelope, took out the money, and threw the empty envelope on the floor.

If Fyodor Pavlovitch took out the money, why didn’t the police find it? Well, some money was found in his cash-box. And maybe he spent or gave away the rest before he died. If it’s possible the money was never there or already gone, how can we say Dmitri stole it? No one really saw these notes.

Fetyukovitch told a story about a boy in Petersburg who really did steal money. The police found the money on him right away, and everyone knew exactly what was taken. That’s real evidence. But in Dmitri’s case, there is no such proof.

People say Dmitri was spending money that night and had fifteen hundred roubles. But only half the supposed stolen money was found, and the other half was missing. Dmitri didn’t have a chance to hide it, because he was always with people. Some people say maybe he hid it somewhere far away, but that idea is like something from a fairy tale.

People also say Dmitri couldn’t explain where he got his money, and that everyone knew he was broke before. But Dmitri told where he got the money, and his story makes sense. Maybe the prosecutor just made up a story about what kind of person Dmitri is, but it might not be true.

Some say witnesses saw Dmitri spend all his money from Katerina Ivanovna a month earlier, so he couldn’t have saved half. But those witnesses only guessed how much he had; they didn’t count it. Maximov even said he saw Dmitri with twenty thousand! People can easily be wrong about money they see in someone else’s hand.

A month before, Katerina Ivanovna gave Dmitri three thousand roubles to send by mail. Did she really give it in a mean way, like she said later? The first time she told the story, it sounded different. Maybe she changed her story in court because she was angry. Dmitri took the money because he thought his father would soon give him the three thousand roubles he was owed, so he could pay Katerina Ivanovna back.

The prosecutor says Dmitri would never save half and sew it in a bag, but even he said Karamazovs have strange personalities. Dmitri wanted the money, not just for partying, but because he loved Grushenka and wanted to be ready to take her away if she chose him. That’s a good reason for him to keep half the money safe.

But time went by, and Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t give Dmitri the money. Instead, Dmitri heard his father might use it to win over Grushenka, the woman Dmitri loved. Dmitri worried he’d look like a thief to Katerina Ivanovna. So he thought about showing her the money he had saved, to prove he wasn’t a thief. This is why he kept the money safe and didn’t spend it.

Dmitri got more upset as he worried about both paying back Katerina Ivanovna and having enough money to run away with Grushenka. He started acting wild and desperate. He sent his brother to ask for the money one last time, but then went himself and ended up hitting his father in front of others. After that, he knew he’d never get the money from his father.

That night, Dmitri told his brother Alyosha (Alexey Karamazov) that he had the money to prove he wasn’t a thief, but he still felt bad. Why doesn’t the prosecutor believe Alyosha’s honest words, but instead wants us to believe in money hidden in some secret place like in a fairy story?

That same night, Dmitri wrote a letter saying he might beg for money, and if he didn’t get it, he would kill his father and take the envelope from under the mattress after Ivan left. The prosecutor says this letter proves everything.

But the letter was written when Dmitri was drunk and angry, and he only wrote about the envelope because of what Smerdyakov told him. He never actually saw the envelope himself. And there’s no real proof that Dmitri took the envelope or the money, or even that the money existed. When Dmitri ran off, he did it in a jealous rage, not because he planned a robbery. And if we can’t even say what was stolen, can we really call it a robbery? And did he even commit murder? Is that proven? Or is it just another made-up story?

“Gentlemen of the jury, please remember a man’s life is in your hands, so you must be careful. The prosecutor said he wasn’t sure the prisoner planned the crime until he saw the drunken letter today. But I say again, the prisoner was running to find Madame Svyetlov (a lady he loved), not to carry out the letter’s threat. If she had been home, he would have stayed with her and not done anything bad. He grabbed the pestle (a heavy stick) only because it was in sight. If the pestle had been put away, he would have run off with empty hands, and no one would be dead. So the pestle isn’t proof he planned the murder.

People say the prisoner talked about killing his father in taverns, and the letter shows he wanted to. But if he really planned such a crime, he wouldn’t have argued in public. He would have stayed quiet so no one noticed him. People shout silly things when drunk, like “I’ll kill you!” but they don’t mean it. Why do we call the letter “fatal” instead of just foolish? Only because his father was found dead and someone saw the prisoner running with a weapon. But does that mean he planned it?

The big point is: “He was there, so he must have done it.” But just being there doesn’t mean he killed his father. Maybe he ran away from the window because he realized Madame Svyetlov wasn’t there. Maybe he even felt scared or respectful. He might have heard something that told him she wasn’t inside. We shouldn’t just imagine things the way we want.

People say, “Grigory saw the door open, so the prisoner must have gone in and killed him.” But only one witness said that, and he wasn’t thinking clearly. Even if the prisoner did go inside, maybe he only rushed in to check for Madame Svyetlov, pushed his father, and then left, happy she wasn’t there and glad he hadn’t done anything terrible. Maybe, feeling relieved, he even helped Grigory after accidentally knocking him down.

The prosecutor described how the prisoner was upset at Mokroe (an inn), unable to love because of his father’s death. But if he really killed his father, feeling loved would make him want to die even more. He would have used his pistols. But he didn’t kill himself, because he was innocent. He only worried about hurting Grigory, not about his father. Why not believe this?
Now people say, “If he didn’t do it, who did?” That’s the main point of the prosecution.

But is it really true there’s no one else? There were five people in the house: the father, Grigory and his wife (they didn’t do it), the prisoner, and Smerdyakov (the servant).
