The prosecutor says the prisoner blames Smerdyakov just because there’s no one else. But maybe the prosecution blames my client only because they’ve decided not to suspect Smerdyakov.

Smerdyakov is accused by the prisoner, his brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. There are also rumors and facts that look suspicious. On the day of the murder, Smerdyakov had a fit, then killed himself before the trial. Ivan Karamazov (the prisoner’s brother), who used to believe the prisoner was guilty, now says Smerdyakov did it. Maybe Ivan is sick in his mind, but Smerdyakov’s name keeps coming up. There’s still a mystery.

The prosecutor described Smerdyakov as weak and simple, but I met him and he seemed clever, suspicious, and jealous. He was angry about being poor and being called the son of Lizaveta, and jealous of his master’s sons. He dreamed of having money and going to France. He helped Fyodor Pavlovitch (the father) put the money in an envelope, and seeing all that money might have made him want it even more.
The prosecutor asked why Smerdyakov would fake a fit. But maybe he really had a fit, then woke up after a deep sleep, as happens with people who have epilepsy.

Maybe Smerdyakov woke up when Grigory shouted “Parricide!” and, feeling confused, went toward the noise. He could have learned what happened, and then decided to take the money and blame the prisoner.
Smerdyakov could have picked up any heavy thing as a weapon. Maybe he knew where the money was kept, so he took it and left the torn envelope behind.

The prosecutor says only the prisoner would leave the envelope behind, but Smerdyakov himself told me that, maybe to make me think it was my own idea. Maybe he suggested the same thing to the prosecutor.
Some say Grigory’s wife heard Smerdyakov moaning all night, but sometimes people just remember being woken up a few times and think it lasted all night.
The prosecutor asks why Smerdyakov didn’t confess in his last letter. But maybe he felt only despair, not guilt or regret. Some people who end their lives feel angry, not sorry.

Gentlemen of the jury, be careful not to punish the wrong person! If there’s even a little doubt, you should not condemn him. All the facts the prosecution brings are not definite. Don’t let scary words and stories make you forget your great responsibility.
Even if I pretended to agree my client was guilty (though I do not believe it!), I want to say one more thing to you, from my heart. Please listen sincerely.

At this point, people in the court clapped loudly because they felt the lawyer was very sincere. The President (the judge) told everyone to be quiet, and Fetyukovitch (the lawyer) continued his speech with even more feeling.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” the lawyer began, “my client is in trouble not just because of many facts, but because of one big thing—his father is dead. If this was just a normal murder case, you might not believe the weak and strange clues. You might even let my client go, even though people have reasons to dislike him. But this is not an ordinary murder. This is a father being killed by his own son, called parricide. Just hearing that makes people feel shocked. Even if the clues are small, everyone wonders, ‘What if he did it and goes free?’ That is why it is so hard to think about letting him go.”

“It is terrible to think of killing your own father—the person who brought you into the world, who loved you, cared for you, and wanted you to be happy. A real father loves and helps his child. But Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, my client’s father, was not a good father. And some fathers are not good—they can be a problem for their children. We must look at this problem closely because your decision is very important.”

“The prosecutor, who spoke before me, said he both blames and defends my client. But if my client could be thankful for just a pound of nuts given to him as a child, can’t you imagine how much he remembered running around his father’s yard, poor and barefoot?”

“Why blame my client for being wild and uncontrolled? Who is really responsible for how he turned out? Did anyone teach him or care for him when he was little? No. He was left alone like an animal. Maybe he wanted to see his father after so many years and forgive him. But when he came back, he was met with mean words, money fights, and saw his father try to take his girlfriend away using his own money. That was very cruel. And the father always said his son was bad, told lies about him, and even tried to get him thrown in jail.”

“People like my client may seem rough and out of control, but inside they can be very gentle. They just don’t show it. The prosecutor laughed because my client loved Schiller, a great writer. But it’s true—people like this often want kindness and justice, even if they act wild. They can love deeply, even if it doesn’t look like it. They want to be good, even if they make mistakes.”

“About my client’s engagement, I must say what we heard was not good evidence, just a hurt woman speaking in anger. She has betrayed him herself. Don’t believe she is right when she calls him a monster. He is not!”
“Jesus once said, ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.’ We should not cause someone to lose his soul because of us.”

“I said ‘father’ is a great word, but you must be honest. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov was not a real father. You cannot force a child to love a father who does not deserve it. Love can’t come from nothing.”

“The Bible says, ‘Fathers, do not make your children angry.’ I say this to all fathers. We are not here on earth for long, and we do many bad things. Let us use this time to say something good to each other. Fathers, do not make your children your enemies by treating them badly. If you do, you are not real fathers.”

“Not long ago, a servant girl in Finland was found to have hidden a box with the bodies of three babies she had killed. Was she really a mother to them? She gave birth to them, but did not care for them. The true father or mother is the one who cares for the child.”

“Some people say no matter how bad a father is, he is still your father because he gave you life. But that is just something we believe without proof. In real life, we must act with kindness and reason, not just follow old rules. We must not hurt people by following ideas that do not make sense.”
Many people in the court clapped loudly at these words, but Fetyukovitch asked for quiet so he could finish. The room became silent again.

“Children grow up and start to wonder about these things. If a father is not good, and the child sees other fathers treating their children better, he will ask, ‘Why should I love my father if he never cared for me?’ The usual answer is, ‘Because he gave you life.’ But the child might think, ‘He never cared for me after I was born. Why must I love him for that?’”

“These are hard questions, but we must answer them honestly. If a son asks his father, ‘Why must I love you?’ and the father can give a good answer, then they have a real family bond. But if he cannot, then the son may feel he is not really his father. Our court should teach people to think in this way.”
(People in the court clapped and cheered again. The President was annoyed but did not clear the room. Fetyukovitch, feeling excited, kept speaking.)

“Think about the night my client went to his father’s house. He did not go there for money, as some say. He did not plan to kill his father. If he had wanted to, he would have brought a weapon. He grabbed the brass pestle without thinking. Even if he tricked his father by tapping on the window, I do not believe it, but let’s pretend he did. If it had been anyone else, he would have just pushed him away. But seeing his father, who had been so mean to him, made him angry. All his feelings came out at once. It was like going crazy for a moment.”

“But even then, my client did not mean to kill his father. He just waved the pestle in anger, not knowing it would hurt him so badly. If he had not grabbed it, maybe he would have only pushed his father. When he ran away, he did not know if his father was dead or not. This is not real murder. It is not truly parricide. Only prejudice makes it seem so.”

“But I ask you again, did this murder really happen? If you send my client to prison, he will think, ‘No one ever helped me grow up or taught me to be good. Now they just punish me. I owe them nothing.’ He will feel even worse and will not want to become a better person.”
“If you want to punish him in a way that might save him, show him mercy! He will be shocked and ask, ‘How can I deserve so much kindness?’ His heart will change.”

“I know my client’s heart. It is wild but thankful. If you show him mercy, he will feel sorry for what he did and want to be better. He will say, ‘Others wanted to help me, not destroy me.’ Your kindness can help him change.”

“It is better to let ten guilty people go free than to punish one innocent person! Russian courts are not just to punish, but to help people become better. If you do this, you will show the world that Russian justice is good and wise. My client’s future, and the future of Russian justice, is in your hands.”

When Fetyukovitch finished his speech, the whole courtroom burst into cheers and tears. Many women cried, some men cried too. Even two important people cried. The President let everyone have their moment and did not try to stop it. The speech had touched everyone, even Fetyukovitch himself.

Then Ippolit Kirillovitch stood up to make objections. People looked at him angrily. Some ladies whispered, "How dare he!" But he could not be stopped. He was pale and shaking. At first, he could hardly speak, but soon he found his voice. He said, "You say I made up a story, but your defense is also a story. For example, who saw Fyodor Pavlovitch take out the money? Who heard what he said? And calling Smerdyakov a hero is just silly. You can't say Mitya both did and did not kill his father. That makes no sense."

Ippolit Kirillovitch went on, "If we say killing a father is just an old idea, what will happen to families and society? Some say parricide is only a silly fear, but it's very serious. The defense says we should have mercy, but is that right for such a crime? And the defense says things about the Gospel that are not true. Jesus teaches us to forgive, but he also teaches us not to do wrong. We should not change what the Gospel says just to help someone."

The President stopped Ippolit Kirillovitch and told him not to go too far. The crowd was uneasy. Fetyukovitch did not argue back. He just went up and said a few proud words, making a joke about "romancing" that made the audience laugh. He also said he would not answer the idea that he was teaching young people to hurt their fathers. He ended his speech with a bow, and the crowd approved. The ladies thought Ippolit Kirillovitch had lost.
Now the prisoner, Mitya, could speak. He was very tired and looked defeated. He spoke quietly and seemed humble.

Mitya said, "Gentlemen of the jury, my time has come. God is judging me. But I tell you, I am innocent! I did not kill my father. I have done wrong things, but not this. I thank the prosecutor and my lawyer, but they are both wrong about me. I am not crazy, just sad. If you let me go, I will be a better man. If you punish me, I will try to accept it. But please, do not take away my hope in God. My heart is heavy—spare me!"
Mitya almost collapsed as he finished speaking. Then the judges began asking questions and both sides gave their final arguments.
I will not describe every detail, but soon the jury stood up to leave and decide. The President was tired and told the jury to be fair and careful.

The jury left, and everyone in the courtroom waited anxiously. It was very late, but no one wanted to leave. Most people thought Mitya would be found not guilty. Some were happy, some were worried, and some did not want him to go free. Fetyukovitch felt sure he had won.
Fetyukovitch told people he could feel a special connection with the jury and was confident they would decide in Mitya's favor.
In the crowd, people talked about the jury. Some wondered what the local peasants would say. Others pointed out that not all jurors were peasants; some were clerks and merchants.
In another group, people wondered if Mitya would really be set free. Some said he might be, others thought it would be a shame. They argued about what the lawyers had said and how the case had gone.

Then the bell rang. The jury had been gone for exactly one hour. Everyone fell silent as the jurymen walked back in. The President asked, "Did the prisoner commit the murder for robbery and on purpose?" The youngest juror answered loudly, "Yes, guilty!"

The same answer came for each question: "Yes, guilty!" No one expected such a strong answer. The whole court was silent. Then suddenly there was a loud noise as people reacted. Some men were happy, some were sad. The women were shocked and started crying out. They hoped the decision could be changed, but it could not.
Mitya stood up and shouted, "I swear to God I did not kill my father! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers and friends, please have pity on the other woman!"

Mitya could not say more and began to sob loudly. From the back of the room, Grushenka screamed. She had managed to get into the court again. Mitya was taken away. The sentence would be given the next day. The court was in chaos as people left.
As I left, I heard people saying, "He'll be sent to the mines for twenty years." Others agreed, "Yes, at least that long." Some thought, "Our peasants did their job," and, "They have finished Mitya."

Early one morning, five days after the trial, Alyosha went to visit Katerina Ivanovna. He had something important to tell her. They talked in the same room where Katerina Ivanovna had once met Grushenka. In the next room, Ivan Fyodorovitch (Alyosha’s brother) was very sick and could not wake up. After the trial, Katerina Ivanovna brought Ivan to her house to take care of him, even though other people talked badly about her for it. One of her relatives left for Moscow, but the other stayed. Even if both had left, Katerina Ivanovna would not have changed her mind. She wanted to care for Ivan day and night. Two doctors, Varvinsky and Herzenstube, visited Ivan. Another famous doctor from Moscow had come but would not say if Ivan would get better. The doctors tried to give hope, but no one really knew if Ivan would recover.
Alyosha visited Ivan twice a day. But today, he had something urgent to discuss with Katerina Ivanovna and he was in a hurry, because he had another important thing to do later that morning.
Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna had been talking for about fifteen minutes. Katerina Ivanovna looked tired and pale, but she was also upset and excited. She guessed why Alyosha had come.

“Don’t worry about Ivan’s plan,” Katerina Ivanovna said. “He will go through with it. He wants Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya) to escape from prison. Ivan told me about the escape plan a long time ago. The escape will probably happen when the prisoners are being taken to Siberia, but that is still a long way off. Ivan has even talked to the person in charge of the third stage of the journey, but we still don’t know who will be guarding the prisoners. I can show you the whole plan tomorrow. Ivan left me the details in case something happened to him. Do you remember when you found us arguing? That was what we were fighting about. He had just left, but I called him back when you came in. Do you know why we argued?”

“He didn’t tell you because we argued about his plan to help Dmitri escape. I was angry when he said Dmitri would leave the country with that woman—Grushenka. I didn’t want her to go with him. Ivan thought I was jealous and still loved Dmitri, but I really didn’t. I only cared about Ivan. But Ivan didn’t believe me, so we argued for three days. Then he gave me an envelope with the escape plan, and told me to use it if he died or got very sick. He left me money too, to help Dmitri. I was so moved that Ivan still wanted to help his brother, even though he thought I loved Dmitri. That was a big sacrifice, but I couldn’t show how grateful I was, because I thought he would misunderstand. So I got angry again. When you came in, I was mad, and I shouted something mean—to hurt Ivan. I told you it was Ivan who made me think Dmitri was a murderer, but that wasn’t true. I was the one who made Ivan believe it. My bad temper caused everything, even the terrible scene at the trial. I am to blame for it all!”

Katya had never told Alyosha so much before. He saw that she was suffering a lot and was too sad to keep her feelings hidden. Alyosha knew she also felt guilty for what she did at the trial, but she didn’t want to talk about it. Alyosha wished she wouldn’t bring it up, because it would be too painful. He tried to talk about Dmitri instead.

“Don’t worry about Dmitri,” Katerina Ivanovna said quickly. “He will agree to escape. Ivan will be better by then and will help, so I won’t have to do anything. Dmitri has already agreed. He won’t stay in prison when he can’t see Grushenka. He’s only worried you won’t think it’s right for him to escape. But you should let him go.”

“Dmitri keeps talking about a hymn and a cross he has to bear,” she said, “like he has some big duty. Ivan told me a lot about it. Ivan loved Dmitri so much then, even though he was angry too. I just listened and didn’t care. I am to blame for Ivan’s sickness. But I don’t think that man in prison can really suffer. People like him don’t suffer.”
“I called you here to make you promise to convince Dmitri to escape,” Katerina Ivanovna said. “Or do you think it’s wrong or cowardly to run away?”
“No, I’ll tell him everything,” Alyosha answered. “He wants you to go see him today,” he added, looking at her.
“Me? Really?” Katerina Ivanovna said, turning pale.

“Yes, you must go,” Alyosha said. “Dmitri needs to see you right now. He is very upset and keeps asking for you. He knows he hurt you and doesn’t ask for forgiveness, but he wants you to come to his door and just show yourself.”
“It’s so sudden,” Katerina Ivanovna said. “I thought you might come and tell me this. I knew Dmitri would ask, but it feels impossible.”

“Even if it feels impossible, you should do it,” Alyosha said. “He realizes how much he hurt you for the first time. He said, ‘If she does not come, I will be unhappy all my life.’ Even though he is going to prison for twenty years, he still hopes to be happy. Please go see him. He is innocent, and his hands are clean. For all his pain, you should visit him now. Just stand at his door.”
“I should... but I can’t,” Katya said, very sad. “He will look at me... I can’t.”
“You need to see each other,” Alyosha said. “How will you live if you don’t do it now?”
“It’s better to suffer all my life,” she whispered.
“You should go, you should go,” Alyosha repeated.
“But why today? I can’t leave Ivan—”
“You can go for just a moment. If you don’t, Dmitri will get even sicker. I am telling you the truth. Please have pity on him!”
“Have pity on me!” Katya cried, and she started to cry.
“Then you will come,” Alyosha said gently. “I will go tell Dmitri you are coming.”
“No, don’t tell him yet,” Katya said quickly. “I might go, but maybe I won’t go in. I don’t know yet—”
She couldn’t speak anymore and tried to catch her breath. Alyosha stood up to leave.
“What if I meet someone?” she asked in a quiet voice, turning pale again.
“That’s why you should go now, so you won’t meet anyone. There will be no one there, I promise. We will expect you,” Alyosha said, and left the room.

Alyosha hurried to the hospital where Mitya (his brother Dmitri) was staying. After being found guilty, Mitya got very sick and was sent to the prison hospital. But Doctor Varvinsky (the kind doctor) let Mitya have his own little room, instead of staying with the other prisoners, because he knew it would be too hard for Mitya right away. There was a guard nearby and bars on the window, so it was safe. Only Alyosha and Grushenka (Mitya’s beloved) had come to visit him. Rakitin tried to visit, but Mitya didn’t want to see him.

Alyosha found Mitya sitting on his bed, looking pale with a wet towel on his head. Mitya seemed worried and quiet, lost in thought. He looked happier when Grushenka came to visit, even if they didn’t talk much.
Alyosha sat down next to Mitya without saying anything. Mitya was waiting for news about Katya (Katerina), but was too nervous to ask. Alyosha understood how he felt.
Mitya started talking about Trifon Borissovitch, the man who owned the inn. He said Trifon had been tearing the inn apart looking for the money the prosecutor said Mitya hid there.
Alyosha told Mitya that Katya would come to visit, but he didn’t know when—maybe today, maybe in a few days.
Mitya was very affected by this news. He wanted to ask more but was afraid Katya might say something mean.
Alyosha said Katya wanted Mitya not to worry about escaping. If Ivan (their brother) wasn’t well, Katya would handle everything herself.
Mitya said Grushenka knew Katya was helping, and Grushenka understood it was important. He thought Grushenka now realized Katya loved Ivan, not him.
Mitya said Ivan was better than all of them and deserved to live. He hoped Ivan would get well.
Alyosha said he believed Ivan would get better.
Mitya agreed, but thought Katya was so worried because she was afraid Ivan would die. Mitya felt very anxious.
Suddenly, Mitya said he loved Grushenka very much, and his voice shook with tears.
Alyosha told him Grushenka wouldn’t be allowed to go with him if he was sent away.

Mitya said if anyone treated him badly during the journey, he wouldn’t stand it and might fight back. He was scared he couldn’t handle being punished for years. But for Grushenka, he would try to bear anything except being hit.

Alyosha gently said Mitya wasn’t ready for such a hard punishment, especially because he was innocent. Alyosha said if Mitya escaped, he wouldn’t blame him, since it wasn’t fair for him to suffer so much. He promised he would never judge Mitya.
Mitya said he would still feel guilty if he escaped, and would pray for forgiveness forever.

Mitya explained his plan: if he escaped to America with Grushenka, it wouldn’t be for fun, but it would be another kind of exile, just as hard as Siberia. He didn’t like America already. Grushenka was Russian and would miss home. Mitya wanted to live somewhere far away, maybe with wild animals, and work on the land. He and Grushenka would learn English, then someday sneak back to Russia and live hidden. He would change how he looked so no one would recognize him. He just wanted to die in Russia. He asked Alyosha if he agreed.
Alyosha said yes, not wanting to argue.
Mitya complained how the trial made things look worse.
Alyosha said Mitya would have been found guilty anyway.
Mitya felt people were tired of him and it was hard.
Mitya begged Alyosha to tell him if Katya was coming and what she said.
Alyosha said Katya promised to come, but it was hard for her.
Mitya said it was driving him crazy. He wanted Katya, but also didn’t understand his own feelings.
Suddenly, Alyosha saw Katya arrive.

Katya came into the room and looked at Mitya. He stood up, looking scared but hopeful, and held out his hands. Katya hurried to him, made him sit down, and held his hands tightly. They looked at each other for a long time, not speaking.
Mitya finally asked, “Have you forgiven me?” He looked at Alyosha with joy.
Katya said forgiveness didn’t matter, because they would always care about each other. She said she loved him, even though it hurt, and hugged his hands, crying.
Katya said their love was over, but the past was dear to her. She said they would always love each other, even though they each loved someone else now.
Mitya said he still loved Katya, even five days ago, and always would.
They said many frantic, loving words to each other. At that moment, they both believed it all.
Mitya suddenly asked Katya if she really believed he killed his father.
Katya said she never truly believed it, even while she gave evidence at court. She only convinced herself for a moment, but stopped believing it right after.
Katya said she had to go, because it was too much for her.
As Katya stood up, Grushenka suddenly came in. Katya tried to leave, but when she reached Grushenka, she stopped, turned very pale, and whispered, “Forgive me!”
Grushenka answered coldly, “We are both full of hatred. As if we could forgive each other! Save him, and I’ll worship you all my life.”
Mitya was upset Grushenka wouldn’t forgive Katya.
Katya whispered quickly she would save Mitya, then ran out.
Mitya was upset Grushenka wouldn’t forgive Katya even when Katya asked.
Alyosha told Mitya not to blame Grushenka.
Grushenka said Katya’s words came from pride, not her heart. She said if Katya saved Mitya, she would forgive her for everything.
Grushenka was still upset and quiet. She hadn’t expected to see Katya.
Mitya told Alyosha to run after Katya and not let her leave like that.
Alyosha promised to come back later and ran after Katya. He caught up with her outside. Katya said she couldn’t punish herself in front of Grushenka. She liked Grushenka for not forgiving her.
Katya told Alyosha she couldn’t go to the funeral with him but had sent flowers and would help if needed. She told him to go quickly, as the bells were ringing for the service.

Alyosha was late. The boys, who were Ilusha’s school friends, had been waiting for him. They were ready to carry Ilusha’s small coffin to the church. Ilusha had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. There were twelve boys, all with their schoolbags. When Ilusha was dying, he told them, “Father will cry, be with father.” The boys remembered his words. Kolya Krassotkin was the leader.
Kolya greeted Alyosha and said, “I’m glad you’re here, Karamazov! It’s so sad inside. Snegiryov isn’t drunk, but he acts strange. Before you go in, can I ask you a question?”
Kolya asked, “Is your brother innocent or guilty? Did he kill your father or was it the servant? I keep thinking about it.”
Alyosha said, “The servant did it. My brother is innocent.”
Kolya said, “So he is an innocent victim! He is ruined, but happy. I wish I could be brave like him!”

Alyosha was surprised. Kolya explained, “I want to do something brave for the truth one day.” Alyosha said, “Not with so much sadness and trouble.” Kolya said, “I would like to do something good for everyone, even if it means people forget my name. I respect your brother.” Another boy, who once talked about Troy, agreed and blushed.

Alyosha went into the room. Ilusha was lying in a blue coffin with white frills. His face looked serious and peaceful. Flowers were everywhere, sent by Lise Hohlakov and Katerina Ivanovna. Captain Snegiryov, Ilusha’s father, was laying more flowers on the body. He barely noticed Alyosha or anyone else, not even his crying wife, Ilusha’s mother, who tried to stand up to see her son. Nina, Ilusha’s sister, sat close to the coffin and was quietly crying. Snegiryov kept calling Ilusha “old man,” which was his loving nickname for his son.
Ilusha’s mother begged for a white flower from his hand to remember him by.
Snegiryov shouted, “No! They are his flowers, not yours! Everything is his!”
Nina asked her father to give their mother a flower, but he refused and started crying, remembering when Ilusha gave his toy cannon to his mother. The mother cried silently.
The boys saw that the father would not leave the coffin, so they gathered around it and began to lift it.
Suddenly, Snegiryov cried, “I don’t want him buried in the churchyard! I’ll bury him by our stone. Ilusha told me to.”
For three days, Snegiryov had said he wanted to bury Ilusha by the stone, but Alyosha, Kolya, the landlady, and the boys said no.
The landlady said, “He should be buried in the churchyard, where prayers are said.”

At last, Snegiryov gave up. The boys carried the coffin. They stopped by the mother so she could say goodbye. She shook with grief and beat her chest. Nina kissed Ilusha one last time as the coffin passed. Alyosha asked the landlady to care for the family, and she promised to stay.

They carried the coffin to the church. The day was cold but clear. The church bells rang. Snegiryov ran after the coffin, worried and confused. He tried to help carry it, but only got in the way. When a flower fell, he picked it up quickly.
Suddenly, Snegiryov remembered, “We forgot the bread!” The boys reminded him he had the bread in his pocket, and he felt better.
Snegiryov told Alyosha, “Ilusha asked me to crumble bread on his grave so the sparrows would come. That would make him happy.”
Alyosha said it was a good idea.
Snegiryov said, “Every day!”

They reached the church and set the coffin in the middle. The boys stood around it the whole time. The church was old and simple. During the mass, Snegiryov was sometimes calm, sometimes anxious. He fixed the coffin, picked up a candle, and knelt, pressing his head to the floor.

The funeral service began and candles were given out. Snegiryov sobbed and did not want them to close the coffin. He kissed Ilusha many times before they could move him away. He took some flowers from the coffin and was quiet. The coffin was carried to the grave. Katerina Ivanovna had paid for an expensive grave close to the church. Snegiryov leaned over the grave and had to be pulled back. When they filled the grave, he tried to say something but stopped. Then he remembered the bread and threw pieces onto the grave for the sparrows.
“Come, birds, fly down, sparrows!” he called.
Someone told him to put down the flowers so he could crumble the bread, but he held on to them tightly. When everything was done, he suddenly hurried home. Alyosha and the boys followed.
Snegiryov said, “The flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to her.”

Someone told him to wear his hat because it was cold, but he threw it in the snow. Smurov picked it up. All the boys were crying, especially Kolya and the boy who talked about Troy. Smurov even tried to throw a brick at some sparrows, but missed and kept crying. Halfway home, Snegiryov stopped, then ran back toward the grave. The boys caught him. He fell in the snow, crying, “Ilusha, old man!” Alyosha and Kolya tried to help him up.
Kolya said softly, “Captain, be brave.”
Alyosha said, “Don’t spoil the flowers. Mamma is waiting. Ilusha’s bed is still there.”

Snegiryov remembered and hurried home. They all arrived together. He called to his wife, “Mamma, Ilusha has sent you these flowers.” He saw Ilusha’s little boots by the bed. He grabbed a boot and kissed it, crying, “Ilusha, old man, where are your little feet?”
Ilusha’s mother cried, “Where have you taken him?” Nina sobbed. Kolya and the boys left the room. Alyosha left too.
Alyosha told Kolya, “Let them cry. We can’t comfort them now. Let’s wait.”
Kolya agreed, “It’s so sad. If we could bring him back, I would do anything.”
Alyosha said, “Me too.”
Kolya asked if they should visit again tonight. Alyosha said yes, but just the two of them, so they didn’t remind the family of everything all at once.
Kolya said the landlady was setting the table for a funeral dinner. He asked Alyosha if they should go. Alyosha said yes.
Kolya thought it was strange to have pancakes after so much sadness.
The boy who talked about Troy said they would have salmon, too. Kolya told him not to interrupt. The boy went quiet.
As they walked, Smurov pointed out Ilusha’s stone, where Snegiryov wanted to bury him.
They all stopped at the stone. Alyosha remembered how Ilusha once cried there with his father.
Alyosha felt something important and said, “Boys, I want to say something here.”

Alyosha told the boys, “We will soon go separate ways. Let’s make a promise here, at Ilusha’s stone, to always remember Ilusha and each other. Even if we don’t see each other for many years, let’s remember this day. We once threw stones at Ilusha, but later we became his friends. He was brave and cared about his father. Let’s remember him all our lives. Even if we grow up and forget many things, let’s keep this good memory. Good memories from childhood help us stay strong and kind. Even if we become bad one day, remembering this moment can help us be good again. Maybe we’ll laugh about it, but deep inside, we’ll know it was special.”
Kolya said, “I understand you, Karamazov!”

Alyosha continued, “But we don’t have to become bad. Let’s be kind, honest, and never forget each other. I promise I’ll remember all of you. Even Kartashov, who isn’t blushing now, but looking at me kindly. Let’s all try to be brave like Ilusha and Kolya, and kind like Kartashov. You’re all dear to me. Who brought us together? Ilusha. Let’s never forget him.”
The boys shouted, “Yes, forever!”
Alyosha said, “Let’s remember his face, his clothes, his boots, his coffin, and his father, and how Ilusha stood up for him alone.”
The boys agreed, “We will remember! He was brave and good!”
Kolya said, “How I loved him!”
Alyosha said, “Don’t be afraid of life! It is good when we do something kind and right.”
The boys replied, “Yes, yes!”
Someone, probably Kartashov, cried, “Karamazov, we love you!”
All the boys said, “We love you!” Many of them had tears in their eyes.
Kolya shouted, “Hurrah for Karamazov!” and the others joined in.
Alyosha added, “May Ilusha’s memory live forever!”
The boys repeated, “Forever!”
Kolya asked, “Karamazov, is it true that we will all rise again and see each other, even Ilusha?”
Alyosha smiled and said, “Yes, we will all see each other again and tell each other everything that happened.”
Kolya said, “That will be wonderful!”
Alyosha said, “Now let’s go to the funeral dinner. Don’t worry about eating pancakes; it’s an old custom and it’s nice. Let’s go hand in hand.”
Kolya shouted, “Always hand in hand! Hurrah for Karamazov!” The boys all cheered, “Hurrah for Karamazov!”
the end
